full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong dismissed the application for pre-emption. On appeal the learned District Judge, Chittagong, set aside the Judgment of the trial Court and allowed the application for pre-emption in part.

2. The case of the pre-emptor-Opposite party in brief, is that, the case land originally belonged to H.E. Percival and his name was recorded in party statement Khatian Nos 14, 18, 20 and 24 under mouza Kashembazar, in the town of Chittagong. The pre-emptor purchased by a kabala dated 28.12.65 from the said Percival land measuring 1½ kanas and thus the pre-emptor became a co-sharer in Khatian No. 14. H.E. Percival died in August, 1971 and thereafter his properties were looked after by his servant Mofizullah and a near relation Morris Walker. On 3.1.76 the present petitioner got possession of the case land through the Nadir of the Civil Court with the help of Magistrate and Police. On 3.1.76 the pre-emptor came to know that the present petitioner purchased the case land in a certificate sale. According to the pre-emptor he had no knowledge about the auction sale prior to the taking of possession by the petitioner on 3.1.76. The pre-emptor asserted that after enquiry he came to learn that the Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 (separation and amalgamation) the Khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 were amalgamated in one khatian being Khatian No. 18. According to the pre-emptor there was no application for amalgamation and separation of the holding before the Circle Officer (Revenue) by the said H.E. Percival. Certificate cases being certificate case Nos. 408-414/1967-68 were started in the court of the Certificate Officer at Chittagong and in these certificate cases, H.E. Perceival filed an application on 12.3.69 under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 denying liability. In the Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 separation and amalgamation no application was filed by the said Percival and no notice was served upon the pre-emptor who was co-sharer in the disputed property. The preemptor's positive assertion is that the proceeding of amalgamation and separation was collusively taken without serving any notice contemplated under the law to defeat the claim of pre-emption. As the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in khatian No. 14 he is entitled to pre-empt the case land sold in auction in certificate case No. 408/67-68 to the present petitioner.

3. The case of the preempted-petitioner in brief, was that, he purchased the case land in said certificate case on 24.10.73 for Tk. 9000/-. The petitioner got delivery of possession on 11.2.74 through court. After getting possession the petitioner constructed C.I. huts on the hills and another but at the bottom of the hill in March and April. 1974. The petitioner after the auction purchase paid an amount of Tk. 80,000/- to the servant Mofizullah and to the relation of H.E. Percival for the price of the structures standing on the case land. According to the petitioner he also made payment of Tk. 10,000/- to Mofizullah at the request of the son of H.E. Percival. The petitioner spent about 20,000/-. for improvement of the case land after auction purchase. The pre-emptee has denied the date of knowledge of the preempted from 3.1.76. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor knew about the sale from before. According to the present petitioner, the pre-emptors are not co-sharers in P.S. khatian No 14 which was auction purchased by the petitioner for arrears of rent as the remaining land of khatian No. 14 was separated by Misc. case No. 89/72-73. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in old khatian No. 14 as the old khatian No. 14 merged into P.S. khatian No. 18 and this khatian was put to auction sale and the pre-emptor did not remain a co-sharer. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. On appeal the learned District Judge allowed the application for pre-emption in part and remanded the case to the trial court for assessment of the costs of improvement in the case. Mr. S. R. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner has submitted mainly two grounds for my consideration. Firstly, the learned Advocate or the petitioner has submitted that the learned lower appellate Court acted illegally and with material irregularity in holding in a summary jurisdiction that the amalgamation and separation of Tenancy in Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 is illegal, null and void and without jurisdiction and further committing illegality in holding that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in Khatian No. 24. Secondly, he has contended that the application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the bar under section 85 (2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1 will proceed to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner hereinafter.

4. In the instant case it is admitted that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the khatian No. 14 by virtue of his earlier purchase dated 28.12.66. It is also admitted that khatian No. 18 was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the pre-emptors were not co-sharers in this khatian. It is also admitted by the parties that the suit property originally belonged to H.E. Percival who was the recorded tenant in respect of the khatian Nos. 14,18, 20 and 24. From the record it is found that the certificate case being certificate case Nos. 408-414 of 1967-68 were started before the certificate office at Chittagong against the said H.E. Percival for huge arrears of rent in respect of the Khatian mentioned hereinbefore. In the said certificate cases H.E. Percival filed an application on 12.3.69 under section 9 of Public Demands Recovery Act denying his liability with the prayer for dismissing the certificate cases. From a perusal of the records of the Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 a typed copy of the application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act is available. In this application there is no signature of H.E. Percival and no court fee was fixed on the said application. However, this typed and unsigned copy of the said application is found to be on the record. This said application might have been brought on record  by the Revenue Officer for the purpose of amalgamation and separation suo-motu. From the order sheet of the said separation and amalgamation case it is found the first order is dated 17.3.73 wherein it has been stated that this case is started on the basis of the prayer of the petitioner H.E. Percival for separation and amalgamation of his property. From the next order, dated 2.4.73 of the Revenue Officer it is found that he has perused the report of the concerned Tahsilder. The last order is dated 24.4.73 wherein it has been stated that the notices have been duly served and no objection having been filed, the separation and amalgamation was allowed. In the record of Misc case No. 89/72-73 (separation and amalgamation) only the order sheet, copy of the type petition were available and no notices as required under the law were found in the record of this proceeding. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge perused the entire records and came to this finding to the following effect:-

"As regards service and notice in Miscellaneous case for amalgamation, it appears on perusal of the order sheet or Miscellaneous case No. 89/72-73 vide (Ext. 6) which shows that there was order dated 2.4.73 for service of notices on all Concerned. Subsequently order dated 20.4.73 shows that notice was duly served and no objection was filed. Accordingly separation and imagination, was allowed on 24.4.73."

The learned District Judge also perused the entire record of the Miscellaneous case No. 89/72v73 and after careful consideration of the record of that case observed as follows :—

"The total papers according to Firisti appear to be in tact with the record. It is not that any piece of paper was missing from the record. So mere noting in the record that notices were duly served is not sufficient to show that notices were duly served and it is not known at whose instance or under what circumstances it was so noted. In short it may be said that such noting of due service of notices was made without any basis. When it is patent on the face of the record and it is admitted that petitioner Mr. Percival himself died before the order of separation and amalgamation passed and no notice was actually served upon the petitioner appellate-co-sharers, the order of separation and amalgamation was null and void and such order need not be avoided by separate proceeding, as in the eye of law it was no order."

5. Thus, in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant findings of fact on the question of notice in the proceeding in separation and amalgamation, the relevant laws on the subject are to he carefully considered in this proceeding. Section 116 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows :—

"116—Amalgamation of holding of a Tenant in the same village. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject to separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall, under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy.

Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy read as follows :—

"117. Sub-division of holding and restriction thereon. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue Officer may,(a) for the purposes of amalgamation of tenancies under section 116, either on his own motion or on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants in that behalf, or (b) for the purpose of consolidation of holdings of a malice, under section 119, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf, or

(c) for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to hint by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable :

Provided that no such order shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter."

<u>6. Thus, from the reading of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is clear that a Revenue Officer is competent to start with the proceeding of amalgamation, consolidation and subdivision of a tenancy but for this purpose namely, for amalgamation and consolidation the proceeding may be started either on the own motion of the Revenue Officer or on an application made in that behalf by one or more co-sharer tenants. But clause (c) of section 117 says that for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent an application a to be made by one or more co-sharer-tenants and on this application by the tenants concerned the Revenue Officer by order in writing direct such sub-division of a joint tenancy as he may consider fair and equitable. Thus it is clear that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application is to be made by the parties and the Revenue Officer has got no authority on his own motion to sub-division a joint tenancy. The amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of consolidation and amalgamation of holding for the purpose of collection on revenue and for that purpose the Revenue Officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction. This power has been given under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy the legislature though it lit and proper that such a sub-division is only permissible on the application of one of more co-sharer tenants as the interests of the tenants are primary concerned in the scheme of sub-division of a joint tenancy. Thus, it is clear that the legislature provided that the sub-division of a holding may be made when notice has been given to the parties concerned for appearance and being heard in the matter. That it is clear that the legislature intended that when any co-sharer tenant wants division of a holding such a proceeding can be taken. So, I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate caws before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong Under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be roe wale brought in the Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer. I have held earlier that there was in fact no application by H.E. Percival for amalgamation and separation of his holding. The courts below were also of the view that this power was exercised suo-motu by the Revenue Officer in this Misc. proceeding for amalgamation and separation. I may point out here that the application of H. E. Percival denying his liability In respect of the certificate cases was dated 12.3.69 and this proceeding for amalgamation and separation started on 17.3.73 after about 4 years and the admitted position being that H. E. Percival died in August, 1971, the question of filing this application by H.E. Percival thus, in fact, does not arise. Thus, this was a suo-motu exercise of power by the concerned Revenue Officer in this behalf. A reference to the provision of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shows that no order shall be passed unless a notice is given the parties concerned and the matter is heard. This proviso clearly indicates that notice is a must to the partied concerned in cases of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division without service of notice on the parties concerned no final order can be passed in the matter of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division. Thus, after careful consideration of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act I am of the opinion that no proceeding for sub-division of a joint tenancy can be taken without any application by a tenant and in that proceeding notices must be served on the parties concerned. I have indicated earlier that in the instant case there was no application for amalgamation and separation by the tenants and the Lower Appellate Court has correctly come to a finding from the perusal of the records of the Misc. proceeding No. 89/72-73 that no notices were served on the parties concerned and consequently the lower appellate court rightly held that the proceeding taken under amalgamation and separation of the holding was null and void and the same is liable to be set aside.</u>

7. Thus after a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provisions of law as discussed above I had no substance in the first point raised by S.R. Pal in this behalf. Incidentally, I may point out here that proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption is no doubt a summary proceeding but since the question of amalgamation and separation in the proceeding as mentioned above is relevant for the purpose of determination of the fact whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in khatian No. 14 or not, the courts below very rightly proceeded to see whether the tenancy has been separated in accordance with law thereby the pre-emptor remained a re-sharer or ceased to be a co-sharer. Thus the contention of Mr. S. R. Pal that in a summary proceeding in the courts below should not have gone to determine the legality or otherwise of amalgamation and separation of tenancy is without any substance.

8. Thus I hold that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in the Malian No. 14 as if there was no separation under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the pre-emptor was competent to file an application for pre-emption and the lower appellate court has correctly decided this point by holding that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer and he had locus stanch to file this application for pre-emption.

9. Now coming to the second point raised by Mr. S. R. Pal that an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the Bar under section 85(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it will be seen that section 85(2) does not bar an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 85(2) of the Act reads as follows "nothing 'in this act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Central or Provincial Government :—

provided that the right vested in a tenant by the provisions of this Act shall not be divested by the acquisition of the superior right only in the land by the Government."

10. In the connection a reference may be made to the case of Haji Aktaruzzaman Vs. Jadunath Pal and another reported in 17 D.L.R. 384. A Full Bench of the Dacca High Court considered section 80(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in paragraph 16 of that reported decision as follows:

"As soon as the Act had come into force a co-sharer tenant stood vested with a right covered by action 24. And what is the right ? The right to ask for pre-emption in case a share or portion of the non-agricultural land is transferred. With the commencement of the Act whoever answered the description of a "co-sharer" tenant within the meaning of the Act became clothed with the sort of right mentioned above. The proviso, as we read it, simply means that a tenant would not be stripped of his right, merely because of acquisition of superior right by the Government." In the said reported decision at paragraphs 28 and 29 Murshed C.J. observed as follows:-

"We would, therefore, answer the question which has been referred to us as follows :-

In the light of the proviso to section 85(3) of the Act a tenant in respect of non-agricultural land would not be deprived of a right reposed in him by the provisions of Act on the only ground of acquisition of superior tight in the land by Government. The right vested in a tenancy by the provisions of the Act in the right to take advantage of the provisions of the Act, including a right which is immediately enforceable and also a right which is enforceable in future, on the happening of a contingency. The aforesaid answer will also apply in respect of an application under section 24 of the Act. We hold that section 85(2) of the Act does not bee the application filed by the opposite parties under section 24 of the Act. We also hold that the case reported in 16 D.L.R. 77, in which it held that such an application under section 24 was competent, was correctly decided although we have come to the same conclusion by a somewhat different process of reasoning."

The fact of the present case is applicable with all force with that reported decision with which I have dealt herein above.

That I find no substance in the last contention of Mr. S. R. Pal, that the application under section 24 of the Act is not maintainable in view of the proviso of sub-section (2) of section 85 of the Act. In the result, this Rule is discharged.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

End.

TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C.J.-This appeal arises from the judgment of a Single Judge of the High Court Division passed in Admiralty Suit No. 5 of 1981 on April 19, 1982.

The appellant and the proforma-respondent No. 9 filed the aforesaid admiralty suit against the principal respondents for a decree for an amount of Tk. 71,61,724/- and other consequential reliefs.

2. Facts as stated are that in pursuance of negotiations plaintiffs agreed to purchase the Turbine Steamship TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO', defendant No. 1, and defendant No 2, owner of the said ship, agreed to sell it for a sum of US dollar 1,05,8760 at the rate US dollar 1700-00 per LDT CIF Chittagong. The agreement for sale was executed on 3rd July, 1981. Plaintiff-appellant established an irrevocable letter of credit in favour of defendant-respondent No.2 through American International Banking Corporation payable to defendant No. 2 through defendant No. 6. Plaintiff-appellant furnished a Bank guarantee and defendant No. 2 furnished a performance guarantee for the fulfillment of the contract. Terms and conditions mutually agreed upon between the plaintiff-appellant and defendant No. 2 inter alia are:-

(a) that the purchase price is included in the cost of towing the ship from Singapore off port limit to Chittagong.

(b) The plaintiffs shall establish their own irrevocable confirmed at sight 100% letter of credit in favour of the defendant No. 2 not later than 30th July, 1981 which shall remain valid and negotiable until 31st August, 1981, the delivery of which is condition precedent to the fulfillment of the obligation of the defendant No. 2 and the same shall be payable through the defendant No. 6 and the defendant No. 2 shall be entitled to negotiate the letter of credit on delivery to the defendant No. 6.

(i) Legal bill of sale in original duly attested by a Notary Public stating that the vessel is free from encumbrance, all debts, claims, etc.

ii) Certificate of deletion of the vessel from the Panamanian Register of the defendant No. 2's written undertaking for effecting the same as soon as possible.

iii) Notice of Readiness from the Tag Master of Oabale Advice of the arrival of the vessel at Chittagong from the Tag Master is the Tag's agent in Singapore;

iv) Acknowledgement receipt duly signed by the plaintiffs upon receipt of the vessel in afloat condition at Chittagong in Bangladesh to be attached along with the documents required for negotiation of the letter of Credit.

v) Commercial Invoice in Triplicate signed by the defendant No.2:

vi) True copy of certificate of ownership; vii) Buklders plan of certificate is conclusive proof of LTD.

c) That as a security for correct fulfillment of the contract the plaintiffs agree to furnish a Banker's guarantee to the extent of 10% of the price amounting to U.S. dollar 105876.00 only by the American Express International Banking Corporation, Chittagong on condition that the same shall be forfeited and encased by the defendant No. 2 if the plaintiffs fail to establish the letter of credit within the stipulated time; and that the defendant No. 2 agreed to furnish a performance guarantee to the extent of 10% of the price amounting to U.S. dollar 105,876.00 only to the plaintiff to be issued by the defendant No. 6 on condition that the same shall be forfeited and en cashed by the plaintiffs if the Vendor-defendant No. 2 does not complete the sale or fail to deliver the vessel to the plaintiffs within the validity of the letter of Credit;

(d) The defendant. No. 2 shall deliver or came to deliver the vessel at the port of Chittagong;

(e)That the property in the vessel shall vest in the plaintiffs upon delivery of the vessel to the plaintiff and upon release to the defendant No. 2 of the full amount of the purchase price and the vessel shall thereupon be at the risk of the plaintiffs;

(f) That should the vessel become a total or constructive total loss before delivery to the plaintiffs, the said agreement dated 3rd July, 1982 shall be cancelled the defendant No. 2 shall join the plaintiffs to cancelling both irrevocable letter of credit, etc. and

(g)That if there is default by the plaintiffs, in respect of any of the obligations under the contract, the security deposit of 10% shall be forfeited to the defendant No. 2 who shall be at liberty to recall the vessel in such event all loss and damage arising from such default shall be recoverable from the plaintiffs "together with interest @12% per annum and if there is default by the defendant No. 2 in the execution of a legal transfer or in deli very of the vessel and all her stores in the manner and within the time specified, the security deposit of 10% shall be paid to the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 2 shall forthwith join the plantiffs in cancelling the aforesaid letter of credit and pay the plaintiffs interest at the rate of 12% per annum upon the price from the date of such default until the cancelling date."

3. The last date for the delivery of the ship was on 24th August, 1982. In reply to the notice of readiness issued by defendant No. 4 on 21.8.1981, the plaintiff-appellant intimated that in respect of the arrangement to take deli very of the ship, it could not be taken over as it was not in a deliverable condition according to the terms of the agreement and the letter of credit. As a result, the plaintiff's contract of forward sale of the ship with the scrap buyers was frustrated who claimed Tk. 10,00,000/- as compensation, etc. Plaintiff- appellant ad vised their Bankers to encase the performance guarantee as the defendant No. 2 failed to deliver the ship in afloat condition. The cause of action of the suit arose at Chittagong on 24.8.1981 when the ship in question was to be delivered at the port. Defendant-respondents were responsible for all the consequences for the breach of contract. Plaintiff appellant invoked the Jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court under clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 and section 2(2) of the Charter of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act. 1890. Defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed an application under Order 7, rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the plaint did not disclose any cause of action for admiralty suit. Their contention was that the suit did not come within the scope of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. 1861. Further since the suit was filed on the basis of breach of contract in connection with the sale of the ship the suit was triable in the ordinary Civil Court and not in the Court exercising admiralty jurisdiction.

4. In their affidavit-in-opposition to the application under Order 7, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code the plaintiff-appellant stated that "upon application for arrest of the vessel when the Hon'ble Court arrested the vessel and issued injunction re training the defendants from dealing with (it) in any manner including the sale of the vessel, the defendants appeared and after furnishing Bank guarantee for satisfying any claim under final decree for payment has now filed this petition for rejection of the plaint with malafide motive and to make this present suit infructuous and to deprive the plaintiffs of any remedy whatsoever" Further, in their supplementary affidavit- in-opposition the plaintiff-appellant stated inter alia, that TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' was unfit for navigation and it was a dead ship which was bought for scrap. Also, the ship was tugged from Singapore to Chittagong by the 'Challenger,' which was not made a party in the suit. A notice under section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969 was received by the plaintiff appellant from the Customs authority, Chittagong requiring the plaintiffs to clear the under mentioned goods which was presently lying with them -"MV Challenger-PACIFIC ABETO."

5. After hearing the parties the Admiralty Court rejected the plaint on the ground that it did not disclose any cause of action which could be entertained by it. In its opinion the suit did not come within the ambit of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. The court also repelled the contention of the plaintiff-appellant that alternatively the suit was maintainable in the Admiralty Court under the provisions of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 enacted by the British Parliament, the reason being that an Act of the British Parliament was no longer applicable in this country.

6. Being aggrieved the plaintiff moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the Admiralty Court was wrong in rejecting the plaint as, in its opinion rule 11(a), Order 7. Code of Civil Procedure does not empower the Admiralty Court to pass such an order.

7. Mr. K.A. Bakr, Counsel for the plaintiff-appellant, submitted that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure do not apply to proceedings before the Admiralty Court. Hence, the rejection of a plant by mat Court under Order 7, rule 11 (a) was wrong. Secondly, even if such provisions are held to apply to proceedings in an Admiralty Court the decision that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action that can be entertained under the admiralty jurisdiction is not sustainable. Finally, since no materials were before the Court, either by filing the written statement of documents arising out of the transaction or any oral evidence in respect of it, it was clearly unjustifiable to hold that there was no cause of action.

8. As regards the first point regarding the applicability of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code, namely, rule 11(a), Order 7, to proceedings in an Admiralty Court reference was made to rule 3 of Order 49, C.P.C., which is as follows:

"3. The following rules shall Dot apply to [High Court Division] in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction, namely:

(l) rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (a) and (c) of Order VII;

(2)......................................

(3)......................................

(4).....................................

(5).......................................

(6).......................................

From the provisions of the aforesaid rule, it appears that the Admiralty Court exercising original civil jurisdiction has no power to make an order under rule 11(a), Order 7, C. P.C. Consequently, the order of the Admiralty Court rejecting the plaint in exercise of powers conferred by this rule is palpably wrong. Whether in an application filed under rule 11(a), Order 7 C.P.C. the same Court could have returned the plaint for presentation to a Court with proper jurisdiction as mentioned in rule 10 seems to be pointless, in view of the non-applicability of the provisions/of rule 10. Order 7, C.P.C. to proceedings in an Admiralty Court, Rule 10 Order 7 C.P.C. is as follows:

"10. (1) The plaint shall at any stage of the suit be returned to be presented to the Court in which the suit should have been instituted.

(2) On returning a plaint the Judge shall endorse thereon the date of its presentation and return the name of the Party presenting it, and a brief statement of the reasons for returning it."

9. In spite of the clear provisions of rule 3. Order 49, C.P.C., the question remains as to what would the Admiralty Court do if a plaint does not disclose any cause of action entertain able in that Court? If it cannot reject the plaint as provided by rule 11 (a), Order 7, C.P.C. it cannot be returned under rule 10, Order 7, C.P.C. because these provisions have been made non-applicable to proceedings before the Admiralty Court. Whether it relates to the absence of cause of action or lack of jurisdiction, the objection as to exercise of jurisdiction by that Court requires solution.

10. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, Counsel for the respondents, mentioned a few provisions of law in support of the proposition that the Admiralty Court had the necessary power of rejection as well as returning the plaint. First, he referred to section 2(1) of the Colonial Courts of the Admiralty Act, 1890 which empowers the Admiralty Court to "exercise all the powers which it possesses for the purpose of its other civil jurisdiction". Section 2(1) runs as follows:

"2. Colonial Courts of Admiralty (1) Every Court of law in a British possession. which is for the time being declared in pursuance of this Act to be a Court of Admiralty, or which, if no such declaration is in force in the possession, has therein original unlimited civil jurisdiction, shall be a court of Admiralty, with the jurisdiction in this Act mentioned, and may for the purpose of this jurisdiction exercise all the powers which it possesses for the purpose of its other civil jurisdiction.......".

11. Mr. Huq next referred to rules 3 and 51 of the Rules of the Colonial Courts of the Admiralty Act sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Rules 3 and 51 of the Colonial Courts of the Admiralty Act are as follows:

"3. A suit shall be instituted by a plaint drawn up, subscribed and verified according to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure save that if the suit is in rem the defendants may (subject to such variation as the circumstances may require) be described as the vessel or other property proceeded against instead of by name."

"51. Where no other provision is made by these rules proceedings in suits brought in the Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890, shall be regulated by the rules and practice of the Court in suits brought in it in the exercise of its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction."

Sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure provide thus:

"117. Save as provided in this Part or in Part X or in rules, the provisions of this Code shall apply to [High Court Division 1."

"141. The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suit shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of civil jurisdiction."

12. Mr. Huq also referred to a case decided by the Pakistan Supreme Court, namely, Hussain Bakhsh vs. Settlement Commissioner, (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 456=PLD 1970 SC 1. Though the observations related to the extent to which the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure regulate the original jurisdiction exercisable by the High Court under Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962 corresponding to Article 101 of the Constitution of Bangladesh now suspended, the observations made in that case, he submitted, apply equally to the exercise of admiralty jurisdiction by the High Court Division. Since, according to him, the proceedings before the Admiralty Court is a civil proceeding because it involves the assertion or enforcement of a civil right, the following observations made in that case were equally applicable to it;

“A civil proceeding in a Court of civil jurisdiction is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, by virtue of section 117 of the Code a civil proceeding in a High Court is also governed by the provisions of the Code other than the provisions which are specially exempted."

13. Finally, Mr. Rafiqul Huq, in pointing out the difficulty that if it be held that there were no provisions of law for returning the plaint in case the Admiralty Court felt unable to entertain the same, submitted that apart from the provisions referred to by him above, the Admiralty Court can return the plaint by invoking its inherent powers under section 151 C.P.C. if it is necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse of process of the Court. In support of this proposition the learned Counsel referred to the case of R.P.C. Connor vs. P.G. Sam path Kumar, A.I.R. 1953 Md. 897. Among the points discussed there, there is reference to the lack of power to retain a plaint when it is not properly presented to the original side of the High Court. Next, in the absence of provisions of law empowering the return of the plaint when not entertain able by it, the Court can by exercising its inherent powers do the same for ends of justice or preventing the abuse of the process of Court. The relevant observations are:-

"The fact that the Madras High Court is a Court of record does not necessarily imply that it has no power to return any document presented to it and especially so a plaint which it has no jurisdiction to entertain. There is nothing either in the Letters Patent or in any Statute which makes it incumbent on that Court on its Original Side to retain on its file even a plaint which ought not to have been properly presented to it.

Though there is no express provision in the Code or in the rules framed by the Madras High Court for the return of a plaint filed on the Original Side of the High "Court when it is found that the Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, the Court has inherent power to make an order directing the return of the plaint if it is necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of Court. For the purpose; however, of preserving the proceedings taken in the High Court a verified copy of the plaint should be made and filed in place of the original which is returned."

<u>14. The views expressed above seemed to be correct and I am of the opinion that in the absence of express provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure or Rules of tile Admiralty Court it may exercise inherent powers to return the plaint if there is no cause of action triable by it or in case it otherwise lacks jurisdiction.</u>

15. Mr. Huq further submitted that the Admiralty Court was not set up to try cases involving sale of goods. It was established to try cases arising out of carriage of goods by sea.

<u>16. Referring, therefore to the submissions made by the Counsel for the appellant that the Admiralty Court did not consider the terms of contract between the plaintiff and the defendant and also that he did not consider the bill of lading as well, Mr. Rafiqul Huq, Counsel for the defendant-respondents, stated that the contract between the parties did not involve the carriage of goods in a ship. 'TSS PACIFIC ABETO' which was towed from Singapore to Chittagong by the Tug 'Chittagong' was not carried in it. As it has not been carried in a ship, such towing has not been included in the bill of lading. Moreover, the aforesa1d Tug or its owners have not been made parties in the suit. It is true that normally towage from one place to another may not mean carriage in a ship but there may be circumstances where towage may be interpreted as carriage in a ship. Mr. Huq, however, submitted that in the present case towage of "TSS PACIFIC ABETO' from Singapore to Chittagong did riot involve its carriage in a ship. Naturally, he submitted, the bill of lading need not be considered by the Admiralty Court. The facts of the case show the necessity of determining the liability of each party to the contract for the purchase or sale of the 'TSS PACIFIC ABETO.' The Court is to look at the terms and conditions between the parties regarding the sale of the ship and violations of such terms and conditions, if any, either by the seller or the buyer. The consideration of the extent of liability of each party under the contract is to be done by a Court of ordinary civil jurisdiction competent to try such cases and not in an Admiralty Court. It is only when the question of the liability of a carrier arises regarding the carriage of goods by sea that the Admiralty jurisdiction can be invoked. So far as the provisions of the Admiralty Courts Act, 1861 are concerned, they did not apply to the facts of the present case and, therefore, the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court could not have been invoked by the plaintiff-appellant. That has so far been asserted and denied by the parties concerned, it appears that the main question centres round the extent of the liability of the seller of 'TSS PACIFIC ABETO' and correspondingly that of the purchasers, namely, the plaintiff-appellant in refusing to take delivery of the aforesaid ship at Chittagong Port when notice to take delivery was served upon the plaintiff. Even if towage from Singapore to Chittagong is viewed as carriage of goods in a ship the ship here involved being the 'Challenger' is not before the Court as having not been impleaded by the plaintiff-appellant. In such circumstances, submissions by the Counsel for the respondents that the decision of the learned Judge of the High Court Division that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action entertain able by an Admiralty Court was correct cannot be rejected.</u>

17. In this connection Mr. Huq pointed out the distinction between a case where, without considering oral and documentary evidence, the Court can, by merely looking at the plaint, come to the conclusion that it does not disclose any cause of action and can reject the plaint under Order 7, rule 11. C.P.C. and the case where the Court can only, after considering the entire evidence produced by the parties, decide that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action but cannot reject the plaint under the aforesaid provisions. In support, he relied on the following observations in Jagannath Prasad vs. Smt. Chandrawati, AIR 1970 All. 309 FB:

"There is a clear distinction between a case where the plaint itself does not disclose any cause of action and a case in which, after the parties have produced oral and documentary evidence, the Court, on consideration of the entire material on record, comes to the conclusion that there was no cause of action for the suit. In the latter case, obviously, the plaint cannot be rejected under Order 7, rule 11."

<u>18. As on the face of the plaint in the present case, it could be said that it did not disclose any cause of action, there was no necessity for the Court to wait till the parties produced evidence in support of their respective cases in order to come to the conclusion whether there was any cause of action for the suit. According to him, from a reading of the plaint itself in the present case it was apparent that it disclosed no cause of action entertainable by the Admiralty Court. He however, admitted that facts stated in the plaint did, no doubt, constitute a cause of action which were triable in an ordinary Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. He did not deny the existence of any cause of action but he only objected to the choice of venue by the appellant.</u>

19. The distinction between a case in which a mere reading of the plaint would show that there is no cause of action for the suit and a case in which such conclusion would not be possible unless "the Court goes through the entire materials on record is, however, a substantial one.

<u>20. Having regard to this distinction and considering the facts and materials on record in the present case, it appears that it is not necessary to wait for the production of evidence, oral and documentary, before reaching the conclusion that there was no cause of action triable by the Admiralty Court. Facts, as stated in the plaint and the limits imposed by law upon the Admiralty Court are sufficient for the conclusion whether a suit could be tried in the Admiralty Court. In the circumstances, the Admiralty Court rightly concluded that there was no cause of action which it could try.</u>

<u>For reasons stated above, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

Ruhul Islam J.-I have gone through a copy of the judgment prepared by the learned Chief Justice. I regret my inability to agree with the proposed judgment. "

22. Leave was granted to examine the contention that the Admiralty Court was wrong in rejecting the plaint under rule 11(a) of Order VII, of the Code of Civil Procedure although this provision is not applicable to the Admiralty Jurisdiction.

23. The plaintiff-appellants filed Admiralty Suit No.5 of 1981 in the High Court Division under the Admiralty Act, 1891 (Act No. XVI of 1981) claiming a decree for an amount of Tk. 71,71.724.00 by way of damage, compensation, loss of profits, etc. from the principal defendants. Plaintiffs case in short is that the plaintiff company entered into an agreement with defendant No. 2 Everfair Enterprise, owner of the ship defendant No. 1 TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO’ registered in Panama for purchase of their ship for a sum of US dollars 1.05.8760 at the rate of US dollars 170.00 per LDT CIF Chittagong, delivery of which was to be made at Chittagong Port by August 24, 1981. The agreement for sale was executed on July 3, 1981. The terms and conditions of the agreement, inter alia, provided:-

"(a) that the purchase price is included in the case of towing the ship from Singapore off port limit to Chittagong.

(b) The plaintiffs shall establish on their own an irrevocable, confirmed at sight 100% letter of credit in favour of the defendant No. 2 not later than 30th July, 1981 which shall remain valid and negotiable until 31st August, 1981, the delivery of which is condition precedent to the fulfillment of the obligation of the defendant No. 2 and the same shall be payable through the defendant No. 6 and the defendant No. 2 shall be entitled to negotiate the letter of credit on delivery to the defendant No. 6.

(i) Legal bill of sale in original, duly attested by a Notary Public stating that the vessel is free from encumbrance, all debts, claims, etc.

(ii) Certificate of Deletion of the Vessel from the Panamanian Register on the defendant No. 2's written undertaking for effecting the same as soon as possible.

(iii) Notice of Readiness from the Tag Master of Oable Advice of the arrival of the vessel at Chittagong from the Tug Master is the Tag's agent in Singapore;

(iv)Acknowledgment Receipt duly signed by the plaintiff upon receipt of the vessel in afloat condition at Chittagong in Bangladesh to be attached along with the Documents required for negotiation of the letter of credit.

(v) Commercial Invoice in Triplicate signed by the defendant No.2.

(vi) True copy of certificate of ownership

(vii) Buklders plan of certificate is conclusive proof of LTD.

(c) That as a security for correct fulfillment of the contract the plaintiffs agree to furnish a Banker's guarantee to the extent of 10% of the price amounting U.S. dollar 105876.00 only by the American Express International Banking Corporation, Chittagong on condition that the same shall be forfeited and encased by the defendant No.2 if the plaintiffs fail to establish the letter of credit within the stipulated time; and that the defendant No 2 agreed to furnish a performance guarantee to the extent of 10% of the price amounting to U.S. dollar 105,876.00 only to the plaintiff to be issued by the defendant No.6 on condition that the same shall be forfeited and en cashed by the plaintiffs if the Vendor-Defendant No. 2 does not complete the sale or fails to deliver the vessel to the plaintiffs within the validity of the letter of credit;

(d) The defendant No. 2 shall deliver or cause to deliver the vessel at the port of Chittagong;

(e) That the property in the vessel shall vest in the plaintiffs upon delivery of tile vessel to the plaintiff and upon release to the defendant No. 2 of the full amount of the purchase price and the vessel shall thereupon be at the risk of the plaintiffs;

(f) That should the vessel become a total or constructive total loss before delivery to the plaintiffs the said agreement dated 3rd July, 1981 shall be cancelled the defendant No. 2 shall join the plaintiffs in cancelling both irrevocable letter of credit etc. and

(g) That if there is default by the plaintiffs in respect of any of the obligations under the contract. the security deposit of 10% shall be forfeited to the defendant No. 2 who shall be at liberty to re-sell the vessel; in such event all loss and damage arising from such default shall be recoverable from the plaintiffs together with interest @ 12 % per annum and if there is default by the defendant No. 2 in the execution of a legal transfer or in delivery of the vessel and all her stores in the manner and within the time specified the security deposit of 10% shall be paid to the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 2 shall forthwith join the plaintiffs in cancelling the aforesaid letter of credit and pay the plaintiffs interest at the rate of 12 % per annum upon the price from the date of such default until the cancelling date."

24. As per terms of the agreement the plaintiffs established an irrevocable at sight 100% letter of credit in favour of the defendant No. 2 on July 28, 1981 to remain valid and negotiable upto August 31. 1981 for US dollar 105.876.00 only through their American Express International Banking Corporation, Chittagong and payable to defendant No. 2 through defendant No 6 Chartered Bank, Grosby House, Robinson Road. Singapore. The plaintiffs furnished a Banker's guarantee and the defendant No. 2 agreed to furnish a performance guarantee for the amount of US dollar 105,876.00 only being the 10% of the purchase price to remain in force from July 20, 1981 and expire on August 31, 1981 through the said Banker American Express International Banking Corporation and through defendant No.6 respectively. The last date of delivery of the steamship as mutually fixed was 24-4-81. The steamship subject matter of sale though signed at the Dry Dock Jetty on August 23, 1981 but it was not afloat as having listed on one side (Port Side) and as such it was not in deliverable condition in terms of the sale agreement and letter of credit end this fact got support from the letter dated" 24-8-81 of defendant No.3 Master of the ship addressed to Ship Repair (Bangladesh) Limited, requesting them to investigate the reason for port side listing and to make arrangement to make the vessel even keel and submit report of the investigation On 24-8-81 the plaintiff’s informed defendant No. 2 about the vessel that it further deteriorated very badly and the condition of the vessel became alarming and the Dry Dock Authority demanded immediate shifting of the Steamship from the Jetty to avoid any damage to the navigation channel. The plaintiffs by their letter dated 24-8-81 also intimated defendant No. 2 that although arrangements have been made to take over the vessel but since the condition of the vessel as found was not as per terms of the agreement and the letter of credit, the same could not be taken over. Defendant No. 5 the General Manager of the Dry Dock & Heavy Structure Works. P.S. Bandar, Chittagong requested the plaintiffs by the letter dated 25-8-81 to take immediate measures for rectification of the listing of defendant No.1. Time being the essence of the contract and defendant No. 2 having failed to fulfill the terms of the contract and the obligation under the letter of credit to deliver the ship in afloat condition, the plaintiffs by their letter dated 25-8-81 requested their Bankers, American Express International Banking Corporation, Chittagong to encase the bond and credit the proceeds to their account. Thereafter the plaintiffs through their Banker sent a- telex to defendant No. 6 on 29-8-8i claiming encasement of the performance guarantee of US dollar 105, 876.00 furnished by defendant No. 2, on the ground of failure to deliver the ship as per terms of the contract and the letter of credit. Defendant No. 6 expressed its inability to accede to the said request The plaintiffs instructed the said Bankers for cancelling the letter of credit, by issuing the letter dated 28•8-81 since defendant No. 2 could not hand over the vessel in proper condition and time as per terms of the agreement and letter of credit. The said Bankers of the plaintiffs cancelled the letter of credit opened by them. On 12-9-81 the said Bankers of the plaintiffs wrote to defendant No. 6 regarding encashment of performance guarantee No. 412/81/216 dated July 21, 1981 for US dollar 105, 876.00. As a consequence of the breach of contract on the part 9f defendant No.2 in failing to deliver the purchased ship in afloat condition at Chittagong port within the stipulated time the agreement dated July 23, 1981 and the conditions in the letter of credit, stood repudiated. According to the plaintiffs, defendant No. 2 was liable for the breach inasmuch as due to leakage the ship reached Chittagong listing on the port side and there was every possibility of its sinking endangering the Port Navigation. As the defendant No. 2 failed to make delivery of the ship in the specified time at Chittagong Port the defendant No. 2 was not entitled to demand signing of the acknowledgment showing delivery of the ship and the plaintiffs alleged that in order to avoid responsibility for the breach of the contract as aforesaid defendant No. 2 cunningly and fraudulently caused issue of a notice dated 14-9-81 through an Advocate demanding signing of the receipt by the plaintiffs acknowledging delivery of the dead ship "Pacific Abeto"; and for extension of validity of the letter of credit within 3 days from the receipt of the said notice otherwise threatening the plaintiffs that they would be constrained to dispose of the ship at the available price on account of the plaintiffs, and at latter's risk and responsibility and further to take legal action for recovery of balance amount with all consequences and losses incurred by defendant No.2 together with shortfall, if any. In this background the plaintiffs instituted the suit in the Admiralty Jurisdiction.

25. After notice of the suit was served upon the defendants an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by defendants No. 1 and 2 contending inter alia, that in view of the facts disclosed in the plaint the Admiralty Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit inasmuch as the cause of action as shown in the plaint does not come within the scope of the Admiralty Jurisdiction. It was contended that section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 is attracted only when damage is done to the goods or any part thereof due to negligence, misconduct or breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, Master or the Crew of the ship. In the present case the subject matter is not the goods carried in the ship but the ship itself. So, the Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. As the suit has been filed alleging breach of contract for sale of the ship, such suit is not contemplated in the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Court. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent however conceded that the facts stated in the plaint disclose a cause of action, but on the basis of such cause of action a suit in the Admiralty Jurisdiction is not maintainable.

26. Now, the question for consideration is whether the learned Judge in exercising the Admiralty Jurisdiction acted correctly in rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that "it does not disclose a cause of action that can be entertained under the Admiralty Jurisdiction of this Court"?

<u>27. Finding of the learned Admiralty Judge is that the facts stated in the plaint constitute a cause of action but it is not of such a character which can be tried in the Admiralty Jurisdiction. In making this distinction the learned Admiralty Judge apparently made some remarks on the merits of the suit which, it is apprehended by the appellants that it might prejudice the plaintiffs, if any they decide to file the suit in the ordinary Civil Court. One of the reasons for taking the view that the suit is not triable by the Admiralty Court is that the contract relating to the purchase of Turbine Steam ship TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' (defendant No.1) and her towage from Singapore to Chittagong cannot be called a carriage of goods in a ship. The view taken by the learned Judge does not appear to be free from controversy. In the course of arguments it became clear that towage of a dead turbine ship by a ship/tug can be said to be "carriage of goods in a ship." If the expression "carriage of goods in a ship" is given literal meaning, then unless the cargo is placed on board of the ship, there would not be any "carriage of goods" as contemplated in the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, In view of the nature of the contract which specifically mentioned about the bringing of the TSS "PACIFIC ABETO’' by towing by another ship (Tug) the carriage by towing: could not be anything but “carriage of goods in a ship” Sub-section(5) of section 3 of the Administration or Justice Act, 1956 provides that in the case of a claim in the nature of towage or pilotage in respect of an aircraft, the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court, may be invoked in an action in. rem against that aircraft if at the time when the action is brought it is beneficially owned by the person who would be liable for the claim in an action in personem. In the instant suit TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' (defendant No.1) owned by defendant No.2 was under arrest under an order of the Admiralty Court, but Tug 'CHALLENGER' which towed the TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' left the port; and it has not been impleaded, but the Tug Agency for towing the said steamship has been made defendant No.4 Defendant No. 3 is the Master of the steam ship TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO.'</u>

28. Another reason given by the learned Judge is that for bringing a suit in the Admiralty Jurisdiction, there must be a Bill of Lading for carriage of goods, and in the absence of such Bill of Lading the action for damage to the goods carried on board the ship does not lie. Bill of Lading means a paper signed by the Master of the Ship, by which he makes himself responsible for the safe delivery of the goods specified therein. It is true that in the instant case there was no instrument in the form of a Bill of Lading as contemplated in the normal course of business transaction. Here the plaint and the affidavits filed by the plaintiffs show that plaintiffs purchased the dead vessel TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO', and one of the conditions of the sale was that the owner defendant No. 2 took the responsibility of towing the vessel to Chittagong in floating condition. The terms could be ascertained from the sale agreement between plaintiffs and defendant No. 2. Plaintiff's case is that when the owner of the TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO’ took the responsibility of carrying the TSS 'PACIFIC ABETO' by towage to Chittagong and deliver the same there to the plaintiffs, then for this purpose the function of defendant No. 2 was that of a carrier, and the agreement, between the parties will serve the purpose of a Bill of Lading.

29. Mr. K.A. Bakr, the learned Attorney General appearing for the appellants seriously contended that the learned Admiralty Judge acted erroneously in entertaining the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in rejecting the plaint on the ground that "it does not disclose a cause of action that can be entertained under the Admiralty Jurisdiction of this Court" The learned Attorney General submitted that as per requirement of the statute the High Court framed the Admiralty Rules vide Appendix No. V (Admiralty Rules) as incorporated in the Rules of the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal, 1940; and that rule 51 cannot be construed to say that it makes the Code of Civil Procedure applicable to the proceedings in suits brought in the Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. All that rule 51 provides is that where no other provision is made by these rules proceedings in suits brought in the Admiralty Court shall be regulated by the rules and practice of the Court in suits brought in it in the exercise of its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction. According to the learned Attorney General the Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High Court is not governed by the Code of Civil Procedure but original side rules.

30. Civil proceedings in the Original Side of the High Court are governed and regulated by the provisions of the Letters Patent (1965) and the Original Side Rules frame by the Court, wherein by reference only some of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure have been made applicable to applications and suits brought in the Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction, There is nothing to snow that Order VII, rule 11 has been made applicable. The High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal was set up by the Letters Patent, 1862, which was repealed and substituted by the Letters Patent, 1865. The Letters Patent provides the procedure to be followed by the Chartered High Court in dealing with the matters in the Original Side of the Court. The Letters Patent provides the authority to the High Court to frame Rules for its Original Side. The High Court framed elaborate and comprehensive Rule-Rules of the High Court, Original Side, 1914. Chapter VII of the Original Side Rules deals with institution of suits. Rule 1 provides, inter alia, that the plaint shall comply with Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure and shall contain the particulars required by Order VII, rules] to 8 of the Code. Chapter VIII deals with Writ, Summons Process. Chapter IX deals with written statement and set-off. Chapter X deals with List of suits. Chapter XI contains the provisions for Discovery, Inspection Interrogatories. In the Original Side a plaint is presented for admission by the Judge. Rule 4 of Chapter VII provides that when a plaint is admitted, the words "Presented on the day of ................." together with a note of any special leave granted, 'shall be endorsed thereon and signed by the Judge or officer admitting the plaint.

<u>31. The Admiralty Rules were framed for regulating the procedure and practice in cases brought before the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal under the Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890. These rules were gazetted on 27th April, 1912 which came into operation 1st June, 1912. The Admiralty Rules appear to be complete for the purpose of regulating the proceedings in suits brought before the Admiralty Court. In rule 3 it has been provided that a suit shall be instituted by a plaint drawn up, subscribed and verified according to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, and excepting as provided in rule 3, I do not find any mention of the Code of Civil Procedure made applicable for any other purpose in a proceeding in a suit brought before the Admiralty Court. Language of Rule 51 is very' clear, it cannot be read or construed to say that it makes the Code of Civil Procedure applicable to the proceedings in suits brought in the Admiralty Court. Rule 51 reads as under:-</u>

<u>“Where no other provision is made by these rules proceedings in suit brought in the Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act. 1890 shall be regulated by the rules and practice of the Court in suits brought in it in the exercise of its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction."</u>

<u>It brooks no controversy that Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High Court is not governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, and it is governed by the Original Side Rules 1914. Chapter VI of the Original Side Rules contains the rules for guiding the "Chamber Business." Rule 11 enumerate the matters which may be disposed of in Chamber by a Judge. Item 10 relates to admission and rejection of plaints. A Judge sitting in chamber is competent to reject a plaint if it is not drawn up in accordance with rules of the Code. Rejection of a plaint by a Judge taking business in Chamber may be treated as permissible under this provision, that is, at the time of admission of the paint. After a plaint has been admitted by the Judge, it cannot be rejected excepting on merit. There is no scope for rejecting it under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Original Side Rules do not contain any provision for entertaining an application for rejection of the plaint in the manner as has been done in this case.</u>

<u>32. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq is not correct when he says that Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly indicates that Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable to a suit filed in the Admiralty Jurisdiction. Rule 3 inter alia, provides that rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (b) and (c) of Order VII shall not apply to any Chartered High Court in exercise of its Ordinary or Extra-ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction. From this it cannot be said that rule 3 makes Order VII, rule 11 (a) applicable to the Admiralty Jurisdiction. Admiralty Jurisdiction is completely different from both Ordinary Original Civil, Jurisdiction and Extraordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High Court. Part IX of the Code of Civil Procedure contains special provisions relating to the Chartered High Courts Section 116 provides that part IX applies only to High Courts which are, or may hereafter be constituted by His Majesty by Letters Patent. Section 117 provides that save as provided in this part or in part X or in Rules the provisions of this Code shall apply to such High Courts Thus section 117 applies the provisions of the Code to Chartered High Courts, that is, in the exercise of their appellate civil jurisdiction including their jurisdiction in Letters Patent Appeals.</u>

<u>33. On careful examination of the different provisions of the Rules as referred to by the learned Counsels it appears to me that rejection of a plaint filed in the Admiralty Jurisdiction, under Order VII, rule 1l(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure is not permissible under the Rules. In my opinion the learned Admiralty Judge acted without jurisdiction in entertaining the application under Rule 11(a) of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure and rejecting the plaint on this ground alone the judgment of the learned Admiralty Judge is liable to be set aside. In view of the legal aspects stated above the appeal is allowed. The judgment appealed from is set aside. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

<u>Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.-I have gone through the judgments written by the learned Chief Justice and Ruhul Islam, J; I concur with the decision of learned Chief Justice.</u>

<u>Shahabuddin Ahmed J.-I have gone through the judgments written by the learned Chief Justice and Ruhul Islam J. I concur with the decision of learned Chief Justice.</u>

<u>Chowdhury A.T. M. Masud J. I have gone through the judgments written by the learned Chief Justice and Ruhul Islam J. I concur with the decision of learned Chief Justice.</u>

Order of the Court

By a majority decision the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. Let the plaint be returned immediately to the plaintiff for presentation in the Court of proper jurisdiction if the plaintiff is so advised A certified copy of the plaint is to be kept in the record.

The Bank guarantee in this suit is extended upto 15th July, 1982.

End.
