full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J.—This Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against a decision of the Election Tribunal declaring the election of chairman of Govindapur Union Perished as void and further declaring that the respondent No 2 has been elected duly as Chairman of the said Union Parishad.

2. Facts in short are that the election of Chairman of Govindapur Union Perished was held on 14.1.77 under the Local Government Ordinance of 1976; the petitioner having secured the highest number of votes being 2801 as against 2749 votes secured by the respondent No. 2 was duly declared elected Chairman of the Union Perished and the result was accordingly published in the official gate of 19.2.77. The respondent No. 2 thereafter filed an election petition before the Election Tribunal, Faridpur challenging the election of the petitioner as Chairman of the Union Perished nod for a declaration that the petitioner's election as Chairman thereof should be declared as illegal and void and also for a declaration that respondent No. 2 be declared legally elected Chairman of the said Union Parishad. The dispute before the Election Tribunal was with regard to the casting and recurring of votes by the parties in Path rail polling centre. There is no dispute with regard to the manner of casting of votes, its counting and declaration of the result in the other two polling centers, namely, Maksedpur Polling Centre and Gobiadapur Polling Centre.

3. The general allegations made in the election petition in short are that the boxes for chairmanship candidates and that of the membership candidates were not placed in separate compartments and as result illiterate voters specially the women voters could not cast their votes properly and that many ballots for election of members were dropped into the boxes of the Chairmanship candidates and many ballots for election of Chairman were dropped into the boxes of membership candidates. the ease of the respondent No. 2 in respect of path rail polling centre was that respondent No. 2 got 41 votes and the petitioner got 2103 votes in this centre but the Presiding Officer of this centre in collusion with the petitioner took all the election papers to this fishery officer at the Thane Head Quarter and made a mock counting there on the next day and the number of votes in favour of the petitioner were raised from 2103 to 2390 thereby increasing 287 votes in favour of the petitioner. It has also been alleged by the respondent No. 2 in the election petition that at the time of counting of votes the presiding Officer treated many invalid votes of petitioner as valid and many valid votes of respondent No. 2 as invalid; that in spite of the respondent No. 2 having secured the highest number of votes, the petitioner was declared elected as Chair man illegally due to the machination of the said Presiding Officer.

4. The petitioner contested the election petition and filed a written statement denying all material allegations therein. He contended, inter alia, that the election was held legally, peacefully and in accordance with the rules, and the story of mock counting at the Thana Head Quarter of the Presiding Officer and increasing the votes from 2103 to 2190 are false and fabricated. He asserted that in Pathrail polling centre he got 2390 votes and respondent No. 2 got 41 votes and that the petitioner having secured the highest number of votes was validly declared elected as Chairman of the Union Perished. The learned Election Tribunal on consideration of the evidence and materials on record declared the election of the petitioner void and illegal and further declared that the respondent No. 2 had been duly elected as Chairman of the Union Perished. This judgment and decision of the learned Electron Tribunal has been challenged in this Rule.

5. Mr. Khondked Mahbulauddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has submitted that the learned Election Tribunal failed to exercise his jurisdiction in not adverting to the material evidence adduced by the parties and considering time along with the result of the counting by him of the votes secured by the petitioner and the respondent No. 2 in Pathrail Polling Centre. Elaborating his submission he has contended that the learned Tribunal having based his decision to unseat the petitioner upon the result of recounting of the votes by rejecting one hundred membership ballots which were found in the ballot box of the petitioner was illegal inasmuch as that the learned Tribunal was obliged under law as a judicial tribunal to consider other material evidence adduced by the parties along with the result of the recounting He has also submitted that as found by the learned Tribunal the gunny bags in which the election materials were kept though found to be under seal but the packet of the valid ballots in favour of the petitioner having been toned open and torn, the learned Tribunal in the circumstances ought not to have based his decision on recounting the ballots only and that he was obliged as a judicial Tribunal to consider other material evidence of the parties including that of the Presiding Officer to arrive at this decision. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to a decision of the High Court of Bangladesh in the case of Narul Islam Talikder, Versus- Munsif, 4th Court (Sadar) Chittagong reportedin 28 DLR (HC) 375.

6. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2 has submitted that the learned Tribunal committed no error of law apparent on the face of record in deciding the case on the basis of recounting He has submitted that the Tribunal was competent and within its jurisdiction to meter his decisions on the basis of some evidence without adverting to all the evidence adduced by the parties. He has submitted that in certiorari proceeding the High Court can interfere with the decision of the learned Tribunal when the decision is not based upon any evidence, but in the present case the decision is founded on some evidence namely, the parties. According to him, unless the decision of the Tribute is tainted with male Ode motive or based on no evidence the High Court should not interfere with the decision of the Tribunal.

7. The proceeding before the Election Tribunal was a judicial proceeding and not an administrative or quasi judicial proceeding. The tribunal was to determine the election dispute between the parties judicially; as such, to was s which might hare keen adduced of had keen adduced in the proceeding by the parties. In support of their respective cases in the instant case, the parties have adduced oral and documentary evidences and the Tribunal was obliged under law to judicially determine the dispute on consideration of all material evidence on record. We are conscious that in certiorari proceeding this noun exercising power under Article 102 of the Constitution is not a Court of Appeal but exercises supervisory authority aver the actions and decisions of the Tribunals. We have no jurisdiction to review or reassess the evidence to unsettle the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. In the present case however when the parties have adduced evidence which were relevant and material for determination of the case the Tribunal ought to have adverted to those evidence along with result of recounting upon which the decision was based. The Tribunal in its judgment after discussion of the result of recounting and basing his decision to allow the election petition an the basis of such recounting observed that he need not advert to the oral evidence adduced by the parties. In his judgment he has observed as follows:- ফলে মৌখিক সাক্ষ্য আলোচনার কোন প্রয়োজন নাই।

<u>8. It is on record that the petitioner examined 8 witnesses and the respondent No. 2 examined 4 witnesses besides producing some documents as well. The learned Tribunal without adverting and considering those evidence arrived at finding declaring the petitioner's election as void and illegal on the basis of the recounting of the votes of the parties. Now the question is whether failure to consider material evidence adduced by the parties amounted to any error of law apparent on the face of record. This question also came up for decision before the Supreme Court of India in the case of Syed Yukub Ali versus Radha Krishna reported in AIR 1964 (SC) (479-80). It has been held there by their Lordship that a finding of fact may be interfered with by a review court when it is based on no evidence or it is of such a nature as no reasonable person would have arrived at on the basis of material before it. But 'no evidence', in the view of their Lord hips, does not necessarily mean a complete absence of evidence. In this circumstances we are of opinion that a bunt exercising judicial functions is obliged to advert to all material evidence produced before it by the parties before arriving at his decision. In another case reported in 28 DLR (H.C.) page 375 in the case of Nurul Islam Talukder vs. Munsif, 4th Court (Sadar) Chittagong a Division Bench of this Court has held, ordinarily this Court does not interfere with the finding of a Subordinate Court if the findings are arrived at on due consideration of relevant facts and correct appreciation of evidence free from any unfairness of mind. If the findings are not so arrived at this Court has got every power to interfere therewith."</u>

<u>9. In the instant case when the packet of ballot papers of the petitioner was found to be tampered wimp by some malicious hand as has been found on recounting by the learned Tribunal the Tribunal ought to have adverted to other evidence adduced by the parties in support of the respective cases and he ought to have taken decision on consideration of other relevant facts. In this view we hold that the learned Tribunal acted illegally in not adverting to the evidence adduced by the parties in support of the respective cases. We are therefore inclined to declare the judgment and order of the teamed Tribunal as having been passed illegally and without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. We, therefore, make the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and order of the learned Election Tribunal and remand the case back to the Election Tribunal for decision on the basis of existing evidence and in accordance with law. He, however, will not be precluded from receiving further evidence if he considers them to be necessary for arriving at a decision The Election Tribunal is further directed to dispose of the petition within two months flow the date of arrival of the records in his court. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case we make no order as to casts.</u>

<u>Let the records he sent down expeditiously.</u>

Abdul Wadud Choudhury, J.-I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Shafiq Ahmed with S. A. Rahim ----- For the Petitioner.
Abdus Sobhan with Syed J. R. Modassir Hossain ----- For Respondent No.1
parties:
Chandpur Tea Company Ltd. ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Joint Secretary & ors. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
SM Hussain J: Chandpur Tea Company Ltd. being the petitioner in Writ petition No. 427 of 1977 has challenged the legality of certain Certificate cases allegedly on the ground that in view of the provisions of section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the recovery of arrear rents dues therein was barred by limitation. The Certificate cases arose out of non-payment of the balance dues of rent after the final publication of the records of right. The petitioner was assessed provisionally under sub-section (1) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The petitioner bad was paying such provisional rent till such time when such rent was finally determined under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. After adjustment of rent with the previous years the petitioner was served with a demand notice to pay the balance dues being the determining enhanced rent. The petitioner having failed to pay the balance dues of rent the impugned certificate cases were instituted by the Revenue Authority against which the petitioner moved this Court and obtained this Rule under disposal.

<u>2. So far as the impugned certificate cases are concerned they relate to certain Tea gar-dens situated in the district of Sylhet. In such circumstances, the limitation for the recovery of arrear rent dues is governed by the provisions of section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that the period of limitation for the recovery of arrear rent shall be three years running from last day of the year in which the arrear fell due. Sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act further provides that in computing the period of limitation for the recovery of any arrear of rent in the district of Sylhet, a period of twenty-four months that is two years shall be excluded on and from the date of acquisition of the rent receiving interest to which such arrear relate. Reading the aforesaid provisions of section 142 and sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act together it clearly appears that the period of limitation for the purpose of recovery of arrear rent with regard to any land in the district of Sylhet extended up to a period of five years from the last day of the year in which such arrear fell due.</u>

<u>3. In this connection reference may be made to the provisions of clause (ff) of subsection (4) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which provides for the obligation of every owner of any land to pay rent to the Government at the enhanced rate, if any, after the final determination of the rent under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and in such case the tenant in question shall be liable to pay the balance with retrospective effect from the notified date that is the date of final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus it will appear that once the rate of rent is finally determined and published in the final records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, any balance dues there under can be recoverable with retrospective effect from the date of such final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So for the purpose of prospective realisation of rent at the final rate the time for limitation shall run from notified date that is, the date of final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. That being so inevitably the aforesaid period of limitation as provided under section 142 read with sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall normally be a period of five years with regard to any land situated in the district of Sylhet from the date of the final publication of the records of right of that area under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition. and Tenancy Act.</u>

4. The only question now remaining for consideration is whether such period of limitation of five years as aforesaid from the date of the final publication of the records of right is an absolute period or is subject to any extension under section 19 of the Limitation Act. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of section 151(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein it has been provided that apart from sections 6, 7, 8 and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 19 of the Limitation Act all the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall apply as far as possible to all suits, appeals and applications arising under Part V of the said State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but subject to the provisions of the said Part V of the said State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. From the aforesaid provisions of section 151(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it clearly appears that the provisions of section 19 will be applicable in any application arising under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, unless it is found that the provisions of section 19 of the Limitation Act is repugnant to any of the provisions of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the said provisions of section 19 of the Limitation Act shall be applicable in any application arising under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The present proceeding admittedly having taken place under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, section 19 of the Limitation Act applied in the present case in full force.

<u>5. Section 19(1) of Limitation Act provides that where before the expiration of the period prescribed for an application in respect of any right, an acknowledgement of liability in respect of such right has been made in writing by the parties against whom such right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so made. In the present case since the draft publication of the records of right and the provisional determination of the fate of rent, the petitioner had all along paid the provisional rent to the Revenue Authority of the Government periodical and successively every year and such payment of provisional rent continued even after the publication of the records of right and final determination of the rate of rent. Such payment of provisional rent every year by way of a "treasury chalan" signed by the petitioner in favour of the Government bore an acknowledgement on the part of the petitioner its liability to pay the enhanced rate finally from time to time. This has created a legal obligation on the petitioner to pay the enhanced rate of part of the rent as finally determined and published in the record of right under sub-section (3) of Section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This payment from year to year is a clear acknowledgement on the part of the petitioner about its liability to pay the enhanced rate of rent when so finally determined and by making such payment every year the period of limitation was extended from year to year by way of an acknowledgement as contemplated under section 19 of the Limitation Act. That being so for the purpose of computing the period of limitation in the present case, it shall run from the date of the last payment of provisional dues, by the petitioner in favour of the Government by way of "treasury chalan" and shall continue till the completion of five years from such date where after any recovery of arrear rent shall be barred."</u>

6. In the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case and for the reasons stated herein before this case is sent back to the Certificate Officer of Habiganj in the district of Sylhet to dispose of the Certificate cases applying the rule of limitation as aforesaid. For such disposal the Certificate Officer shall first of all determine as to when the last payment of provisional rent was made and from that date five years shall be computed for the purpose of the recovery of any rent from any tenant. Rents due beyond five years form the date of the last payment of provisional rent shall be barred by limitation as aforesaid. The Certificate Officer is directed to dispose of the case accordingly. This Rule is disposed of accordingly. There will be no order as to costs.

The Court records its appreciation about the assistance rendered by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the learned Additional Attorney-General in arriving at a decision of this Court on the point raised herein.

End.

caseno: Appeal from original decree No. 47 of 1975
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmad with Md. Shafiqur Rahman—For the appellants.
Fakir Abdul Mannan with Md. Bazlur Rahman—For the respondents.
parties:
Haji Aklema Khatun and another ------- Appellant
Vs.
Shah Alam and ors ------- Respondent
case_source: With civil rule No. 1035 (F) of 1975 with appeal from original order No. 341 of 1975 with civil rule No. 1002 (F.M) of 1975
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Choudhury, J.:—This appeal by the plaintiffs arises out of a suit for declaration that the plaintiffs are the owners of the property on the basis of a gift and is directed against the judgment and decree passed on 12-2-1975 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dacca in Title Suit No. 64 of 1969 (heard analogously with Succession Certificate case No. 207 of 1969).

2. The plaintiffs' case is that the suit property belonged to late Abdur Rahman Choudhury, husband of the plaintiff No. 1 and father of the plaintiff No. 2. Late Abdur Rahman Choudhury was in exclusive possession of the suit property by letting out the same to M/S. May & Baker Ltd. Abdur Rahman Choudhury for the last several bears before his death was suffering from chronic diabetes. Abdur Rahman Choudhury had no other near and dear relations excepting the plaintiffs and as such he was contemplating to transfer the suit property by way of gift in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs further alleged that on 14-11-68 late Abdur Rahman Choudhury (hereinafter referred to as the donor) had a sudden heart attack of which he survived. After recovery from the heart attack the donor in presence of witnesses, namely, Messrs. Khurshed Ali Choudhury, Abdus Salam Khan and others, orally gifted the suit property on 24-11-68 by a declaration of gift and divested himself of all interest therein and the plaintiffs accepted the said gift along with monthly tenant thereon and became the exclusive owners thereof. The donor, as abundant caution, wanted to execute and register a written instrument of gift with respect to the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs and accordingly, he filed an application on 2-12-68 before the Income Tax Authority for Income Tax Clearance Certificate to which the Income Tax Authority replied by a letter dated 21-12-68 asking the donor to deposit a sum of Rs. 7,500/- as gift tax. Unfortunately, the donor expired on the next day, i.e. on 22-12-68. The defendants are the sons of consanguineous brothers of the grandfather of the donor and during the life time of the donor the defendants had no connection with him.

3. The defendants filed a petition for Succession Certificate being Succession Certificate Case No. 207 of 1969 in Court of the Third Subordinate Judge, Dacca claiming 6 annas share and monthly rent of the suit property and a notice of the same has been served upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs having acquired 16 annas right, title and interest in the suit property on the basis of oral gift and the actions of the defendants having cast a cloud over the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs, they have filed the present suit for declaration of title on the basis of the aforesaid gift from the donor.

4. The defendants filed written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and raised several other objections as to valuation, court fee etc. They further alleged that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of a prayer for recovery of khas possession. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs acquired no title in the suit property on the basis of the so-called oral gift which is an afterthought and concocted with ulterior motive for illegal gains. They further contended that section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 is a bar to the accrual of title to the plaintiffs in the suit property in the absence of a registered written instrument of conveyance. They further contended that even if the gift was genuine as contemplated under Mohammaden Law no title did pass upon the plaintiffs in the absence of a registered written instrument of gift. They, however, stoutly denied the story of the alleged oral gift and contended that the application before the Income Tax Authority for clearance certificate is a manipulated affair. They contended that Abdur Rahman Chowdhury died without making any gift and that the defendants being consanguine paternal uncles of the donor (sons of the consanguine brothers of the grandfather of deceased Abdur Rahman Chowdhury) are entitled to 6 annas share by inheritance under the Mohammaden Law. But the plaintiffs have set up the case of verbal gift to defeat the claim of these defendants in the disputed property and that the suit ought to be dismissed and the succession certificate should be granted to the defendants. The facts relating to the succession case need not be stated separately since the defendants defence in this suit is their case as petitioners in the succession certificate case. This suit was tried analogously along with the said Succession Certificate Case.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge after framing necessary issues and on consideration of materials and evidence on record decreed the suit. On appeal the suit was remanded; mainly on the ground that the defendants had no opportunity to file additional written statement against the belated amendment of the plaint and to examine the witnesses with a view to controvert the genuineness of the documents by handwriting expert if the defendants so desired. In the order of remand it was further directed that both the suit and the Succession Certificate should be heard analogously as before. After remand the learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit. Tie learned Subordinate Judge held that the alleged story of gift of the suit property by Abdur Rahman Chowdhury in favour of the plaintiffs is absolutely false and concocted. The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the witnesses of plaintiffs and its acceptance and the delivery documents with respect to the suit property. He also found that there was no delivery of possession of the suit property by the donor to the plaintiffs. The learned Subordinate Judge also held that section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 is a bar to. the passing of title by oral gift in favour of the plaintiffs, even if the story of alleged gift taken to be a true one. He also found that the Transfer of Property Act being a Central Law and the provision of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act being special law on matters of the transfer of property, Non Agricultural Tenancy Act would prevail over the provision of Transfer of Property Act. He also held that in view of provisions of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, by the alleged transfer of suit property by oral gift, the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the property. Upon these, finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit and allowed the Succession Certificate Case. This appeal is directed against the aforesaid decision of the learned Subordinate Judge.

6. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. Md. Shafiqur Rahman, learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the plaintiff appellants and Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan with Mr. Md. Bazlur Rahman, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the defendants respondents. The learned Advocate for the appellants firstly contended that the court below was wrong in not considering that all the witnesses to a transaction are not supposed to see, note and remember all the facts and aspects relating to the same in the same way and slight variation and deviation amongst the witnesses in stating the facts do not render the evidence adduced by the witnesses to be untrue. He has also submitted that the witnesses of the plaintiffs have proved the oral declaration of gift as oral gift and the handing over of documents relating to the gift and the acceptance of the gift by the donees and these evidences of the witnesses could not be impeached at all with regard to the main ingredients necessary to prove a gift. He has submitted that the trial court was wrong in observing that the plaintiffs did not state anything in their deposition about deli very of possession of the suit property inasmuch as delivery of title deeds of tenanted premises is an act sufficient to constitute delivery of possession. He has also submitted that even if the trial court disbelieved the genuineness of Ext. 5, the fact of handing over the lease deed and letter of extension of tenancy by the donor at the time of gift proved that the gift was completed and effective in law. He has also submitted that the trial Court failed to consider the purport and effect of the evidence of P.Ws. 5, 6 and 8 and was wrong in not relying upon their evidence in deciding the issue as to genuineness of gift. He has also submitted that the court below erred in law in holding that sec. 23(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act rendered the personal law of Mohammadans and section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act nugatory and ineffective. He has also submitted that the provisions of section 23(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 was repugnant and/or inconsistent with the provision of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act and as such it did not affect oral gift by a Mohammadan.

7. With regard to the evidence of oral gift the plaintiffs have, besides themselves, examined 5 witnesses. The defences have also examined 4 witnesses. The plaintiffs' case is that late Abdur Rahman Chowdhury was the husband of plaintiff No. 1 and father of plaintiff No. 2 and he had none else in this world than the plaintiffs. P.W. 1 is the plaintiff No. 1, wife of the donor, She deposed that the donor suffered from diseases for 5/7 years and that excepting the aforesaid daughter they had no other issue or had no other near relation. He deposed that the donor made a heba in their favour on 24th November, 1968. She deposed that the donor called her elder brother P.W 3 Khurshed Ali Chowdhury ; local Chairman Mr. Nazir Hossian, P.W. 8; husband of her sister P.W. 4 through his son-in-law and said "I make oral gift of this house in favour of my daughter and my wife and you bear witness". He further deposed that on saying so he handed over the documents to them and the donor said, "From this day I make heba of this house. Do you accept this?" We replied, "Alhamdu Lillah, we do accept it". P.W. 1 further stated that the donor wanted to write a letter to the tenant. She further stated that there was a talk of executing a deed and it was discussed by the donor with the Chairman and Member of the Union Council at an Ifter Party. These two witnesses namely, the Chairman and the Member (P. Ws. 8 and 6) told the donor, "Your health is now well, you have made oral heba. Now make a regular deed." She further deposed that thereafter her husband applied to Income Tax Authority for income tax clearance certificate and he received letters from the income tax authority asking him to deposit the required money toward gift tax and to obtain the certificate. The donor, however, died on the following day, i.e. 22nd December, 1968. She further stated that the defendants are distant relations of the donor being step-brothers of donor's grand-father and that her husband was not on visiting terms with them and that the defendants did not come to the house of the plaintiff No. 1's husband during the time of his illness. They also did not attend the Janaja of her husband. She further stated that after the death of her husband the defendants wanted to ascertain as to whether her husband left any property and also contended that the defendants had no share in the suit property. In cross-examination P.W. 1 said that 3/4 years before her husband gave the house at 36, Ishwar Chandra Sil Road and 13, Hara Mohan Street to her in lieu of her power by executing a deed. She stated in cross-examination that her husband dealt in paper and stationery articles and sometimes in hosiery business. There were queries with respect to the chairs, tables and other household articles of the donor used before his death, in order to contradict the statements made by the plaintiffs in the reply to the notice sent by the defendants making queries with respect to the properties left by the donor. There the plaintiff stated that the donor left no property. It appears from the cross-examination of this witness that the defendants have sought to bring about the contradiction as to ownership of the household articles used by the donor before his death to suggest that the plaintiffs falsely stated in the aforesaid reply to the lawyer's notice to say that the donor left no property. It appears to us that the contradiction with regard to the matters referred to above are very minor in nature and should not affect the decision on the basis of other evidence as to whether there has been a valid oral gift of the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs. The principal point at issue in this case is whether there has been a valid gift in favour of the plaintiffs and whether delivery of possession was given to the donees. She (P.W.1) denied the suggestion that the letter of the Income Tax Authority was created afterwards with antedating the same and it was a forged letter she stated that her husband received the letter putting his own signature. He also stated in cross-examination that two houses which her husband gave were transferred to her by means of a deed of gift. She also stated that the house at Mohiuddin Lane was given to her daughter. She also stated that at the gate of premises No. 314/16, Lalbagh Road a stone slab bearing the name of Abdur Rahman Choudhury was fixed and this was done because he had business there. She further stated that except this suit house all other properties have been disposed of by the donor to them by written instrument. She also stated that for the purpose of making gift of the suit property discussions were held on several occasion and it stated one or two months before making of the gift and she also stated discussion with his Advocate was also held with regard to gift. She also stated that no stamp was purchased for execution of the document though an application for Income Tax clearance was filed by the donor. She stated that the houses within suit premises were not acquired in the benami of the plaintiffs. She also denied the suggestion that the story of oral gift was a fraudulent affair and has been set up to defeat the claim of the defendants.

8. Next witness for the plaintiffs is Bibi Rahman Khatun P.W. 2 who was the plaintiff No. 2. She stated that her father made a heba of the suit house in her favour and in favour of her mother. Her father was suffering for the last 6/7 years from urinal diseases. She deposed that her father in presence of witnesses said, "I give this property in heba to my wife and daughter and you are the witnesses". Then he handed over the documents of the property to my mother and asked, "Do you accept this property? We said "Alhamdu Lillah, we do accept." Then he asked to write letters to the tenant. She further deposed that the local Chairman and member asked his father to execute a regular deed though he had already made a heba of the property. She also corroborated the deposition of P.W. 1 with respect to filing of application to the Income Tax Authority for income tax clearance certificate and about the receipt of letter from the Income Tax Office just one day before the death of the donor. She also stated that her father left no property besides the suit property. This statement of the witness has been sought to be explained or interpreted by the defence to mean that the suit property had not been transferred by way of gift and it remained with the father of this witness (i.e. Abdur Rahman Choudhury). In our view, this statement seems to mean that Abdur Rahman Choudhury disposed of his property before and only the suit property remained undisposed of before the disposition of the same by way of gift. While cross-examining this witness as well as P.W. 1 the defence suggested that the plaintiffs did not state in the reply to the notice sent to them through the lawyer of the defendants to ascertain about the properties left by the donor, that the suit property was given in heba to the plaintiffs. The reply to the notice Ext.7 (a) stated that, "deceased Janab Abdur Rahman Choudhury left no property", we are of the view that the omission or failure of the plaintiffs to state in the letter Ext. 7 (a) could not in any way affect the case of the plaintiffs. That the suit property was gifted to them by way of heba. The failure of the plaintiffs to state that the property had been gifted to the plaintiffs may have been made by the lawyer sending the letter on various considerations. We have noticed that in cross examination, these witnesses have not been asked as to whether they stated to the lawyer that the property had been gifted by the donor to them. She also stated in her cross-examination that she did not know whether her father informed the tenant, namely M/S. May & Baker and Co. about the gift nor they wrote to the tenant with regard to the gift. She further stated that her father took advance from the tenant and after deduction of the advance per month a sum of Rs, 2,500/- was being received. She also could not say how much money was being deducted from the rent, nor could she say the amount of money which was being deducted from the loan. She stated that they received a total sum of Tk. 2,500/. per month. She further stated that at the time when the Chairman and member talked about the making of the instrument of gift she did not appear before them nor her mother appeared before them. Her father told her mother about the same. She also stated in cross-examination that at the time of making the heba her father called for her Khalu (mother's sister's husband) and her maternal uncle. They were called 2/3 days before the making of the heba. She also stated that some days before making the heba they were called. She also stated the, persons in whose presence the heba was made were called but there was no talk of any writing at the time of making the heba. She further stated that a few days before making of the heba the health of her father deteriorated and he called all these persons and made the heba, for fear that his health might deteriorate and he might die suddenly. She further stated that she did not get any further property through such heba. She further stated in cross-examination that her father handed over to her mother the title deed relating to the suit property. She denied the suggestion that the heba and the story of acceptance of saying "Alhamdo Lillah" were false. She also stated in her deposition that the title deed in respect of other properties of her father were with her father in that very house. This witness was also cross-examined with respect to the household articles used by her father before his death to show that the plaintiffs did not state about these articles which were owned by the donor before his death in Ext, 7 (a).

9. Next witness for the plaintiffs was P.W. 3 Khorshed Ali Chowdhury. He is a brother of P.W. 1. He stated that the plaintiffs are the owner of suit property on the basis of oral gift in presence of Nazir Hossain, Chairman, Lalbagh Union Council, Abdus Salam Khan, his bhagnipati, on 24.8.68 after Asar prayer time. He disposed that Haji Abdur Rahman Chowdhury gave the title deed of the disputed property and the bharanama with May and Baker to the plaintiffs and declared in their presence about the heba that Abdur Rahman was in good health. He stated in cross-examination that he was called by the donor through Shamsul Huda, P.W. 9 on the date of gift. He also stated in cross-examination that before the gift he did not see him taking or giving any property without document. In this connection it is seen from the records that there is no evidence that the donor made any oral gift except the present one and as such question of witnessing or having made any other such gift before did not arise, His further deposition is to the effect that he did not see anyone else taking or giving valuable immovable property without document which was just a suggestion without any purpose since Muslim Law provides for making gift by oral declaration. He also stated in his cross-examination that the suit property could not be valued at less than Rs. five lacs. He further stated in his cross-examination that Abdur Rahman Chowdhury was contemplating to make a gift of the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs since about a month before the date of the gift and had occasion to talk to him in the matter and it did not strike him to advise the donor to make a written instrument of gift. But Abdur Rahman Choudhury, however expressed to him to make a document of gift. He further deposed in his cross-examination that Abdur Rahman Choudhury gave the document of the suit property and another agreement of lease to the plaintiff No. 1. He stated that he did not see giving of any rent receipt book by the the donor to the plaintiff No, 1. He denied the suggestion that the story of gift was false.

10. Next witness for plaintiffs was P.W. 4 Abdus Salam Khan. He is bhaira of the donor (sister's husband of the P.W.1). He stated that the plaintiffs got the disputed property on the basis of verbal gift by the donor in their presence on 24-11-68. He stated that P.W. 3 Khorshed Alam, P.W. 9 Shamsul Huda and Chairman, Lalbagh Union Council P.W.8 were also present at the time of making of the gift.

He stated that gift took place at Asar time and that Abdur Rahman Choudhury handed over the document concerning the disputed property to the plaintiffs through his son-in-law as token of gift in their presence. P.W. 4 also could not state how many papers the donor handed over to plaintiff No 1 through Shamsul Huda but he stated that he gave the title deed of the property, lease deed and some other papers as the token of girt. He further stated that the plaintiffs were sitting behind the screen and could not say when they left from behind the screen. This statement of this witness appears to be contradictory with the statements of P.Ws. 1 and 2 who stated that a title deed with respect to the suit property was handed over by the donor to P.W. 1. In our opinion this discrepancy in the evidence of witnesses are not material contradictions affecting the veracity of the deposition of the witnesses. It is in evidence that P.W. 9 Shamsul Huda, husband of P.W. 2 (Plaintiff No. 2) was present in the sitting where the heba was made. It is not unnatural that at one stage of the sitting the husband of the plaintiff No. 2 might have handled the document after these were handed over to the donees by the donor. This witness in his lapse of memory and in the absence of accurate observation of the whole incident and in view of narrating the same after a long time in not expected to narrate each stage of transaction so accurately as he could state if required to do so soon after the transaction. In our opinion small discrepancies appearing between the statement of this witness would re-impugn their veracity. Hence, in our opinion, the discrepancy between the witnesses with regard to handing over the document or number of documents that were handed over by the donor would not affect the material evidence in this case, i.e., the declaration of gift, its acceptance and the delivery of the document to the plaintiffs.

11. Next witness for the plaintiffs is P.W. 5 Md. Yasin, an Advocate of this court, He stated that he advised the donor to make oral gift of the property. He further stated that before the Eidul Fitre the donor proposed to him that he would make gift of the property. In cross-examination this witness stated that the Plaintiff No. 1 was his argentic cousin. Next witness for the plaintiffs was P.W. 6 Abdul Mannan. He was a Member, Lalbagh Union Council. He deposed that Al-haj Abdur Rahman Choudhury gave the disputed property to the plaintiffs, on the 7 or 8 Ramdan Friday in 1968. P.W. 9 Shamsul Huda called him and the Chairman to an Iftar party at the residence of the donor where the Chairman told the donor that he should make a written document and that then the donor asked his son-in-law Shamsul Huda to have the forms for clearance certificate. Next witness for the plaintiffs is P.W. 7 Md Amjad Ali. He is an Inspector of Income Tax, Circle C. He proves the letter dated 17-4-69 and 22-7-69 bearing signature of Income Tax Officer, Ext. 2 and 2(a), These are letters from the Income-Tax Officer to Haji Abdur Rahman Choudhury asking him to deposit a sum of Tk. 7,500/- as gift tax for making a heba of the suit property in favor of the plaintiffs. This witness denied in his cross-examination that these papers were subsequently manipulated and antedated. Next witness for the plaintiffs is P.W. 8 Nazir liJssain. Chairman, Lalbag Union Council. He was the Chairman at the time when the alleged gift took place. He stated that he knew the donor as he was a resident under his Union Committee. He stated that the donor called him once through his son-in-law on 2nd or 3rd Ramdan in 1968 and he went to his house and also found some other persons there, He deposed that Haji Sb. expressed his desire to make a gift of the property to the plaintiffs in our presence and then he made the verbal gift of the property making over the title deed of the disputed property and another paper to the plaintiffs through his son-in-law. He deposed that females were sitting behind the screen and they accepted the gift by uttering "Alhamdo LiIlah." The donor died on the Eid day of the said Ramjan after making the gift. He also deposed that on the following Friday after making the gift he and P.W. 6 Abdul Mannan were invited to an Ifter Party where he suggested to the Haji Saheb, while discussing about the oral gift he made, to make a written document for the gift and Haji Saheb also agreed to the suggestion. He stated in his cross-examination that he did not know the disputed property or its market value. He, however, stated about the market value of other properties which he knew to have belonged to Haji Saheb. There is no reason why this witness should support the case of the plaintiffs with regard to declaration of oral gift in his presence by the donor unless it was made in his presence. This witness is not a relation of the plaintiffs and, in our view; he has been called by the donor as the leading man of the locality to witness the oral gift.

12. Next witness for the plaintiffs is P.W. 9 Shamsul Huda. He has corroborated the evidence of other witnesses with regard to the declaration of gift to the plaintiffs in his presence and in presence of other witnesses. He stated that the gift was made in presence of the witnesses and the sale deed dated 29-12-60 and the agreement for monthly tenancy between the donor and May & Baker and letter from the May & Baker extending the tenancy were handed over to the donees. Ho also stated that May and Baker made correspondence with the plaintiffs but, did not make any payment of rent without any indemnity bond. He further stated that the plaintiffs. however, took all steps for payment of municipal tax and filing of appeal against enhancement of taxes, etc. through him. He proved certain municipal papers and certain copies of letters written by his wife to the Municipality. He stated that he obtained Income-Tax Form and submitted application for Income Tax clearance certificate Ext. 1 signed by Haji Abdur Rahman Choudhury on 21-12-68. He also stated that chalan was also received from Income Tax Authority for payment of gift tax. He also stated since his marriage in May 1956 he never saw the defendant on visiting and in familiar terms with the donor's house. He stated in his cross examination that May & Baker and Co. paid rent of the disputed house upto November, 1969 and this was paid on 2nd or 3rd December, 1968 when the donor was alive and thereafter no payment was made after that by them. He denied the suggestion that the story of heba was got up and entirely false one. He also denied that the Income Tax papers and Municipal papers were procured after the death of his father-in-law by ante-dating them. These are all the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs besides several documentary evidence which they have produced in support of their case.

13. The defendant No. 1 examined him-self as D.W. 1. He stated that late Abdur Rahman Choudhury was his nephew, i. e. son of his first cousin. He stated that Abdur Razzak was the father of Abdur Rahman Choudhury, and Qudrutullah was the father of Abdur Razzak, and Marbar Bepari was the father of Qudrutullah, Elahi Bux, Nabi Bux and Abdul Sadagar who are all dead. He stated that Abdur Razzak predeceased his father Qudrutullah and no issue of Elahi Bux is alive and that he is the only son of Nabi Bux and that Azizul Huq, defendant No. 2, is the only son of Abdul Sawdagar and as such they inherited 6 annas share in the property left by Abdur Rahman Choudhury. He further stated that they were on good terms with the donor. He asserted that the alleged verbal gift was false and the story of gift in presence of the witnesses is a concocted one. He stated that the donor never expressed his intention to make a gift to the plaintiffs. He stated that the disputed property is worth Tk. 5 to 51 lacs and the monthly rent was Tk. 4,500/- then. He stated in cross-examination that Abdur Razzak was not his first cousin. He stated that Abdur Rahman sold his village house about 10 years ago. This witness has deposed that the other property purchased or standing in the name of plaintiffs were benami property owned by Abdur Rahman Choudhury. He stated that Abdur Rahman Choudhury was suffering from various ailments since these years before his death. He stated that Abdur Rahman died at his Lalbagh House but he did not know personally any of the neighbours of that house, and he denied that he never visited the house of Abdur Rahman Choudhury. He stated that on 12.2.69 they sent a letter to May & Baker demanding deposit of house rent and got a reply from them but could not say if the reply had been filed in court. He denied the suggestion that May & Baker & Co. intimated to them about the gift of the disputed properly and they sent a notice to the plaintiffs to disclose about the properties left by Abdur Rahman Choudhury. He further stated that they filed a Succession Certificate Case claiming 6 annas share in all the properties left by Abdur Rahman Choudhury. This witness further stated in his deposition that after remand of the case May & Baker requested them to obtain necessary Succession Certificate.

14. Next witness for the defendant is P.W. 2, a Handwriting Expert. He stated that he could not give any definite opinion about the identity or otherwise of the signatures with those in 'Y' and 'Z' as these signatures were not contemporaneous. He also stated that it could not be said from examination of 2 signatures only whether the full stop as appears at the end of the word 'Chowdhury' in 'Y' and ‘Z' constitutes the individual characteristics of the author in the writing.

15. Next witness for the defendant, P.W. 3, is another handwriting expert. He stated that he looked into the disputed signatures marked 'X' and the admitted signatures in the registered deed marked 'Y' and 'Z' He deposed that the signatures in Ext ‘X' is defective, hesitant and lacks individual characteristics and are dissimilar to those marked 'Y' and 'Z' in the registered document. He stated in cross-examination that general features of a writing are changed with old age. He further stated in cross-examination that it is not a fact that the difference in the writings 'X' and 'Y' and 'Z' are due to infirmity of old age of the writer. He denied that his opinion was not correct and he was induced to depose falsely. These are all the oral evidences adduced by the defendants in this suit in support of their case.

16. In the background of the evidence let us consider whether Haji Abdur Rahman Choudhury made declaration of oral gift in presence of the witnesses as alleged and whether the said gift was accepted by the plaintiffs and delivery of possession of the disputed property was given. In this connection it may be mentioned that the disputed property is in possession of the tenant under an agreement of tenancy. It is in evidence that the plaintiff No. 1 is the widow and plaintiff No. 2 is the only daughter and only issue of late Abdur Rahman Choudhury. It appears that late Abdur Rahman Choudhury left no near relation besides the plaintiffs. The defendants are step-brothers of, grandfather of late Abdur Rahman Choudbury. It is not disputed that the defendants are distant agnates and that they would inherit a share of the property left by Abdur Rahman Choudhury if there was no disposition of the suit property by the impugned oral gift. The plaintiffs have filed this suit for declaration of their title on the basis of oral gift. We do not think that the plaintiffs are required to pay ad valorem court fee as they were not seeking recovery of khas possession after establishment of their title. The relief for declaration is competent and as such the suit as framed is maintainable.

17. As stated earlier the plaintiffs are the near and dear ones of late Abdur Rahman Choudhury and that the defendants are consanguine paternal uncles in the 4th category of distant kindred under Muslim Law. In our opinion the facts of declaration of gift by the donor and acceptance of the gift by the donees have been well proved by the evidence of P.WS. 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 & 9. It is true that excepting P.Ws. 8 Chairman of the Local Union Council, all other witnesses of the gift are near relations of the donor and the donees. In a transaction like a heba made by the husband in favour of his widow and by father in favour of his only daughter and issue, the person expected to be present and witness the heba would naturally be the near relations. The donor, however, in his wisdom called the chairman of the locality to witness the gift. He has corroborated the evidence of other witnesses with regard to the declaration of the gift, acceptance of the same and delivery of the document relating to the property. We do not find any reason to reject the evidence of P.W.8, the local Chairman who corroborated the evidence of other witnesses. We also find that the plaintiffs being near and dear relations of the donor in the world, it would not be unnatural to make a gift in their favour, affecting inheritance of the defendants who are consanguine paternal uncles and distant kindred under the 14th category under Musalman Law. It is seen in deposition that the material fact with regard to the making of gift and its acceptance by the donees could not be impugned by cross-examination of the witnesses. Serious criticism has been put forward by the defendants about the number of papers and documents handed over during the declaration of gift but the material evidence of the declaration of gift by the donor and the acceptance of the gift by the donees could hardly be impugned in cross-examination. The discrepancy about the number of papers and documents banded over to the donees by the donor as we have discussed earlier would be natural in view of lapse of time that passed between the time when the transaction took place and the witnesses deposed in the Court. It is not natural for the witnesses to remember the details of the transaction at the time of making of the gift witnessed by them with meticulous accuracy. Small discrepancies bring truthfulness in their evidence. With regard to the discrepancies about how many papers were handed over by the donor to the donees at the time of making of the gift it is seen for the evidence that P.Ws. 1 and 2 stated that the donor passed all the documents relating to the disputed property. There is no discrepancy between the evidence of those two witnesses about the handing over of the document of title with respect to the suit property to them by the donor. P.W. 3 stated the donor handed over the title deed of the disputed property and bharanama with May and Baker and Co. to the plaintiffs. P.W. 4 stated some other papers beside the title deed and bharanama were handed over to the plaintiffs as a token of gift P.W. 8 Chairman stated that the donor handed over the title deed and another paper to plaintiff, through the son-in-law, P.W. 9 stated that few other papers besides the title deed were banded over to the donees. This discrepancy with regard to the handing over of some other papers including the lease agreement besides the title deed appear in the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2. But the evidence that the title deed with respect to the property was handed over to the donees by the donor is consistent and there is no discrepancy with regard to the handing over of the title deed to the plaintiffs. In our view the discrepancy appearing in the evidence of some of the witnesses with regard to the number of papers and documents banded over to the donees by the donor should not affect or impair the veracity of the evidence with regard to the declaration of gift and its acceptance by the donees. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiffs have proved successfully by cogent evidence the fact of declaration of gift in presence of witnesses and its acceptance by the donees.

18. Now with regard to the delivery of possession of subject of the gift by the donor to the donees as the subject was susceptible, it is consistent evidence of all the witnesses on behali of the plaintiffs that the title deed of the disputed property was handed over to the plaintiffs at the time of making the gift. It is in evidence that the suit property was under occupation of May and Baker & Co., Ltd, as tenants at the time of the gift. The plaintiffs produced Ext. 3, Ext. 4, and Ext. 4 (a) to prove delivery of possession of the subject matter of the gift by the donor to the donees. Since the property is in physical possession of the tenant, it is untenable to hold that short of actual physical possession of the property gift the would be invalid. In present case if the evidence of handing over of other documents and papers Exts. 3, 4 and 4 (a) are not accepted as being discrepant with evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 the handing over of title deed is consistent with all the depositions of the witnesses. In that view of the matter we hold that the delivery of title deed with respect to the property which is in occupation of a monthly tenant would constitute a valid delivery of possession of the property in favour of the donees.

19. With regard to the handing over of the lease deed executed between May and Baker & Co. and the donor we are inclined to accept evidence of P.Ws. 3, 4, 8 and 9 because of the donor having made the gift of the property handed over the title deed to the donees there is no reason why he should not be banding over the lease deed on the basis of which the then tenant of the property were in occupation. It is possible that P.Ws. 1 and 2 may not have noticed as how many documents the donor gave to them or due to the lapse of time that passed between the transaction and their deposition in court they may not have remembered about the number of documents that donor gave to them. In this view we hold that in pursuance of the gift and its acceptance, the donor delivered possession or the disputed property to the plaintiffs by delivery of the title deed, and the deed of lease in favour of the tenant.

<u>20. It has been submitted on behalf of the appellants that Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is a Special Law with respect to the incidence of tenancy and it is not a law of transfer, and that even if section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act deals with transfers relating to Non-Agricultural Tenancy land, the provision of Transfer of Property Act, it being a central Law, shall prevail over the provision of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has submitted that the transfer by a gift by a Muslim to a Muslim will be governed by the personal Law of the Muslims. It has been so stated by section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act. He submits that although by virtue of the assent of the Governor-General under sub-section (2) of section 107 of the Government of India Act. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was a valid legislation but the provision with regard to transfer of Non-Agricultural Tenancy cannot override the provision of general law. For that purpose the provision of Muslim Law relating to transfer shall prevail. In our view Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not a special law of transfer. General law of transfer may be affected by the special law of transfer and in that event the provision of special law will prevail. In our view, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not a special law of Transfer. This is a law with respect to the incidence of tenancy of Non-Agricultural lands and the provisions in section 23 of the Act cannot over-ride the provision of general law relating to the transfer of immovable property, namely, the Transfer of Property Act and for that purpose the provision of Muslim Law. We are, therefore, of the view that with regard to a transfer of immovable property between a Muslim and another Muslim, the Muslim Law relating to gift will be applicable, i.e., an oral transfer by gift in accordance with Muslim Law may be made in the absence of a registered written instrument of gift.</u>

<u>21. Mr. M. H. Khondker, the learned Advocate who appeared as amicus curiae on our request to assist the court on the question whether a Muslim can make a valid oral gift in respect of immovable property submitted that section 12 of the Transfer of Property Act having accepted the Rules of Mohammadan Law and the provisions of Transfer of Property Act relating to gift was not affected by the provisions of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has submitted that whether if the provisions of Chapter on gift in. Transfer of Property Act is in conflict with the Mohammadan Law the latter shall prevail. The Transfer of Property Act requires that a gift must be made by a registered instrument. But under the Mohammadan Law a gift of immovable property may be made orally and by delivery of possession. Mr. Khondkar has also submitted that Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not apply to a premises with structure and that the transfer of a land and building is not attracted by section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has referred to the decision reported in 1968 SC, M. R. 341 and to the case of Abdul Mutate Vs Musammat Rezia Begum reported in 22 D.L.R. (SC) 134. Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan, learned Advocate, on the other hand, submitted that it is a Non-Agricultural Tenancy and in spite of the building standing therein section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will apply with all force as the tenancy is Non-Agricultural tenancy. tie has referred to the decision of G. Narayana-swami Naidu and others Vs. Inspector of Police," Mayavaram and another reported in A, L R. 1949 (Madras) 307 (Special Bench) and to an unreported decision in Afsaruddin Ahmed Vs. Nahar and others in F. A.. No. 79 of 1963. In our view the provision in section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act prohibiting the transfer of Non-Agricultural Tenancy without registered document shall not apply to gifts of immovable property by a Muslim. A valid gift of immovable property with buildings and structures inter vivos can be made under the Muslim Law by oral gift. In this connection their Lordships of the Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Abul Vs. Fakir Jan an Begum reported in 49 I.A. 195 (209-10) have stated as follows ;</u>

<u>"For a valid gift inter vivos under Mohammadan Law these condition are necessary ; (a) manifestation of the wishes to give on the part of donor, (b) acceptance of the donee and (c) taking of possession of the subject matter of the gift of the donee either actual or constructively."</u>

<u>In our view, according to Muslim Law an oral gift is complete as soon as the declaration of gift and the delivery of possession is given by the donor to the donee. When these essential conditions are complied with the gift, in our opinion, becomes perfectly valid and if a written deed is executed afterwards and registered the oral gift would be valid notwithstanding the latter written instrument of gift. With regard to the delivery of possession it is in evidence that the disputed property is in occupation of the tenant and in that view the property is not susceptible to actual physical delivery of possession. In our view, in a gift of immovable property which is in occupation of tenant, the delivery of possession can be effected by delivery of title deed. Reliance may be placed for our view in the case of Gani Mia and ors Vs. Wajid Ali reported in 39 C.W.N. 882, in the case of Gani Mia and anr Vs. Wajid Ali reported in 61 C. L. J. 328 as also in the case of McEvoy Vs. The Belfast Banking Company Limited reported in 1935 A. C. 24. In this view of the matter, we find substance in the contentions of the learned Advocate for the appellant and hold that a valid gift has been made by the donor in favour of the plaintiffs and delivery of possession has been made to the plaintiffs in pursuance of the gift.</u>

22. In view of our discussion above, we allow the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Court below and decree the suit declaring that the plaintiffs are 16 annas owner of the suit property. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case we do not make any order as to costs. We also allow the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 341 of 1975 and dismiss the application for Succession Certificate. The connected Rules being C.R. Nos. 1035 (f) of 1975 and 1002 (fm) of 1975 are made absolute.

Sultan Hossain Khan, J.—I agree.

End.
