full_judgment:
In this Rule the petitioner has challenged decision of the 3rd Subordinate Judge of Comilla made on 23rd June 1980 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 1978 allowing an application directing the restitution of a land claimed in a pre-emption proceeding. The only question that arises for disposal in this Rule is whether the provision of section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the restitution of any property upon the variation of a decree of a Court is applicable in relation to an order passed by a court in a proceeding under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. Before deciding this question the short fact leading to this Rule may be stated. An application for claiming preemption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was allowed ex-parte against which an application for setting aside such ex-parse order was also dismissed by the Trial Court against which a miscellaneous appeal was filed before the lower appellate court which in turn set aside the ex-parte order of the Trial Court allowing pre-emption. Against the aforesaid decision of the lower appellate court a Rule was obtained from the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 510 of 1977 which having been disposed of by a Division Bench on 30th June, 1977 set aside the decision of the lower appellate court setting aside the ex-parte order of the Trial Court allowing preemption on the ground that there could not he any appeal in such case. Consequently, subsequent thereto another Rule was issued by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 852 of 1977 which was disposed of by a Single Bench on 8th February, 1978 wherein the ex-parte order cattier passed by the Trial Court allowing the pre-emption case was set aside and the pre-emption case was restored to its file and number. After passing of the ex-parte order allowing the preemption case the preemptor obtained possession of the land in question by virtue of the proceeding u/s. 96 of the S.A. & T. Act. Such ex-parte order in the previous cane having been allowed but ultimately set aside as aforesaid and such preemption case having been restored to its file and number the preempted purchaser filed an application before the Trial Court for the restitution of the land claimed in the pre-emption application which having been rejected by the Trial Court was allowed by the lower appellate court against which the present Rule under disposal was obtained.

3. As already the question to be decided in this Rule is whether such restitution of the land claimed under pre-emption can be allowed u/s. 144 of the Civil Procedure Code or under any provision of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is undisputed that apart from section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no other provision in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or for that matter any other law for the restitution of any property in view of the variation of any order made by any appellate court. Than the whole question is whether section 144 C P.C. would be applicable in a proceeding u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So far as section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code is concerned, it must be re-id along with section 141 of the Code which says that the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable. in all proceedings in any Court of Civil Jurisdiction. What is referred to in section 144 of the Civil Procedure Coda is that the procedure of the Code shall be made applicable in all proceedings in any Civil Court, Section 144 of the said Code is not a procedural law as such. It is a substantive right of any party to any litigation fur restitution of any property in case of any variation of the deck on of the Court. Sub-section (1) of Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure while providing for this substantive right of restitution of any property makes a clear reference that where and in so far as a decree is varied or reversed, the court shall cause such restitution to be made and place the parties in the position which they would have occupied but for such decree as has been varied or reversed. From the language quoted in subsection (1) of section 145 of the Civil Procedure Code it clearly appears that such restitution could only be available where a decree is varied or reversed. The question now is whether an order passed by a Civil Court in a proceeding u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act can be construed to be a decree within the meaning of section 144 C.P.C. So far as the definition of decree and order is concerned, it has not been defined anywhere in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or for that matter is any other relevant law. Such definition has only be given in the Civil Procedure Code. Decree has been defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereas order has been defined in sub-section (14) of section 2 of the said Code. Decree has been defined as meaning the formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties with regard to any of the matters in controversy in a suit. What is important to note in this definition is that such decree can only be passed in a suit. An order has been defined to mean the formal expression of any decision of the civil court which is not a decree.

<u>4. Considering the aforesaid definition of a decree and an order as given in the Civil Procedure Code and reading them together, it would clearly appear that a proceeding u/s 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which though makes a formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties with regard to any matter in controversy, being not a suit as referred to in the definition of a decree in the Code of Civil Procedure, can nor be said to be a decree within the meaning of the definition of a decree given in the Code as aforesaid. The definition of an order given in the Civil Procedure Code fully applies in the case of an order passed by a civil court in a proceeding under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

5. A Division Bench of the High Court Division while disposing or the Civil Revision No. 510 of 197, on 30th June, 1977 between the same parties in the collected matter as already referred to hereinbefore has held that an order passed by a civil court u/s 96 of the S A. & T Act is not a decree of the court as contemplated under the Civil Procedure Code. In this connection, reference may also he made to a Single Bench decision reported in 4 D.L.R. (1952) at page 671 and 53 CWN in Dacca Reports at page 61. In both the cases it has been held that an order passed in a pre-emption proceeding is not a decree of a civil court. In a recent decision of a Division Bench of the High Court Division reported in 33 D.L.R. (1981) at page 168, a different view has however been taken holding that an order passed in a proceeding u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in a pre-emotion case has the Force of a decree. Considering all the aforesaid decisions it appears that the majority view of this Court reported in 2 Single Bench decisions and one Division Bench decision as against another Division Bench decision is that an order passed by a civil court in a pre-emption proceeding is not a decree of a suit. Upon such proposition it thus clearly appears that what is contemplated in caption 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that a decree in a suit must be varied or reversed in order to apply for restitution of any property. An order passed by a civil court in a pre-emption proceeding u/s 96 of the S.A. & T. Act being not a decree in a suit, in such proceeding no application for restitution of property can be made at least under section 144 of the Civil procedure Code.

6. In the result, the impugned decision 1981. Special Original Jurisdiction of the 3rd Subordinate Judge of Comilla made on 23rd June, 1980 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 1978 allowing restitution of the land claimed in a pre-emption proceeding must be held to have been made illegally and it is accordingly net aside. Since the preempted-purchaser has lost possession of the land claimed in a pre-emption-proceeding in view of the ex-parte order of the Court allowing the pre-emption case, and such case having been restored to its file and number for regular hearing again, it is necessary for ends of justice and equity that the pre-emption case now revived and pending before the Trial Court should be heard and disposed of as expeditiously as possible. In that view, the 3rd Munsif of Comilla is directed to decide and dispose of the Miscellaneous Case No 192 of 1974 at the latest by 31st December, 1981.

With the aforesaid observation and direction this Rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
M. Gholam Rabbani ----- For the Petitioner. 
Shah Md. Sharif ----- For opposite party No. 30.
parties:
Giri Bala Das ----- Petitioner. 
Vs. 
Basudev Dey and others ----- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
S. M. Husain, J—This Rule is directed against a judgment of the Lower Appellate Court affirming an order of the Trial Court dismissing the petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949. The petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land was con-tested by the opposite parties as co-sharers alleging that neither the transferee nor the transferee had any right, title and interest the suit land and the question of pre-emption of the basis of the said transfer does not wise. In the impugned transfer under pre-emption one Profullya Kumar Dey was the transferee on his death his right, title and interest if any devolved on this heirs. The alleged transfer took place on 12.8.61 and the present pre-emption case were filed on 21.5.62 Although the pre-emption case was filed beyond the statutory period of four months from the date of the alleged transfer but the courts below concurrently found that the case was filed within four months from the date of the knowidea FA of" the petitioner about the said alleged transfer. However, when the pre-emption case was filed by that time the transferee Profullya Kumar Dey had already died and the heirs of the transferee were accordingly made parties in the preemption case. It appears that one of the heirs of the aforesaid transferee was left out, that is opposite party No. 6 and he was impleaded in the proceeding on 26-9-64, almost after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case. The courts below dismissed the petitioner's pre-emption case holding firstly, that the addition of opposite party No. 6 after 2 years makes the application for pre-emption itself barred by limitation and even if the pre-emption case in allowed against other heirs of the transferee, the same cannot be allowed against opposite party No. 6 since it was barred by limitation and on that account the pre-emption case shall fail since no partial pre-emption can be allowed in favour of other heirs of the said transferee.

2. In this Rule 2 questions have been raised by the petitioner, firstly, whether by adding Opp. Party No. 6 after 2 years from the date of the filing of the pre-emption case, the pre-emption case itself becomes barred by limitation and secondly, whether partial pre-emption against other heirs of the said transferee can be allowed in this case. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under Sub-Section (1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, if the main application for pre-emption to have been filed within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the alleged transfer, any subsequent addition of any party would not make the application as barred by limitation. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act partial pre-emption has not been prohibited as has been found in the case of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>3. So far as the addition of parties in the present case is concerned opposite party No. 6 being an admitted heir of the aforesaid transferee is not only a necessary but a proper party. In a pre-emption case the proper party is the transferee whose transfer is challenged. The transferee being dead the heirs of the transferee must be held to be the parties in the pre-emption, case. In that view the opposite party No. 6 was one of the proper and necessary party in this pre-emption case and the case itself would have remain  defective for non-joinder of such proper and necessary parties. The question now is whether such joinder of a proper and necessary party after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case shall make the pre-emption case itself, barred by limitation at least as against the aforesaid added party as such. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. Thus, an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act before a Civil Court is governed the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure provides, that subject to the provisions of section 22 of the Limitation Act, the proceeding as against any person added as defendant shall be demand to have begun only on the service of the summons. Section 22 of the Limitation Act provides that whether after the institution of the suit if a new defendant is added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party, provided that such addition has not been made owing to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suite Considering the provisions of section 141 and sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 22 of Limitation Act as aforesaid it clearly appears that in a pre-emption case either under the State Acquisition Act or under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act if a proper and necessary party like an heir of transferee is added as a party to the proceeding evidently after the statutory period of limitation such pre-emption case must be held to be barred by limitation at least against such party added after the period of limitation as such. In the present case it is on admission that when the pre-emption ewe was initially filed, the opposite party No. 6 was already born by then and was a minor heir of the aforesaid transferee and that he was added as such in the pre-emption case after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case, long after the statutory .period of limitation. Thus the irresistible conclusion is that this pre-emption case is barred by limitation at least as against the opposite party No. 6.</u>

4. The next question is, if the pre-emption case is barred by limitation as against opposite party No. 6 why the same shall not be allowed with regard to the other heirs of the transferee, who were on record admittedly within the period of limitation, that is opposite parties No. 1-4. This question in certainly leads to a vital issue as to whether partial pre-emption is allowed under the law. So far as pre-emption under Section 26 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 F of the State Acquisition Act are concerned, there are consistent Judicial pronouncements that partial pre-emption could not be allowed both under the law and equity. Single Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 38 C.W.N. 654 and 49 CWN 242 and a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 19 DLR 659 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. A Single Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 13 DLR 323, a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 14 DLR 847 and another Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 28 D.L.R, 400 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act.

<u>5. The question still remains as to whether partial pre-emption could still be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, Section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides that one or more co sharers-tenants of the holding, a portion or share which is transferred may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. Under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act provides that if a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharers tenants of the holding may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to him or themselves. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, provides that if a portion or share of the non-agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more cashiers tenants of such land may apply to the court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Thus basically the language of sub section (1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, sub-section(1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and sub-section(1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is almost in the similar language that where if a portion or share of any holding or land is transferred, one or more co-sharers-tenants of such holding or laid may apply to the Court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Taking into consideration the aforesaid similar .language in the relevant statutes concerned it clearly appears that the provision of pre-emption both under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act are similar excepting that under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, all the co-sharers of the holding must be impleaded in the pre-emption case whereas under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a co-sharer may apply for being added as a party in a pre-emption case, The aforesaid decisions of the Calcutta High Court and Dacca High Court referred to above disallowed partial pre-emption in view of the language imported in sub-section(1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and sub-section (I) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, The language imported in sub-section (I) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is also similar to that of the language imported in sub-section (i) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that view, the aforesaid judicial decisions disallowing partial pre-emption under Bengal-Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act are also applicable in the case of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Partial pre-emption has been disallowed under the Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act on equitable ground and for the same reason partial pre-emption should be disallowed under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In that view no partial pre-emption can be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949.</u>

6. In the result the petitioner's application for under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no substance and it must fail since the impugned judgment and order of the Courts below do not suffer from any illegality or material irregularity calling for any interference by the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This Rule is accordingly discharged.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Shah Md. Sharif with Fakrul Islam and Nizamul Huq ----- For the Petitioners
M. Nurullah with Syed Sakhawat Ali ----- For the O.P. No. 1 and 2.
parties:
Md. Abdul Majid and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Sarina Begum and ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
In this Rule the petitioner has challenged a decision of the lower appellate court reversing the decision of the trial court in a pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The trial court returned the application for pre-emption to the petitioner to file it before a court with appropriate pecuniary jurisdiction. Such order of the trial court was challenged before the lower appellate court who held that the order of the trial court returning the application was bad and the pre-emption case should have been dismissed outright. Against the aforesaid order of the lower appellate court the petitioner obtained this Rule under disposal.

2. There was a transfer of land measuring 3.72 acres at a consideration of Taka 40 thousand. The petitioner claiming to be a contiguous owner of the land claimed the pre-emption with a part thereof measuring 0.35 acres. While making the application for the pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the petitioner deposited Taka 2 thousand alleging to be the consideration amount as contemplated under clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The trial court proceeded upon the determination of the amount that would be required to be deposited by the petitioner under clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and found that the consideration money for 0.35 acres of land shall be Taka 4,323/- instead of Taka 2 thousand as deposited earlier. The trial court having assessed the consideration money at Taka 4,323/- had to return the application to the petitioner for filing it before another court with appropriate pecuniary jurisdiction since the court concerned had no such jurisdiction to try a suit valued at above Taka 4 thousand. Consequently the application for pre-emption was ultimately filed before the First Munsif of Dacca and the balance consideration money was also deposited therein. The opposite party being the purchaser pre-emptee however challenged the earlier order of the Second Munsif of Dacca in returning the plaint and consequently an appeal was preferred before the court below. The lower appellate court found that the balance consideration amount was deposited beyond the period of statutory limitation as contemplated under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the pre-emption case was liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation. The petitioner has challenged the aforesaid order of the lower appellate court in this Rule under disposal.

3. The only question for determination is whether the balance amount of consideration money has been deposited by the petitioner beyond 4 months from the date of the transfer of the pre-empted land and, if so, whether the petitioner was entitled to the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act in view of the provision of section 151 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>4. The land in question was transferred by a deed of conveyance executed on 8th April, 1974 and it was presented for registration on the aforesaid date before the appropriate sub-registry at Dacca. The pre-emption case was filed within one month from the date of the execution of the deed of conveyance in May, 1974 before the Second Munsif of Dacca. It is an admitted fact that during the pendency of the pre-emption case before the Second Munsif of Dacca the registration of the deed of conveyance was completed under section 60 of Registration Act and pursuant to section 47 of the Registration Act it took effect from the date of execution of the deed i.e. from 8th April, 1974. On 26th June, 1979 the Second Munsif of Dacca having proceeded to determine the final amount to be deposited by the petitioner found that the consideration amount in question would be Taka 4,323/- which was beyond the jurisdiction of the Second Munsif of Dacca and consequently the application of pre-emption case was returned to the petitioner who duly filed the same before the First Munsif of Dacca having pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the case on 15th July, 1976 and also deposited the balance consideration money of Taka 2,323/- in addition to Taka 2,000/- already deposited earlier. It appears that upto 26th June, 1972 the petitioner was pursuing the pre-emption case before a wrong forum which lacked the appropriate pecuniary jurisdiction. The question is whether time from the date of the filing of the pre-emption case in May, 1974 before the Second Munsif of Dacca till the returning of the application on 26th June, 1976 would be computed and excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act read with section 151(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In this connection it may be observed that if section 14 of Limitation Act is made applicable in the present case and if the entire period of the pre-emption case remaining pending before the Second Munsif of Dacca is taken into consideration for the purpose of exclusion from the period of limitation in that event the deposit of balance consideration money on 15th, July, 1976 is well within the statutory period of 4 months from the date of the transfer of the land under pre-emption. Coming into the application of section 14 of the Limitation Act in a pre-emption case reference may be made to section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Sub-section (1) of Section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act says that excepting sections 6, 7, 8, 9 & 29 of the Limitation Act the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall apply to all suits, appeals and applications arising under part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Admittedly section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act being in Chapter XIII is included within Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In such circumstances, it is quite clear that section 14 of the Limitation Act is applicable to an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Sub-section (2) of section 151 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act however has stated that all suits, appeals and applications referred to in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall be instituted within the time prescribed therein and any such suit, appeal and application made after prescribed period of limitation shall be dismissed. This provision merely reiterates the application of such limitation in such Act without any reference to the period of limitation provided in the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>5. This provision of sub-section (2) of Section 151 shall however be read subject to sub-section (1) of section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein section 14 of Limitation Act is made applicable to an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So far as the section 14 of Limitation Act is concerned once it has been found that a party was delinquently pursuing a matter before another court such period shall be computed and excluded from the period of limitation. Thus, it is quite clear that the period when the pre-emption case remains pending before the Second Munsif of Dacca till the order returning the application for filing before another court with appropriate pecuniary jurisdiction shall be excluded for the purpose of computing the period of limitation under section 14 of the Limitation Act. That being done evidently the deposit of the balance consideration money made before the First Munsif of Dacca on the date of the filing of the application for pre-emption on 15th July, 1976 was done within 4 months from the date of the transfer of the impugned land claimed under pre-emption. In such circumstances deposit made can not be held to have been done beyond the period of limitation and the pre-emption application can not be dismissed on that account and consequently the order of the Second Munsif of Dacca made on 26.6.76 by order No. 27 in Miscellaneous Case No. 114 of 1974 returning the application for pre-emption can not be said to be not in according with law.</u>

6. Be that as it may. for the foregoing reasons the decision of the 5th Subordinate Judge of Dacca made on the June, 1979 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 369 of 1976 must be held to have suffered from error of law and is accordingly set aside. The First Munsif of Dacca is directed to proceed with the hearing of miscellaneous Case No. 157 of 1976 in accordance with law and dispose it of as expeditiously as possible. This Rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Abdur Rouf -----for petitioners.
Syed J.R. Modassir Hossain, A.A.G. -----for respondents.
parties:
Shahar Ali alias Safar Ali and others ----- Petitioners.
Vs. 
A.R. Chowdhury, Sessions Judge, Mymensingh, as the Special Tribunal and another ----- Respondents.
case_source: In the Matter of an Application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
Syed Muhammad Husain, J.— This Rule arising out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, is directed against a criminal proceeding by way of a prosecution and trial of the petitioners before a Tribunal under the Special Powers Act (No. XIV of 1974) The Petitioners have challenged such proceeding, prosecution and trial mainly on the ground that a criminal prosecution and trial before a Tribunal under the Special Powers Act is violative of Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh.

2. Before proceeding with this case reference may be made to Article 7 of the Constitution of Bangladesh regarding the supremacy of the Constitution. Under Sub-Article (2) of Article 7, the Constitution is the supreme law, and if any other law is inconsistent with the Constitution, that other law shah be void, in order to ascertain and decide the constitutionality of the proceeding, prosecution and trial under the Special Powers Act, it is necessary to find out me correct position of the Judiciary under the Constitution of Bangladesh. The Constitution of Bangladesh as adopted and amended from time to time, is primarily based upon the age old theory of separation of powers. Article 22, of the Constitution has mandated the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive organs of the State. Upon such theory of separation of powers, the Constitution has provided for three separate but consecutive parts for the establishment of three distinct organs of the Government. Part IV of the Constitution has laid down the provisions with regard to the Executive Branch of the Government headed by the President, whereas Part V of the Constitution has laid down the provision for the Legislature headed by the Parliament, it has been immediately followed by Part VI of the Constitution laying down the provision with regard to the Judiciary headed by the Supreme Court. The provisions for the exercise of the judicial powers of the state have been provided in three Chapters in Part VI of the Constitution between Articles 94-117 thereof. In Chapter X of Part VI of the Constitution, detail provisions have been made with regard to the Supreme Court comprising of the Appellate Division and the High Court Division. Under Article 101 of the Constitution, the High Court Division shall have such original, appellate and other jurisdictions, powers and functions as or may be conferred on it by the Constitution or any law. Under sub-article 1 of Article 103 of the Constitution, the Appellate Division shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from judgments and orders of the High Court Division. So far as Courts other than the Supreme Court are concerned, provisions thereof have been made in Chapter 11 of Part VI of the Constitution.

<u>3. Article 114 of the Constitution says, "There shall be, in addition to the Supreme Court, such courts subordinate thereto as may be established by law". It clearly appears from the aforesaid provision that the Constitution has permitted the establishment of other Courts, other than Supreme Court, but subordinate to the Supreme Court. Article 114 of the Constitutions makes all Courts established by law subordinate to the Supreme Court ; in other words, no Court can validly exist which is not subordinate to the Supreme Court. This proposition based upon the clear mandatory provision of Article 114 of the Constitution as mentioned therein before fits with the very scheme of the Constitution based upon the principle of separation of powers" wherein the judicial powers shall be exercised through various Courts headed by the Supreme Court. Thus it is quite clear that according to the aforesaid constitutional position the judiciary shall function with the Supreme Court as its apex and all other Courts shall be subordinate to Supreme Court. Thus assuming that all Courts established by law remain subordinate to the Supreme Court, the necessary consequence is that the Supreme Court in its turn shall have superintendence and control over all such Courts subordinate thereto. This is quite evident from the provision of Article 109 of the Constitution which says that "the High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all courts subordinate to it". In such circumstances Article 114 of the Constitution must be read along with Article 109 of the Constitution, in order to finally determine the position of all courts visa the Supreme Court. Considering the aforesaid provision of Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution, it is clearly evident that all Courts established by law shall remain subordinate to the Supreme Courts and the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in its turn shall have superintendence and control over all other Courts subordinate thereto. Consequently considering the various provisions of Chapters 1 and 11 of Part VI of the Constitution with particular reference to Article 109 and Article 114 thereof, it must be held that the Constitution does not provide for the establishment of any Court under any law which is not subordinate to the Supreme Court, where the High Court Division thereof shall have no superintendence and control over such Courts. Any attempt to establish any Court under any law refusing its subordination to the Supreme Court and thereby avoiding the superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court over such Courts is in direct conflict with the scheme of the Constitution and is violative of the mandatory provision of the Constitution under Article 114 read with Article 109 thereof and thereby becomes ultra vires of the Constitution.</u>

4. In this connection it may be observed that any provision similar to Article 114 of the Constitution of Bangladesh did not find its place either in Government of India Act, 1915 and 1935 or in the Constitution of Pakistan 1956 and 1962. Even in the Constitution of India there is no provision that all Courts established under the law shall be Subordinate to the High Courts as such. This omission has however been mitigated to a great extent by the provisions of Article 136 and Article 227 of the Constitution of India as it existed prior to 42nd Amendment in 1976. Under Article 127(1) of the Indian Constitution as it, existed prior to 42nd Amendment in 1976 the High Courts could exercise their superintending authority over all Courts and Tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction irrespective of the fact whether such Courts and Tribunals were subordinate to the High Courts as such. Under Article 136(1) of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court can grant special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any Court or Tribunal in India. A similar provision was incorporated in the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956 in Article 190 thereof, where under the Supreme Court could grant special leave to appeal from any judgment and order of any Court or Tribunal in Pakistan irrespective of the fact whether such Court or Tribunal were subordinate to the Supreme Court or the High Courts concerned. Considering the aforesaid position it must be held that the provision of Article 114 of the Constitution of Bangladesh is unique in the sense that it makes all Courts established under the law subordinate to the Supreme Court and thereby bringing it within the superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 109 of the said Constitution.

<u>5. The next question is whether Tribunals under the Special Powers Act can be considered to be Courts as contemplated under the Constitution. In Article 152 (1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh a Court has been said to mean any "Court of law" including the Supreme Court, meaning thereby that Court is a Court of law as such. Although in the Code of Criminal Procedure 'Court' as such has not been specifically defined in section 4 thereof, various classes of Criminal Courts have been provided in section 6 of the said Code. It has been provided in section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that besides the High Court and the Courts constituted under any law for the purpose of this Code, there shall be various classes of criminal courts being courts of Session and Magistracy Courts of Session include Courts of Additional and Assistant Judges and Courts of Magistrates include Court of 1st class, 2nd class and 3rd class Magistrates. Considering the provisions of Section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with the definition of Court Article 152 (1) of the Constitution apart from the Supreme Court and the High Court, Court of Sessions and Magistracy as such are Criminal Courts. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of section 26 (2) of the Special Powers Act wherein every. Session, Additional Session and Assistant Session Judge as such within the Sessions Division shall be a Special Tribunal for the purpose of original trial of offences under the Special Powers Act. By a recent amendment a first class Magistrate can be designated as an Additional Special Tribunal for the purpose of original trial of offences under the Special Powers Act. Thus it appears that it is only such Criminal Courts as have been classified in Section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which have been made Special Tribunal or Additional Special Tribunal for the purpose of original trial of offences under the Special Powers Act. In this connection reference may also be made to Section 29 of the Special Powers Act wherein the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure have been made applicable to the proceedings before the Special Tribunals subject to the provisions of Special Powers Act; such Tribunals have been vested with all the powers conferred by the Code of Criminal Procedure on Courts of Session exercising original jurisdiction. Considering the foregoing provisions of sections 26 and 29 of the Special Powers Act, it clearly appears that Special Tribunals or Additional Special Tribunals constituted thereunder are for all purposes criminal Courts classified in section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, exercising all the powers conferred on it by the Code of Criminal Procedure, but subject to the specific provisions of the Special Powers Act. In such circumstances it becomes unmistakably clear that a Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act is net only a Criminal Court as classified under section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but is also a Court meaning a Court of law as defined in Article 152 (1) of the Constitution such definition being applicable to the reference of Court made in Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution. In that view a Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act is purely a judicial tribunal exclusively exercising the functions of a court of law and constituting a Court within the meaning of a Supreme Court subordinate to the Supreme Court as contemplated under Article 114 of the Constitution whereupon the High Court Division of the Supreme Court shall have superintendence and control as contemplated under Article 114 of the Constitution. This is all the more so, because the Court of Session and first class Magistracy having constituted the Special Tribunals and Additional Special Tribunals are already under the superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court being subordinate thereto, both under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Constitution. In this connection reference may be made to the earlier version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act where under an appeal from the judgment of a Special Tribunal used to lie to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court thereby making the Special Tribunals subordinate to the Supreme Court, subjecting itself to the superintendence and control of the High Court Division thereof.</u>

6. Subsequently, however, the earlier version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act has been specifically and drastically amended and under the amended version, for the purpose of the appeals from the judgment of Special Tribunal, an Appellate Tribunal has been constituted. For purpose of deciding the constitutionality of a proceeding, prosecution and trial under the Special Powers Act, at present it is necessary to examine the frame work of the amended version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act which runs as follows:

"30. APPEALS AND CONFIRMATION OF DEATH SENTENCES.—

(1) An appeal from the judgment of, or sentence passed by, Special Tribunal may be preferred to the Appellate Tribunal. constituted under sub-section (2) within thirty days of the delivery or passing thereof, but save as aforesaid there shall be no appeal from any order, judgment or sentence of a Special Tribunal and no Court shall have authority to revise such order, judgment or sentence.

(2) The Government shall, for the purpose of this Act, constitute an Appellate Tribunal consisting of one member to be appointed by the Government.

(3) The member of the Appellate Tribunal shall be a person who is, or is qualified to be appointed as, a judge of the Supreme Court.

(4) The Appellate Tribunal may, on appeal, confirm, set aside, enhance, vary or modify any judgment of, or sentence passed by, a Special Tribunal including a direction under section 344, (3)and the decision of the Appellate Tribunal in an appeal shall be final.

(5) The Appellate Tribunal shall, for the purpose of hearing an appeal under this Act, have the same powers and follow, as nearly as possible, the same procedure as are vested in and followed by the High Court Division under the Code.

(6) Where a Special Tribunal passes a sentence of death, the proceedings shall be submitted forthwith to the Appellate Tribunal and the sentence shall not be executed unless it is confirmed by the Appellate Tribunal."

<u>7. While Analysing the provisions of the amended version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act, reference may be made to the concluding provision of sub-section (1) thereof to the effect that no Court shall have authority to revise any such judgment, order or sentence of the Appellate Tribunal. Under sub-section (2) of section 30 the Government is required to constitute an Appellate Tribunal. Under sub-section (3) a member of the Appellate Tribunal is required to be a person who is or is qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court. Under sub-section (4) of section 30 of the Special Powers Act, it has been further provided that the decision of the Appellate Tribunal shall be final. In sub-section (5) of Section 30, it has been provided that the Appellate Tribunal shall have the same powers and follow the same procedures as are vested in and followed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the concluding provision of sub-section (6), the Appellate Tribunal has been vested with the power to confirm a sentence of death passed by a Special Tribunal. Considering the aforesaid provisions of the amended version of Section 30 of the Special Powers Act in the context of its earlier version, it clearly appears that while in the earlier version, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court was the direct Appellate Court over a Special. Tribunal, whereas in the amended version the High Court Division has been substituted by an Appellate Tribunal constituted by a person who is or can be a judge of the Supreme Court, exercising all the powers and functions and following the same procedure as that of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure, but keeping such Court outside the purview and pale of the Supreme Court as such. Any judgment or sentence of the Appellate Tribunal shall not only be final but no Court including the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court shall have any such normal power to revise any appellate judgment and sentence even when it involves the confirmation of a death sentence. This is an unprecedented innovation in the history of common law countries. There is no Commonwealth country where a sentence of death has been normally kept out of the scrutiny by the highest constitutional court of the country. This was evidently an attempt not only to exude the supervisory and superintending jurisdiction of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court but at the same time it was also an attempt to create a Court parallel to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court outside the pale and purview of the Supreme Court as such because of the fact that even under Article 103 (4) of the Constitution, the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has no jurisdiction over any judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal which is for all practical purpose exercising the function of the High Court Division in that regard. This attempt to establish a purely judicial Tribunal exclusively exercising the functions of a Court of law in its criminal jurisdiction outside the purview and pale of the Supreme Court is clearly in conflict with and violative of Article 114 of the Constitution and thereby negativing the inherent supervisory and superintending jurisdiction of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 109 of the Constitution, In such circumstances the attempt of the Legislature establish an Appellate Tribunal under the amended version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act independent of the Supreme Court of either Division must be held to be ultra vires of the Constitution.</u>

<u>8. Since it has already been observed that no Court of law including a judicial tribunal exercising the functions of a Court of law can be established by law, which is not other wise sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court and which is not otherwise subject to the superintendence and control of High Court Division of the Supreme Court as contemplated under Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution, the Appellate Tribunal constituted under amended version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act must be amended to be a Court sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court and subject to the superintendence and control of the High Court Division thereof, otherwise the very existence of such judicial tribunal exercising the functions of a Court of law is negatived and straightaway goes out of statute books, being hit by Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution. Under Article 101 of the Constitution, the High Court Division shall have such original, appellate and other jurisdictions, powers, and functions as may be conferred on it by any law. The Legislature thus has the power to create and establish a separate exclusive Appellate Court to hear appeals from the Trial Court as such, thereby taking away the appellate jurisdictions, powers and functions of the High Court Division. The appellate jurisdictions, powers and functions of the High Court Division have been created by law and such jurisdictions, powers and functions can be taken away by law by vesting such jurisdictions, powers and functions to some other Courts created and established by law. But such Appellate Court must be made sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court subject to the superintendence and control of the High Court Division thereof as contemplated under Article 114 read with Article 109 of the Constitution. In this connection it may be mentioned that such Appellate Court may be called an Appellate Tribunal but such judicial tribunal purely and exclusively exercising the functions and powers of a Court of law does not cease to remain as a Court simply because of its description as a Tribunal. With reference to Court, Tribunal is a generic expression; all Tribunals are not Courts, but all Courts are Tribunals. A tribunal having all the trappings of a Court for all purposes is a Court within the meaning thereof under Article 152(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Considering the aforesaid position, it must be held that the Appellate Tribunal under the amended version of section 30 of the Special Powers Act being purely a judicial tribunal exclusively exercising the functions of a Court of law in its appellate jurisdiction under the Code of Criminal Procedure, is a Court sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court under Article 114 of the Constitution and is subject to the superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 109 of the Constitution, that being so, any party aggrieved by any judgment of order or sentence of the appellate tribunal may move the High Court Division of the Supreme Court with a prayer to exercise its superintendence and control over such Appellate Tribunal by interfering with the judgment, order and sentence thereof under Article 109 of the Constitution, which is quite separate, distinct and independent from the extra-ordinary prerogative jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 109 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>9. The question that comes up for consideration consequently is, the exact nature of the jurisdictions, powers and functions of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court relating to superintendence and control over Courts sub-ordinate thereto as contemplated under Article 109 of the Constitution are both Judicial and Administrative in nature or only Administrative as such excluding the Judicial one. In this connection it may be mentioned that Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh substantially corresponds to Article 102 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962, Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 and Section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915. This power of superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Courts sub-ordinate thereto as contemplated under Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh is almost similar in nature to the preceding provisions of Article 102 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962, Article 227(2) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 and section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915. In Article 227(5) of the Constitution of India as per 42nd amendment of 1976 following the provision of section 224(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, the High Courts have been debarred from questioning any judgment of any court sub-ordinate thereto under the said provision.</u>

<u>This specific exclusion of the powers of the High Courts to make any judicial interference with any judgment of any Court sub-ordinate thereto under Article 227(5) of the Constitution of India as per 42nd amendment of 1976 following the provision of section 224(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, made the powers of the High Courts under Article 102 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962, Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976and section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 to have superintendence over all Courts sub-ordinate thereto as of both Administrative and Judicial in nature. Article 227(5) of the India constitution as per 42nd amendment of 1976 following section 224(2) of the Government of India act. 1935 having made an exception to the powers of Judicial superintendence of the High Courts with regard to Courts sub-ordinate thereto, the aforesaid provision of general superintendence and control by the High Court's over Courts sub-ordinate thereto under Article 102 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962, Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 and Section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 have been held to be both Administrative and Judicial in nature. In such circumstances it clearly appears that under Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the power conferred on the High Court Division of the Supreme Court to have general superintendence and control over all courts sub-ordinate thereto, inevitably includes judicial superintendence and control. In that view of the matter, any party aggrieved by any judgment, or order or sentence of any Court of law or a judicial tribunal exercising the function of a Court of law including an Appellate Tribunal under the Special Powers Act may apply before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court for a judicial interference with regard to such judgment, order or sentence of the Appellate Tribunal under the superintending power of the High Court Division under Article 109 of the Constitution as used to be done Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd Amendment of 1976. This is quite separate, distinct and in-dependent from the extraordinary prerogative jurisdiction of the High Court division under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>10. Having accepted such power of the High Court Division to make a Judicial Interference with any judgment, order or sentence of the Appellate Tribunal Constituted under the Special Powers act, the question now arises as to what is the exact nature and limitation of such jurisdiction by way of a judicial interference by the High Court Division under its supervisory and superintending authority over Courts sub-ordinate thereto under Article 109 of the Constitution. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 where the High Courts were vested with the powers of superintendence over all Courts and Tribunals throughout the territory in relation to which the High Court's concerned exercised its jurisdiction. The main distinction between the provision of Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and the erstwhile Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment 1976 is that whereas under Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh the supervisory and superintending authority of the High Court Division extend to the Courts sub-ordinate thereto, whereas under erstwhile 227(1) of the Indian Constitution prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 the superintending jurisdiction of the High Courts extended over all Courts and Tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction irrespective of the fact whether such Courts and Tribunals were sub-ordinate to the High Courts concerned. This difference between the two provisions in the Bangladesh and Indian Constitutions as before has been further narrowed down in view of the fact that Bangladesh Constitution as per Article 114 thereof does not contemplate the establishment of any Court of law including any judicial tribunal exercising the function of a court of law which is not otherwise sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court. Erstwhile Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 came up for consideration before the various High Courts and Supreme Court in India to determine its scope and authority with relation to the power of the High Courts to make judicial interference with any judgment or order of any other court as such. The extent and scope of the judicial superintendence of the High Court over other courts came for consideration in various High Courts and Supreme Courts in India and the consensus view on such question appears to be that where there is a patent absence or excess erroneous assumption of jurisdiction and grave error of law apparent on the face of the record, such power of the High Court is to be exercised most sparingly in appropriate cases only in order to keep the courts concerned within the limits of their authority under the law. The power of judicial superintendence of the High Courts over the Courts below by its nature is a revisional one short of an appeal; it is not intended to correct any and every mistake of law but only such grave error of law which causes miscarriage of justice as such. Taking into consideration the views of the Indian Supreme Court from time to time with regard to the power of the High Court to make judicial interference with any judgment and order of the Courts below under erstwhile Article 227 (1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976, it can safely be said that Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh has conferred upon the High Court Division of the Supreme Court such superintending authority over the courts below where under the High Court Division can make judicial interference with any judgment and order of any other Court of law including a judicial tribunal exercising the functions of a court of law, such as the Appellate Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, by way of a revision short of an appeal to rectify any patent absence or excess or erroneous assumption of jurisdiction, or any grave error of Jaw apparent on the face of the record which might cause serious miscarriage of justice. The High Court Division in exercising such jurisdiction as contemplated under Article 109 of the Constitution may refer to the inherent residuary revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division short of its appellate powers under the normal procedural law, and even without such reference can also directly resort to the jurisdiction conferred upon it under Article 109 of the Constitution, as a distinct forum for a separate proceeding thereunder, being quite separate, distinct and independent from the extraordinary prerogative jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>11. In view of the aforesaid constitutional position of the Supreme Court and its High Court Division with regard to its authority over other Courts established by other law including any judicial tribunal exercising the function of a court of law like the Appellate Tribunal under the Special Powers Act and considering the implications of Article 114 along with Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, it must be held that the prosecution and trial of the petitioner under the Special Powers Act can proceed before a Special Tribunal or an Additional Special Tribunal and therefrom also before the Appellate Tribunal, but any judgment, order or sentence of any such Appellate Tribunal shall be subject to a revision short of an appeal under the normal procedural law before the High Court Division and in any event even directly under Article 109 read with Article 114 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, being quite separate; distinct and independent from the extraordinary prerogative jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. While arriving at the aforesaid decision reference has been made to various decisions of the Supreme Court of India reported in A.I.R. 1954 ( SC) 215, A.I.R. 1958 (SC) 398, A.I.R. 1961 (SC) 222, A.I.R. 1975 (SC) 1297 and also to a decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 32 DLR (AD) 1, with the aforesaid observation this Rule is accordingly disposed of without any order as to costs.</u>

12. Since this case involves substantial question of law as to the interpretation of Article 109 and Article 114 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, a certificate for leave to appeal before the Appellate Division is granted under Article 103 (2)(a) of She Constitution of Bangladesh.

Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the Secretary in the Ministry of Law of the Government of Bangladesh.

End.
