parties:
Ashutosh Mali & ors ------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Shamsunnahar & ors ------- Opp. Parties.
full_judgment:
This rule at the Instance of the pre-emptee is directed against the Judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Noakhali dated 8.6.79 in Misc. Appeal No. 78 1978 affirming those passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court Lakshmipur in Misc. Case No. 79 of 1966 and arises out of an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The opposite parties Nos. 1 to 11 who were pre-emptors filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the disputed land detailed in the schedule, by the original pre-emptee who was the father of the petitioners Nos. 1 and 4 here on obtaining a decree for Specific Performance of Control by a kabala dated 18.1.63 registered on 13.3.66.

2. The pre-emptors case was to the effect that they were co-sharers with regard to the disputed holding by prior purchase and came to know of the sale only for the first time on 3.4.66. They after taking certified copy of the kabala came to know of the sale definitely and thereafter depositing the consideration money along wish the statutory compensation filed the application for pre-emption on 16.5.66. They further contended that the opposite party No. 1 was a stranger to the holding. The application for pre-emption was contested by opposite parties Nos. 1 to 3 and 11 who contended, inter alit, that the petition was not maintainable in its present form and was barred by limitation and the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and was bad for defect of parties. They also denied the allegation and statements made in the application. They, however, claimed, that they too are co-sharers In the case holding and in case Pie petition for pre-emption is allowed, they are also entitled to rateable pre-emption according to their shares.

3. The learned Munsif on consideration of the facts, circumstances and evidence on record found that the opposite party No 2 did not press for pre-emption at the time of the trial; opposite party No. 11 to the application was not a co-sharer in the disputed holding and the petition for rateable pre-emption by the opposite party No. 1 was barred by limitation. As such he allowed the pre-emptors application for pre-emption. Against the said judgment and order of the learned Munsif the heirs of the opposite party No. 1 before the learned Munsif and the opposite party No. 11 filed an appeal before the Court of appeal below. The learned District Judge on consideration of the facts, circumstances and evidence on record upheld the judgment and order of the learned Monsif and dismissed the appeal preferred by the pre-emptee opposite parties. He also held that notices of the pre-emption proceeding were properly served upon the opposite parties and that the petition for rateable pre-emption by opp. party Nos. 1, 2 & 3 was barred by limitation as they put forward their claim beyond two months from the date of service of notice of pre-emption case. He also found that the opposite party No. 11 did not acquire any interest in the disputed holding and was not a co-sharer with respect to the said holding. A ground was taken before the Court of appeal below that the Misc. Case abated on the ground of non-pleading of the heirs of the opposite party No. 2 but the learned District Judge found that the opposite party No. 11 was the only son and heir of the opposite party No. 2 and as such the question of substitution did not arise. Moreover the claim for rateable pre-emption filed by the opposite party No 2 before the learned Munsif was barred by limitation and he was therefore not entitled to get any rateable pre-emption. In that view of the matter he found that the application for pre-emption did not suffer from any defect and that she learned Munsif has rightly allowed the application for pre-emption. As against the said order of pre-emption the petitioners who were the heirs of pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 before the learned Munsif have obtained the present rule.

4. Mr. M.H. Khondker with Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury and Mr. M.L. Bhowmic the learned Advocates appeared for the pre-emptee petitioners and Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. Mahbubey Alam the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the pre-emption opposite parties.

5. Mr M. H Khondker, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued only one ground which he formulated to the following effect:

“For that the land in question being a part of a tenure (Sikkimi Maddya Satia) there was no right of pre-emption in respect thereof under the Bengal Tenancy Act and the transfer is dispute based on the agreement to sell dated 24 5 57 which was the date of transfer on the passing of the decree for specific performance of the contract for sale on 2. 1962 (though the kabala executed by the learned Munsif on 18.1.1963 was registered on 18.3.66) there did not arise any right of pre emption under section 96(1) of E.B. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1951, which was applied to the area by enforcing Part V of the said Act on 1.8.1963. So, the case was governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act and not the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the learned Courts below exercised Jurisdiction not vested in them by law in allowing the application for pre-emption as the land of a holding of a raiyat".

In elaborating his arguments Mr. Khondker submits that in vie v of the decree passed in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, It will date back to the date of agreement since this transfer in dispute was based on an agreement to sell dated 24.5.57 and on that date the right of pre-emption under section 96 was not available. As such the case was governed by e. 2e (F) of the Bengal Tenancy Act.

He further submits that Part V of the State Acquisition Act came into force in the area on 1.8 63 and only on that date of coming Into force or this part, there shall be within that area only one class of agricultural tenant. Before that the Bengal Tenancy Act was in force and section 26 (F) B.T. Act did not apply to the class of holders of tenure, called "Sikkiml Maddya Satta tenure".

<u>6. Mr. Khondker Mahbabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, on the other hand, submits that the right of pre-emption accrued from the date of registration r f the document and after its registration, it will take effect from the date of execution. He submits that the contract was dated 24.5.57 but since the specific performance was not effected a suit was brought by the opposite party No. 1 before the learned Munsif which was decreed on 7.2.62. Pursuant to the decree the Court executed the kabala for sale on 18.1.61 and the same was registered on 18.3 66. So on the date when the kabala was executed i.e. on 18.1.63 Part V of the Sate Acquisition Act came into force in the area In which the case land is situate and by the time, which the kabala was executed, the provisions of 26(F) B T. Act lost i's force and the matter was governed by section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. He further submits that the right of pre-emption accrued only on registration of the document and not earlier. Here the date of registration was 18.3.66 and on that date the Bengal Tenancy Act was not in existence and there was no existence of Sikkim, Maddya Satta. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, last paragraph, is to the following effect:</u>

<u>“A contract for the sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties. It does not of itself, create any interest in or charge on such properties."</u>

<u>So a property can be transferred only by a conveyance and not by mere agreement between the parties. A contract for sale by itself does not create any interest or charge in the property. Law requires a conveyance for the purpose of transfer of title and this cannot be made by agreement. Of course, under the English Law, a purchaser, by virtue of contract of sale, becomes complete owner of the property from the date of contract but that principle of English Law has no application to a place where toe Transfer of Property Act is in force. In that view of the matter the contention of the learned Advocate of the pre-emptee petitioners that the transfer dates back to the date of agreement for sale cannot be accepted. Mr. Khondker in support of his arguments relied upon a decision reported In 16 D.L.R. (SC) page 706 but that case was with regard the put performance of contract. The facts and circumstances of that 16 D.L R. (SC) 706 case are completely different from the facts and circumstances of the present case and has no application here. In that case a suit for specific performance of contract was decreed on 3.11.51 and an appeal was preferred to the High Court against the decree which was dismissed on 6.2.58. The contract was entered into on 30.9 47 and some consideration passed. On 13.12.58 a portion of the land was compulsorily acquired by the Government and compensation for the acquired laud was assessed. The decree-holder applied for amendment of the decree for the purpose of getting the kabala in respect of the compensation money awarded by the Government and the Court accordingly directed that the defendant shall execute the kabala in respect of the award money as fixed by the Government On appeal a point was taken that the contract has become frustrated in respect of the land which was compulsorily acquired by the Government and could not be enforced to that extent. There it was held that in view of sections 12 & 14 of the Specific Relief Act there was no question of frustration of the contract, and it being clear that at least after the making of the decree, the land vested in the purchaser which tad already gone into his possession, the right to the compensation money for the land. lost by reasons of the acquisition by the Government, clearly vested in the purchaser who shall have exclusive claim to the compensation money. But here in the present case the contract as stated earlier was dated 4.5.57 and the decree was dated 7.2.62 and the date of execution of the kabala was dated 18.1.63. So the kabala being executed on 18.1.63 and the registration being completed on 18.3.63 the right to transfer accrued from the date of registration of the kabala dated 18.3.63 and that would be the date for determining the status of class of tenancy. In case of transfer, the Dalton which the transfer takes effect is the date of instrument and not the date of registration but in case of pre-emption the date of registration gives rise to the accrual of the right of pre-emption (17 D.L.R.(Dacca) 365 and 21 D. L. R. 599). So, in that view of the matter, right of pre-emption hiving accrued on 18.1.63 the contention of Mr. H. M. Khondker the learned advocate that the tenancy was governed by the provision of section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the nature of the Tenancy being Sikkimi Maddya Satta was not liable to pre-emption his no force. Registration of document having been completed in 1968, the tenancy would be governed by the law applicable at that time. By that time Part V of the State Acquisition Act has come into force and there existed only one class of holders of agricultural land. The tenancy was therefore governed by the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and section 96 was applicable to the facts and circumstances of the oats. No other point has been urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

<u>In the result, the rule is discharged. In the facts and circumstances of the case, however, there will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.

caseno:
Writ Petition No. 189 of 1976.
In the matter of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
lawyer:
S. R. Pail with S.C Das & Zakir Ahmed  -----For the Petitioner. 
Syed J. R. Mudadsir Hossain -----For Respondents No. 1 & 2.
parties:
Srimongal Pourashava ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms & others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
S. M. Husain, .J.—This Rule arising out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against a decision of the Government to take over possession of all hats and bazars within the jurisdiction of Srimongal Pourashava with effect from 5th February, 1976.

2. Srimongal Pourashava was constituted under Assam Municipal Act of 1923, Thereafter the said Municipality came within the purview of the Municipal Administration Ordinance of 1960 and finally under the Pourashava Ordinance of 1977. Under Clause (e) of sub-section (1) of section 55 of the Assam Municipal Act of 1923, all markets, slaughter houses and public buildings of every description which have been constructed andiron maintained out of the Municipal fund are the properties of the Municipality. Under section 63 of the Municipal Administration Ordinance, 1960 a Municipal Committee may establish and maintain public markets or may provide places for use as public markets. Under section 64 of the said Municipal Ordinance private markets can only be established under a licence granted by the Municipal Committee and in conformity with the conditions in such licence. Sections 84 and 85 of the Pourashava Ordinance of 1977 provide for similar provisions as mentioned in sections 63 and 64 of the Municipal Administration Ordinance of 1960. From the aforesaid provisions of law it is quite clear that a Municipality can own, hold and establish any market within its area.

<u>3. In this connection reference may be made to the provisions of Hats and Bazars (Establishment) and Acquisition Ordinance 1959 (Ordinance No XIX of 1959). Sub-section (1) of section 2 of the said Ordinance provides that no person shall establish any hats and bazars except without a license for that purpose from the Collector in such form as may be prescribed by rules. Sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Ordinance provides that any hats and bazars established in contravention of the aforesaid provisions shall be forfeited to the Government. Hats and Bazars (Establishment) and Acquisition (Amendment) Act of 1966 (Act XII/67) had amended the provisions of section 2 of the aforesaid Ordinance No. XIX of 1959 where under at present no person shall establish any hats or bazars excepting the Government or any local authority with the approval of the Government The local authority means local-councils as defined in sub clause (24) of clause 1 of Article 3 of the Basic Democracy Ordinance of 1959 and subsequently it included a Municipal Committee under the Municipal Administration Ordinance 1960 followed by the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. Subsequently Bangladesh Government Hats and Bazars (Management) Order of 1972 (P.O. 73/72) was introduced providing for the management of all Government hats and bazars. P.O. No. 73 of 1972 stood repealed by Bangladesh Government Hats and bazars (Management Repeal) Ordinance 1975 (Ordinance No. 59 of 1975). Considering the aforesaid provisions of law it now appears that there is no special provisions for management of Government hats and Bazars but the Government has an absolute right to establish any hat and bazar. A local authority including a Municipality or Pourashava can also establish a hat and bazar with the prior approval of the Government. All the references made to the various provisions of law made herein-before are prospective in nature providing for powers of the Government and any local authority including a Pourashava to establish and to maintain any hat or bazar or a market as the case may be after the promulgation of the laws referred to hereinbefore. The aforesaid statutes are completely silent with regard to the powers of the Government to take over such hats and bazars and markets in possession of a local authority like a Pourashava. It appears that apart front the general provisions of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there is no other special statutory provisions authorising the Government to acquire and to take over any hat and bazar and market already remaining under the ownership and possession of a local authority and a Pourashava.</u>

<u>4. Under sub-section (1) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, on acquisition of the interests of rent-receiver in any area under Chapter V of the Act no rent receiver, cultivating raiyat, cultivating under raiyat or non-agricultural tenant shall be entitled to retain any khash land in such area except as provided in sub-section (2) thereof. By virtue of the provisions of section (2) (a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act any land or building in a hat or bazar have been excluded from the retainable khash land contemplated under sub-section (2) thereof. Now the question is whether any,land or building in a hat or bazar which inevitably includes a market as such can be retained by a local authority like a Pourashava. In the category of persons who are entitled to retain possession of any khash land under sub-section (1) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act a Municipality or Pourashava does not come within the definition of a rent-receiver or a cultivating raiyat or under raiyot as such. As to the non-agricultural tenant, it appears from the definition thereof from sub-section (17) of section 2 with reference to State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also with reference to the definition of tenant as provided in sub-section (27) of section 2 the said Act, it appears that the language used thereunder is "a tenant" meaning "a person". There is no statutory provision whereby a local authority like a Municipality or a Pourashava has been specifically omitted from being a person like a tenant under the Government Thee scheme of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which extends to the whole of Bangladesh, contemplates only 4 classes of persons who can own lands under the Government as aforesaid and there is no other class as such. In such circumstances a Pourashava for the purpose of owning and holding any land is a tenant under the Government. From the paltan of the Srimongal Pourashava relating to the markets in question it also appears that the Government has been shown. as the landlord and the Srimongal Municipality as aperson in possession thereof. Considering the aforesaid circumstances it must be held that the Government can acquire and take over any hat or bazar including a market since the lands thereunder are non-retainable by any tenant. But in the absence of any specific proceeding under Chapter V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, non-retainable hat or bazar or market of a Municipality or Pourashava is not liable to be acquired by the Government. Thus acquisition of any Municipal market by the Government can only proceed according to the provisions of Chapter V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act culminating in the final publication of the compensation Assessment roll under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Only after such publication the Government by a special order takes possession of any market belonging to any Pourashava. In this connection it may be mentioned that subject to the ultimate right of the Government to acquire and take over any Municipal market, a Municipality or a Pourashava can establish and run any market as provided under sections 84 and 85 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977.</u>

<u>5. Considering the aforesaid provisions of law the position is that a Pourashava can establish and maintain a new market under section 84 and 85 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977, with the permission of the Government as contemplated under Ordinance No. XIX of 1959 as amended by Act No. XII of 1967 With regard to such markets which existed before coming into force of the provisions of Ordinance No XIX of 1959 as amended by Act XII of 1967, the Government is not prevented from acquiring and taking over any such old markets under the provisions of sub-section 2 (a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But in any case to enable the Government to acquire and to take over any such Municipal market there must be an order to that effect after the final publication of the compensation assessment roll in the Official Gazette under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Be that as it may, admittedly in the present case there is nothing on record to show that there has been any final publication of the compensation assessment roll in the Official Gazette with regard to the areas in question under the Srimongal Pourashava and further admit only there is no order specifically acquiring the markets in question of the Srimongal Municipality as such. In that view of the matter it must be held that the decision of the Government to take over the markets in question of the Srimongal Municipality was done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. As such the decision of the Government as communicated to the petitioner by Annexures B and 1 to the petition am set aside. This rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

Sultan Hossain Khan J—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker, J:- This Rule was issued upon an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the petitioner who was elected Chairman of the Nalchity Upazila Parishad against the judgment and order dated 24.2.87 passed by the learned District Judge, Jhalakati in election Appeal Nos. 2 of 1986 and 3 of 1986 modifying the judgment and order dated 19.8.86 passed by the Election Tribunal and Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati in Election Case NO.2 of 1985. 

2. The petitioner and opposite party No.4 con- tested for the post of Chairman of the Nalchity Upazila Parishad in the election held on 20.5.85 and in the election the petitioner received in total 54,870 votes as against 8,749 votes received by the' opposite party No.4. The result of the said election was published in the official Gazette on 24.5.85 and the petitioner assumed the office of Chairman of said Upazila Parishad. 
3. After the publication of the result in the official Gazette on 24.5.85 the opposite party No.4 filed an Election Petition being Election Case No.2 of 1985 before the Election Tribunal and Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati on 22.6.85 praying for declaring the result of the election of Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad void as a whole on the allegations of corrupt and illegal practices adopted by the petitioner in the election. The petitioner appeared before the Election Tribunal on receipt of the follicle and submitted a written objection on 21.11.85 denying the allegations-made in the election petition and asserting that the election was held legally without any irregularities for which the election could not be declared as void. 

4. In the meantime there was an election to the Parliament in which the petitioner was elected a member" of the Parliament on 7.5.86 and the name of the petitioner was published by the Election Commissioner in the official Gazette dated 12.6.86 declaring the petitioner as a member of the Parliament. Since the petitioner was elected as a member of the Parliament he ceased to be a Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad in view of still-section (3) of section 6 of the Local Government Upazila Parishadand Upazila Administration Re-organisation) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. LIX of 1982) and the office of the said Upazila Parishad has become vacant with effect from 12.6.86 in view of the Gazette notification dated 21.6.86. 

5. The opposite party No.4 filed an application for amendment of the Election Petition on 7.7.85 praying for impleading the Returning Officer and the A.D.C, Jhalakati as opposite party in the election petition which was allowed by the Election Tribunal by the order of the same date. Thereafter the opposite party No.4 filed another application for amendment of the election petition praying for substituting the cause title of the election petition, adding a paragraph after paragraph 6 of the election petition and for substituting the relief of declaring the election of the returned candidate as void and declaring the opposite party No.4 as elected Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad in place of declaring the election void as a whole. Simultaneously with this application for amendment of the election petition the opposite party No.4 also filed an application on 4.6.86 praying for calling the election materials from Returning Officer. The application for calling the election materials however was not ultimately pressed. The Election Tribunal took up the application for amendment of the election petition on 19.6.86 and allowed the same directing to amend the original election petition. 
6. The election petition was taken up for hearing on 13.8.86 in the absence of the petitioner when 7 witnesses including the opposite party No.4 was examined and on. 14.8.86 another 8 witnesses were examined on behalf of the opposite party No.4 and certain papers were admitted into evidence and marked Exts. 1-6. After hearing the arguments the Election Tribunal adjourned the case to 19.8.86 for delivery of judgment. 

7. The Election Tribunal on consideration of the evidence of the witnesses found that out of 45 polling centres there were peaceful votes in 15 pol- ling center’s but in the other 30 polling centres the election was not held properly due to the illegal activities of the supporters of opposite party No.4. On consideration of the documentary evidence, namely, the F.I.R, the report of the Investigating Officer and the order dated 18.8.85 of the NalchityUpazila Magistrate in G.R. case No.24 of 1985, the Election Tribunal accepted the contention of the opposite party No.4 that the supporters of the petitioner hijacked a speed boat and illegally used the same by force and came to the conclusion that opposite party No.4 has proved his case beyond any dispute. Upon this finding the Election Tribunal declared the election of the returned candidate, the petitioner as void; but in consideration of the facts that the petitioner polled 54,870 votes as against 8,749 polled by opposite party No.4 and in view of the fact that according to the opposite party No.4 the election was held in a le- gal and peaceful manner in 15 polling centres out of 45 polling centres rejected the prayer of opposite party No.4 to declare him to be duly elected as a Chair- man of the said UpazilaParishad. 

8. Against the aforesaid judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal, opposite party No.4 filed Election Appeal No.2 of 1986 and the petitioner also filed Election Appeal No. 3 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Jhalakati. The learned District Judge after hearing both the parties dismissed Election Appeal No.3 of 1986 filed by the petitioner but allowed election Appeal No.2 of 1986 filed by opposite party No.4 by his judgment and order dated 24.2.87 upholding the order of the Election Tribunal as to the declaration that the election of the returned candidate is void and declared opposite party No.4 as duly elected Chairman of the said Upazila setting aside the order of the Election Tribunal in that respect. Hence this provisional application by the petitioner, the returned candidate.

9. Mr. Khandker Mahbub Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule has con- tended that the Election Tribunal has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in allowing the application for amendment of the election petition after the statutory period of limitation for the purpose of declaring the election of the petitioner void and the learned District Judge has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in declaring the opposite party No.4 as Chairman of the said UpazilaParishad in place of the petitioner inasmuch as by allowing the belated application for amendment of the election petition. The nature and character of the election petition has been materially changed. The learned Advocate secondly, contended that the Election Tribunal as well as the learned District Judge acted illegally and without jurisdiction in not dismissing the election petition for want of cause of action after the office of the Chairman of the said Upazila has been declared vacant by operation of law. 

10. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite party No.4, on the other hand, has contended that by the impugned amendment the nature and character of the election petition has not been changed but only the relief sought for was amended inasmuch as any relief can be granted which emanates from the pleadings and evidence led in the case. The learned Advocate further contended that notwithstanding the cessation of the office of the Chairman of the said Upazila by the petitioner due to his election as member of the Parliament the election case will continue and the learned District Judge legally held the opposite party No.4 to be elected as a Chairman of the said UpazilaParishad. 

11. As to the first contention of NIT. Khandker Mahbub Hossain, the learned Advocate that since the election petition is to be filed within 30 days next after the publication of the name of the returned candidate in the official gazette, the election petition was filed on 22.6.85 within 30 days from the gazette notification dated 24.5.85 but the application for amendment was filed long after the statutory period on 4.6.86 which completely changed the nature and character of the election dispute arid the relief prayed for and "as such the Election Tribunal acted illegally and without jurisdiction in allowing the application for amendment of the election petition. The learned Advocate has referred to the case of Hosne Zaman Sarker vs. Election Tribunal and others reported in B.C.R. 1986 (HC) 141 same as 38 D.L.R. 435 in support of his contention. 

12. Rule 44 sub-rule (1) of the Upazila Parishad (Election of Chairman) Rules, 1983 ( herein- after referred to as the said rules) provides that an election petition shall be presented to the Tribunal within thirty days next after the publication of the names of the returned candidate in official Gazette under rule 39. Surrule (5) of Rule 44 provides that an election petition shall set forth clearly the ground on which the petition is filed and the relief sought rule 45 of the said Rules provides that the petitioner in an election petition may claim either for a declaration that the election of the returned candidate is a void one and that the petitioner or some other person has been duly elected or for a declaration that the election as a whole is void. Rule 46 provides that every election petition shall be signed by the petitioner and verified in the manner provided for the verification of the plaints in the Code of Civil Procedure Rule 47 provides that every election shall be tried as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 48 provides that the Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure and shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

 13. It may be mentioned here that the application for amendment of the election petition was filed under Order 6, rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and by the said application opposite party No.4 prayed for amendment of the election petition in three places; (1) for adding a paragraph after paragraph No.6 of the election petition which is as follows:-
“১নং প্রতিপক্ষ জাল জালিয়াতি ও কারুচুপির মাধ্যমে বেআইনিভাবে নির্বাচিত উপজেলা চেয়াম্যান ঘোষিত হইয়াছেন। প্রকৃত পক্ষে সুষ্ঠ নির্বাচন হয় নাই। ১নং প্রতিপক্ষকে নির্বাচীত উপজেলা চেয়ারম্যান ও বেআইনী সাব্যস্ত করিয়া তদস্থলে দরখাস্তকারীকে নির্বাচীত উপজেলা চেয়ারম্যান ঘোষনা করা অবশ্যক। কারুচুপি ও জাল জালিয়াতীর আশ্রয় ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ গ্রহণ না করিলে অত্র দরখাস্তকারী অবশ্যই নির্বাচীত চেয়ারম্যান ঘোষিত হইতেন। নির্বাচন সংক্রান্ত ব্যালট কাগজ ও অন্যান্য কাগজপত্রাদি পরিক্ষা করিলে কারুচুপি ও জালজালিয়াতী ধরা পরিবে এবং ১নং প্রতিপক্ষকে নির্বাচিত ঘোষনা বাতিল ঘোষিত হইয়া তদস্থলে দরখাস্তকারী নির্বাচিত ঘোষিত হইবেন।”

(2) For declaring the election of the returned candidate as void and to declare the opposite party No.4 to be duly elected Chairman of the said Upazila in place of the original prayer for declaring the election void as a whole ; 

(3) and to amend the cause title by incorporating that the election of the petitioner As returned candidate of the Chairman of the said Upazila to be void and to declare opposite party No.4 to be elected as a Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad in place of the prayer to declare the election void as a whole. 

14. From a bare reading of the application for amendment it appears that not only the cause title has been changed and a completely new relief has been prayed for but also a new allegation as to fraud and corruption has been ascribed to the returned candidate and to ascertain the position sought for inspection of the ballot papers and other connected papers to find out fraud and corruption committed by the petitioner. By this amendment the opposite party No.4 prayed about a complete change in the nature and character of the election petition and also the relief prayed for.

 15. Although rule 47 of the said rules pro-vides that the election petition shall be tried as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure and rule 48 provides that the Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure and shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it is now well settled that the Election Tribunal is not a Civil Court constituted under the Civil Court Act. In that view of the matter the power of an Election Tribunal trying an election petition under section 23 of Ordinance No.LIX of 1982 is that of a statutory tribunal with limited jurisdictions. This view of ours is sup-ported by the case reported in (1986) 38 D.L.R. 435 referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Similar view has been taken by a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Sk. Tabibar Rahman Vs. Election Tribunal reported in 1981 B.L.D. 298. A similar view was also taken in the case of Management Board, A.R. Howlader Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Chairman, 1st Labour Court reported in (1976) 28 D.L.R. 368 in which it has been held that the Labour Court has the power as a statutory Tribunal of limited jurisdiction to allow an amendment of the pleadings. 

16. Thus although the Election Tribunal has the limited jurisdiction to allow amendment of the election petition, it has no power to allow any amendment, so as to relate hack to the date of filing of the election petition. It is so because sub-rule (1)of Rule 44 prescribed the limitation of 30 days next after the publication of the result in the official Gazette to file an election petition and sub-rule (5) specifically provides that an election petition shall set forth the ground on which the petition is fixed and the relief sought. In other words the ground for the election petition and the relief sought must be stated within the period of limitation. 

17. In the instant case by the amendment petition opposite party No.4 introduced fresh facts and prayed for different relief long after 30 days of the publication of the result of the election in the official gazette. As such the Election Tribunal has no authority to allow such amendment to give retrospective effect to the election petition long after the period of limitation prescribed by rule 44 of the said rules. Both the decisions reported in 38 D.L.R. 435 and 1981 B.L.D. 298 supports this view of our". Hence ware of the view that the Election Tribunal has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in allowing the application for amendment of the election petition. As such the declaration by the Election Tribunal as well as by the learned District Judge that the election of the petitioner was void cannot be sustained in law. 

18. The learned District Judge upheld the finding of the Election Tribunal that the election of the returned candidate was void. The Election Tribunal in coming to this conclusion has relied upon the F.I.R, the police report and the order passed by the learned Upazila Magistrate, Nalchity, Exts.4, 5 and 6. We 'have looked into those Exts. The F.I.R. Ext. 4 shows that it was lodged at 4.10 P.M. by the Driver of the D.C's speed boat, that he kept the speed boat at the Nalchity Ghat and went to take his meals in a hotel at 2.45 P.M. and on his return he found six un- known persons driving the speed boat in the mid river. On his signal those persons did not return to the Ghat but went towards the east. The police report Ext. 5 shows that on inspection the police found that the accused persons did not take the speed boat with bad intention but the accused’s were known to the in- formant from before and they used to drive the speed boat to learn how to drive the same and used to board the speed boat along with the informant and as such the police found no fault with the accused persons and submitted final report in the case which was accepted by the learned Upazila Magistrate on 18.8.85. These Exts.do not support the finding of the Election Tribunal that the speed boat was hijacked by the supporters of the petitioner or that it established the case of opposite party No.4 that the election of the petitioner was vitiated by any corrupt practice. The findings of the Election Tribunal in this regard is palpably wrong and without any basis. 

19. The learned District Judge without any scrutiny of the evidence upheld the finding of the Election Tribunal that the election or the returned candidate was void. The learned District Judge on consideration of the evidence found that out of 45 polling centres polling was peaceful in 11 centres and the election was vitiated by corrupt practice in the remaining 34 polling centres. The learned District Judge took the view that the Election Tribunal was wrong in directing fresh election since there was peaceful election in 11 polling centres and should have directed re-election in the remaining 34 centres but since the petitioner has been elected a member of the Parliament he cannot contest the election for the post of Chairman of the Upazila Parishad in view of the amendment of section 6 of Ordinance Nq.LIX of 1982 by Ordinance No. XXXIV of 1986 which came into force on 31.5.86. The learned District Judge rejecting the contention of the petitioner that the office of the Chairman of the Nalchity Upazila Parishad has become vacant by operation of law held that the opposite party No.4 was entitled to be declared as Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad as the petitioner became disqualified to be a contesting candidate. Repelling the contention that the amendment of the election petition beyond the period of limitation was illegal and without jurisdiction the learned District Judge declared the opposite party No.4 as the Chairman of the said Upazila Parishad on the basis of the amended prayer made in the election petition. In view of our finding that the amendment being beyond the statutory period was illegal and without jurisdiction the declaration made by the learned District Judge cannot be sustained in law. In as much as the only declaration that could be made is that the election was void as a whole. 

20. In view of our above discussion, this Rule is made absolute'. The judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge is set aside and the judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal is restored with the modification to the extent that the election of the chairman of the said Upazila Parishad is void as a whole. 

21. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs. 
End.

full_judgment:
In these two Rules arising out of two pre-emption cases between the same parties the common question is whether the deposit of the consideration amount as contemplated under sub-section 3(a) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made though subsequent to the filing of the application but within the period of limitation as contemplated under sub-section (i) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act can be deemed to have been made at the time of making the application as such, in the present cases while filing the application for pre-emption no deposit of consideration money was male but it was done immediately thereafter and within the period of limitation. The courts below however rejected the claim of pre-emption only on the ground that the deposit of consideration money was not accompanied along with the application for pre-emption against which the present rules were obtained.

<u>2. Clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act says that the deposit of the amount of consideration money or the value of the transferred holding shall be made in court at the time of making the application for pre-emption under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It would, however, appear from sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that an application for pre-emption may be made within 4 months of the service of notice upon the pre-empties or within 4 months from the knowledge of the alleged transfer under pre-emption. Thus, if an application for pre-emption is made within the period of limitation and the consideration money is also deposited in court within the period of limitation, in such circumstances it shall be deemed that the deposit of the consideration money has been made while making the application for pre-emption. In this connection it may he mentioned that it has not been said in clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the application for pre-emption shall be accompanied along with the deposit of consideration money or the value of the holding simultaneously. Clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 96 must be read along with the provision of limitation provided in sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. That being so, if the application for pre-emption and the deposit of consideration amount or the value of the transferred holding are made both within the period of limitation though separately, they shall he deemed and held to have been made validly within the given statutory period.</u>

3. In the aforesaid circumstances, the decisions of the courts below dismissing the pre-emption cases on the ground that the deposit of consideration amount or the value of the transferred holding was made subsequent to the filing of the pre-emption cases though evidently both within the period of limitation suffers from clear error of law and such decisions are set aside. The Second Munsif of Gaibandha in the district of Rangpur is directed to re-hear Miscellaneous Case Nos. 192 and 193 of 1977 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and decide and dispose of the case on met it finally and expeditiously, These Rules are made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Nani Gopal Saha -------- Appellant
Vs.
Jatindra Lal Chowdhury and others -------- Respondents
case_source: From the judgment and order dated 21-11-1979 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 60 of 1976.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.-This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 60 of 1976. Leave was granted to consider the question raised by the appellant-whether under the provisions of the President's Order No. 13 of 1972 the Tribunal has any power to remand; and whether the High Court Division took the correct view that the Tribunal could not direct for re-hearing of the case, and as provided under the Statute, should have adjudicated and decided the case fully and finally, if necessary after taking further evidence in the matter.

2. The facts, in short, necessary for proper appreciation of the contention under consideration may be stated thus: Respondents 1 and 2 challenged legality of the order of the Tribunal and filed an application under Article 7(5) of the President's Order No. 13 of 1972 with Boxirhat Union Arbitration Court. The Arbitration Court forwarded the record of the case to the Thana Magistrate recording that the appellant did not appear before the Arbitration Court, and as such it has no jurisdiction to make any order. The Thana Magistrate caused notices to be served on the parties, who as required in the law, appeared, on consideration of the report submitted by the Magistrate as per direction of the Thana Magistrate and after hearing of the parties and holding local enquiry the Thana Magistrate by his order dated March 15, 1975 directed for restoration of possession of the premises in question to respondents 1 and 2, and possession was delivered to them on March 20, 1975. Against this order the appellant filed an appeal before the Tribunal being Tribunal Appeal No. 3 of 1975 contending, inter alia, that the Arbitration Court was not properly constituted. The Tribunal accepted the contention and after setting aside the order of the Thana Magistrate remanded the case for re-hearing by a properly constituted Arbitration Court according to law. Validity of this order was challenged by the respondent by filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution on the ground that the Tribunal acted in excess of its jurisdiction in remanding the case to the Thana Magistrate for re-hearing inasmuch as statute does not provide any such power to the Tribunal. A Division Bench on examining the different provisions of the President's Order No. 13 of 1972 held that judgment of the Tribunal directing re-hearing of the case by the Arbitration Court afresh suffers from clear want of jurisdiction and was made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. This decision is under challenge in this appeal on the ground that the learned Judges committed a substantial error of law in setting aside the judgment of the Tribunal on an erroneous view that the Tribunal has no power to remand.

3. Before the Tribunal it was contended, inter alia, that the order of restoration of possession passed by the Thana Magistrate was illegal and without jurisdiction, inasmuch as the recommendation of the Arbitration Court on the basis of which the order was made, was not the recommendation of a properly constituted Arbitration Court. On examining the record the Tribunal found that the Arbitration Court was not properly constituted, because, there is nothing on record to indicate that the case was dealt with by a properly constituted Arbitration Court as contemplated under Article 4 of the President's Order No. 13 of 1972. According to the Tribunal, there is nothing to show on record that any member other than the Chairman ever participated in the proceedings. Consequently, the Tribunal held that the findings made in the case were made by the Chairman alone, and as such the same could not be the findings of the Arbitration Court; and that possession could not be delivered on the basis of such illegal findings. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, however, took the view that if the Arbitration Court was not properly constituted, the Tribunal being the final appellate authority constituted by the statute itself, and the Tribunal being a special forum created under the special law in the absence of any power specifically given for remanding a case for fresh hearing, the order of remand was wholly unauthorised being in excess of its jurisdiction. On this finding the learned Judges set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the Tribunal to decide the case fully and finally by itself on the merit.

<u>4. Article 5 provides for constitution of a Tribunal for each Sub-Division. A Tribunal consists of a Chairman and two members, all to be nominated by the District Judge. The Chairman is to be nominated from amongst the Additional District Judges and Senior Subordinate Judges and members to be nominated from amongst other Subordinate Judges and Massif. A Chairman or a member shall hold office for such period as the District Judge may determine. Clauses (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5) of article 7 contained the procedure to be followed by the Arbitration Court. Clause (1) provides that when the parties have agreed to Arbitration, the Arbitration Court shall, on the basis of its findings under clause (3), pass an order either allowing the prayer of the applicant or rejecting it; and this order shall be final and binding on the parties. Clause (5) provides that when the parties have not agreed to the arbitration, the Arbitration Court shall send its findings under Clause (3) along with the record of the case, to the Thana Magistrate, having jurisdiction, for such order as he may deem fit. Clause (6) provides that the Thana Magistrate shall on a consideration of the findings of the Arbitration Court and other evidence on record and after such further enquiry as he may consider necessary or after hearing both the parties, pass an order in writing either allowing the prayer of the applicant or rejecting it; and this order shall, subject to the provision of clause (7) be final and binding on both the parties. Clause (7) provides for an appeal to the Tribunal against ante order of Thana Magistrate; and the order of the Tribunal on such appeal shall be final and binding on the parties, Clause (8) provides that where the prayer for restoration of possession is allowed under clauses (4), (6) or (7) the Arbitration Court, in the case of an order passed by it, or the Thana Magistrate in the case of an order passed by it or by the Tribunal, shall cause the possession of the property concerned to be delivered to the applicant by evicting the unauthorised occupant therefrom, and may, for this purpose, cause such force to be used as may be necessary. Article 10 gives the power to an Arbitration Court, a Thana Magistrate or a Tribunal to issue summons to any person to appear before any Court and give evidence or to produce or cause the production of any document. Clause (2) of article 10 provides that if any person to whom an Arbitration Court, a Thana Magistrate or a Tribunal has issued summons to appear and give evidence or to produce or cause the production of any document before it or him willfully disobeys such summons the Court, the Magistrate or the Tribunal may take cognizance of such disobedience, and, after giving such persons an opportunity to explain, sentence him to a fine not exceeding twenty rupees.</u>

<u>5. The above provisions clearly show that the Tribunal has not only been given the power to hear an appeal from the Thana Magistrate but also the power of adjudication after taking evidence and give necessary direction for giving possession to the applicant. In an appropriate case the Tribunal has been given the authority to adjudicate the question of possession as a Court of first stage. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have correctly construed the statutory provisions, and we concur with the view taken by the learned Judges that the Tribunal being a specially constituted forum under the special law, its procedure and substantive powers are regulated by the special law; and that the Tribunal cannot pass an order in excess of its power as provided Articles 3 and 7 of the President's No. 13 of 1972. In the result, the fails and it is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.

Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, represented by its Managing Director ------ Petitioner 
VS.
Chairman, First Labour Court &ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed, J : This Rule was obtained on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution challenging an order passed by Mr. Nazrul Islam Khan, Chairman 1st Labour Court, Dhaka, on 3.11.88 in I.R.O. Case No. 267 of 1988 whereby he stayed operation of the order of transfer of the Respondent No.2, an employee serving under the petitioner, the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. 

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the Respondent No.2 had been serving as an employee under the petitioner, the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation and that he was posted at the Dhaka Office of the said Corporation, The Petitioner transferred the Respondent No.2 to its Office at Comilla. The Respondent No.2, thereafter, filed I.R.O. Case No. 267 of 1988 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka challenging the said order of transfer on the ground that he being a Trade Union Leader was not liable to be transferred to any station outside Dhaka in view of section 47B of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, and the learned Labour Court stayed the operation of the order of the said transfer by passing the impugned order on 3.11.88. 

3. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, challenges the order passed by the Labour Court mainly on the ground that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application of the Respondent No.2 giving rise to the I.R.O. Case No. 267 of 1988 inasmuch as the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation had been brought under the Administrative Tribunal Act, , 1981 as amended by the Administrative Tribunal (Amendment) Act, 1984 (ordinance No. LX of 1984) He has further submitted that in view of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981 the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all applications made by any per- son in the service of the Republic or in any Corporation, Bank or institution to which the said Act is made applicable, in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or in such Corporation, Bank or institution and the order of transfer of the Respondent No.2 being an order in respect of the terms and conditions of his service the Administrative Tribunal set up under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981 will have exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the said matter and that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to deal with the said matter is ousted. In support of his submission be has placed reliance on a decision reported in (1988) 40 .D.L.R. page 163. 

4. Mr. AshrafulHossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the Respondent No.2, submits that the right of the Respondent No.2 having been created and guaranteed by section 47B of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 the Labour Court which is the forum provided in the said Statute for enforcing the said right must be deemed to have jurisdiction to decide the matter and such jurisdiction cannot be ousted by any other enactment. In sport of his contention he has cited a case reported in (1981) 33 DLR (AD) page 305. 

5. It is not disputed that the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981, has been made applicable to the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation by the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 (Ordinance No. LX of 1984) 

6. Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1981 runs as follows:- 4. "Jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal-(1) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic. 

(2) A person in the service of the Republic may make an application to an Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (1), if he is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic: Provided that no application in respect of an order, decision or action which can be set aside, varied or modified by a higher administrative authority under any law for the time being in force relating to the terms and conditions of the service of the Republic or the discipline or that service can be made to the Administrative Tribunal until such higher authority has taken a decision on the matter: 

Provided further that 00 such application shall be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal unless it is made within six months from the date of making or taking of the order, decision or action concerned or making of the decision on the matter by the higher administrative 'authority, as the case may be. 

(3) In this section "person in the service of the Republic" includes a person who is or has retired or is dismissed, removed or discharged from such service, but does not include a person in the defence services of Bangladesh. " 

7. It, therefore, appears that in view of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981, the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to decide matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of the Respondent No.2. The order of transfer of the Respondent No.2 is undisputedly a matter relating to the terms and conditions of his service as such, the legality or otherwise of the order of transfer of the Respondent No.2 affecting the terms and conditions of his service is exclusively triable by the Administrative Tribunal. 

8. Moreover, apart from section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, we must refer to Article 117 of the Constitution whereby the Administrative Tribunal was created. It runs as follows :-117. (1) "Notwithstanding anything herein before contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of- 

(a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic Including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishments 

(b) the acquisition, administration, management and disposal of any property vested in or managed• by the Government by or under any law, including the operation and management of, and service in any nationalised enterprise or statutory public authority; 

(c)any law to which clause (3) of Article 102 applies. (2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal: 

Provided that Parliament may, by law, pro- vide for appeals from, or the review of decisions of any such tribunal. Clause (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution, therefore, specifically bars the Jurisdiction 'of any Court or tribunal other than an Administrative Tribunal, to entertain any proceedings in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. It, therefore, appears that section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act confers exclusive jurisdiction on the Administrative Tribunal to deal with any dispute relating to the order of transfer of the Respondent No. 2 and clause (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution specifically bars the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to entertain any proceeding relating to such matters were therefore, of the view that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. 
9. Relying on a case reported in 33 DLR (AD) (1981) 305 it was contended by Mr. Ashraful Hossain that the right of the Respondent No.2 not to be transferred having been guaranteed by section 47 B of .the Industrial Relations Ordinance, the forum provided by the said 'Statute alone is empowered to enforce that right. In the said case, an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was filed by a Co-sharer in the holding for pre-emption of a portion of the said holding transferred to a stranger. The purchaser resisted the application on the ground that he was no longer a co-sharer as the original holding had been sub-divided and the rent thereof had been split up by the Revenue Officer under section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The question arose whether the order of the Revenue Officer could be held to be without jurisdiction for non-compliance with certain provisions of section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act, in a collateral proceeding pending before the Civil Court and it was held by the learned Appellate' Division of this Court, "in this view of the matter the opinion is that non-compliance with proviso (a) to sub-section (1) of Section 88A will not render the proceeding without jurisdiction inasmuch as a remedy has been provided by way of appeal and therefore the Civil Court cannot knock it out by holding it as having been made without jurisdiction in a collateral proceeding:- 

"13. The reason can be stated in the words of Asquith, L.J. "It is undoubtedly good law that where a statute creates a right and in plain language gives a specific remedy or appoints a specific tribunal for its enforcement, a party seeking to enforce that right must resort to this' remedy or this tribunal and not to others" 

(Wilkinson- Vs-Banking (Sic) Corporation (1948) I.K.B. 721 (724)." For a decision in that case this finding of the learned Appellate Division was not, however, necessary and was merely academic since the Courts below found that the requirements of provision (a) to sub-section (1) of section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act were complied with in the proceeding before the Revenue Officer. Mr. Ashraful Hossain seems to have depended mainly on the observation of the learned Appellate Division in para 13 of their Lordships' Judgment as quoted above. 

10. In the English case of Wilkinson Vs. Banking Corporation reported in 1948 Law Reports I.K.B. page 721, from where the relevant portion in para 13 of their Lordships' Judgment in the case re- ported in 33 DLR (AD) page 305 has been quoted, a person brought an action against a local authority claiming superannuation allowance and the same has been refused by the said local authority. Section 35 of the Local Government Act, 1937, provided that "any question concerning the rights and liabilities of an employee of a local authority 	shall be decided at the first instance by the authority concerned, and if the employee is dissatisfied with any such decision shall be determined by the Minister, and the Minister's determination shall be final." A point was raised by the defendants that since the plaintiff’s right to superannuation was required to be determined by the Minister under the above Statute in the event of the plaintiffs being dissatisfied with the decision of the local authority, the plaintiff had no cause of action to approach the Court. It was held that since the Parliament, by en- acting section 35 of the Local Government Act, 1937, appointed a specific tribunal for dealing with the rights and liabilities of the employees of a local authority no act of the parties could create in the Court a jurisdiction which Parliament had vested exclusively in some other body. To quote Asquith, LJ No act of the parties can create in the Courts a jurisdiction which Parliament had said shall vest not in the Court but exclusively in some other body." 

11. Apart from the fact that the points at issue in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) page 305 are not at all similar to those in the case before us, the principles of law involved therein and the context in which the above observations of Asquith, LJ., in Wilkinson Vs. Banking Corporation were quoted by their Lordships are totally different from those in the present case. Moreover, in Wilkinson Vs. Banking Corporation it was held that when by a Statute a specific forum is created for deciding a particular matter, by consent of parties the court cannot assume jurisdiction in such matters. We are also of the same view. In the present case, Article 117 of the Constitution read with section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act provides a particular forum with exclusive jurisdiction for deciding the dispute in question and also bars jurisdiction of any other forum. Consequently, the case relied upon by Mr. Ashraful Hossain does not, in our view, assist him. In the instant case, the jurisdiction of the Labour Court was not sought to be ousted by consent of the parties but by the provision of the Constitution as well as by a Statute. So the decision in Wilkinson Vs. Banking Corporation rather lends support to the view taken by the petitioner. 

12. In the case reported in 40 DLR page 113 cited by Mr. Rafiqul Hoq, an employee of the Bangladesh Railway filed an application under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance before the Labour Court in respect of certain matters affecting his conditions of service and it was held that since the Administrative Tribunal Act was made applicable to the employees of the Bangladesh Railway by operation of law, the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the said application. The principle enunciated in that case is also applicable to the present case. 

13. In view of the above, we are of the opinion that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. 

14. The Rule is, therefore, made absolute. The order dated 3.11.88 passed by the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka in I.R.O. Case No. 267 of 1988 is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

End.
