case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 10th November, 1988  passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 324 of 1988.)
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J.: This appeal by the defendants following leave is from Judgment and Order dated 10 November, 1988 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka discharging the Rule in Civil Revision No. 324 of 1988 and upholding the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court.

<u>2. The matter arises out of an acquisition proceeding of 1959-60 requisitioning and then acquiring large areas of land in mouza Khilgaon, presently within P.S. Motijheel, for the Railway Board. Plaintiff-respondents' 6.4650 acres of land had also been acquired and included in the total of more than 70 acres of such acquired land. The facts of the case have grown pretty long as the plaintiffs are campaigning from 1963 with the only grievance that proper notices not having been served, the acquisition of their land was illegal and invalid. Thus while it will be necessary to recount briefly all the facts for a proper appreciation of the plaintiffs case (and of the defendants also) the decision will turn only on one question, namely, whether the acquisition of the plaintiffs land was illegal for want of proper service of notices as required under the law. Accordingly leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division has correctly decided the issue as to service of notice of acquisition in the facts of the present case while upholding the decree passed in favour of the plaintiffs.</u>

3. The predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-respondents, Basharatullah, and his wife respondent No. 2 as plaintiffs brought Title suit No. 147 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on the averments, inter alia, that the suit land owned by them was requisitioned in L.A. Case No. 63/59-60 by a notice dated 21.6.60 under section 3 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) for the defendant-respondent No. 3, the Railway Board. The requisitioning authority took over possession of the suit land from the plaintiffs on 21.6.60. The suit land was requisitioned with the object of permanent acquisition, but no notice under section 5(1a) and (3) of the Act was served in the locality or on the plaintiffs as required by law for acquisition. An Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) passed an order to serve fresh notice on the opposite parties under the said sections, being satisfied that no such notices were served before, but the file mysteriously disappeared. On 13.9.67 the successor Additional Deputy Commissioner noting that an injustice will be done by depriving the plaintiffs of due compensation, passed an order to serve fresh notices on the plaintiffs. But the officers concerned having dragged their feet in the matter of serving fresh notices the plaintiffs were constrained to file a suit being Title suit No. 36 of 1968 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka against the defendant-appellants and respondent No. 3 challenging their claim of acquisition of the suit land without service of legal notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the Act. The present appellants contested the suit by filing a written statement asserting that the said notices have been duly served upon the plaintiffs. By his judgment and decree dated 8.7.69 the learned Munsif decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. The learned Munsif came to the conclusion that notice under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the said Act were not served on the plaintiffs and as such there was no valid acquisition of the disputed property.

4. Against the said judgment and decree the defendant-appellants preferred Title appeal No. 28 of 1970 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka, who, by his judgment and decree dated 24.5.71 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif. The plaintiffs thus became entitled to fresh notices for valid and legal acquisition of the suit land.

5. Instead of issuing fresh notice the defendant-appellants formulated a fraudulent device to serve a copy of the alleged original notice under section 5(1) dated 21.6.60 putting a fresh date of issue in the notice under section 5(1a). This alleged copy of the old original notice under section 5(1) of the said Act was served on 23.4.73 directing the plaintiffs to appear before the concerned authority on 30.12.60 to object to the acquisition proceedings, if any. This action was fraudulent and absurd on the face of it. The defendant-appellants also served a fresh notice under section 5(3) of the said Act on the same day, i.e. 23.4.73 upon the plaintiffs giving 7 days notice to object to the acquisition of the suit land. The statute requires the concerned authority to give notice of 15 days to state the owner's objection. But in the notice served on 23.4.73 the plaintiffs were asked to file their objections on 30.4.73 i.e. within 7 days. The notice was illegal, invalid and void.

6. The plaintiffs made representations against such wrong actions before various authorities including Mr. Mirza Golam Hafez who was the Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. After a detailed discussion of facts and law involved in the matter, he came to the view that there had been no legal or valid acquisition of the suit property as no notice under section 5(1a) and 5(3) were served. Upon "the Minister's order an opinion was obtained from the Ministry of Law which also opined that fresh notices under section 5 (la) and 5(3) were required to be served for valid acquisition of the suit property. Thereafter, Mr. Abdul Haque took over charge as Minister of Land Administration and Land Reforms. But before passing any written order in the matter he went out of office. His successor Mr. Md. Ismail passed an order simply rejecting the plaintiffs representation. They then submitted a representation on 12.3.82 to the then President of Bangladesh. Subsequently they made a representation on 4.6.82 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator and submitted all relevant papers. They received a communication in January, 1983 from the Secretariat of the Chief Martial Law Administrator advising them to seek relief in a Civil Court.

7. The present suit was filed on 13.5.84 stating further that the defendants by a Gazettee Notification No. DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73 purporting to be under section 5(7) of Act allegedly acquired the suit land which was illegal.

They, therefore, prayed:

(a) for a decree declaring that required and valid notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of Act-XIII of 1948 have not been issued or served in L.A. Case No. 63/59-60 in respect of the suit property as per provisions of law;

(b) for a declaration that Gazette Notification No. DA 72/71/355 dated 25.6.73 has no legal basis or validity or binding force ...

(c) for a declaration that the notice under section 5(3) along with enclosed copy of notice under section 5(1) served on the plaintiff on 23.4.73 are fraudulent, defective, invalid and without any legal effect and as such the title and ownership of the suit land has always rested and continues to rest with the plaintiffs and has never been vested with the defendants;

(d) for an order of mandatory injunction directing the defendants to perform their statutory duties by making proper and lawful assessment for the period of requisition through requisition order dated 21.6.60 till the filing of the suit for use and occupation of the suit land as well as start valid acquisition proceeding afresh under part-Il, section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, and other provisions of law in force for ex- pressed intent of acquisition within 3 months failing which the possession of the suit land be restored to the plaintiff.

8. The appellants contested the suit contending, inter alia, that there was no cause of action for the suit, that the suit was barred under the Act, the Law of Limitation and Specific Relief Act and that it was also barred by res judicata. It was stated that the plaintiffs' land measuring an area of 6.4650 acres along with other lands was requisitioned on 21.6.60 with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter under L.A. Case No. 63 of 1959-60. Vacant possession of the land in question was handed over to the requiring body on 2.7.60 and since then the Railway Board is possessing the suit land after constructing their buildings except approximately an area of 0.16 acre of land which is still under the occupation of the plaintiffs. The land in question has already been acquired and vested in the Government vide Gazette Notification No. DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73. From the office record of the office of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) it appears vide order sheet at page 20 dated 30.12.60 that the notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) was issued to the plaintiffs in the year 1960. It was further stated that as per order of the then Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) on the body of the re- port of the then Kanungo, the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms was informed vide T.O. No. 2095-L.A. dated 14.6.72 for a fresh requisition and acquisition of the land in question of the plaintiffs. The Ministry thereupon issued instructions along with the Attorney General's minutes dated 15.3.73 whereupon the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) served upon the plaintiffs a fresh notice under section 5(3) fixing 30.4.73 for filing objection, if any, against acquisition along with the true copy of the notice under section 5(la) as already served in the locality in the year 1960. It is claimed that the said Gazette Notification is quite legal, valid and binding upon the plaintiffs and the suit land vested in the defendants absolutely and free from any encumbrances with the publication of the aforesaid Notification. Fresh notice or fresh acquisition proceedings under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 is neither necessary nor can be conceived of in respect of the suit land which has already vested in the defendants. The object of filing of the suit is to get a fresh notice for fresh assessment of compensation causing loss and injury to the defendants.

9. The learned Subordinate Judge by judgment and decree dated 31.8.85 dismissed the suit upon finding that the first prayer was superfluous and redundant as the plaintiffs had already obtained the declaration in T.S. 36/68, that notice under sections 5 (1a) and (3) of the Act had not been served upon the plaintiffs, that the present suit was barred under Order 2, rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure as the plaintiffs omitted to pray for recovery of possession in the earlier suit, that the instant suit for the said relief was hit by Art 142 of the Limitation Act, that the declaration as in prayer (b) (c) was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as no consequential relief was prayed for and that the prayer (d) was Vague, indefinite and cumbrous. He, however, found that "there is no doubt that the attempt of the Government to legalise the disputed acquisition which has been declared invalid by the Court, by fresh service of old notice on 23.4.73 after the disposal of the said suit and appeal, is of no legal effect, the service of notice contemplated in section 5(la) and 5(3) of the Act must be prior to the initiation of acquisition has been rendered invalid for the want of statutory notice, the service of notice which is posterior to the acquisition, can not legally have any restrospective effect and as such a subsequent fresh service of old notice cannot have any legal effect of legalising the illegal acquisition."

10. On appeal by the plaintiffs, the learned Additional District Judge, by judgment and decree dated 20.6.87 reversed the aforesaid decision and decreed the suit in terms of prayer (b) (c) and (d). As to prayer (a) he agreed with the trial Court that it was unnecessary and held further that it was also barred by res judicata. The learned Additional District Judge, however, did not reverse any of the findings as to bar of the suit made by the Trial Court but having concurred with the finding that the service of the old notice under section 5(1a) along with that under sub-section (3) of the Act on 23.4.73 upon the plaintiffs giving only 7 days time to file objection was not valid and legal, held that the Notification dated 25.6.73 under section 5(7) of the Act acquiring the suit land was illegal and liable to be set aside.

11. In the revision taken by the appellants against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the learned Judges of the High Court Division found in the impugned judgment no reason to differ from the concurrent finding of the courts below (as to the invalidity of the notices served in 1973). Defendant-appellants raised several points including bar of the suit under section 14A of the Act but they were all negatived by the learned Judges. The learned Judges before finding invalidity of the notices served in 1973 devoted a large part of the judgment in construing the decree passed in T.S. 36/68 and ultimately held that "when a decree declares that the notice under section 5(1a) was 'not served on the plaintiffs', it cannot be understood to mean that a personal notice on the plaintiffs under section (5(1a) was not served. The decree will be understood to mean that the mode of service prescribed in section 5(1a) was not resorted to as a result of which the plaintiff-opposite parties were not served with the notice under section 5(la)."

It will have to be examined whether this finding can be justified in the facts and ircumstances of the case.

12. It may be mentioned that the lower appellate Court relied entirely on the opinions given by the Hon'ble Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms and other officials in the official notes in order to hold that fresh notice under section 5(1a) was required to be issued following the decree in T.S. 36/68. The learned Judges of the High Court Division disapproving the same observed that opinions etc of certain officials have been marked as exhibits without examining the makers thereof or without proving them in the manner provided by the Evidence Act, but the absence of notice under section 5(1a) or 5(3) in 1960 is a matter already decided in T.S. 36/68 and therefore, it needs no further proof in this suit. The interpretation of the decree in T.S.36/68 as made by the learned Judges was found necessary, it seems, to cover up the aforesaid lacuna in the judgment of the lower appellate Court.

<u>13. The main issue in this suit, therefore, is whether in the absence of a fresh notice under section 5(la) following the decree in T.S. 36/68, the impugned acquisition could be held to be valid on the basis of notices served in the manner on 23.4.73.</u>

14. The learned Additional Attorney General appearing in support of the appeal submitted that notice under section 5(la) provides for a public notice, but the respondents having obtained a decree in T.S. 36/68 that notices under section 5(1a) and (3) "were not served on the plaintiffs", the respondents could only be served (in terms of the decree) with copy of the public notice already served in 1960 and accordingly the authority served fresh notice under section 5(3) (which is a personal notice) along with a copy of the public notice dated 14.12.60 on 23.4.73 and the respondents having failed to file any objection to such acquisition notice, the authority lawfully issued the gazette Notification on 25.6.73 and thus the suit land stood validly acquired. As to the grievance that clear 15 (fifteen) days' time was not given for filing objection even in the notice under 5(3) as required under the law, the learned Additional Attorney General submitted that the notice under 5(3) having been issued on 12.4.73 by competent authority with Jurisdiction and served on 23.4.73 fixing 30.4.73 for filing objections and the respondents not having raised any grievance as to shortage of time nor having prayed for any further time and they having not ever challenged the validity of the public purpose for acquisition at any stage (which could not be challenged in any case) and the Gazette Notification acquiring the suit land having been issued 2(two) months after the service of notice under 5(3), no prejudice was caused to the respondents and, further- more, no suit would lie for such small irregularity and thus the suit itself was barred under section 14A of the Act.

15. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, submitted that even though the decree in T.S.36/68 mentions that notice under 5(1a) and (3)" were not served on the plaintiffs", it is abundantly clear from paragraphs 7 and 3 of the plaint of the former and present suit respectively that the plaintiffs always alleged that public notice under 5(1 a) was not served in the locality and the judgment in T.S. 36/68 read as whole can- not but mean that the court referred to non-service of public notice as required under the law. The learned counsel upon making reference to Ext. 1 order sheet in L.A. Case No. 63/59-60 and other exhibits official notes etc (vide supplementary paper book filed by the respondents) submitted that the appellants clearly understood both before and after the decree in T.S. 36/68 that public notice under 5(1a) was required to be served afresh and as such the service of copy of the old notice of 1960 under 5(1a) in 1973 was no compliance either of the law or of the decree in T.S. 36/68 and thus the view taken by the High Court Division was fully justified. Mr. Huq submitted that even if it is conceded for argument's sake that public notice under 5(la) was issued in 1960 as claimed by the appellants, it was required to be served afresh after the decree in T.S. 36/68 as notices under 5(1a) and 5(3) are required under the law to be served simultaneously and not separately with several years intervening. Mr. Huq argued that the plaintiffs are entitled to at least 15 days time for objection even in a notice under 5(3) and this period starts from publication of the notice under 5(1a) and thus in any case upon a true construction of section 5(1a) and (3) of the Act, fresh notice was absolutely necessary. He argued that admittedly the plaintiffs got less then 7(seven) days time from the service of notice under 5(3) on 23.4.73 which has vitiated the proceeding because procedural provisions relating to acquisition of private property have always been enforced by Court with utmost rigour.

16. In support of his submission as to the requirement of simultaneous notice, Mr. Huq referred to and relied upon 1984 BLD (AD) 283, AIR 1973 S.c. 552, AIR 1975 Allahabad 202, AIR 1976 Punjab 279 and other decisions. For the purpose of showing necessity and requirement of strict compliance with statutory notice, Mr. Huq cited AIR 1971 (SC)306, ATR 1978 Mad. 201, AIR 1988 Bombay 18 and other decisions.

<u>17. Before considering the submissions on merit the provisions as to notice for requisition and permanent acquisition of a property under the Act may be considered. An order of requisition is made under section 3 by the Deputy Commissioner and section 4(1) provides for service of the same "on the owner of the property by delivering or tendering it to him" etc. It further provides that an authentic copy a of such order shall also be affixed on the notice board of the local Union Council and the order shall also be proclaimed by beat of drum in the locality in which the property is situate. Thus both a personal and public service of the order of requisition is contemplated.</u>

18. It may be observed that in the case of Md. Ismail Vs. The Province of East Pakistan 16 DLR (SC) 438 it has been held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that if the person concerned has full knowledge of the contents of an order (of requisition) service of the notice on him is not necessary. Hamoodur Rahman, J. however held that although non-service of the order will not render the order itself in-effective but its service would still be necessary not only for taking over possession but also for determining the compensation payable under section 7(a)(i).

19. The procedure for acquisition of a requisitioned land is provided in section 5 of the Act. The process begins with the Deputy Commissioner giving a public notice under 5(Ia) which is as follows:

"The Deputy Commissioner shall, if he considers that the acquisition of any requisitioned property is expedient for a public purpose or in public interest cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired."

20. Sub-section (1) and (La) were substituted for the former sub-section (1) by E.P. Ordinance XL of 1961 which was as follows:

"(I) The District Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property and if he proposes to so acquire, he shall cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the property to be acquired stating that he intends to acquire the property."

21. In the instant case, according to the appellants, notice was given under 5(1) which was dated 14.12.60 (vide paper book Part II page 3) but the Additional District Judge referred to the said notice as dated 21.6.60 (obviously erroneously) which is the date of the requisition notice and this error has crept into the judgement of the High Court Division also. Be that as it may section 5(3) provides for a personal notice which is as follows:

5(3) "Notice shall also be served to the above effect on the owner of such property and on all such persons known or believed to be interested therein or to be entitled to act for persons so interested as reside or have agents authorized to receive service on their behalf within the revenue district in which the property is situated."

22. It will be seen that though the purpose of both the notices under 5(1a) and (3) is to inform the affected persons as to the proposed acquisition enabling them to raise objection, claim, etc they are distinct notices and are to be complied with differently. Rule 4 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 provides for different forms for the aforesaid notices and a reference to those forms (BC) would show that whereas notice under 5(la) is an omnibus notice meant for all to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property, that under 5(3) is addressed to a particular person, the owner, etc. The appellant's consistent case is that both the notices were served in 1960 but in view of the finding and decree in T.S. 36/68 that the notices were not served on the plaintiffs, the fact of non- service of the personal notice under 5(3) can no longer be questioned and accordingly it was served afresh on 23.4.73. The important question, however, is whether it was proved and found in that suit that public notice under 5(1a) also was not served and therefore required to be served afresh.

23. It has been noticed that the acquisition proceeding was in respect of more that 70 acres of land involving many persons including the plaintiffs and notice under 5(1) was a pre-requisite for initiating acquisition proceeding. Service of public notice being an official act, a presumption is available under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act that it has been regularly performed unless the contrary is proved. Notice under 5(3) being a personal notice, a denial by the owner is prima facie evidence of non-service. Therefore, consideration is bound to be different when allegation is made as to non-service of both the aforesaid notices.

24. We shall now consider whether there has been any evidence at any stage that the public notice under 5(1a) was not served in the manner required. It is true that in the plaint of both the suits it has been stated that no notice under 5(1a) was served in the locality. It is also true that in the subsequent suit (T.S. 147/84) it has been found that the question of non-service of notice having already been decided in T.S. 36/68, the issue was barred by res judicata. But then it is important to consider the only evidence given by P. W. 1 the plaintiff himself in the present suit. Nowhere he stated that public notice under 5 (1a) was not served in the locality. All he said was: আমার উপর বা আমার স্ত্রীর উপর নালিশী সম্পত্তি একুইজিশিন এর ব্যাপারে কোন নোটিশ জারি হয় নাই, আমার নালিশী সম্পত্তি রিলিজ করার জন্য হাইকোর্টে এর রিট পিটিশন দাখিল করি এবং উক্ত রিট পিটিশন শুনানীর সময় সরকার এইমর্মে undertaking দেন যে, সরকার আপোষে নালিশী সম্পত্তি বাবদ আমাদের ক্ষতিপূরণ দিবেন। বিবাদী সরকার নোটিশ না দিয়া ও আমার উপর নোটিশ দিয়াছেন বলিয়া আমরা ঢাকায় ১ম মুনসেফী আদালতে সরকারের বিরুদ্ধে এক মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করি এবং তাহাতে ডিক্রি লাভ করি।

25. The all-important decree in T.S. 36/68 which is the main plank in the plaintiffs case may now be examined. The operative part of the judgment reads thus; "that the suit be decreed on contest with cost. Let it be hereby declared that the notices under section 5(1a) & 5(3) of the Requisition Act for the purpose of acquisition were not served on the plaintiffs. Let it be further declared that there is no valid acquisition of the disputed land."

26. It is clear from the above that notices were not found to have been served on the plaintiffs; but can it be said that since reference has been made to 5 (1a) it has to be read that public notice was also not served. It is not only permissible but rather incumbent to refer to the judgment itself for construing a decree on the dicta of the Privy Council in the case of Seth Manakchand, AIR(II)1944 Privy Council 46 that "For the purpose of interpreting a decree no other document is so directly in point as the judgment or can in the nature of things have comparable force". The learned Additional Attorney General assailed the interpretation sought to be given by the High Court Division of the said decree, it seems with good deal of force, because the judgment of all things was not taken into consideration in holding that "the decree will be understood to mean that the mode of service prescribed in section 5(1a) was not resorted to as a result of which the plaintiff-opposite parties were not served with the notice under section 5(1 a)".

27. Is there anything to show in the said judgment of the learned Munsif that the mode of service prescribed in section 5(1a) was not resorted to, or, rather is there any evidence in that behalf? It will be seen that the brief Judgment of the learned Munsif rests only on consideration of Ext. 1 (ordersheet in L.A. Case No. 63 of 1959-60). The material part of the judgment is reproduced below:

"It appears from the said ordersheet that on 13.9.67 A.D.C(D) came to a finding of that "there is no conclusive evidence that there has been a proper service of notices since there is some genuine doubt in respect of a service of notice on the plaintiff. We might agree to serve fresh notice on the petitioner. The above observation and finding by the A.D.C(D) in the absence of anything to the contrary goes to prove that the notices under section 5(1)(a) and 5(3) were not served. The notices are mandatory. So, the plaintiffs are entitled to get fresh notice.

28. In view of the above findings, the Court came to the conclusion that the notices under section 5(1)(a) and 5(3) of the Requisition Act were not served on the plaintiffs and as such there was no valid acquisition of the disputed property."

29. We have carefully considered the source material, i.e. the entire ordersheet Ext. 1 (pages 2-9 of the Supplementary Paper Book filed on behalf of the respondents) and are in no doubt that the L.A. authorities have at all relevant time been considering the grievance of the plaintiffs as to non-service of personal notice, but so far as public notice was concerned, it was never an issue nor held by them that there was any doubt as to service of the public notice. The opinion of the Minsters and other officials have been rightly discarded by the High Court Division as the fact remains that the government ultimately rejected the representation made by the plaintiffs and on the opinion of the Attorney General directed the L.A. Office to issue fresh notice only under 5(3).

30. Having considered the fact of the case carefully we are clearly of the opinion that there was neither any evidence that public notice was not served nor the decree in T.S.36/68 could be construed to mean as such requiring fresh public notice to be served. Accordingly, the interpretation sought to be given by the High Court Division or the decree in question must be held to be unsustainable, Had the Courts below and the High Court Division considered the matter in their correct perspective they would have found that giving a copy of the old notice under 5(1a) along with fresh notice under 5(3) in 1973 was only in compliance with a misconceived decree but it did not vitiate the fresh notice under 5 (3) or the acquisition proceeding in any way.

31. Now coming to the contention of Mr. Rafiqul Huq that in any case, there ought to have been fresh notice under 5(la) also in 1973 when fresh notice under 5(3) was served pursuant to the decree In T.S.36/68 because the law contemplates a simultaneous service of notice under the said sub-sections, we find it plainly difficult to accept the same. It. is true that the law provides for a simultaneous service of the public and the personal notice. But there may be a case where the public notice is not in dispute but the personal notice is, as in the present case.

<u>32. A fresh service of the personal notice may be necessary but the public notice which concerns many other people which has already been served does not need to be served afresh even though the fresh personal notice is served fairly long after the public notice. If it were not so and a fresh public notice were necessary as contended by the learned counsel it would lead to a paradox, for, it would be tantamount to an admission that no public notice under 5(1a) was served earlier and the acquisition proceedings taken against others properties on the basis of the said notice were a nullity. The consequence is too serious to be ignored.</u>

33. The Indian decisions referred to by Mr. Huq have considered the question of failure to give public notice or delay in giving such notice after publication of Gazette Notification as to intended acquisition by the Government under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act,1894. Provisions of the said Act and the Act under which the present proceeding has been taken are different and the principles laid down in interpretating section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act are not applicable either in terms of the provisions of section 5 of the Act or m facts of the present case. Thus we do not think that the decisions referred to are of much help to the respondents. 1984 BLD (AD) 283, relied upon, however, will be referred to at the end of this discussion.

34. The grievance as to less than 15 days notice in connection with the fresh notice under 5(3) in 1973 also does not seem to have much force in the context of the facts of the present case. Provisions of section 5(1a)(2) and (3) read together would indicate that the intention of law is to provide at least 15 days time from the publication of the notice under 5 (1a) to the affected person to appear before the Deputy Commissioner to state the nature of their interest in the property and objection (if any). As it has been found that no fresh notice under 5(1a) was required to be served, it follows that 15 days time for answering a personal notice under 5(3) was not strictly necessary. Even so it must be held that the authority was bound to give reasonable time. The question is, was it given? It has been noticed that the notice under 5 (3) was dated 12.4.73 and was served on the plaintiffs on 23.4.73 requiring them to appear on 30.4.73 at the office of the L.A. Collector, Dhaka, Admittedly the plaintiffs did not appear on the date-fixed nor prayed for any further time. The gazette notification under 5(7) was made on 25.6.73 about 2 months after the said notice. In the circumstances it cannot be said that the plaintiffs have been deprived of a reasonable opportunity to appear due to shortage of time.

<u>35. It, therefore, follows that the view taken by the Additional District Judge and endorsed by the High Court Division to the effect that service in 1973 of an alleged copy of an old notice dated 21.6.60 under section 5(1) is no service of notice at all and service of a notice under section 5(3) giving only 7 days time to file any objection against acquisition is also no notice under the said Act, is not tenable because of want of proper appreciation of the law and the decree in T.S. 36/68. The plaintiffs do not challenge the public purpose of the requisition/ acquisition proceeding nor do they allege any malafide to the respondents. In view of our findings made above, there is also no substance in the contention of the plaintiffs that valid notices were not served under 5(1a) and 5(3) thus vitiating the acquisition of the property under 5(7) of the Act. The High Court Division held that the impugned notices in prayer no (c) are no notices at all in the eye of law, far less notices under the Act and , therefore, the bar of section 14A his no application in the present case when a statutory authority acts without jurisdiction or acts in a manner without following the procedure provided in the statute itself and the bar of suit does not apply, As already observed, we could not agree with the views and findings made by the High Court Division as to the relevant notices and therefore, there was no question of the authorities acting without Jurisdiction or acting in a manner without following the procedure provided in the statute. The table now b being turned the bar of the suit under section 14A of the Act is inexorably attracted and it must be held that the suit itself was barred.</u>

36. In view of the discussion above, we find substance in the contentions raised by the learned Additional Attorney General and, accordingly, hold that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

<u>37. There is, however, one matter, though not in issue in this suit, at the centre of all this litigation being carried on by the plaintiffs right from 1963 and that relates to compensation. They have been fighting for fresh notice apparently because it has a direct bearing on the determination of compensation. In the writ petition Nos. 518 and 519 of 1963 filed by them the senior Government Pleader gave an a surance before the Court that the Government would expedite the acquisition of the lands in question and on such assurance their counsel did not press the writ petitions. If the Government were issue to the assurance given and completed the publication of the Gazette Notification under section 5(7) of the Act, say, with in a year or two then the matter of C compensation would not have been very matenal. But now that a whole decade has passed between the public notice under 5(la) dated 14.12.60 and the publication of the gazettee under 5(7) of the Act on 25.6.73, the matter of compensation assumes great importance because of the phenomenal rise in the value of land since 1960. The observation made by this court in the case of Abdul Gafur Khan Vs. Government of Bangladesh 1984 BLD(AD) 283 is pertinent in the circumstances of the present case. It was said in that case that though notice for acquisition under section 5(la) was served in 1962 the land was actually acquired in 1968, that is, after the expiry of six years when the value of the land increased to a great extent. Government did not explain why notice was served in 1962 but acquisition was made in 1968. Although there is no particular period within which a requisitioned land is to be acquired after notice for acquisition has been served, yet when the value of the land was increasing but that of money was decreasing the compensation to be paid now on the valuation of the year 1962 would cause substantial injury to the land owner. There should be some proximity between the date of notice for acquisition and that of actual acquisition.</u>

38. When though we have found the acquisition in the present case to be valid, we have felt it on our conscience to refer to the above observation so that the authorities may take into consideration the fact of the long time gap between the notice of acquisition under 5(1a) and the actual acquisition by Gazette Notification under 5(7) of the Act while determining compensation. It may not be for the validity of the acquisition itself but the fact remains that the L.A. authority admittedly served a copy of the old notice under 5(1a) upon the plaintiffs on 23.4.73 while Gazette Notification was made on 25.6.73. It will be, in our opinion, in consonance with justice and equity if the authorities reckon the aforesaid date (23.4.73) for the purpose of section 7(e) proviso (1) of the Act in the special facts of the present case.

39. In the result, however, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment is set aside and the suit dismissed.

Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.: I agree with the judgment proposed to be delivered by my brother A.T.M. Afzal, J: I would add the following. The entire case centres round the interpretation of the decree in the earlier suit, T.S. No. 36 of 1968, filed by the respondent, owner of the land acquired: Now his contentions are that neither the public notice was served in the locality under sec. 5(1), nor the personal notice was served upon him under sec. 5(3), of the Act and that this is what was held in the said decree. These contentions however, are not supported by the facts established.' The decree, and the judgment on which it is based, do not say so. The decree is that "notices under sets. 5(1) and 5(3) were not served upon the plaintiff (emphasis supplied). According to law, the notice under see 5(1) was not required to be served upon the "plaintiff it was to be published in the locality. And case of the appellant IS that such notice dated 14.12.60 was published in the locality. In addition to the public notice, a personal notice under sec. 5(3) was to be served upon the plaintiff, owner of the land; finding in that suit is that such notice was not served. By the expression, "notices under sees. 5 (1) and 5(3) were not served upon the plaintiff the learned Munsif acted under the wrong impression that both the notices were to be served upon the plaintiff. Whereas in fact, only the personal notice was not served upon him. The plaintiff did not dispose either in the earlier suit or in the instant suit that no public notice was served. In the locality the clear and categorical statement In his deposition IS that "no notice was served upon him personally". This makes the whole thing clear. Again in the same. L. A. Case, No. 63/59-60, seventy acres of land belonging to several persons including the plaintiffs 6½ acres was requisitioned and taken over on 21.6.60 and then acquired by one and same public notice dated 14.12.60. If all other land owners had known about the notice there is no reason why the plaintiff would not know of it. In the earlier suit, it was held that personal notice was not served, and in compliance with the decree in that suit, personal notice dated 12.4.73 was served upon him on 23.4.73. Along with this personal notice a copy of the public notice dated 14.12.6q which .had been served already, was given Just for information. There was nothing wrong in it for, the public notice was served in 1960, and according to law this is the date for acquisition of the land and assessment of compensation. But, as my learned brother has observed, in the interest of justice and equity and when the personal notice should be more or less simultaneous with the public notice and when there were some laches on the part of the Government servants-in this matter the date of acquisition for the purpose of compensation in the case of this plaintiff-respondent only, should be the date of the personal notice, that is, 12.4.73.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J:-This Rule Nisi obtained under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic' of Bangladesh calls upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 16.12.85 passed by the respondent No. 1 the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, Dhaka in L.A. Miscellaneous Petition No. 38 of 1985 (Annexure E) and the decision dated 24.3.86 arrived at by the respondent No. 2 the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj in L.A. Case No. 32/81-82 (Annexure F) shall not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. The father of the petitioners was owner in possession of the premises situated on a land measuring about .047 acre of C.S. Plot No. 9209 corresponding to S.A. Plot No. 10753F appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 6334 and S.A. Khatian No. 5136 of Mouza, P.S. and District Kishoregonj. The respondent No.3, Sub-Divisional Co-operative Multipurpose Society, Ltd., Kishoregonj took monthly lease of the said premises and started cloth business therein. The respondent No. 3 is a private body engaged in profit earning businesses. It has many buildings at Kishoregonj which have been let out. The respondent No.3 defaulted in the payment, of rent. It also sublet a portion of the demised premises. The present petitioners succeeded to the estate of their father after his death and they needed the demised premises for their own use and occupation. The petitioners instituted O.C. Suit No. 264 of 1975 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Kishoregonj for ejectment of the respondent NO.3 and the suit was decreed on contest on 25.7.78. The petitioners instituted O.C. Execution Case No. 36 of 1978 for khas possession of the demised premises. The respondent No.3 preferred O.C. Appeal No. 216 of 1978 before the learned District Judge, Mymensingh and obtained stay of execution. The appeal was dismissed on 21.3.80. The respondent No.3 obtained a Rule in Civil Revision Case No. 975 of 1980 from the High Court Division and obtained a stay of execution of the Execution case. The Rule was discharged on contest with costs on 19.1.84. The petitioners were taking steps for eviction of the respondent No.3, when suddenly on 15.3.84 they received a notice under Section 6 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) for acquisition of the demised land as well as the structures thereon from the office of the Land Acquisition Officer at Mymensingh. On inquiry the petitioners came to know that having failed to resist the decree for eviction, the respondent No. 3 in collusion with the staff of the Land Acquisition Office at Mymensingh started L.A. Case No. 32/81-82 to grab the demised premises by way of acquisition. Notice under Section 3 of the said Ordinance was shown to have been issued on 20.6.83, but the petitioners never received such notice. Before issuance of notice under Section 3 no agreement was entered into by the respondent No.3 with the Government, as mandatorily required under Section 15 of the Ordinance. On 29.3.84 another notice purportedly issued under section 7(3) of the Ordinance was served upon the petitioners. On 1.2.84 Kishoregonj which was a sub-division was elevated to a District. A separate Land Acquisition Office started functioning from the very same date at Kishoregonj, Mymensingh Land Acquisition Office had no jurisdiction to proceed with the disputed property after 1.2.84. But the respondent No.3 got the file of L.A. Case No. 32 of 1981-82 moved in hot haste and some orders were shown to have been passed showing that on 15.3.84 notice under Section 6 of the Ordinance was issued, that on 16.3.84 the said notice was served, that 1.4.84 was fixed for giving formal delivery of possession and that on 2.4.84 certificate of possession was issued in favour of the respondent No.3

3. Upon receipt of the notice on 15.3.84 under Section 6 of the Ordinance the petitioners filed an objection on 1.4.84 to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) at Mymensingh stating the aforesaid facts and contending specifically that no notice under Section 3 of the Ordinance was ever served on them or at or near the acquired property. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Mymensingh fixed 8.4.84 and then 20.4.84 for hearing of the objection but ultimately did not hear the matter and sent the records of the case to the Land Acquisition Office at Kishoregonj. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Kishoregonj heard the objection and by order dated 2.5.85 recommended to the higher authority, namely, the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, Dhaka for cancellation of the proposal for acquisition of the disputed property on the following amongst other findings:

a) Notice u/s. 3 of the Ordinance was not served   as per law;

(b) Requiring body wanted to grab the property by any means;

(c) Non-Governmental body like the requiring body being a private body could have purchased any land, if necessary;

(d) The requiring-body has many buildings which

they have let out;

(e) Mymensingh District Land Acquisition Authority had no jurisdiction to pass any order after 1.2.84;

(f) The requiring body collusively obtained the orders :

(g) The disputed property was lying unused for a long time.

4. Against the aforesaid order the respondent No. 3 moved the respondent, No.1 being L.A. Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1985. The Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, Dhaka, the respondent No.1, discussed only the issue of jurisdiction and held that with effect from 1.2.84 the Mymensingh District Land Acquisition Office had no jurisdiction to deal with L.A. Case No. 32/81-82. He however did not advert to the above findings of fact by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Kishoregonj and simply directed that fresh proceedings be initiated by the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj from the stage of Section 4 (3)(b) of the said Ordinance.

5. Thereafter the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj entered into an agreement with the requiring body, respondent No.3, on 24.3.86 in respect of acquisition of the disputed property and clearly decided to go ahead with the acquisition proceedings from the stage of Section 4 (3) (b) of the Ordinance.

6. Being aggrieved affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by all the 3 respondents and a separate affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the respondent No.3. It has been stated that the Executive Officer of the Kishoregonj Sub-Divisional Multipurpose Society by a memo dated 17.11.80 submitted a proposal for acquisition of the disputed land under the provisions of Ordinance No. II of 1982. This very statement is a contradiction in terms, because there could be no proposal in 1980 for acquisition of a property under the Ordinance of 1982. Thereafter it is stated that the proposal was approved by the Mymensingh Land Allotment Committee after holding a joint inspection. Notice under Section 3 of the Ordinance was served on 23.6.83. No objection was received. After approval of valuation, per acre notice under Section 6 of the Ordinance was served and an award was prepared on the basis of the approved valuation. Then a notice under Section 7 of the Ordinance was served on the owners of the disputed land and they were asked to be present on the spot on 1.4.84 to receive the compensation money, but they did not appear. Although Kishoregonj was made a separate district from 1.2.84, the records of the Land Acquisition Department reached the new district headquarter on 26.4.84. Before the records reached the new district head quarter the Mymensingh, District Land Acquisition Office legally completed the procedure of acquisition including service of notice under Section 6 and 7 (aa) of the Ordinance. It is further stated that the deed of agreement with the respondent No.3 was signed by the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh on 21.3.85. It is claimed that the notice under section 3 was duly served on the spot and that the property has been acquired in the public interest.

7. The requiring body in the separate affidavit-in-opposition has only stated about the co-operative society and its performance and has generally supported the case of the Government-respondent.

8. In the affidavit-in-reply the petitioners have denied the averments made by the respondents. The first point urged by Mr. Abdur Rashid, learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that under Section 15 of the Ordinance, when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the Government in such form as may be prescribed "before a notice under Section 3 is published." He submits that the requiring body, the respondent No. 3, having not entered into any agreement with the Government before the alleged notice under Section 3 was published, the proceeding is absolutely without jurisdiction.

9. We find substance in the contention of Mr. Abdur Rashid. The provision of Section 15 is not directory but mandatory. Before the Deputy Commissioner acquires the jurisdiction to publish a notice under Section 3 an agreement with the non-Government requiring body is a sine qua non for the exercise of such power. It is a condition precedent. It cannot be whittled down by any device. It cannot be even accepted that an acquisition proceeding may be started without any agreement, but if a subsequent agreement is reached then it amounts to validation. The principle of subsequent validation cannot be entertained in a matter where the property rights of the citizen are involved. The affidavit-in-opposition filed by the 3 respondents together states that the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh signed the deed of agreement with the respondent No. 3 on 21.3.85. Mr. Fakhrul Islam, learned Assistant Attorney-General, could not show any such agreement from the files. On the contrary the petitioners have annexed a copy of the agreement entered into between the respondent No. 3 and the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj which shows that it was signed by the parties on 24.3.86. It is the case of the respondents that notice under Section 3 of the Ordinance was served on 23.6.83. Therefore on the very admission of the respondents the cart was put before the horse and the entire proceedings commenced without jurisdiction.

10. Mr. Abdur Rashid then assails the alleged notice under Section 3 on several grounds. He shows from the photocopy of the order sheet of L.A. Case No. 32/81-82 that it is the Land Acquisition Officer who signed the notice under Section 3 on 20.6.83. Under section 3 of the Ordinance it is the Deputy Commissioner who has to cause a notice to be published under the said Ordinance. Under Section 2(b) "Deputy Commissioner" includes an Additional Deputy Commissioner and any other officer authorised by the Deputy Commissioner to exercise any power conferred, or perform any duty imposed, on the Deputy Commissioner by or under this Ordinance. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has failed to produce any order by which the Deputy Commissioner authorised the Land Acquisition Officer, either by a general order or by a special order, to exercise the powers of the Deputy Commissioner under the said Ordinance. The notice under Section 3 also shows that it was not signed by the Deputy Commissioner. It was signed by the Land Acquisition Officer, Mymensingh. In the absence of any authorization we have no other alternative but to hold that the order under Section 3 and the notice under Section 3 were passed and issued unauthorisedly and are therefore without jurisdiction.

11. The recital of the notice under Section 3 is as follows:-

"Whereas the property described in the schedule is needed or is likely to be needed for the public purpose of Kishoregonj Sub-Divisional Central Co-Operative Society Ltd. and in the public interest

12. Mr. Abdur Rashid submits that it is no doubt in exercise of Section 3 of the Ordinance that a property can be acquired if it appears to the Deputy Commissioner that any property in any locality is needed or is likely to be needed for any public purpose but in the notice under Section 3 the Deputy Commissioner cannot simply quote the provision of Section 3. He has to say whether the property in question is needed, or, alternatively, whether it is likely to be needed. But he cannot say at the same time that it is both needed or is likely to be needed. If he says so, then he is not sure whether the need is immediate or proximate. He has not applied his mind. The order, the notice, he submits, will fail for non-application of mind.

13. We do not find any escape from this submission of Mr. Abdur Rashid. The law of acquisition gives the Deputy Commissioner the power to acquire property in the likelihood of two situations. First, if the property is needed. Or, if the properly is likely to be needed. A property is either needed or it is likely to be needed, but while acquiring a property the Deputy Commissioner cannot keep both the alternatives in his pocket. He has to choose between the two. If he keeps both the options open, then he docs not know whether the property is needed for immediate use or it is likely to be needed for some future use. The use of both these alternative expressions in the notice under Section 3 is indicative of a lack of application of mind and the nonce under Section 3 is liable to be struck down on will ground as well.

14. Mr. Abdur Rashid next submits that there is no disclosure of public purpose or any public interest in the notice under Section 3. Mr. Fakhrul Islam submits that the public purpose can be gathered from the notice, first, because it is acquired for a co-operative society which runs its businesses for public benefit and, secondly because, the agreement between the requiring body and the Government dated 24.3.86 shows that the respondent No. 3 shall operate co-operative consumers in the acquired land.

<u>15. This explanation is far from satisfactory. Acquisition for a co-operative society per se is not a public purpose. The purpose for which the Co- operative Society proposes to use the acquired land is the ultimate test for a decision as to whether the acquisition is for a public purpose or not. There is a total lack of disclosure in the notice under Section 3 as to for what purpose the Co-operative Society needs the acquired land. The need to state the precise public purpose in the body of the notice under Section 3 is imperative, because under Section 4 of the Ordinance any person interested in the disputed properly has the right to object to the acquisition of the property challenging the public purpose stated therein, but if no specific public purpose is stated in the notice then the right given to the objector under Section 4 is rendered nugatory and illusory. Beside's, under Section 17 no property acquired under the Ordinance shall be used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it is acquired, without the prior approval of the Government. If it is so used, the requiring body shall be liable to surrender the acquired property to the Deputy Commissioner on being directed by him to do so. If the public purpose is left completely vague and unspecified then this will give a handle to the requiring body to use the acquired property in any manner it deems fit and the acquiring authority can subsequently do nothing about it. Further, the petitioners are not supposed to look into the agreement between there querying body and the Government executed long 3 years after the notice under section 3 was published to know for sure the precise public purpose for which the land was sought to be acquired. Hence on the ground of lack of public purpose the acquisition proceedings fail.</u>

16. Coming to the impugned order of the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, Dhaka Mr. Abdur Rashid submits that the Additional Commissioner did not advert to the findings of fact given by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Kishoregonj, who found that notice under Section 3 of the Ordinance was not served in accordance with law, the requiring body wanted to grab the disputed property by any means, non- Government body like the requiring body being a private body could have purchased any land if necessary, the requiring body has many buildings which they have let out, the requiring body collusively obtained the orders and that the disputed premises was lying unutilised for a long time. Without setting aside the aforesaid findings of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Mr. Abdur Rashid submits, the Additional Commissioner acted illegally in sustaining the notice under Section 3 and in directing the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj to proceed from the stage of section 4(3)(b) of the Ordinance.

17. When the Additional Commissioner directed the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj to proceed from the stage of Section 4(3)(b) of the Ordinance, there is a presumption that he rejected the petitioner's contentions upheld by the Additional Deputy Commissioner. In all fairness the Additional Commissioner should have given a finding on those issues. Without disposing of those issues the Additional Commissioner could not have directed the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj to proceed under Section 4 (3)(b) of the Ordinance. As we have independently found that the notice under Section 3 suffers from a total lack of jurisdiction, we need not dwell at length on this point.

18. Mr. Rashid finally submits that the impugned proceedings are malafide and have been taken recourse to by the requiring body in collusion with the staff of the Land Acquisition Office at Mymensingh in order to thwart and subvert the decree obtained by the petitioners for the ejectment of the respondent No.3.

19. The litigations and the results thereof are not denied by the respondent No.3. The way the acquisition proceedings were started, even without any agreement with the requiring body under Section 15, the way the various notices were hurried through and the way the Mymensingh Land Acquisition Office chose to exercise powers over the disputed property even after it ceased to have any jurisdiction over the same, lead to the inevitable conclusion that the respondent No.3 had devised this novel means of circumventing and thwarting a valid decree of the Civil Court. The acquisition proceedings are therefore a colourable exercise of powers.

20. The learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that the petitioners have not exhausted the remaining remedies available to them after the Additional Commissioner passed his order. Since the proceedings have been found by us to be without jurisdiction, the petitioners need not have pursued any other alternative remedy.

21. For all the above reasons we hold that the impugned orders have been passed without lawful authority and that those are of no legal effect.

The Rule is accordingly made absolute but without any order as to costs.

End.
