parties:
Muzahiduddin Ahmed, Chairman, Deokapan, Union Parishad ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Munsif, Sunamganj, Sylhet and 48 others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.—This Rule arises out of an order passed by the Election Tribunal, Sunamganj, Sylhet rejecting an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as not maintainable.

2. Facts leading to this application in brief ate that the petitioner was elected as Chairman of the Deokapan Union Parishad under P.S. Chattak, district Sylhet. Respondent No. 2 filed an application before the Election Tribunal challenging the election of the petitioner. On the date fixed for hearing the petitioner who was respondent before the Tribunal, failed to appear and the case was heard ex-parte, and the Tribunal by its order dated 10-4-75 declared the election of the returned candidate, namely, that of the petitioner as illegal and void. The petitioner thereafter filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte order dated 10-4-75 being Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1975. The Tribunal held that the application under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable on the ground that there was no provision in the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973 for setting aside or reviewing an order passed by the Tribunal. The respondent No. 2 entered appearance and contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition.

3. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has urged only one ground in support of the Rule that in view of the provisions of Rules 61A and 61B of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973, the Tribunal acts as a Civil Court and as such the Tribunal is entitled to exercise all the powers conferred upon it under the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 61A relating to the Procedure before the Tribunal runs as follows :

Rule 61A: "Subject to the provisions of these rules, every election petition shall be tried, as nearly as may be, in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil, Procedure 1908.

Provided that the Tribunal may—

(a) make a memorandum of the substance of the evidence of each witness as his examination proceeds unless it considers that there is special reasons for taking down the evidence of any witness in full ; and

(b) refuse to examine a witness if it considers that his evidence is not material or that he has been called on a frivolous ground for-the purpose of delaying the proceedings."

Rule 61B:—Power of the Tribunal runs as follows :—

"The Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1898."

<u>4. A perusal of the above quoted rules would clearly show that it was never the intention of the Legislature to convert the Election Tribunal into a full fledged Civil Court or to invest it with all the powers under the Code of Civil Procedure. The expression "as nearly as may be" occurring in rule 61A and the expression "shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898" occurring in rule 61B clearly show that the Tribunal would be deemed. to be a Civil Court only for a limited purpose. The use of the word 'deemed' in this Rule definitely indicates that the Tribunal is not ordinarily a Civil Court but it shall be considered to be so ill respect of the proceeding before it for some specified purpose but not for all purposes. Then again, rule 57 which deals with the appointment of Tribunal is as follows:-</u>

<u>Rule 57  "For the trial of election petitions, the Election Commission shall by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint an Officer to be an Election Tribunal for such area as may be specified in the notification:</u>

<u>Rule 58 which deals with the power to transfer election petitions is as follows ;-</u>

<u>Rule 58; "The Election Commission, either of its own motion or on an application made in this behalf any of the parties, may, at any stage, transfer an election petition from one Tribunal to another Tribunal and the Tribunal to which the petition is so transferred shall proceed with the trial of the petition from the state which at it was transferred;</u>

<u>Provided that the Tribunal to which an Election petition is so transferred may, if it thinks fit, recall and examine any of the witnesses already examined."</u>

If we examine. the rules 61A and 61B along with the rules 57 and 58 it would be evident that the power of appointment of Tribunal has been vested with the Election Commission and the Election Commission can appoint any person, not necessarily a judicial officer, to constitute the Election Tribunal. The fact that in this particular case a Munsif, namely, a judicial officer or in other cases other Munsifs, were appointed as Election Tribunals, would not automatically convert them into a Civil Court. Under rule 58, the Election Commission is the only authority to transfer an election petition from one Tribunal to another either suo-motu or on the application of a party. This shows that the Election Commission is the controlling authority over an Election Tribunal. Another significant feature to note is that the decision or the Election Tribunal has been made final under Rule 62 (3) and no appeal has been provided for against the decision of the Tribunal. Then again, in the procedure prescribed for the trial of election petitions significant departures have been made from the ordinary procedure as will be evident from Rules 6IA(a) and 61A(b) quoted above. The sole purpose of constituting the Election Tribunal is for expeditious trial of the election petitions under the Rules in order to avoid delay which is inevitable under the ordinary procedure, otherwise the ordinary Civil Courts could have been empowered to try the election petitions without the necessity of framing these specific rules for the purpose. These facts to our mind, is clear and unmistakable manner detract from the character of a Civil Court. These rules, in our opinion, clearly show that the Tribunal is neither a full pledged Civil Court nor has it been invested with all the powers available under the Code of Civil Procedure. The only relief which can be granted to a party is laid down in rule. 60 and the Election Tribunal is 'not competent to travel beyond the said rule.

<u>5. The view we have taken also finds, support from a decision of this Court in the case of Shamsul Huq Sikdar Vs. Election Tribunal, reported in 27 DLR 188 to which one of us was a party. In the said case the question for consideration was whether the Tribunal had the power to grant temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After elaborate discussion the Court held that the Election Tribunal not being a Civil Court it had no power to grant temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

6. The position may be further clarified with reference to the Constitution of the Labour Court under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 wherein a similar provision," namely, section 36(2) which is almost identical to rule 61B of the Rules runs as follows :-

Section 36 (3)-"A Labour Court shall for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute, be deemed to be a civil court and shall have the same powers as are vested in such Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) including the powers of-

(a) enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath

(b) compelling the production of documents and material objects; and

(c) issuing commission for the examination of witnesses and documents.

7. Section 36(2) of the Industrial Relation Ordinance came in for interpretation before a Division Beach of this Court In the case of Bangladesh Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. Vs. The Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong reported in 27 DLR 367, wherein a question arose whether the Labour Court adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute is a Civil Court. Notwithstanding the provision that the Chairman of the Labour Court must be a judicial officer of the status of a District Judge as per section 35(3) of the said Ordinance, it has been held in the said case that the Labour Court is not a Civil Court but it shall have all the powers of a Civil Court for regulating the procedure for deciding an industrial dispute.

8. Having regard to these facts and circumstances we are clearly of the view that the Election Tribunal is not a Civil Court and as such the Tribunal was justified in rejecting the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as not maintainable.

The Rule is accordingly discharged. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we make no order as to costs.

Ruhul Islam, J.—I agree.

End.

caseno:
Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 with Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989. 
Writ Petition No. 374 of 1990 and Writ Petition No. 644 of 1989.
lawyer:
M. Amir-ul Islam with Tania Amir and Shirin Sharmin Chowdhury, Advocates—For the Petitioners in all the four writ petitions.
Md. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General with Md. Altafur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General — For the Respondent Nos.1-4 in all the four writ petitions. 
Zainul Abedin with Zakir Hossain Munshi, Advocates — For the Respondent No.6 in all the four writ petitions
MA Hannan with M Khaled Ahmed, Advocates — For the Respondent No.7 in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989
parties:
Abed Ali and others  ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed J : These four writ petitions have been heard together and are disposed of by this judgment.

2. The facts giving rise to these four writ petitions and the questions of law involved therein are the same.

3. The case of the petitioners in all the four writ petitions are that they were respective owners of the lands described in Annexure-A respectively in the four respective writ petitions and these lands were at first requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 on 29.1.1963 in Land Acquisition Case No. 159 of 1961-1962 hereinafter called as LA Case No. 159 of 1961-1962. Thereafter the Government decided to acquire these lands and accordingly notified the same for the purpose of acquisition under section 5 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act of 1948. There is no dispute that the procedures required for requisition and acquisitions under the said Act were followed. Compensation was also assessed and was also duly paid to all the owners of these lands including the petitioners and the predecessor in-interest of some of the substituted petitioners in these writ petitions. It is also the accepted position that these lands were acquired for setting up a satellite town for settlement and rehabilitation of the people on the outskirts of Dhaka City. Although initially it was alleged by the petitioners that these lands were acquired for the purpose of settling the refugees arrived here from India, at the time of hearing this case it was not pursued and it was accepted by the petitioners that in fact these lands were acquired for the purpose of settlement and rehabilitation of people by establishing a satellite town there. It is then alleged by the petitioners that although the lands described in the respective schedules of the four writ petitions were acquired with other lands in the said LA Case No. 159 of 1961-1962 the lands described in the respective schedules of the four writ petitions were not at all utilized by the Government or by the agencies for which these lands had been acquired and these lands were left vacant and totally unutilized. It is further alleged that the petitioners are in occupation of these lands despite acquisition thereof and by constructing their houses, etc. they live there. The further case of the petitioners is that since the Government did not utilized these lands for the purpose for which these were acquired the Government is under an obligation to release these lands from acquisition. In all these writ petitions in the prayer portion it has, however, been prayed that a direction may be issued by this Court for the purpose of releasing these unutilized lands from 'requisition' and the word 'acquisition' has not been used in any of the prayer portions of these writ petitions, although admittedly these lands had been acquired after initial requisition thereof under the Act of 1948. It has further been alleged in the writ petitions that in fact the Government adopted a policy of releasing these unutilized lands in favor of the previous owners and in pursuance of this policy asked the petitioners to appear before the respondent No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka with all necessary papers. In pursuance of the above instruction the petitioners in fact appeared before the respondents Nos. 2 and 3 with all their papers relating to these lands but no action was taken by the respondent to release these lands and ultimately the petitioners have come to know that they have no contemplation to release these lands according to the Government policy adopted earlier.

4. As such, the petitioners approached this Court with these four writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution praying for a direction to the effect that the above lands may be released in favour of the respective owners by the respondents and obtained the present Rules.

5. The respondent Nos. 1-4 entered appearance in all the four writ petitions and contested these writ petitions by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition contending that after acquisition of these lands under the provision of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 these properties has vested in the Government and the petitioners had been completely divested of their ownership and title in these lands and, as such, they cannot claim to get back possession of these lands as a matter of right. It is also contended that the petitioners have also received compensation for their respective lands acquired by the Government in the above LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 and after receiving payment of compensation there is no scope for them to claim release of these lands from acquisition. The next contention of the respondent Nos.1-4 is that the disputed lands are being utilised for the very purpose for which these had been acquired and the work of setting up the satellite town and the work of settlement and rehabilitation of people are taking place since their acquisition and, as such, there is no substance in the allegation of the petitioners that these lands are unutilised and would also remain unutilised. It has been further contended by them that if any of the petitioners are in occupation of any portion of these acquired lands then such occupation by them is without any authority and as trespassers.

6. The respondent No. 6, Chairman, T & T Board in all the writ petitions also entered appearance and contested these writ petitions by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition contending that certain lands out of the aforesaid acquired lands were allotted to the T & T Board for construction of quarters for the staff of the said Board and the Board is in occupation of these lands and they had already taken up the work of construction in the lands allotted to them.

7. The respondent No. 7, Bangladesh Film Development Corporation in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989 also entered appearance and contested this writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it has been contended that the said Corporation has also been allotted some lands out of the acquired lands for the purpose of construction of quarters for the staff of the Corporation and the Corporation is already in possession of these lands and also proceeded with the work of construction of the staff quarters.

8. In view of the above, the contesting respondents contend, all the writ petitions are liable to be dismissed and the Rules are liable to be discharged.

9. In all these four writ petitions certain facts are admitted.

10. Before we enter into the merits of the case of the parties in these four writ petitions we like to point out certain technical errors and omissions in framing the writ petitions such as, in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989 petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif has prayed for releasing as many as 8 plots being Plot Nos. 5, 10, 29, 60, 66, 83, 87 and 90 comprising an area of 1.33 acres of land of Mouza Lalasarai, JL No. 273 as at Annexure-A to this writ petition. The petitioners have also filed the notice under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 served on this petitioner while requisitioning his property under the said Act before acquisition of his property under the same Act. This notice under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 as at Annexure-B to this writ petition shows that only one plot being Plot No. 83 of Mouza Lalasarai JL No. 273 belonging to petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif was requisitioned and ultimately acquired. We have not been able to understand why along with this plot No. 83 seven other plots were included in Annexure-A to this writ petition by the petitioners against the name of petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif. Such discrepancies are in almost in all the writ petitions and in respect of many of the petitioners. Be that as it may, for these technical errors in framing the writ petitions, the writ petitions cannot be knocked down holding that these are not maintainable, because, in spite of these technical errors we feel relief can be granted if the court ultimately finds the petitioners have been able to make out their case.

11. In all these writ petitions the basic facts are admitted. It is admitted that in LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 the lands attracted in the writ petitions, hereinafter called as the disputed lands, were at first requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 with effect from 29.1.63. It is also admitted that thereafter these lands were finally acquired by the Government under section 5 of East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 with effect from 22.10.70. It is also not disputed that the Government paid compensation to all the respective owners of the lands attracted in LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 and these owners including the petitioners received payment of their respective shares of the compensation.

12. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has argued that the lands as described in the four writ petitions are still lying vacant and unutilised by the Government and are in possession of the respective petitioners of the four writ petitions. He has also argued that in view of the above situation, from equitable standpoint and for the purpose of enforcing the purpose of the Constitution of Bangladesh which its Preamble vows as securing economic and social justice for its citizens, should be returned to the respective previous owners by releasing these lands from acquisition. He has also drawn our attention to certain Government policy decisions in the matter whereby, according to him, the Government expressed its intention to release all unutilised acquired lands in favour of the previous owners and has argued that after announcing this policy decision the Government is not empowered to go back on the said decision and is estopped from doing so and, as such, this Court in exercise of its power under Article 102 of the Constitution may issue a direction on the Government to implement the policy decision as the said policy decision is completely in conformity with the vows of the Constitution-makers as expressed in its Preamble, that the Constitution would secure economic and social justice for all its citizens. Mr. Islam has also drawn our attention to section 17 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 wherein it has been laid down that no property acquired under the said Act should, without prior approval of the Government, be used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it is acquired and, if so used, or does not use it for the purpose for which it is acquired, the Deputy Commissioner may take possession of such property and has then argued that this provision has been enacted in the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 only to give effect to the above vows in the preamble of the Constitution to secure economic and social justice to all its citizens, by returning such lands to the previous owners.

13. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General representing the respondent Nos. 1-4, has advanced a very simple contention submitting that since the disputed lands had been acquired by the Government under section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. 1948 these lands had been completely vested in the Government and the petitioners had been divested of their ownership, right and title therein and, as such, the petitioners have no vested right of any sort whatsoever in these lands. Consequently, according to the learned Deputy Attorney General, they cannot claim release of these lands in their favour as a matter of right. He has further drawn our attention to section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and has contended that under the said section the Government could release any property from acquisition only before compensation was paid to the effected owners and after the compensation had been paid no acquired property could be released by the Government. He has further contended that the provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 having been promulgated long after the disputed lands had been acquired by the Government under the provision of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and had completely vested in the Government, the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, is not at all applicable.

14. Mr. Zainul Abedin, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 6 in all the four writ petitions, has contended that the Government have already allotted some portions of the disputed lands to them for construction of quarters for their staff and they had already taken possession thereof and proceeded with some construction thereon and, as such, the allegations of the petitioners that these lands are still unutilised have no substance.

15. Mr. M A Hannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 7 in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989, has also submitted that some portions of the above acquired lands were allotted to the respondent No. 7 for construction of quarters for the staff and the respondent No. 7 have also taken possession thereof and have also proceeded with some work on the said land and, as such, the petitioners are not entitled to get these lands released and delivered to them.

<u>16. Since the disputed lands were admittedly at first requisitioned under the provision of section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and then acquired under section 5 of the said Act let us first of all decide the legal effect of such requisition and ultimate acquisition of these lands. In this connection sub-section (7) of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 may be referred to but before doing so, it may be stated briefly that sub-sections (1) to (6) of section 5 lay down the procedure which, before an order for acquisition under section 5, were to be undergone. We do not like to elaborate the above sub-sections since it is not disputed by the petitioners that the procedures laid down in sub-sections (1) to (6) of section 5 for completing the acquisition processes were duly and correctly undergone by the Deputy Commissioner concerned who under the said section was empowered to effect acquisition.</u>

<u>Sub-section (7) of section 5 runs as follows:</u>

<u>"(7) The Government shall then publish in the official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such property shall end."</u>

<u>It is not disputed that the Gazette Notification as required by sub-section (7) of section 5 of the above Act was duly published in the Dhaka Gazette, November, 5, 1970 at page 148. So by operation of sub-section (7) of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 the above lands completely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and from the date of vesting of the property in the Government the petitioners were completely divested of their ownership, right and title in these lands, so the petitioners have no legal right to claim release of these properties unless such right is conferred on them by any statutory provision. We have not been able to find any statutory provision conferring such right except section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, which runs as follows :—</u>

<u>"8B. Withdrawal from Acquisition: When the owner of any property which has been acquired under section 5 is willing to receive back the property, the Government may, at any time before the payment of compensation, withdraw from the acquisition of any such property by notification published in the Official Gazette, and on such withdrawal, the property shall be restored to the possession of the owner, and with effect from the date of such restoration, the property shall vest back in the owner the rights which he had before such property was acquired.</u>

<u>"A close reading of the above provision shows that when the owner of any property which had been acquired under section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, was willing to receive back the property, the Government might, at any time before compensation was paid, withdraw from the acquisition of any such property. The section appears to confer full discretionary power on the Government either to withdraw from acquisition or not, if any owner of acquired property expressed willingness to receive backs such acquired property. The said section did not impose on the Government absolute liability to release such property in case the owner of the acquired property was willing to receive back the property. This is absolutely clear from the word "may" occurring after the word "Government" in the said section. The second condition was that the Government was also empowered to release such property if compensation had not been paid to the affected owners. So this section did not confer absolute right on the petitioners to get back the acquired property, on the other hand, it was left to the discretion of the Government either to release such property or not. Moreover, such withdrawal from acquisition could not be affected if compensation had already been paid to the affected owners. In the present case, admittedly compensation had already been paid to the affected owners and, as such, the question of applying section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 could not arise. Similar view was taken by this Court in two similar cases in Writ Petition Nos. 526 of 1992 and 146 of 1989 and this view was affirmed by the learned Appellate Division of this Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 249 and 255 of 1993.</u>

17. Moreover, since the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is no longer in existence having expired on 15th August, 1982 (section 1(4) of the said Act read with the notification published in the Dacca Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 16th August, 1948, whereby this Act came into force on 16th August 1948) section 8B thereof cannot be applied now for releasing the disputed properties.

18. Acknowledging the difficulty of applying section 8B of the said Act Mr. Islam has taken shelter not under any provision of the said Act but under the umbrella of section 17 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and has argued that the intent of section 17 is that if any property, whether acquired either before or after the enactment of the said ordinance, is utilized for any purpose other than for which it has been acquired the Deputy Commissioner is empowered to take possession of such property which means that the Deputy Commissioner will in such circumstances release the property in favour of the previous owner. Mr. Islam has also argued that this section should be read with the intent of the constitution-makers as expressed in the Preamble of the Constitution which vows for securing economic and social justice for the citizens of this court.

19. We have not been able to subscribe to the views expressed by Mr. Islam.

<u>20. A plain reading of section 17 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, clearly shows that this section is applicable when a property is acquired under Part II of the said Ordinance. It is also clear that this section is not applicable if the acquisition has been made under the provision of any other law for the time being in force. If the intention of the legislature was, while enacting this section, to include all the acquired lands under the provisions of any law, whatsoever, the legislature would have clearly stated that the section would be applicable to all lands acquired under the provision of any law whatsoever and not only to lands acquired under Part II of the Ordinance, Consequently, section 17 of the Ordinance cannot be applied to secure release of the disputed lands as has been argued by Mr. Islam.</u>

<u>21. It further appears from section 17 of the Ordinance that the said Ordinance has not conferred any right on the owners of the acquired lands but simply empowers the Deputy Commissioner to take possession of such acquired lands as are left unutilised or are not utilised for the purpose for which they have been acquired. There is nothing in the section to show that after resuming possession of such unutilised lands the Deputy Commissioner or, so to say, the Government will be under any liability to return the lands to the previous owners. It appears to us that the manner of dealing with such resumed land has been left completely to the discretion of the Government and the Government in its discretion can also hand over these lands to the previous owners or to utilise these lands for any public purpose. As such, we are unable to subscribe to the view expressed by Mr. Islam that in view of section 17 of the Ordinance the Government is under a legal liability to return the disputed lands to the petitioners.</u>

22. Mr. Islam has also undertaken considerable exercise in order to emphasise that this Court should apply the object of the Constitution as expressed in its Preamble and should apply the principles of equity.

<u>23. In answer to the above contention of Mr. Islam it can be said that in its writ jurisdiction conferred by Article 102 of the Constitution, the object set forth in the Preamble cannot be enforced although the Preamble can be used as an aid to interpretation of the Constitution or any other statutory provision if there is any equivocality or ambiguity in such provision of the Constitution or such statute. Article 102 of the Constitution empowers this Court to issue mandate only for enforcement of fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution (clause (1) of Article 102) and also to compel a person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to do which he is required by law to do (clause (2) of Article 102). The power to issue mandate or any writ in the nature of mandamus is, therefore, limited by the purposes mentioned in clauses (1) and (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution, Consequently, this Court in its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot issue a writ for enforcement of an equitable right, because, this court while exercising its power under Article 102 of the Constitution, is not a Court of Equity. Moreover, assuming that it will be most inequitable and repugnant to the concept of social justice to acquire private properties of citizens, it may be pointed out that the said concept of equity and social justice enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution is hedged in by Article 42 of the Constitution as well as Article 47 of the Constitution. Article 42 of the Constitution has guaranteed the right to property of every citizen on the one hand and immediately thereafter by enacting clause (2) has put restriction on the right of an individual to enjoy his property by authorizing the Government to nationalize, acquire and requisition private property and also laying down that no law enacted relating to the acquisition, nationalization or requisition of private property can be called in question in any Court even on the ground that any provision in such law relating to payment of compensation is inadequate in any Court. In addition to enacting Article 42(2) of the Constitution, the makers of the Constitution have provided that no law relating to compulsory acquisition, nationalization or requisition of any property can be called in question and can be deemed to be void even on the ground that such law is inconsistent with or takes away any of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution. As such, however inequitable the principle of acquisition of private property may seem to appear the above provisions of the Constitution itself have provided that such inequity cannot be remedied by the Court.</u>

24. Last of all, Mr. Islam has drawn our attention to certain decision of the Government whereby the Government expressed its intention to release such acquired properties as are left unutilised or are not utilised for the purpose for which such properties had been acquired and has argued that the Government is bound by this decision. In this connection, Mr. Islam has referred to certain communication and certain news-items appearing in newspapers. The first communication to which Mr. Islam has referred is a semi-official letter from the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to all the Secretaries to the Government. This letter is at Annexure-C to Writ Petition No.167 of 1989. A perusal of this letter shows that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms observed that since the area of land in Bangladesh is very limited it is necessary to utilise every inch of such land. It has also been observed that many agencies get private lands acquired for various public purposes but do not utilise these lands and leave these lands unutilised for years together. It was then suggested that land in excess of what is absolutely necessary for the purpose for which it is acquired should not be acquired and, lastly, it was informed that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms had taken a decision that if any land was left unutilised for more than a reasonable period of time such land would be released from acquisition and would be returned to the previous owners. Mr. Islam has also referred to another semi-official letter addressed by the Hon'ble Minister of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to all the other Hon'ble Ministers. In these letter also similar observations as in the letter as at Annexure-G were made and the Hon'ble Ministers to whom this letter was addressed were requested to surrender the land left unutilised in favour of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. There is, however, nothing in this letter to show that the Government intended to return the lands to the previous owners. Mr. Islam has then referred to another news item published in the Bangladesh Observer, dated 23rd August, 1983 as at Annexure-C 1 to the writ petition. In this news item news was published to the effect that the Government had decided to return unutilised lands to the respective affected owners and accordingly, according to this news item, the District Administration, Dhaka requested all the previous owners to bring to its notice all cases of unutilised lands.

25. From the above it appears that the Government was considering a proposal for returning unutilised lands to the previous owners. It also appears that in this respect, the Government also took certain steps and called for certain particulars of such unutilised lands. We have now to see whether such proposal and such decision taken by the Government have vested any right in the petitioner to get the disputed lands released. It appears to us that the above decision or proposal of the Government was an internal matter of the Government and the Government had been considering the said proposal. It also appears that the said proposal of the Government did not mature into any enactment or rule or even notification or final decision to return the unutilised acquired lands to the previous owners. Consequently, we find that on the basis of such proposal pending for consideration of the Government no right was created in the petitioners to claim back the disputed lands which had vested in the Government by operation of law. Moreover, it appears to us that even if such decision to return such land to the previous owners had been finally taken, it would remain the sole discretion of the Government as to which land should be returned and which land should be retained in its possession. To our view, such decision and such proposal cannot create any right in the petitioners to claim back the acquired lands which previously belonged to them. We are also of the view that the said proposal and the said internal decision of the Government cannot act as estoppel to prevent the Government from altering the decision. We are also of the view that no mandate can be issued by this Court in its power under Article 102(2) of the Constitution to direct the Government to implement the aforesaid proposal expressed in the letter as at Annexure-C and the news item, Annexure-C1.

26. The petitioners have alleged that the disputed lands were acquired for the purpose of settlement and rehabilitation of people by establishing a satellite town but even more than 30 years after the Government took possession of these lands large areas of these lands are still lying vacant. In reply to this the contesting respondents contended that these lands are being utilised step by step. It has also been averred in the affidavit-in-opposition sworn by the respondent No. 6 in Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 that they have taken possession of the portion of the disputed lands which had been allotted to them and they have preceded with the work of construction of their staff quarters. Similarly, the respondent No. 7 in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989 have averred in their affidavit in opposition that they have also taken possession of that portion of the disputed land which had been allotted to them and they have proceeded with the work constructing quarters for their staff to some extent. These facts are not disputed by the petitioners. Moreover, in a supplementary-affidavit sworn by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 a report of enquiry made by the office of the Deputy Commissioner Dhaka has been produced. This report is at Annexure-Kha to the supplementary-affidavit sworn on 19.7.95. This report shows that some of the plots are vacant and in these lands there are still houses in which some of the petitioners live. It has also been stated that various portions of the disputed lands had been utilised by various organizations to whom these lands had been allotted. It appears to us that these lands are being allotted to various organization’s from time to time and the establishment of satellite town for settlement and rehabilitation of people are taking place step by step. It, therefore, appears to us that the allegations that these lands are not likely to be utilised for the purpose for which these had been acquired, is not correct.

27. In the result, we find that the petitioners cannot get any relief in these writ petitions.

28. The Rules in all the four writ petitions are, accordingly, discharged without any order as to costs.

29. The orders of status quo granted by this Court earlier in all the four writ petitions are vacated.

End.

Bangladesh ----- Appellant in all the appeals.
Vs.
Haji Abdul Gani Biswas and others ----- Respondent in C.A No. 31 of 1974 ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haidar Chowdhury, J :-These appeals arise out of judgment passed by the High Court Division in writ petition Nos. 85, 96, 100, 109, 111, 113, 126, 136, 137, 142, 145, 151, 152, 153, 154, 176, 177, 192, 200, 361, 382, 422, 450, 514, 159, 163, 190, 197 and 303 of 1973 and 11, 12, 14, 19, 24, 26, 27, 52, 56, 57, 58, 59, 117, 139, 232, 261, 367 add 565 of 1974 which were heard analogously under Article 102 of the Constitution making the said Rule absolute. These are certificated appeals under Article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution.

Facts of all the appeals need not be recounted except one as the matters were proceeded on one common ground of validity of some laws which will be mentioned hereafter.

2. Facts of the case in writ petition No. 85 of 1974 are that the respondent No. 1 purchased the land from respondent No. 3 with an agreement to reconvey the said land. The agreement is dated 26.4.63 which stipulated that the land will be reconvened if the money is repaid within 10 years. The respondent No. 3 made an application under section 9(4) and (5) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to the Respondent No. 2 for restoration of possession of the said land. This petition was allowed on 30-3-73 and thereafter the respondent No. 1 filed the writ petition urging inter alia that the said order is without lawful authority inasmuch as section 95A of the aforesaid Act does not cover the case of the pure sale with an agreement to recovery. An out and out sale accompanied by an agreement for reconveyance is within the purview of the President's Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 whereby provisions of section 95 of the Act have been amended and a new section being section 95A has been inserted in the said Act. A number of writ petitions were filed and the High Court Division disposed of these petitions by one judgment as the same question of law of public importance had been rayed and on consideration of which a certificate was also granted. Vires of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 was also challenged whereby section 95A was inserted and the constitutionality of President's Order No. 24 of 1973 was also challenged. The High Court Division after hearing the arguments came to the conclusion that (a) a transaction of out and out sale; with an agreement to reconvey within the meaning of section 95A must be in sense a mortgage: (b) a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey is not a transaction within the am bit of section 95A; (c) section 95A has no application to a transaction which has been passed and closed before the relevant President's Order was promulgated (d) section 95A cannot be invoked in respect of a transaction which has been entered into before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation in the area in which the land in question lies. Bangladesh is the appellant. The learned Attorney General appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court Division erred in holding that the word transfer" in section 95 of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act must be construed as meaning a transfer by mortgage. It is contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed substantial error of law in adding words into the Statutes. It was canvassed that the intention of the legislature was to cover even sale with an agreement to reconvey and the High Court Division was wrong in applying the different rules of Interpretation to construe the work transfer as transfer by mortgage. It was further contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong in applying the so-called mischief rule as enunciated in Heydorm’s case to hold that the words out and out sale with agreement to reconvey refer to a Mortgage by conditional sale. It was overlooked that a sale with an agreement for reconveyance is distinct from mortgage by conditional sale. The High Court Division had erred in holding that the President's Order 24 of 1973 has led to the constitutional difficulty which, however, was a mere amendment of a grammatical error, Lastly it was contended that the High Court Division had erroneously taken the view that President's Order No. 24 of 1973 affected certain vested right to .property which is vocative of the fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.

3. Before we consider the relevant contentions it will be relevant to consider section 95A which was inserted by amendment. It will also be relevant to note that sub-section (4) and (5) were added to section 95 of the Act by Article 2 of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. The words and comma within brackets i.e. either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey'' was inserted by amendment by Presidents Order No. 136 of 1972 and the word 'or' was inserted after words and comma "agreement to reconvey" by President's Order No. 24 of 1973. Again sub-Section (4) of section 95 was substituted for the former sub-section (4) by President's Order No. 24 of 1973. After all these amendments section 95 and 95A as stand today are as follows:-

"95 (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, a raiyat shall not enter into any form of unfructuary. mortgage other that a complete unfructuary mortgage in respect of his holding or of a portion or share thereof; and every such complete unfructuary mortgage shall be subject to the same limitation as are imposed by section 90 on a transfer of the holding of a raiyat or of any share or portion thereof and the period for which such compete unfructuary mortgage may be entered into by any raiyat shall not exceed by any agreement, express or implied, seven years;

provided that any such unfructuary mortgage may be redeemed at any time before the expiry of the said period, on payment of an amount which shall bear the same proportion to the total consideration money received by the mortgagor, as the unexpired period bears to the total period for which the mortgage had been entered into.

(2) Every such complete unfructuary mortgage shall be registered under the Registration Act, 1908.

(3) If any unfructuary mortgage entered into by a raiyat does not fulfill any of the conditions specified in sub-section (1) or is not registered as requited under sub-section (2) it shall be void.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, if any mortgagee prevents the redemption of a unfructuary mortgage after the expiry of the period of such mortgage to any officer authorised in this behalf by the Government, for such redemption or restoration and, on such application and in the case of redemption also on payment by the applicant of the amount by due to the mortgagee under the said proviso the Sub-divisional Magistrate or the Officer so authorised shall pass an order directing the mortgagee to restore possession of the mortgaged land to the applicant and to deliver up to the applicant all document in his possession or power relating to the mortgaged land by such date as may fixed in the order.

(5) If the mortgagee does not restore possession of the mortgagee land to the mortgagor by the date fixed under sub-section (4) the Sub divisional Magistrate or any Officer authorised in this behalf by the Government shall, on application made by the mortgagor, put the applicant in possession of such land by evicting the mortgagee therefrom and may, for such eviction, use or cause to be used such force as may be necessary.

95A. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof, either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete unfructuary mortgage for period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Second Amendment) Order 1972".

The learned Attorney General has placed the Judgment of the High Court Division which certainly cannot be assailed for brevity. The learned Judges had taken pains to consider the rules of interpretation which would be applicable for interpreting the relevant sections. Considerable attention was devoted as to which of the rules of interpretation should be applied, namely whether the literal rule or golden rule as propounded by Lord Wendeydal or Heydon's rule or mischief rule as suggested by Lord Coke. The High Court Division considered that the effect of impugned law in its literal interpretation is virtually a prohibition against the common form of transaction which is invoked in the society and further this legislation may well be considered discriminatory. It considered that the vested right to a property cannot be extinguished as purported to have been done President's Order No. 24 of 1973 and speculated that the consequences flowing from the impugned Presidential Orders construed literally would amount to a virtual embargo upon this common form of transaction and "if is more than likely that such a form of transaction shall fall into disuse in no time". It considered that the right of repurchase is a privileges granted (or the benefit of the seller which is essentially personal in character. The Pesiderit's Orders were considered in the background of previous law, namely, section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and disposed of the point by noting that "it is not necessary to speculate whether in view of this prohibition against creating a complete unfructuary mortgage in favour of a person other than a bonafide cultivator, some of the beneficial measures for giving relief to indebted agricultural tenants which were incorporated in the amended section 26G were not considered to be necessary to be included in section 95 at the time when the East Pakistan State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was enacted or where the legislature lost right of those judicial authorities which gave strict interpretation to the unfructuary mortgage as used in section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act in accordance with the terms of section 95(a) of the transfer of Property Act". The High Court Division on such consideration made the rules absolute and set aside the orders passed under section 95 read with section 95A.

4. The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 is a law relating to the landlord and the tenant. East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was promulgated for the acquisition by the State of the interest of the rent-receivers and certain other interest in land and "to define the law relating to tenancies to be held under the State after such a acquisition and other matters connected herewith". Part- V of the Act mainly deals with the rights and obligations of agricultural tenants which was so long controlled and regulated under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act and came in to force in different areas at different points of time, the earliest being 5-8-54 in the Subdivision of Patuakhali and the last being 5-8 65 in the District of Faridpur.

<u>5. Section 26G was introduced by amending Act IV of 1982 which came into force on 22-2-29. The object of the legislature was to protect a raiyat "so that no mahajan can keep a raiyat out of his land for more than 15 years at the most" in return for a, petty loan. This section permitted an occupancy raiyat to create a complete unfructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 15 years and did not allow him to create any unfructuary mortgage as defined in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act but the amending Act Of the Bengal Tenancy Act introduced a new definition of "complete unfructuary mortgage" by section 3(3), which says complete unfructuary mortgage means of transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interests thereon shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profit arising from the land during the period of mortgage". Under this sub-section the gradual process of reduction may not follow the strict rules of arithmetic. In other words no question of accounting arises unless an earlier redemption is proposed as contemplated by section 26G(2). It envisages automatic extinction of the loan both principal and interest within the stipulated period no matter whether the profits of land taken by the mortgagee had been of sufficient value to cover the total amount of the loan with interest thereon. The legal effect of it is that after expiry of the stipulated period the property automatically comes back to the mortgagor and the maximum period allowed by law was 15 years. The effect is that no unfructuary mortgage of the raiyati holding when even created can endure for a longer period than 15 years and they will be statutorily redeemed. Registration of documents creating a complete unfructuary mortgage for exceeding 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage was also forbidden and such documents were declared inadmissible in evidence., Thus a drastic change was made by Act IV of 1928 and a new type of mortgage being "complete unfructuary mortgage" was brought as a concept for the benefit of the raiyat. Litigations cropped up as to the retrospectively of his amendment and by Act IV of 1928, the legislature introduced section 26G(1) (a) and declared that every unfructuary mortgage created before 22-2-29 and which was subsisting on or after 1-8-38 (date of the commencement of the amendment) was to be deemed to be a complete unfructuary mortgage for period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years whichever is Jess. Sub-sections (5) and (6) were also inserted by Act VI of 1938 whereby it was provided that after the expiry of the period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years from the date of registration of the compete unfructuary mortgage or from the date of mortgagee’s entering into possession, as the case may be whichever is earlier, a complete unfructuary mortgage or an unfructuary mortgage sha1l be deemed to have been extinguished and the mortgagor there after would on application made either to civil court or revenue court be restored to possession. The Calcutta High Court in a number of decisions held that anomalous mortgage with possession given to the mortgagee, namely mortgage by conditional sale when the mortgagee had entered into possession was not covered by sub-section r) (a) and (5) [Badsha Mia Vs. Mobarrak Ali. 50 C. W.N. 578). Thereafter by amending Act XVIII of 1940 obviously for nullifying those decisions section 260 was further amended which provides that every form of mortgage executed before 22.2.29 and subsisting on or after 1.8.37 was to be deemed complete unfructuary mortgage if possession had been delivered to the mortgagee including a mortgage by conditional sale." The sub-section thus included a1l mortgages executed before 22.2.29 whether unfructuary or "anomalous" provided they were subsisting on 1-8-37 and as regards mortgages executed after the Act of 1928 it came to embrace all such mortgages whether "complete" unfructuary mortgage or "anomalous" mortgage provided they were executed before the Act 1940 and subsisting after the commencement of that Act. Sub-section (4) which created a bar against registration of documents creating unfructuary mortgage for more than 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage now added the "anomalous mortgage" to the list. Thus it is apparent by the amending Acts of 1928 and 1940 the legislature relieved the raiyat from all sorts of mortgages, namely (a) unfructuary mortgage. (b)a mortgage by conditional sale and (C) anomalous mortgages which are known concepts of the Transfer of Property Act. The raiyat can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage for which the definition was supplied by the Amending Act IV of 1928. It is not necessary to consider the incidents of unfructuary mortgage and mortgage by conditional sale or anomalous mortgage which are mentioned in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act. The law extricated the raiyat from those mortgages and laid down that he can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage which is to be valid for a period not exceeding 15 years after which such mortgage is extinguished and on application before the Civil Court or revenue court his possession is restored. Then came East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951). All the rent receiving interest were acquired with effect from 14-4-56 Section 95 of the Act provided that a raiyat could not enter into any form of unfructuary mortgage other than the complete unfructuary mortgage and every such complete unfructuary mortgage is subject to the limitation of section 90. Section 2(b) defined complete unfructuary mortgage which means a transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the purpose of securing the payment of money on the return of grain advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interest thereon, shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profits ensuing from the land during the period of the mortgage".</u>

<u>Originally it provided that the period would not exceed 15 years and the registration of documents was made compulsory. It further provided that if it is not a complete usufructuary mortgage or if the documents are not registered then the usufructuary mortgage is void. By the East Pakistan Ordinance XXI of 1969 the period was reduced to 7 years. Thus, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act placed an embargo that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force a raiyat shall not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than complete usufructuary mortgage." The Transfer of Property Act so far as mortgage of a raiyat holding is concerned is thus displaced Sub-sections (4) and (5) provided for less expensive and less time consuming remedy of redemption and /or restoration of possession by means of application before the authorised officer who will pass the order of restoring possession and, if necessary, by evicting the mortgagee by use of force. The amendment was made by President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and section 95A was inserted by the same President's Order. Section 95A provides that in any transaction when the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct of such holding, etc. for a specified period in lieu of such consideration then such transfer shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for not exceeding 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) will apply for restoration of possession. Thus, the historical background of this legislation is obvious, namely, that the raiyat is to be rescued from the clutches of the money lenders or mohajans who taking advantage of the property of the raiyat would force him to enter into a disadvantageous deal. To protect a raiyat from such transactions, the law-makers came to his rescue prohibiting him from entering into any kind of mortgage other than complete usufructuary mortgage and the maximum period for which he could transfer his land was reduced to 7 years whereupon the debt including the principal and interest stands liquidated and on an application before the authorised officer the raiyat could be put back into possession. Human ingenuity devised new contrivances and the hairsplitting decisions given by various courts as to whether the instrument in question created mortgage by conditional sale or usufructuary mortgage or anomalous mortgage led the legislature to come again to the rescue by disowning all sorts of mortgage other than the "complete usufructuary mortgage." The question as to what about a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to recovery has led to numerous litigations and on 4-11-72 President's Order No. 136 of 197). was enacted and section 95A was amended by insertion of the clause :</u>

<u>"either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey."</u>

<u>Then again on 29-3-79 by President's Order No. 24 of 1973 amendment was further made by an insertion of an expression 'or'. Thus, another kind of transaction was brought within the mischief of the law, namely "out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey" and the law provided that it should be "deemed to be the complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years and the provision of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the amendment order.</u>

<u>6. The High Court Division missed the real intent of the legislation which originated since 1928, although it seems that it was in the view of the learned Judges, because they themselves considered the laws as "beneficial legislations" but the learned Judges wondered why in enacting section 95 the provisions of section 26G were not kept in view by the legislature. The answer is simple, that by the operation of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act no complete usufructuary mortgage by a raiyat would subsist beyond 15 years, that is why when the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in 1966 all such mortgages were extinguished by operation of law. The legislature, in section 95; provided that the raiyat shall not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than the complete usufructuary mortgage and to give the complete shape to the social thinking the legislature also prohibited a contract of out and out sale with reconveyance and by a deeming clause had made such transaction as complete usufructuary mortgage. In other words in Bangladesh a raiyat cannot enter into any other transaction of his raiyat-holding except a complete usufructuary mortgage. Thus the process that was started in 1928 found its full expression by the amendment caused by President's Order No. 24 of 1973. The view of the High Court Division that such transactions are an embargo upon the common form of transaction is unwarranted. It is for the legislature to decide that question whether the raiyati's interest will be best protected by creating such embargo. The High Court Division was wrong in saying "that consequences flowing from the President's Order construed literally in undoubtedly absurd and unjust in the context of prevailing legal norms". It is neither absurd not unjust because the vast majority of our people are illiterate agriculturists living in abject poverty and the legislature passed the law to protect their interest in order to save them from the clutches of the money lenders or mohajans from reaping benefits out of their unconscionable bargains. The High Court Division considered that the word "transfer" used in section 95A must be given a restrictive connotation. It means only a transfer in the nature of a mortgage with respect, this kind of construction has been considered as "new terror" in the construction of statute. It would be a new terror in the construction of Acts of Parliament if we were required to limit a word to an unnatural sense because in the same Act which is 'not incorporated or, referred to such interpretation is given to it for the purposes of that Act alone" per Lord Lovedura, LC in Macbeth vs Chistell, 1910 (AC) 220 (223). Lord Mac-Naghten observed in the same case :</u>

<u>It seems to me there is no ground what-ever for introducing the definition of the word "seamen" found in the Merchant Shipping Act into the Employers Liability Act. In the latter Act, I think the word must have its ordinary signification.</u>

<u>The anxiety of the High Court Division for interpreting the presidential orders is perceptible when it devoted considerable attention as to whether the Haydon's rule or mischief rule propounded by Lord Coke or Golden Rule of Lord Wendaydal or the learned Judges to devote their attention for the Canons of construction and interpretation when they themselves have found the "broad unanimity" is "to take the whole statute together and construe the said proviso as a part of the said statute." The learned Judge addressed themselves we shall have to interpret the words literally at the first instance by applying the literal rule, but if we find that as a result of such literal interpretation certain consequences do arise which are absurd or unjust, it would set the court to inquire if it was the intention of the law-maker to use the words in their ordinary significance. Having propounded the principle correctly, the learned Judges took pains to find that the amendment by President's Order No. 24 of 1973 in inserting the word "or" the legislature created a new legislation. If section 1959 is perused then it will be evident that the word "or" has been inserted for grammatical reasons because the expression "either" is to be associated with the expression "or". When President's Order No. 136 of 1972 inserted the expression "either" by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey the expression or was a mere grammatical requirement which as has been contended by the learned Attorney-General is that in the absence of any amendment such expression could have been supplied by the Court as cause omisus. Even Lord Wensbydale who pro pounded the golden rule of construction stated:</u>

<u>"In construing wills and indeed statute and all written instruments the grammatical, and ordinary sense is to be adhere to, unless that would lead to some absurdity or some repugnance or inconsistency with the rest of the instrument (Grey vs Pains, 1888, 6 HL Case, 61 at 106)".</u>

<u>It has not been shown how the grammatical and ordinary sense of the word would lead to inconsistency "with the rest of the instrument". It has not been made clear how the word "or" would lead to some absurdity or repugnance or inconsistency. Plain reading of section 95A shows that any transfer of a holding either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or whether the transferor delivers the property after a consideration to the transferee to enjoy the usufruct of such holding, such transfer be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage and the period must not exceed 7 years and the provisions of section 95 will apply for restoration or redemption. The observation of the learned Judges that "it cannot be conceded that relief can be granted to such kind of debtor by converting a transaction which was clearly intended by the parties thereto to be a pure sale with an agreement to reconvey into one of complete usufructuary mortgage" is not correct because the law intended to give such relief and for that reasons resort was taken since 1928 to the deeming provision.</u>

<u>7. Mr SR Pal, Amicus Curiae has rightly pointed out that the High Court Division missed the deeming provision in section 95A which categorically says "shall notwithstanding anything contained in the documents relating to the transfer be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage". Since 1928 recourse was taken of the deeming provision by the legislature and all sorts of mortgage, usufructuary mortgage, mortgages by conditional sale, anomalous have been displaced by providing that all such mortgages by a raiyat shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage" for which a definition was given in the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Judges then considered that the literal construction of the President's Orders would entail "constitutional difficulties". The learned Attorney-General has pointed out that the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a protected legislation with all the amendments. Exception has been taken by the High Court Division to this argument and it is said it cannot be accepted unless clear indication has been given in the constitution in this behalf. Article 47 read with the 1st Schedule of the Constitution has protected this law and clear indication has been given in the Constitution itself and when the parent legislation is immune from attack the consequential amendments are to be viewed in that light, namely, for giving effect to the parent legislation unless it would be shown that the amendment minus the protection, is otherwise unconstitutional. No such case has been or could be made out in any of these appeals and no argument was advanced on behalf of the respondent.</u>

8. Lastly, the High Court Division considered that section 95A is a discriminatory piece of legislation although they themselves have found 'the law regulating the right of an agricultural tenant to mortgage his land may not be considered to be discriminatory in as much as indebted agricultural tenants who constitute poorer section of the people may be regarded as a class apart for which there appears to be a rational basis having a just and reasonable relation to the objection of the legislation". In view of this observation the conclusion that literal interpretation would show that there was no reasonable basis for which they termed section 95A as discriminatory one, does not stand logically. The removal of by legislation is not only sanctioned by the constitution, it is supported by well established canon of interpretation viz, the beneficial rule.

<u>9. Mr Shamsul Huq Chowdhury appearing for the respondents could not show as to how discrimination has been made when the legislation was passed to save a class of people for whom even the learned Judges have found a rational basis. As for the violation of fundamental right, the right to property is given in Article 42 of the Constitution but subject to reasonable restriction. Clause (2) of Article 42 has no relevancy because that operates in a different context, namely, compulsory acquisition, nationalisation or requisition. The High Court Division has fallen into error by construing the expression "transfer" in the context of the Transfer of Property Act which is evident from their own observation "the agreement to recovery shall have to be incorporated in the deed affecting the transfer in view of the provision to section 58 (c) of Transfer of Property Act". Here lies the error because since 1928 the legislature wanted to take out the transaction of the raiyat from the purview of Transfer of Property Act for which specific definition was supplied, namely, "complete usufructuary mortgage" in the Bengal Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>10. The expression "transfer" is an ordinary word which is used in construing the word of Presidential Orders. The High Court Division observed that the vested right of the property should be extinguished "except in the manner as provided in the second part of Article 42(1) or 47 (1)". The learned Attorney-General has rightly pointed out that there is no question of vested right because the complete usufructuary mortgage presupposes the restoration of land to the transferee actual, social and economic discrimination either by redemption or by efflux of time whichever is earlier. The Privy Council has held that whatever form is used, nothing more than an interest is transferred and that interest is subject to the right of redemption (Ram Kindkar vs Satya Chaman, 66 IA 50). The High Court Division considered that the restoration would amount to "windfall" which to say again is unwarranted because a transferee enjoyed the rights during these years before redemption or restoration and the transaction known in vernacular is "Khai Khalashi" for which both the principal and interest are liquidated. Therefore the question of vested right does not arise, nor can it be said the raiyat gets it as a windfall because after all the property is his and he had to transfer it as complete usufructuary mortgage or "Khai Khalashi" in order to obtain loan.</u>

11. Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos. 88 and 116 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for affecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vices. (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of sections 95 (4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question :(4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to recovery, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 : and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed.

12. It is for the High Court Division now to scrutinise the respective documents and dispose of the matters in the light of observations made herein before.

In the result, therefore, all the appeals are allowed, decision of the High Court Division set-aside and remitted back to the High Court Division for disposal. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
