parties:
Md. Sharifullah Petitioner in Petition No. 201 of 1977.
Vs.
Election Tribunal (Munsif, Second Court Habiganj and anr. Khan Ataur Rahman Petitioner in Petition N. 209, Ashraful Huq Petitioner in Petition No. 211 of 1977 
Vs.
Election Tribunal Munsif Court Rajshahi and anr. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.-These three applications were heard analogously as common question of law is involved therein. Writ Petition No. 201 of 1977 the petitioner was declared elected as Chairman of No. 10 Umednagar Union Parishad under Police Station Baniachong, District Sylhet on 25th January 1977 and it was duly published in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) dated19th February; 1977. After the publication of the result respondent No. 2, filed an election petition before the Election Tribunal, Munsif, Second Court Hobiganj, alleging malpractices adopted by the petitioner and prayed for setting aside the result of the election. An application was filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 24th February, 1977 by respondent No. 2 praying, or an order of injunction restraining the petitioner from taking over charge of the office of the Chairman and also retraining the Returning Officer, from administering oath of office of Chairman to the petitioner. Election Tribunal by the order dated 19th March, 1977 restrained the petitioner from taking oath of his office as Chairman and taking charge from the respondent No. 2 till the hearing of the case. Against this order the petitioner moved this court when rule was issued.

2. In Writ petition No. 209 of 1977 the petitioner having secured the highest vote, was declared the elected Chairman of the Rishikul Union Parishad and the result was duly published in the official Gazette dated 20th February 1977. Oath of office was administered to him on 2nd March, 1977. The petitioner was given training by the authority from 7th March to 9th March, 1977 to efficiently run the Union Parishad as Chairman. In the meantime respondent No. 2 filed an election petition before the Election Tribunal challenging validity of the election with a prayer for declaration that the election of the petitioner is void and respondent No. 2 be declared as the elected Chairman. After filing the election petition respondent No. 2 filed an application on 25th February, 1977 praying for injunction against the petitioner restraining him from taking charge of Union Parishad. The Election Tribunal on 25th February, 1977 issued notice upon the petitioner to show cause within seven days from the date of the receipt of the notice as to why he should not be restrained from taking over charge of the office of Chairman of the Union Parishad, and granted an order of ad interim injunction. The petitioner contested the said application for injunction, contending inter alia, that the Election Tribunal is not competent to grant injunction as per decisions of the High Court, Election Tribunal, however, found it a fit case for granting injunction and accordingly made the order of ad interim injunction absolute by his order dated 17th March, 1977. The petitioner moved this Court against this order when the rule was issued.

3. In Writ Petition No. 211 of 1977 the petitioner was declared elected as the Chairman of No. 8 Basudebpur Union Parishad under Police Station Godabari, District Rajshahi in the election held on 13th January 1977. The result of the election was published in the official Gazette dated 20th February, 1977 and oath was administered to the petitioner on 23rd February, 1977 and he was given training from 7th March to 9th March, 1977. Respondent No. 2 filed election petition challenging validity of the election before the Election Tribunal at Rajshahi with a prayer for a declaration that respondent No. 2 be declared to be the elected Chairman of Union Parishad or declare the election of the said Union Parishad null and void. On 1st March 1977 respondent No. 2 filed an application praying for order of injunction against the petitioner restraining him from taking charge of the, office of Chairman. Election Tribunal by an order dated 1st March, 1977 issued notice upon the petitioner to show cause as to why the injunction as prayed for should not be granted, and the petitioner was restrained by an order of ad-interim injunction. The matter of temporary injunction was heard on 7th March, 1977 and Election Tribunal made the ad interim injunction also lute till disposal of the case. Against this order the petitioner moved this court when rule was issued.

4. While issuing rule in Writ Petition Nos. 201 and 211 of 1977 direction was given upon the Election Tribunal concerned to explain as to why two reported decisions of this court namely, .................(1)

Shamsul Huq Sikder Vs. Election Tribunal and to (1.975) 27 D.L.R. 388; and (2) Masehiduddin Ahmed Vs. Munsif Sunamganj, Sylhet and others (1976) 28 D.L.R. 189, were ignored while granting temporary injunction under Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure although it has been clearly held therein that Election Tribunals not being Civil Courts are not competent to grant injunction.

5. Writ Petition Nos. 201 of 1977 and 211 of 1977, explanations submitted by the Election Tribunals have been received by this Court. In both the explanations Election Tribunals have practically pleaded ignorance about the rulings of this Court and begged to be excused. On perusal of the explanations we do not consider that any action need be taken. However, we observe that as judicial Officers they are expected to keep themselves abreast with the current rulings of the Superior Courts of the country.

6. Only question for our consideration in these applications is as to whether Election Tribunal constituted under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance, 1976 is "Civil Court" and as such, is competent to grant temporary injunction under Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submitted that the Election Tribunal not being a civil court is not competent to exercise any of the powers provided under the Code of Civil Procedure for gran-ting temporary injunction. As against this the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, however, argued strenuously that in view of clear language of the present Election Rules, and the Election Tribunal having been clothed with all the powers of the Civil Court, for all practical purposes, is a civil court, and as such is competent to grant injunction.

8. Let us first deal with the argument advanced on behalf of the respondents One of the main arguments advanced from the Bar is that on the authority of the decisions in the case of Shamsul Huq Sikder Vs. Election Tribunal and others 27 D.L.R. 388, and Mazehiduddin Ahmed Vs, Munsif, Sunamganj Sylhet and others, 28 D.L.R. 189, it cannot be held that the Election Tribunal as constituted under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance, 1976 and the powers conferred under Rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1979 is not a Civil Court as contemplated under the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of this argument the learned Advocate with reference to rule 57 of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973 submitted that since the power of appointing Election Tribunal was given to the Election Commission without confining the appointment to only judicial grounds for taking the view that the Election Tribunal so appointed could not be a Civil Court. But in the present election laws, namely, section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance, 1976 the power of appointment of Election Tribunal having been given to the Government with clear specification that Judicial Officers are to be appointed as the Election Tribunals, the reasons-advanced in the reported cases are not applicable in the instant cases. Here the appointment is having been made by the Government and Judicial Officers having been appointed as Election Tribunals by the Government enjoy for all practical purposes-the powers of Civil Court.

9. Learned Advocates further argued with reference to Rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1976 that the Election Tribunal appointed by the Government, shall be deemed to be Civil Courts. Since Rule 48 provides that every election petition shall be tried, as nearly as may be, in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suit under the Civil Procedure Code, and since Rule 49 provides that the Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Civil Procedure Code there cannot be any doubt that the Election Tribunal is a Civil Court.

10. Learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners contends that there being a difference in the language of the two provisions, namely, 'rule 57 of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973 and Section 27 of the. Local Government Ordinance 1976 there is hardly any scope for contending that Election Tribunals appointed by the Government under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance of 1976 stand 'on different footing, that is to say, those are to be treated' as Civil. Courts. According to the learned Advocates Election Tribunals so appointed under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance are nothing but Election Tribunals as appointed under the former Rules. Mere change in the authority to appoint Election Tribunals makes no difference, With reference to Rules 61 A and 61 B of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973, and rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parisians (Election) Rules, 1976 the learned Advocate submitted that there being no difference in the powers conferred under the two sets of Rules, there is hardly any scope to contend that the Election Tribunal appointed under the Union Parishad (Election) Rules. 1976 are Civil Courts and as such competent to exercise any of the powers as conferred under the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of this argument the learned Advocates referred to a decision of this court in the case of A. CA fur Vs. Election Tribunal and Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni, Noakhali and another (1977) 29 DLR 111.

<u>11. We have considered the subdivisions made by the learned Advocates of the parties and perused the relevant provisions of the Statute and the Rules and also the decisions referred to above. On careful examination of the relevant provisions with election laws we do not find any change in the status of the Election. Tribunals as appointed under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinacne, 1976 and powers conferred under Rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parishad (Election), Rules; 1976. Merely because the Election Tribunal have been appointed by the Government, and the appointment is confined to Judicial Officers, that itself does not lend support to the argument that the Election Tribunals so appointed are Civil Courts. To find out the status of the Election Tribunal one is to examine the powers conferred under Rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1976 Rule 48 core spends to Rule 61A of the Union Parishad and 'Paurashava (Election) Roles, 1973. Similarly, rule 49 corresponds to rule 61 B Of 'the said Rule's. Rules 48 and 49 are identical to Rules 61A and 61B. In the case reported in 29 D.L.R.111, the question raised before us has been elaborately discussed and question fully answered. It  has been 'held therein that Election Tribunals appointed under section 27 of the Local Government Ordinance, 19.76 and exercising powers under rules 48 and 49 of the Union Parishads (Election) Rules, 1976, are not Civil Courts, and as such are not competent to exercise the powers of Civil Courts in granting temporary injunction.</u>

<u>12. In our opinion, the Election Tribunals cannot be treated as Civil. Courts" as contemplated under the Code of Civil Procedure, and as such, the Election Tribunals are not competent to grant injunction under Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter we hold that the Election Tribunals in the instant cases acted without jurisdiction in granting temporary injunction either under Order 39 Rule 1 or under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore the Rules are made absolute and the impugned orders granting injunction are quashed. We make no order as to costs.</u>

M. H. RAHMAN, J.- I agree.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 2nd February, 1979 passed by the High Court Division In Writ Petition No. 847 of 1978.)
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave arises out of the Judgment and Order passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 847 of 1978.

2. Respondent 2, Abdul Jalil filed the above writ petition stating that he and the appellant, Afzal Khan along with to others were the contesting candidates in the election of Chairman for Comilla Pourashava held on 11-8-1977. The election was held peacefully in 32 polling centres and the Respondent 2, Abdul Jalil, was declared elected by the Returning Officer defeating his nearest rival Afzal Khan by a merging of 61 votes.

3. The defeated candidate Afzal Khan filed election petition making number of allegations of corrupt and illegal practices in holding the election including improper and perfunctory counting of votes. His grievance was that at the 18 polling station mentioned in the petition the counting of votes was done most hurriedly improperly and perfunctorily and in some polling stations he alleged that known supporters of Respondent No. 2 were allowed to handle the ballot papers and due to this, many valid votes of the appellant were illegally invalidated and good number of votes were counted in favour of Respondent 2."

Abdul Jalil in the writ petition denied the material objections and stated that at the time of counting of all votes, no objection was taken by anybody regarding the counting of votes.

4. The Election Tribunal thereafter considered an application which was filed on 31.7.78 for amendment of the election petition giving up his entire allegation regarding corrupt and illegal practices in holding the election and pressed the prayer for recounting of the ballot papers of the 18 polling centres. This amendment was allowed in spite of the objection of Respondent 2, Abdul Jalil, who filed the petition stating that if the prayer for recounting was allowed then recounting should be held for all the 32 polling centres. His petition was, however, rejected by the Tribunal.

5. The Election Tribunal after hearing the parties and considering the evidence recounted the ballot papers of the 18 polling renters and found that Afzal Khan had a lead of 153 votes over Abdul Jalil? Accordingly, it declared Afzal Khan elected.

6. Thereafter Abdul Jalil filed the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division after hearing the parties decided to recheck the ballot papers of the 18 polling centres which were rejected by the Election Tribunal as Invalid. In this process it was found that the Respondent 2 had still margin of 66 votes. The High Court Division, however, considered the prayer of Abdul Jalil for checking the ballot papers in respect of the 14 polling centres which, however, were objected to by the appellant, Afzal Khan. The High Court Division however, checked the valid ballot papers of these 14 polling centres. Finally this process recounting showed that the Respondent 2, Abdul Jalil, had a lead of 20 votes and accordingly it declared him elected as Chairman after setting aside the decision of the Election Tribunal,

7. Leave was granted on the ground that the High Court Division had acted illegally in recounting the ballot papers of 14 polling centres and further in counting 35 ballot papers which did not bear any official mark in contravention of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1971.

8. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court Division had adopted a double standard in rechecking the ballot papers which was rejected by the Tribunal in respect of the 18 polling centres, whereas in the case of remaining 14 polling centres over which there was no dispute, the High Court Division had erroneously checked only valid ballot papers. The learned Counsel forcefully argued that the rechecking of 14 polling centres by the High Court Division was illegal and without jurisdiction.

9. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed the learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent 2 argued that no case had been made out before the Election Tribunal for recounting or the ballot papers and the Tribunal itself was not justified in recounting. It was argued further that if the Tribunal had decided on recounting, then it should have recounted the ballot papers of all the 32 polling centres which, in fact, was prayed for by the Respondent Mr. Ahmed canvassed that sufficient foundation was not laid for the exercise of the jurisdiction of Tribunal for recounting. The High Court Division, it was contended, had rightly checked the ballot papers of the 14 polling centres since the whole case of the appellant was for counting of ballot papers, submitted that the High Court Division had adopted a correct course in checking the ballot papers of the 14 polling stations and this and this cannot be termed as adopting double standard.

10. As has been noticed, Abdul Jalil, Respondent No. 2. was declared, elected by the Presiding Officer by a margin of 61 votes. Rule, 37(4) of the Pourashava Election Rules 1977 provides for counting. As has been noticed no objection was taken either before the Presiding Officer or to the Returning Officer that the ballot papers were counted improperly and illegally or hurriedly. Nothing was said about the counting by any body, It is only when the election petition was filed that a general allegation was made about 18 specified polling centres stating that in these centres counting was done hurriedly and improperly" and in some centres the Polling Agents of the rival candidate "were allowed to handle the ballot  boxes" This allegation was not brought either before the Presiding Officer or to the notice of the Returning Officer. Not only this, when the election petition was about to tried, then the aIlegation for corrupt and illegal practices were given up and simply a case of counting was put before the Tribunal.

11. Normally mere counting of votes may not a sole issue before any Election Tribunal unless sufficient foundation for such exercise is laid by evidence In the present case no allegation was made before the Returning Officer specifically regarding the error in counting but this was raised before the Tribunal along with, the allegation of corrupt practice.

12. The case of Afzal Khan was based on corrupt or illegal practices and as a component part of it he prayed for recounting in 18 polling centres. This prayer, as has been noticed, was objected to by the Respondent 2 who prayed for recounting of all the stations. That was not done by the Tribunal. The High Court Division did it but in doing so the High Court Division only re-checked the ballot papers which have been taken as valid in the 14 polling centres. It must be said that the High Court Division took sufficient precaution while deciding the Writ matter in the exercise of jurisdiction whether the High Court Division should recount the ballot papers of the 14 polling centres but it considered that in the "interest of justice'" these ballot papers should be rechecked keeping in the mind "though such a course should be avoided as far as possible." The High Court Division was careful that the prayer of a defeated candidate "for recounting of ballot papers should be rejected if he had not requested the Presiding Officer for recounting on the spot. It noticed that in the case of the 18 polling centres the Election Tribunal had recounted the ballot papers and the High Court Division had verified "whether rejection by the Tribunal of some votes got basis whereas in the later (14 centres) in which the Tribunal did not do the recounting we did it and completed thereby process of the recounting started by the Tribunal". The High Court Division observed:

"This petitioner filed on the eleventh hour containing the allegation of double yardstick has got no substance and is rejected."

The High Court Division had rightly noticed the principles namely, (a) that the counting was not asked for before the Presiding Officer, (b) foundation for the exercise of jurisdiction of the Tribunal merely for recounting was not laid, (C) when the Tribunal had counted only 18 polling centres the process of counting could not be completed unless the other 14 centres are checked. The High Court Division had correctly judged that this was necessary to complete the process of counting which was started by the Tribunal and, therefore, it cannot be assailed as having a double standard.

We fully subscribe to this view and no exception can be taken to this part or the High Court Division's judgment.

<u>13. As for the 35 ballot papers the High Court Division noticed correctly that these ballot papers which do not bear official mark should be rejected under rule 37 (3) (b) of the Pourashava Election Rules, 1977. It accordingly checked the ballot papers which was not done by the Tribunal itself correctly, so the High Court Division rechecked the ballot papers of the candidates and excluded them from the counting which did not bear official mark. The contention that the High Court Division in a Writ jurisdiction should not count the ballot papers because it is not convenient for such jurisdiction to do the recounting has some force but on exception can be taken to this endeavor of the High Court Division of counting ballot papers as it was done in the interest of justice and fair play. The jurisdiction of counting eminently lies elsewhere and even the Election Tribunal cannot count the ballot papers, unless the recounting became a necessary part of the case itself which has been brought on the basis of certain allegations of corrupt and illegal practices. It is well settled that if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal in connection with an election which cannot be determined without such recounting, then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recounting the ballot papers provided sufficient foundation has been laid to come to the finding that the recounting is indispensably necessary for adjudication of the election petition. This was not the position before the Election Tribunal. The High Court Division therefore had acted correctly in the exercise of its jurisdiction of ends for justice in counting and rechecking of the ballot papers the process of which was started by the Election Tribunal itself. No exception can be taken to the procedure adopted by the High Court Division in as much as the High Court Division is itself aware of the limitations of its jurisdiction in taking such steps which is done, however, solely for the purpose of doing complete justice in the matter.</u>

<u>In the result, therefore, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 18th July, 1977 passed by the High Court in F.A. No. 262 of 1969)
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, C. J:- The short question of law involved in this appeal is when land is acquired under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act and in the absence of Tribunal constituted there under, whether the Land Acquisition Court in assessing compensation in terms of section 93A(5)(b)(ii) read with 91A of the Act is competent to direct for payment of interest on the compensation assessed.

2. Facts are that the land recorded in C.S. Plot Nos. 59, 60, 89 and 90 measuring 2.55 acres of land of Mouza Bhola under P.S. Tejgaon, District Dhaka of the respondents were requisitioned on January 27, 1969 and its possession was taken over on the same date by the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca under sub-section (1) of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953. The land was subsequently acquired on June 23, 1969 after serving notices on the respondents on April 30, 1960 as required under sub-section (4)(a) and (b) of section 93A of the Act. The Deputy Commissioner, Dacca, assessed compensation of the lands at Tk. 8,286-12 but the respondents did not accept, they made an application for arbitration before the Tribunal In terms of section 91A of the Act for determination of the compensation claiming much higher rates. In the absence of the Tribunal set up under the said Act, the land Acquisition Court set up with the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dacca under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 acted as the Arbitrator in the case. The claim was contested by the then Government of East Pakistan contending that the claim was highly inflated that the Deputy Commissioner awarded a fair and reasonable amount of compensation having regard to the quality of the land, the situation and all other advantages and disadvantages there for according to Jaw prevailing at the time of final acquisition. The Land Acquisition Court by an order dated July 5, 1968 determined the compensation at Tk. 32,076/00 which included a sum of Tk. 4,765/00 as compensation for some trees and plants standing on the land. The land Acquisition Court directed the payment of interest at the rate of 6% percent per annum on the compensation if not paid within the date fixed in the award, as against that award there was an appeal before the High Court being F.A. No. 262 of 1969 which was allowed in part. Leave was granted to consider the question set out above.

3. The learned Judges of the High Court Division with reference to the decision of this Division in the case of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Mannan (1977) 29 DLR (S.C.) 17 held that the Land Acquisition Court holds the power of granting interest on the compensation assessed. It is being challenged by the Additional Attorney-General appearing for the Government appellant. On finding the Importance of the question involved we required the assistance of an amicus curiae and requested Mr. T. H. Khan to render his assistance to this Division and had the advantage of hearing a very learned argument on the exposition of the law.

<u>4. To appreciate the question, it is to be observed that under the terms of the Town Improvement Act 1953 land can be acquired in three ways under three different sections; One is by purchase on agreement under section 78, the other is by compulsory acquisition under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act 1894 under section 79 and the third is acquisition on requisition of land under section 93A(4) (a) of the Act. It is to be noted that for the land acquired under section 79 of the Act, the mode of payment of compensation and the settlement of dispute in the assessment of compensation have been elaborately provided in the Act, which has been enacted for setting up of Tribunal under section 80 with the provision for appeals from the award made by the Tribunal under certain circumstances and for that purpose a schedule has been appended to the Act. Reading the relevant provisions of the Act it is found that sections 93A and 93B of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 are related to the acquisition of land preceded by an order of requisition and they provide almost a self-contained code for the specific purpose, the third mode of acquisition under the Act.</u>

5. If we look at the provision for assessment of compensation in this section, we find that it has been provided under sub-section, (5) which consists of three clauses. Clause (a) enacts for payment of compensation on agreement and clause (c) as to the right of the contending parties to state their cases before the Tribunal. The Provision regarding the power of the Tribunal and mode of assessment of compensation is in clause (b) It may be set out:

"Section 93A (b) (i) Where no such agreement can be reached, the Deputy Commissioner shall assess a compensation for the immovable property having regard to the provisions of sections 23, 24 and 24A, as modified by section 81 of this Act, and sub-section (2) of section 36 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, so far as the same can be made applicable, and he shall give immediate notice of the assessment to the person or persons interested;

Provided that in determining such market value the Court shall take into account the average value of the properties of the similar description and with similar advantage in the vicinity during twenty-four months preceding the date of service of the notice under clause (a) of sub-section (4) of this section;

Provided further that in assessing compensation for the acquisition of any immovable property to which the provisions of any other law for the time being in force, for the control of house-rent, apply, the Deputy Commissioner shall have regard to those provisions, so that the compensation awarded may not exceed the amount of rent allowable in respect of such property under those provisions: and

(ii) Any person interested who has not accepted assessment, may, by written application, move the Tribunal to determine the matter;

(iii) The application shall state the grounds on which objection to assessment is taken;

Provided that every such application shall be made within 6 weeks of the service of notice by the District Magistrate under clause (b) or within 3 months from the date of the order of assessment, which ever period shall later expire".

<u>6. The reading of the above provisions indicates that for the assessment of compensation of land acquired under section 93A a complete Code has been provided which is quite distinct from the acquisition made under section 79. On the failure of agreement, the Deputy Commissioner shall assess the compensation. If a person is not interested in accepting the compensation assessed by the Deputy Commissioner, he can under sub-clause (b)(ii) move the Tribunal means one constituted under section 80 read with section 82 of the Act. But when no Tribunal is constituted under the said section the contingency has been met by the provisions of section 91A, which says that when no Tribunal has been set up, any reference to the Tribunal under section 93A shall be construed as referring to Court under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.</u>

<u>7. The question is how far by reference to the Court under the Land Acquisition Act, the Tribunal referred to under sub-section (ii) of clause (b) of sub-section (5) of section 93A, acquires power to grant interest requires, to be examined It is to be observed that Mr. T. H. Khan concedes that the Tribunal under the Act in assessing compensation does not possess the power to grant interest though the power is available when the acquisition is under the provisions of Land Acquisition Act. The question is could this power be exercised by the Court while acting as such under the provision 91A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953? Mr. T.H. Khan refers to some observations made in Bangladesh vs. Abdul Mannan 29 DLR (SC) 17, to say that the Court will be entitled to take recourse to section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act. How far Mr. T.H. Khan's contention on the authority of Abdul Mannan's case be accepted?' In the cited decision the question was, when the land was acquired under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act and no Tribunal was set up, whether the award of the Court under the Land Acquisition Act, by reference to section 91A of the Act was appealable. It has been held that the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Town Improvement Act are to be read together with the first supplementing the latter, in other words the general provision of the Land Acquisition Act will apply where there is no specific provision in the Town Improvement Act: It was held that as there was nothing specifically said about the trial procedure or the character of the award made by the Court under the Land Acquisition Act read with section 91A of the Town Improvement Act, tie provision of power, procedure, jurisdiction and appeal of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 shall apply in such case. Mr. T.H. Khan argues from this observation that the power shall include the power to grant interest. The power the of the Court under Land Acquisition Act to grant interest is enacted in section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and Mr. Khan says that this section is available. We think, it is not permissible to extend the meaning of an expression which has no logical bearing with the question, nor any legal rule to support. It is to be noted that since there was a lack of provision as to trial procedure or the character of the award or the mode of execution in the Town Improvement Act, 1953 regarding an award made under this special provision, the observation set out was made. Nothing has said on the power to grant interest or could such power be conferred by reference. A glance at sub-section (5) clause (b) will reveal that the power as welt as mode of assessment of compensation under the special law has been provided for an application of provisions of Land Acquisition Act is not called for. The provision of special law fits in with the fact of the case and so the general provision of Land Acquisition Act is not called into play. There it no scope fur invoking the general provision of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to invest the said Court with a power to grant interest.</u>

8. Looking from another stand point, the soundness of Mr. T.H. Khan's contention of invoking sec. 18 of the Land Acquisition Act could be tested, Mr. Khan has conceded that the Tribunal set up under the Town Improvement Act, could not grant interest under section 93A (5) (b)(ii) of the Act. How could then the Court deemed to be set up under the same provision by reference to section 91A of the Act acquire a higher power than the former. It is neither possible nor desirable to bring about a conflict of power under the same provision of law, only because two sets of forums may be called into existence. We therefore, find it difficult to uphold the decision of the learned Judges of the High Court on the question.

In the result appeal is allowed without any order as costs. The orders of the High Court and the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court Dacca, as awarding interest are set aside.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated July 25, 1996 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in AAT No. 12 of 1994).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : In this appeal by leave the short question for consideration is whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka was right in dismissing the appellant's case, Administrative Tribunal Case No. 13 of 1991, only on the ground of defect of party, although on merit there was a concurrent finding in favour of the appellant.

2. Material facts for disposal of this appeal are that the appellants filed the aforesaid case before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka against the respondents for a declaration that notification dated 26-1-89 issued by respondent No. 1 promoting respondent No. 4 to the post of Administrative Officer in the Labour Directorate in supersession of the claim of the appellant was illegal and of no legal effect and also for a direction upon respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to reconsider the case of the appellant for promotion. The appellant's case, briefly, is that he was appointed steno-typist on 15-11-68 in the Directorate of Labour and on 6-11-74 he was appointed Stenographer-cum-Confidential Assistant temporarily on ad hoc basis in the same Directorate. Under a circular dated 10-7-82 the Establishment Ministry regularized his service as Stenographer (CA) with effect from 1-5-75 and in terms of the Enam Committee report dated 10-10-83 his post was declared as Stenographer (PA). In the Recruitment Rules 1983 published by the Labour Directorate in the official Gazette on 27-3-84 requisite qualification for the post of Administrative Officer of the Labour Directorate was 5 years-experience as Head Assistant or Stenographer-cum-Confidential Assistant. On 13-12-88 respondent No. 1 sent the names of 5 employees including that of the appellant in serial number 1 and that of respondent No. 4 in serial number 4 to the Public Service Commission for consideration for promotion to the post of Administrative Officer of the Directorate with the recommendation for same and except the appellant none completed 5 years-service in the feeder post but the Public Service Commission recommended the case of respondent No. 4 for promotion and accordingly he was promoted to the post of Administrative Officer by the impugned notification dated 26-1-89. The appellant's representation to respondent No. 1 and then appeal to the Government-respondent No. 2 having been dismissed, the case was filed before the Administrative Tribunal for the aforesaid reliefs.

3. Respondent Nos. 1 and 4 contested the case by filing separate written statements taking similar defence and contending, inter alia, that respondent No. 4 was promoted on the merit of his case on the recommendation of the Public Service Commission.

4. The Administrative Tribunal by its judgment and order dated 14-12-93 allowed the case of the appellant declaring that the promotion of respondent No. 4 to the post of Administrative Officer together with the recommendation of the Public Service Commission being illegal and violate of the principle of natural justice were void and of no legal effect and further directing respondent Nos. 1-3 to reconsider the case of the appellant for promotion fairly and on correct principle of law.

5. Respondent No. 4 took an appeal, No. 12 of 1994, to the Appellate Tribunal against the aforesaid decision whereupon the Administrative Appellate Tribunal by the impugned judgment and order dated 25 July, 1995 dismissed the appellant's case, as already noticed, only on the ground of defect of party holding that "although we agree with the learned lower Tribunal that the Respondent-petitioner has a good case on merits, yet the Government being his employer is a necessary party who having not been impleaded the application before the lower Tribunal is not properly constituted and the case is bad for defect of party on which ground alone the appeal succeeds".

6. In coming to the said finding the Appellate Tribunal relied on. the case of Abdul Naim vs. Chairman, Board of Directors, Sonali Bank, Head Office referred to by respondent No. 4 which was not reported till then but has since been reported in 1 BLC (AD) 80.

7. The appellant while praying for leave to appeal from the impugned decision of the Appellate Tribunal submitted that the decision relied upon by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was not applicable in the facts of the present case and further the decision was under review by this Division and that at any rate the Appellate Tribunal upon a misapprehension and misconception of the facts of the present case wrongly held that the Government of Bangladesh was not impleaded in the petition of the appellant.

8. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan learned Advocate for the appellant, at the hearing of the appeal, shifted his argument a little because the judgment on review in the case of Abdul Naim 3 BLC (AD) 1 has in the meantime been delivered. Mr. Khan submitted that the review in that case failed because the Court did not find any differential factual basis for taking a differential view but in the present case the differential factual basis squarely exists and a differential view is aptly called for without disputing the principle of making the employer a party as laid down in the judgment before review 1 BLC (AD) 80.

9. The submission of the learned Advocate requires an examination of the facts of the two cases in order to appreciate his point. In Abdul Naim's case, the petitioner was dismissed from the service of the Sonali Bank when he was on leave preparatory to retirement. Among other, he made the Chairman, Board of Directors, Sonali Bank, Head Office as opposite party in his application before the Appellate Tribunal challenging his dismissal. He succeeded in the Tribunal but on appeal by the opposite parties he lost on the ground that the Sonali Bank which is a legal entity and capable of being sued having not been made a party to the case, the petitioner's application was not maintainable. The petitioner came to this Division seeking leave to appeal from that order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. His leave petition was dismissed upholding the view of the Appellate Tribunal.

10. It was held that under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal can be invoked only by a person in the service of the Republic or in the service of the Statutory Public Authority. In other words, his employer is a necessary party. The officers whom the petitioner made opposite parties in his application might be his appointing authority and/or appellant authority but the petitioner was not in the service of those officers. The petitioner was in the service of the Sonali Bank and his cause of action was against his employer and not against his appointing authority or appellate authority. It was obligatory for the petitioner to make his employer a party to the application or else any decree in his favour will be in executable, his employer not being bound by the decree.

11. The petitioner in that case filed a review application from the said order and leave was granted giving rise to Civil Appeal No. 52 of 1996, 3 BLC (AD) 1.

12. It was argued in the said appeal that when the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Sonali Bank and other officials were made parties, there was a substantial compliance of the requirement of law even though the Sonali Bank was no doubt the employer of the appellant. It was argued that the respondents did not object to the joinder of the Sonali Bank as a party before the Administrative Tribunal taking upon themselves the full responsibility of the outcome of the litigation.

13. It was only at the appellate stage that the objection was taken and the technical error in the draftsmanship of the petition by a lawyer could have been conveniently corrected and the Appellate Tribunal could have conveniently read the cause title as Sonali Bank represented by the Chairman, Board of Directors thereof. The appellant further argued that the objection as to non-joinder of proper party was taken long 6 years after the case was filed and decided before the Administrative Tribunal and this conduct of the respondents was not noticed while dismissing the leave petition.

14. The appellant relied upon the case of Murari Mohan Deb vs. Secretary to the Government of India, AIR 1985 SC 931 where the Judicial Commissioner of Tripura while considering the writ petition challenging the order of compulsory retirement suomotu raised the objection that the Union of India having not been made a party, the petition was not competent. The Supreme Court of India observed as follows:

"We have not been able to appreciate why the learned Judicial Commissioner should have taken upon himself to raise this untenable contention even though the respondents did not raise such a contention."

15. The Supreme Court of India found that an "oral request to correct the description of the first respondent". Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Afairs, would have satisfied the procedural requirement. By raising and accepting such a contention after a lapse of 6 years the law is brought into ridicule. The Court could have conveniently read the cause title as "Government of India" instead of the description set out in the writ petition.

16. The said decision was distinguished and review was not allowed by this Division because in that case it was found that the objection as to defect of party was taken by the respondents at the beginning, namely, in the written statement filed in the Tribunal and the appellant never corrected the said mistake.

17. In the present case, admittedly, neither respondent No. 4 nor respondent No. 1 who contested the case took any objection in their written statement as to defect of party. Respondent No. 4 who preferred an appeal against the decision of the Tribunal did not also take that objection in the Memorandum of Appeal. It was only during argument before the Appellate Tribunal that the question of defect of party was raised. The Appellate Tribunal permitted the objection to be raised on the basis of the case of Abdul Naim holding that since this was a point of law, there was no bar to raising it for the first time in the appeal.

<u>18. It is true that a point of law can be raised even at the appellate stage but it is important that if an objection as to defect of party is taken it should be raised at the earliest opportunity so that the applicant has opportunity to correct it. Under the Administrative Tribunals Rules, 1982 a Tribunal before rejecting an application on the ground of the application not being in accordance with sub-rules (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) of rule 3 may give the applicant an opportunity for making the application in accordance with those provisions. In other words, if the necessary party was not there or had not been properly described as in the present case, the applicant should get an opportunity to correct his application and he should not be taken by surprise at a later stage. The respondents not having taken any objection as to defect of party at the earliest stage, this case meets the tests for differential treatment and calls for taking a differential view as indicated in 3 BLC (AD) 1.</u>

19. Further there was an interesting aspect in the present case in that although the appellant described opposite party No. 2 in his application before the Tribunal like this সচিব, শ্রম ও জনশক্তি মন্ত্রণালয় গণপ্রজতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার, বাংলাদেশ সচিবালয়, ঢাকা, Respondent No. 4 in his written statement properly described the opposite party as follows : মোঃ আলী এমদাদ-দরখাস্তকারী-বনাম বাংলাদেশ সরকার গং-প্রতিপক্ষ From the judgment of the Tribunal also it is found that the opposite parties have been described thus: Md Emdad Ali, Petitioner vs. Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh represented by Secretary, Ministry of Labour Director and three others.

20. The Government of Bangladesh was there in the application of the appellant but it was not properly described, that is to say, the word "Secretary" should have followed the words "Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh" and not preceded it. There was a misdescription no doubt but it seems to have been corrected by respondent No. 4 himself and the corrected description of the necessary party, namely, the Government of Bangladesh appeared in the judgment of the Tribunal.

<u>21. Therefore, notwithstanding the requirement of making the employer a party in an application under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act as laid down in 1 BLC (AD) 80 which is a correct proposition of law, we think for the reasons stated above an exception should be made in the present case for not describing the employer, namely, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh properly. In an application by a person in the service of the Republic the correct method is to follow Article 146 of the Constitution which provides that the Government of Bangladesh may sue or be sued by the name of Bangladesh. The applicant has of course to mention a competent official in the facts of a particular case who can represent Bangladesh. If the Government or the Statutory Public Authority is not made a party or is not properly described in the application, the opposite parties must raise objection if they want to at the earliest stage so that the applicant may get an opportunity to take necessary steps. If the proper party is not before the Tribunal then whether any objection is raised or not the applicant will run the risk of having an ineffective order to his peril and his application may be adjudged as incompetent. It will be, however, a matter for consideration in each case whether the irregularity of describing a necessary party properly the same should prove fatal or whether it can be condoned. In the present case, we have indicated the reasons above for which the condemnation principle should apply.</u>

22. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The decision of the Administrative Tribunal is restored subject to the following observation of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal which reads:

"We cannot but uphold the finding of the lower Tribunal striking down the impugned order of promotion of the appellant (before the Appellate Tribunal) but for obvious reason we cannot uphold the declaration made in the order portion of the judgment against the recommendation of the Commission."

End.

case_source: In the matter of An application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.-. This is directed against an order of conviction passed in Martial Law Case No. 6 of 1977 by Special Martial Law Court No. II, Dacca sentencing the accused to death for declaring the same to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and for directing the respondents not to execute the sentence pending hearing of the Rule add for such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. This rule was issued on 14-4-1978 and it has been fixed for hearing on 27-4-1978.

2. Facts giving rise to this proceeding are as follows: on 31-1-76 one Rahim Aktar Khatun lodged a petition of complaint before the Sub divisional Magistrate, Kishoregonj alleging, inter alia, that on 18-3-75 at about 4 P.M. accused Chand Mia and six others who were not named being armed with deadly weapons called out her husband Erpon Ali and killed him by gun shot.

3. The learned Sub-divisional Magistrate taking cognizance forwarded the petition to the Q.C. Bajitput P.S. whereupon Bajitpur P.S. Case No 203(3)/76 dated 9-3-76 was started against 7 accused persons under sections 148/149/448/302/364 B.P.C.read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act The F.I.R. is dated 9-3-76 In that F.I.R. names of the 3 condemned prisoners, Shamsuddin, Abulal and Rouf were not mentioned as accused. Charged-sheet was submitted on 31-3-76 under sections 148/149/448/364/302 and 201 B.P.C. read with Special Powers Act. After submission of the charge-sheet some of the accused persons surrendered before the Sub divisional Magistrate and obtained bail pending trial.

4. The case was sent to the Special Tribunal, Mymensingh for trial and it was registered as Special Tribunal Case No. 350 of 1976. While the case was pending before the Special Tribunal it was transferred to the Special Martial Law Court No. If, Dacca, vide Notification No. 991-JIV/2T-17/76 dated 23-12-76 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary.

5. Thereafter the Special Marital Law Court was constituted being Martial Law Court No. II by (1) Wing Commander Sabaruddin Ahmed, E.A.B.A.F. Chairman (2) Major Wajiullah Chowdhury, BSc. Engg. (Elect), BSc. Engg. Aero, MIE (SD) (Avionics), Member and (3) Mr. A.M. Safiuzzaman, M A. L.L.B. Magistrate, 1st Class, Member

6. Martial Law Court tried the 5 accused persons namely, (1) Chand Mia (absconding), (2) Shamsuddin (in custody), (3) Abulal (in custody), (4) Kanchan (in custody) and (5) Rouf (in custody). The Martial Law Court on consideration of the evidence convicted all the accused under section 302/34 B.P.C. and sentenced them to suffer punishment of death by hanging by neck till death (Annexure-C).

7. Kamal, the brother of Abulal the condemned prisoner was informed by the Deputy Jailor, Dacca Central Jail that the date of execution of the condemned prisoner has been fixed on 18-4-78 and he was instructed to take delivery of the dead body, if he so desired, on 19-4-78 in the morning (Annexure-B).

This Rule, as has already been mentioned, was issued on 14-5-78 and by the order of this Court the execution of the sentence was stayed.

8. The respondent have filed affidavit-in-opposition along with supplementary affidavit. Point has been taken that offence was committed on 18-3-75 and complaint was lodged on 31-1-76 and the charge-sheet was submitted on 31-3-76. But the case transferred to the Martial Law Court from the Special Tribunal on 23-12-76 as per Notification. It has been sated in the affidavit-in-opposition that none of the provisions containing Article 31 or any other Article of the Constitution is attracted as the case was tried under Martial Law Regulation. It includes all offences under ordinary law whether committed before or after the Martial Law came into existence, it is stated that the petitioner is not a competent person to file the writ petition.

9. Mr. Serajul Haq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner canvassed that (1) Regulation 3(2) cannot be given retrospective effect as it is hit by Article 27 of the Constitution being violative of the equality clause. Alternatively since retrospectivity has not been given expressly this would be treated as prospective legislation; (2) transfer of the case which was pending in a special jurisdiction to a jurisdiction of general nature is not permissible and assumption of jurisdiction by a Tribunal which has not been vested by law for determination is illegal and anything done in illegal manner is a nullify; (3) procedural provision contained vested rights and deprivation of procedural law, namely, by way of appeal is illegal; and (4) superior Court is vested with power to determine whether any authority has exercised the power conferred on it in accordance with law and this jurisdiction is preserved and cannot be taken away.

10. Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney-General canvassed that (1) the petition has not been filed by the aggrieved party (2) transfer of a case from Special Tribunal to Special Martial Law Court is permissible by regulation 3, (3) the word "offence" finds mention in the proclamation and therefore, it is not subject to any limitation as to the time of occurrence; and (4) proceedings in the Martial Law Court cannot be questioned as bar has been created by Regulation.

11. The first question is whether this Court has the jurisdiction to examine as to whether any authority has exercised the power in accordance with law or whether any Tribunal has acted within the jurisdiction. In other words, whether this Court can exercise its jurisdiction that has been conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution to pronounce as to whether the Martial Law Court has acted within the lawful authority or not.

12. This jurisdictional aspect was argued mainly on the proclamation of Martial Law dated 20th August, 1975. Mr. Serajul Huq has placed the entire proclamation of 20th August, 1975 and canvassed that the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has continued to remain in force subject to the proclamation and Martial Law Regulation and Orders. In clause (g) the jurisdiction of the superior Courts has been ousted on a very limited ground, namely (i) the Court shall have no power to question in any manner whatsoever or declare illegal or void the Proclamation or any Martial Law Regulation or Order; (ii) nor any order made under the Proclamation or action taken or anything done under the Proclamation are liable to be challenged, Mr. Huq has argued that unlike Martial Law of 1958 which was proclaimed by Md. Ayub Khan and the Martial Law of 1969 of General Yahya Khan the Constitution was not abrogated by the Proclamation of 20th August, 1975. The jurisdiction of the superior Courts have been curtailed for specific purpose with limited objective because the consideration of Martial Law is that the "security, peace and progress, prosperity and development of the country" and for paving the way for general election, vide Proclamation dated 8th November, 1975 which is to be read with deeming clause "to be a part of the Proclamation of the 20th August, 1975". Mr. Huq has argued if this is the overt policy of Proclamation of Martial Law which was done by the Proclaimed on 20th August, 1975 while seizing the full power of the Government with the help and mercy of the Almighty Allah and relying upon blessings of the people the authority Who is to discharge the functions of Martial Law cannot act in a manner which is a negation of it. Since jurisdiction of the superior Court is to determine the question between the litigating public in accordance with law this function has been saddled upon the Judges of this Court for achieving the end of law which is human happiness. Therefore, it is argued that the Martial Law which was proclaimed for establishing peace, order, security, progress and prosperity has no reason to curtail the jurisdiction of the superior Courts.

13. By the Charter of 1774 the Supreme Court was established in Bengal and the Judges of that Court had been assigned by clause 4 the powers, functions of Kings Bench Division. When the High Court Act of 1861 was passed functions and power was preserved by section 9. Letters Patent of 1865 declared that the High Court is a Court of record and empowered to punish for contempt. Government of India Act, 1919 by section 106 preserved all the jurisdiction of the High Court and the same was retained in Government of India Act, 1935. When the India Independence Act 1947 was passed and two Dominions were created, Government of India Act, 1935 continued till the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. High Court was established by Article 165 and writ jurisdiction was conferred by Article 170. By Article 224 Letters Patent constituting the High Court was declared as "existing law" and by Article 227(5) it was stipulated that the High Court will have the same jurisdiction and power as it had before the Constitution day.

14. So the High Court under the Constitution of 1956 was the successor of the High Court that was created by Act 1861 and the Judges of that High Court had all the powers, function and jurisdiction that was given by charter of 1774 which again was the same powers, functions of the Kings Bench Division.

15. This power continued, till 7-10-58 when the Constitution was abrogated by Md. Ayub Khan. By Continuance of Laws Order 1958 post proclamation order that jurisdiction was retained subject to proclamation of Martial Law and its regulation. Challenge was given before the Supreme Court as to whether the superior Courts could call in question the grievances, the propriety or finding and legality of the order passed by Military Court. In the case of Ayub khan reported in P.L.D. 1960 (SC) 237. Munir. C.J. declared that the jurisdiction of the Court exists. In that case the Supreme Court of Pakistan quashed the conviction.

16. When in 1962 the Constitution was promulgated the powers and jurisdiction was mentioned in Article 98 of that Constitution. For the first time the nomenclature of prerogative writs such as Mandamus, Certiorari, Habeas Corpus and quo warranto were omitted from the constitutional vocabulary and the language was adopted which is in identical terms of the present constitutional terms and finds place in our Constitution in Article 102. Judicial pronouncement in the highest level have explained that the jurisdictional aspect has been enlarged by the introduction of the new constitutional terms and tenor and expression "without lawful authority" and "is of no legal effect" is not hedged by the constitutional limitation as found in prerogative writ of certiorari. The command for directing a person for refraining from doing which is not permitted to do or to do with which he is required by law to do has wider scope than prerogative writ of mandamus. While considering the writ of habeas corpus the constitutional term is not only that he is not held in custody without lawful authority, but "in an unlawful manner".

17. This Constitution of 1962 was abrogated in 1969 when the Martial Law was promulgated. But the power of the Court was preserved in Article 5(b) subject to the condition that the Court will not call into question the proclamation of Martial Law and no writ could be passed against the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Again, the question was raised as to the jurisdictional aspect. Lahore High Court in a Full Bench decision in the case of Mir Hasan, reported in PLD 1969 Lahore, 786 declared that this power of the Court cannot be taken away. No appeal was filed against that decision. However to notify the decision the Government attempted a device by way of passing a. Martial Law Order being Martial Law Order No. 3 of 1969. The Supreme Court declared that that Martial Law Order No. 3 of 1969 was illegal in Asma Jilani PLD 1972 (SC) 139. Hence the debate as to the jurisdiction of the superior Courts though continued the trend of decision shows that the jurisdiction was not only claimed but was exercised.

18. Through the liberation war when Bangladesh came into existence the High Court of Bangladesh was set up by Provisional Constitutional Order, P.O. No. 11 of 1972 dated 22-1-72. The jurisdictional aspect was clarified in P.O. 5 of 1972 where in Article 4 it is declared that all jurisdiction, original, appellate, special, revisional, etc. and all other powers which the old High. Court at Dacca had the new High Court of Bangladesh will have the same power, function and jurisdiction. And further it declared it as the Court of record. It expressly stated that this High Court of Bangladesh shall not have |he power to issue writ in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari and quo warranto, etc. but in August 1972 by P. O. 91 of 1972 the entire writ jurisdiction was reconferred vide Article 6(B)(1).

Thus the High Court has come into existence in its pristine glory to exercise the same power, function and jurisdiction which have been handed over Jo it from the 18th century.

19. Then the Constitution of Bangladesh was enacted and in the 4th Schedule original, appellate and other jurisdiction at the High Court was preserved and recognized. This continued till 15th August, 1975 when the Martial Law was proclaimed. Save and except clause (g) of the proclamation nothing was said as Jo the power, functions and jurisdiction of the superior Courts, namely, Supreme Court.

20. By the Second Proclamation (7th Amendment) Order being Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1976 the then president while bifurcating and creating a Supreme Court and a High Court inserted a new paragraph being paragraph 6A. The declaration was that the same power, function and jurisdiction of the High Court Division will be continued by the High Court (vide 6(6).

21.Then by Second Proclamation (10th Amendment) Order 1977 being Second Proclamation Order No. 1 of 1977 dated 27th November, 1977 the Supreme Court was restored as was in the Constitution having two divisions, namely, Appellate Division and High Court Division. By Article 6B the same functions, power and jurisdiction was conferred in the High Court Division which was exercised by the High Court previously.

22. The present dispensation is continuing. High Court Division is exercising all powers of the High Court and erstwhile High Court of Dacca. The conclusion therefore, is that the writ jurisdiction of the High Court has not only been preserved, but recognition has been given by the proclamation of Martial Law which was proclaimed on 20th August, 1975: In the proclamation of 20th August, 1975 an amendment was made that if the incumbent is unable to discharge the functions of the office of the president for any reason or he is to vacate the office of the president he may, however, nominate, any person as president of Bangladesh who shall enter upon only after talking an oath before the Chief Justice of Bangladesh or any Judge of the Supreme Court designated by him.

The emphasis is that the oath is to be taken before the Chief Justice of Bangladesh.

23. This office was vacated on 6-11-75 by the person who proclaimed Martial Law on 20th August, 1975. The mantle of the Martial Law fell upon a person who was none but than the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. This is unique in the history of Martial Law that the highest judicial authority had to take and perform the task of Martial Law. He, therefore, declared that it is necessary to assume the powers of the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Be it noted when the 20th August proclamation was made the form of Article 148 was changed. The oath as was required by the constitution was to be administered by the Speaker but the proclaimed who declared Martial Law in August, 1975 decided to take oath from the Chief Justice of Bangladesh and after taking oath entered into office.

24. This Martial Law therefore, had come not for destroying the legal order, but supplement it where there has been some breaches. The argument therefore, is that the Martial Law as supra constitutional law is not to be accepted in its entirety. It is a mere constitutional deviation.

25. Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney General frankly placed argument that this Martial Law was not by any coup of the armed forces. It was proclaimed by civil authority and the armed forces had to come as and to maintain the civil administration. This point is correct because reading two proclamations together as we have already analyzed the whole purpose of Martial Law was to bring the country on the even keel by way of fair election. In the case of Abdus Shukoor Vs. The State, reported in (1976) 28 DLR 441 a Division Bench of this Court has observed thus:-

“Martial Law is now known concept of jurisprudence. We have had series of Martial Laws in this Sub-continent since 1953, Martial Law is proclaimed when normal machinery breaks down and for taking certain corrective measures which are beyond the reach of normal laws.”

It was further mentioned in the case of Majibur Rahman Vs. The State, reported in (1977) 29 DLR (HD), 141 that:-

“Though the jurisdiction of the ordinary Court has been ousted, the scheme of Martial Law shows that the traditional system of Justice was retained...”

In the case of Malik Mir Hasan Vs. The Stale, reported in PLD 1969 Lahore, 786 the point was considered by a Full Bench. The question was whether a case under Act 11/47 could validly be transferred from ordinary criminal Court to a Martial Law Court. If was claimed that Martial Law Regulation 42 had conferred such power. The Full Bench repudiated the contention. When the question of jurisdiction of the High Court was raised the answer was given that the High Court of judicature at Lahore was constituted by Letters Patent of 1919 and it was constituted as a Court of record. Reference was made to section 29 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that when no Court is so mentioned, it may be tried by the High Court. Therefore, the High Court is the highest Court exercising criminal jurisdiction and in that view of the matter considering article 191 of their constitution the conclusion was thus :-

“The aforesaid enactment was temporary...which has become existing laws and the High Court continued to enjoy and exercise all the powers that were conferred time to time.”

The other learned Judge expressed the view that it is the inherent jurisdiction of the superior Court to interpret law. If was observed:-

“If an order is passed by a Martial Law authority or a Military Court which is in excess of or without jurisdiction its legal position is open for examination by the High Court or the Supreme Court, though these Courts would not and could not interfere if the order in question was one with jurisdiction.”

In that case it was held that the order of transfer of a case from Central Special Judge to Special Military Court was illegal. It was further held that the transfer was, therefore, liable to be quashed. We shall deal with this case more elaborately in another place.

26. In the case of Asma Jilani, reported in PLD 1972 (SC) 139 his Lordships, Hamoodur Rahman, C.J. considering the question of power and jurisdiction appreciated the frankness of Attorney-General who conceded that the Courts have and must have power to determine all questions of their own jurisdiction. His Lordship observed:

“The learned Attorney-General does not seriously dispute the correctness of the contention that "judicial power'' is different from "jurisdiction" and so far as judicial power is concerned it must exist in Courts as long as the Courts are there. In fact, he has been bold enough, and I admire him for his holdness, in characterizing these provisions of the presidential Order No. 3 of 1969, which seek to take away the judicial power itself as ''absurdities". He frankly concedes that the Courts have and must have the power to determine all questions of their own jurisdiction. It is a proposition so well-settled that no one can challenge it.”

His Lordship further considered the contention that in certain circumstances the Constitution can confer or restrict the jurisdiction of even the superior Courts and then observed :-

“But this is not the same thing as saying that it can also restrict or curtail the judicial power, because, that, in effect, would be denying to the Court the very function for which it exists i.e. to decide a controversy even if it relates to its own jurisdiction.”

27. Yakub Ali, J., another Member of the learned Court, while repudiating the contention that the power of the superior Court can be restricted (dealt that point at page 235) his Lordship after discussing that what is law and citing from various authors and text-book writers came to the conclusion as under :-

“The preponderant view appears to be that law is not the will of a sovereign. Law is a body of principles-called rules or norms-recognized and applied by the State in the administration of justice. It must have the contents and form of laws.”

His Lordship considered Article 3 that no Court, tribunal or other authority, including the Supreme Court and High Court shall question the proceedings and receive complaint, etc. against Martial Law and held that it was not law because it is essentially within the jurisdiction of Courts to determine whether their jurisdiction to try a dispute is barred by law. The learned Judge declared them as "offensive provision" and characterized the purpose of the order "was to deny the performance of judicial function". It was observed:

“It did not contain a body of principles which may be recognized and acted upon by the Courts. It reflected only the will of the Chief Martial Law Administrator who ordained that no action taken by him or by any Martial Law Authority, howsoever unjust such action may be, shall be open to judicial review.”

In this view of the matter it was held that both the Presidential Order No. 3 of 1969 and Martial Law Regulation 78, which authorized for Preventive Detention were intended "to deny to the Courts the performance of their judicial function, an object opposed to the concept of law. Neither would be recognized by the Court of law."

28. The last word has been said in the Pakistani jurisdiction in the case of Nusrat Bhutto. While considering the validity of the Martial Law that was proclaimed in 1977 the Supreme Court of Pakistan concluded that that Martial Law of 1977 is merely "a constitutional deviation for a temporary period end have specified limited objective, namely, the restoration of law and order and normalcy in the country and in earliest possible time holding of free and fair election for the purpose of restoration of democratic institutions."

29. In that context the Pakistan Supreme Court rejected the contention that the superior Court has been denuded their power and function. It observed:-

“The 1973 Constitution provides for a clear trichotomy of powers between the executive, legislative and judicial organs of the State. However, owing to reasons of necessity, the Executive and the Legislative powers now stand combined in one authority, for the reason that these two organs of the state had lost their constitutional and moral authority in the circumstances arising since the 7th of March 1977, but no such considerations arose in regard to the judicial organ of the State. Accordingly, on no principle of necessity could powers of judicial review vested in the superior Courts under the 1973 constitution, be taken away". (PLD 1977 (SC) 657)."

The learned Judges observed:

“The necessity which justified the proclamation of Martial Law did not arise owing to the failure of the Courts to adjudicate on these matters. Such matters must, therefore, continue to fall outside the purview of the Martial Law authorities and the only remedy to the citizens against any such encroachment be by way of judicial review in the superior Courts.”

30. In the case of Anisminic Ltd. Vs. Foreign Compensation Commission, reported in 1969 (2) Appeal Cases 147 the House of Lords considered section 4 of the Foreign Compensation Act, 1950 "the determination by the Commission of any application made to them under this Act shall not be called in question in any Court of Law." Their Lordships by majority came to the conclusion that this section cannot prevent the Court from making any declaration that the commissioner's declaration was a nullity. This is the last word from the English jurisdiction.

31. Hamoodur Rahman, C.J. brought out the distinction between "judicial power" and "jurisdiction". Rejecting the contention of the Attorney-General that where there is a written constitution the Courts are themselves creatures of the constitution and have only such jurisdiction as the constitution chooses to confer upon them. His Lordship observed:-

“I have no cavil with this pro position, as I myself in several cases indicated that the constitution can confer or restrict the jurisdiction of even superior Courts but this is not the same thing as saying that it can also restrict or curtail the judicial power, because in effect it would be denying to the Court the Very function for which it exists i.e. to decide a controversy even if it relates to its own jurisdiction. (p. 198).”

32. Mr. M. H. Khandkar, the learned Advocate appearing as Amicus Curiae developed this point further by citing the decision in 24 Calcutta Weekly Notes (Full B each) and A.I.R. 1972 (SC), 237 (para 9).

33. In the case of Keshabanonda Vs. State of Kerala, reported in A.I.R. 1973, (S5C) 1461 the Special Bench of 13 learned Judges considered amongst others the vires of Article 31-C which excluded judicial review by insertion of a clause of conclusiveness of the de termination, The majority opinion was that the second part, namely, "and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall he called in question in any Court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy" is invalid.

34. The noted author on constitutional Administrative Law by Wood philips (5th Edn) at page 543 after considering the Anisminio case referred to above remarked:

“Statutes have purported or appeared to exclude the jurisdiction of the Courts by the use of various drafting formulas though with scant success.”

Wade philips in "Constitutional and Administrative Law" (9th Edn at page 629) observed:-

“One frequently found clause was that a particular decision shall be final, but it is settled law that such a clause does not restrict the power of the Court to issue certiorari either for jurisdictional defect or for error of law on the record. Such a clause means simply that there is no right of appeal from the decision.”

35. From the trend in the decision in Robinson vs. Minister of Town and Country Planning 1947 (KB) 702; Commissioner of Customs and Excise Vs. Cure and Decky (1962) (1 QB) 340; Padfield Vs. Minister of Agriculture, 1968 (AC) 997 the noted authors have remarked:

“More recent decisions suggest a marked trend towards more interventionist brand of judicial review.”

36. It is not necessary to quote volume on this particular point. The conclusion is that the judicial power of the superior Courts can never be taken away. This power exists as long as the Court exists. This power is available even where the jurisdiction of the superior Courts have been barred.

37. In view of the above the conclusion is that judicial power of this Court cannot be taken away by Martial Law Regulation No.1 which has been passed in pursuance of the proclamation by saying no judgment, decision or sentence of a Martial Law Court shall be called in question in any manner whatsoever including the Supreme Court.

38. If the Court is validly constituted and in seisin of the case lawfully then it will be a case of exercise of jurisdiction. But if it is a case of absence of jurisdiction then by no declaration can such judgment be saved because such judgment is a nullity. The question is what about the present conviction which is under challenge.

39. Now we shall consider the present case. The learned Deputy Attorney General has raised a question of locus standi of the petitioner to file the writ petition. The petitioner Raji Joyhal Abedin is the father of condemned prisoner Abulal and uncle of other 3 condemned prisoners. It is stated in paragraph 20 of the petition "the petitioner will be highly aggrieved by the aforesaid death sentence as passed by Martial Law Court and he has locus standi to move this writ petition for the protection of their lives". In the petition as annexure-F which was filed by the learned Advocate requesting the Superintendent of Dacca Central Jail for allowing the condemned accused person to execute a power for moving this Court by way of writ against their conviction and sentence. The same, however, was denied and the petition was rejected vide the endorsement on it. So the petitioner is the father of one condemned person and uncle of other condemned persons. This point may be dismissed by a short remark where there Lordships of the Privy Council in 1969 I.A.C. at page 720 was considering a detention case which was challenged by his wife. The point was raised that she was not an aggrieved party and she had no right to file the appeal. The contention was rejected on the ground that her husband is in detention and deprivation of his liberty is sufficient for her to file the legal proceedings and therefore, she was aggrieved party. In Manzoor Elahi Vs. State (PLD 1975 (SC) 66 the Supreme Court of Pakistan entertained a petition although it was not moved by the detenue himself but by his brother. In the present case, the vakalatnama could not be obtained from the jail and the petition was filed by the father of one of the condemned prisoners who is also the uncle of other three condemned prisoners. The opinion is that he is an aggrieved party within the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution.

40. Now the Regulation 3 empowers the Government to transfer a case from one Court to another Martial Law Court or from a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal to a Martial Law Court. The Notification reads thus:-
