41. Special Tribunal is a creation of Special Powers Act 1974. Section 26 provides that offences specified in the schedule to the Special Powers Act "shall be triable exclusively by Special Tribunal constituted under sub-section (2). Sub-section (2) provides that every Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge and Assistant Sessions Judge shall, for the areas within his sessions division, be a Special Tribunal for the trial of offences triable under this Act. Sub-section (3) provides that a Special Tribunal consisting of the Sessions Judge may transfer, at any stage of the trial, any case from one Special Tribunal to another Special Tribunal within his sessions division. Paragraph (5) of the schedule provides that any offence punishable under any law committed being armed with fire arms or explosive substance will be tried under Special Powers Act.

42. The legislature has created special jurisdiction for special purpose, namely, for more speedy trial and effective punishment of certain grave offence. The jurisdiction of Special Tribunal is exclusive and it ousts the jurisdiction of the ordinary criminal Court. The case under section 302/201 is triable exclusively by Sessions Court under the normal law. But since fire arms were used the case was before the Special Tribunal and cognizance was accordingly taken.

43. Subsequently Martial Law was promulgated in 1975. Proclamation of Martial Law specified that by Martial Law Regulation the President has been empowered to set up Special Court or Tribunal for trial of offences under such Regulation or orders or for contravention thereof, and offences under any other law (clause b (i). Clause (iv) provides for barring the jurisdiction of any Court or Tribunal from trying any offence specified in such Regulations or Orders. Reading clause (i) and (iv) side by side the impression is that the President contemplated for, setting up special Court or tribunal for offences under the Regulation or orders and also under ordinary law and vide clause (iv) also contemplated the barring the jurisdiction of any Court or tribunal from trying offences specified by Regulation or orders. In other words the special Court can try offences under the Martial Law Regulation and under the ordinary, Court law; the ordinary Court will not try cases under Martial Law Regulation.

44. When the Court was constituted by Regulation I no special Court or tribunal was mentioned. Regulation 2 provides that the Government may by notification in the official gazette, constitute special martial law Courts and summary martial law Courts for such areas as may be specified in the notification. The marginal notes mentions "Martial Law Courts" although in the proclamation it has mentioned only "Special Courts or Tribunals". In the previous two Martial Laws in 1958 and 1969 when the Constitution was abrogated Special Courts were created, namely. Special Military Court and Summary Military Court and these were legal conceptions known to law. But the conception of Martial Law Court is something new which is not found in Army Act or any other enactment. In the Proclamation of 1969 the power was reserved for providing for setting up Military Court. By regulation 2 special Court of criminal jurisdiction were created, namely, Special Military Court and Summary Military Court. But it was provided that this Special Military Court should be constituted in the same manner and should exercise the same powers and should follow the same procedure as a Field General Court Martial convened under the Pakistan Army Act, 1952 and the provisions of that Act and of the Rules made thereunder should apply to and govern all such proceedings.

45. The present Martial Law Court that was created by Regulation 1 does not stipulate any such requirement. But provides in sub-regulation (3) that Chairman of a Special Martial Law Court shall be appointed from among Sessions Judges or Officers of the Defense Service of Bangladesh Rifles not below the rank of Lieutenant Colonel or equivalent, and of the two other members of such Court, one shall be appointed from among officers of the Defense Services or Bangladesh Rifles not below the rank of Major or equivalent and the other from among Magistrates of the first class. Thus a new conception has been introduced in the jurisprudence by introduction of a Court termed "Martial Law Court". This Martial Law Court had been set up without having specific class of cases which will be tried by it. In 1969 when Martial Law was promulgated series of Regulation were passed. Regulation No. 3 reads thus:

Notwithstanding anything contained in these Regulations, the Criminal Courts as by law established shall continue to exercise jurisdiction over persons accused of:

(a) offences other than offences created by these Regulations;

(b) offences not connected with present disturbances;

(c) offences which though connected with the present disturbances, have been transferred under these Regulations, for trial by such Courts.

Martial Law Regulation 42 was promulgated in the following terms:

Regulation No. 42

1. A Zonal Martial Law Administrator may direct that any case or class of cases, under the ordinary law pending in any criminal Court, irrespective of whether the case or cases relate to period before or after the imposition of Martial Law or whether trial has commenced or NOT, shall be transferred for trial to a Military Court specified by him and the Military Court shall try the case according to its own procedure. Where a case in which trial has commenced is transferred the Military Court to which the cafe is transferred shall NOT, by reasons of such transfer, be bound to recall and rehear any witness who has given evidence in the case before transfer, and may act on the evidence already recorded by or produced before the Criminal Court from which the case has been transferred.

2. All applications, of whatever nature, made to any Court, including a High Court, in respect of any case transferred to a Military Court and all proceedings connected with such applications shall-abate.

It will be noticed that in Regulation 3 of 1969 care was taken to define the jurisdiction and what type of cases can be tried by the ordinary criminal Courts. Further by Regulation 42 power given to Zonal Martial Law Administrators to transfer any case or class of cases under ordinary law "irrespective of whether the case relates to period before or after imposition of Martial Law."

Regulation 3(2) of 1975 which reads thus:

“Government may transfer a case from one Martial Law Court to another Martial Law Court or from a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal to Martial Law Court.”

No attempt was made as to which of the cases are to be tried by ordinary Court or which cases are liable to be transferred to. Martial Law Court. The learned Deputy Attorney General could not show any Regulation or Order which has laid down the guide-line or classified the cases to be tried by the respective Courts. Government has the power to set up Special Court and this is not disputed. Once a Special Court is established it is at once the duty to supply the norm as to how concurrence of the jurisdiction are to be regulated. This was noticed by Munir, C J. in the case of Ayub Khuro thus:

“Thus the effect of these two regulations was that Martial Law Courts and Ordinary Criminal Courts were invested with concurrent jurisdiction to try offences under the ordinary law as well as offences under the Martial Law Regulations and Orders. Nothing was said in any of the Regulations as to how this concurrent jurisdiction was to be regulated and a possible conflict between the two classes of Courts avoided. (PLD 1960 (SC), 237).”

Special Tribunal has been created under Special Powers Act and it has exclusive jurisdiction over the offences mentioned in the schedule to the Act. Martial Law Court does not appear to be invested with any special jurisdiction. This may be taken as general jurisdiction because no particular offences or class of offences have been allotted to if. A Special Tribunal is created by law and another extra constitutional authority had created another set of Courts e, g. Martial Law Courts without making them Court of special jurisdiction and they are now running paripasu. In the case of Majibur Rahman Vs. State (1977) 29 D.L.R. 141 it was pointed out:

“Martial Law Courts have been set up by the Regulation No. 1 of 1975 by virtue of the Proclamation of 20th August, 1975 and 8th November, 1975. Ordinary Criminal Court as established by law on constitutional authority had been retained and Martial Law Courts had been set up for dealing with the cases which come within the purview of the Martial Law Regulations. Both the Courts are running paripasu.”

When these two jurisdictions exist side by side they obviously have concurrent jurisdiction. The Martial Law Courts have been empowered to try also the offences under ordinary law and again the ordinary Courts have been continued with their respective jurisdiction. Then the special tribunals created under the Special Powers Act, 1974 are also functioning and exclusive jurisdiction have been vested by law. The present case was pending before Special Tribunal, Mymensingh and by notification mentioned above the case has been transferred to Special Martial Law Court. The question is when there is such concurrent jurisdiction if at all can be said so, how the case was transferred. Article 119 of the Corpus Juris Secundum is in the following terms;-

“19. Where a Court has jurisdiction of a crime, a statute simply conferring the same jurisdiction on another Court does not deprive the former of its jurisdiction, in the absence of an express provision or clear implication to that effect, but merely confers concurrent jurisdiction. Thus a statute conferring on a justice of the peace or other inferior Court jurisdiction to try a crime which is indictable in a superior Court does not by implication oust the superior Court of jurisdiction, Similarly, where a statute confers jurisdiction on a Court to try and to determine offences against the state, it will be presumed that such jurisdiction is concurrent with a municipal Court enforcing an ordinance which provides for the punishment of the same criminal act. Nevertheless where, from the terms of the statute conferring jurisdiction, it is apparent that the legislature intended the jurisdiction thus conferred to be exclusive, other Court is deprived of its jurisdiction, and any criminal prosecution pending therein when the statute goes into effect should not be transferred to the Court acquiring such exclusive jurisdiction, unless it appears that no such transfer was contemplated or intended by the statute. The exclusive character of a statutory Court's jurisdiction of an offence is destroyed by a statute conferring concurrent Jurisdiction thereof on other Courts, where the legislative intent to do so is clear.”

46. The principle quoted above can be appreciated thus; when the Special Powers Act was promulgated and created special tribunal for trying scheduled offences it was created as Court of exclusive jurisdiction qua ordinary sessions Court under the normal law. The question is when the Martial Law Courts were created whether these Courts were created as Courts having exclusive jurisdiction over certain criminal offences? Research does not show that any such exclusive character was detailed by any Regulation. On the contrary when Martial Law of 1969 was proclaimed such jurisdiction was detailed by Regulation No. 3 which has been quoted above. Regulation 3 continued the jurisdiction of criminal Courts over persons accused of:

(a) offence other than offences created by Regulations;

(b) offences not connected with disturbances;

(c) offences though connected with disturbances have been transferred, under the Regulations, for trial by such Courts. This was not done by the proclamation of 20th August not by any Regulation.

The position thus appears :-

(1) Criminal Courts and Martial Law Courts are having concurrent jurisdiction over offences under the normal law of the land.

(2) Special Tribunals under Special Powers Act, 1974 are Courts of exclusive jurisdiction qua Martial Law Courts.

(3) The exclusive character of Special Tribunal is not destroyed by Martial Law Proclamation or Regulation.

47. Therefore, the transference of the case from the Special Martial Law Court was without any lawful authority because Regulation 3(2) is mere an enabling provisions which at best can come into play in the circumstances as in (1) above e. g. between Martial Law Court and Criminal Court. Mere mention of Special Tribunal in Regulation 3(2) will not alter the position because from a conviction by Special Tribunal an appeal as of right lies to the Appellate Tribunal whereas from conviction by Martial Law Court no such appeal lies as of right. This point will be considered at a later stage.

48. The charge-sheet was submitted and the case was pending before the Special Tribusunal, Mymensingh. The case transferred to the Martial Law Court which was not declared by law to be a Court of Special jurisdiction nor any class of cases were allotted to it. Alternatively if the two have concurrent jurisdiction, if at all, in the matters of crime under ordinary law the one which was created especially for trying these cases, namely, Special Tribunal, cannot be divested from its jurisdiction by mere order of a transfer passed in the executive jurisdiction. This view was also accepted in the case of Mr. Hassan Vs. State, reported in PLD 1969 Lahore. 786 where it was noted that the Special Judge appointed under the Pakistan Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958, is a Court of special jurisdiction, its jurisdiction being confined only to specific class of cases under a prescribed procedure. Martial Law Regulation No. 42, therefore, would not be attracted to this category of Cases pending in the Court of Special Judge. Accordingly the Full Bench held that the order transferring the case from the Court of the Special Judge to the Special Military Court was defective on the legal plane and was without jurisdiction.

49. In this view of the matter also the opinion is the transfer of the present case from the Court of Special Tribunal to the Special Martial Law Court was illegal and without jurisdiction. If a decision is given without jurisdiction that is nullity and no amount of confirmation by a superior authority will make valid an order which is nullity. In the words of Munir, C.J. that will be a case that confirmation would be void and void added Jo void is doubly void.

"49A. Mr. Serajul Huq, the learned Advocate attacked the conviction from another angle, namely, the retrospective operation of the Regulation 3(2) is hit by Article27 of the Constitution. Article 27 is found under Part III captioned "Fundamental Rights" proclaiming: equality before law--"All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal projection of law."

50. Mr. Huq has argued that the procedure which is laid down under the Special Powers Act provides for an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal whereas the Martial Law Regulation No. 4 provides that no appeal shall lie from any unanimous judgment or decision of a Special Martial Law Court. If the judgment is not unanimous then an appeal is provided for and an appeal will lie to Appellate Tribunal. This provision was recast by Regulation No. 3 of 1976 wherein paragraph 4(2) was substituted by new clause as under:

“All proceedings of Special Martial Law Courts shall immediately after the termination thereof to be submitted to the Government for review and all sentences of death or transportation for life shall have to be confirmed by the President.”

51. The net result was whatever appeal was provided for owing to any unanimity of the judgment that itself was taken away and the provision for appeal was totally abolished. The inchoate right for appeal as was given earlier was now taken away without ceremony. This discrimination affected the accused prejudicially because an apple is a vested right.

52. The argument deserves fuller consideration as to whether fundamental right under Article 27 is at all available. The contention of Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney- General that this fundamental right came within the mischief of Proclamation of Emergency dated 28. 12. 74 because the president by Order declared that the right to move the Court for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Articles 27, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 42, 43 of the Constitution and proceeding pending in Court for the enforcement of the said rights shall remain suspended for the period during which the proclamation of emergency is in force. The proclamation of Martial Law in clause (f) mentions that all Acts, Ordinances, President's Orders, and other orders, Proclamations, rules, regulation, bye-laws, notification and other legal instruments in force on 15th August, 1975 shall continue to remain force until repealed, revoked or amended. Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury contended that since the Proclamation of emergency and Presidential Orders made in pursuance thereto dated 28.12. 74 is still in force, Article 27 of the Constitution will not be available to the petitioner.

53. The main question is whether these rights are now available. It will be seen that Article 33 also was mentioned in the Presidential Order dated 28. 12. 74. Article33(4)(5) of the Constitution prohibits any law providing for preventive detention unless it ensures four things in case of preventive detention, namely, (1) right to be informed regarding the grounds of his detention, (2) right of the representation, (3) reference to Advisory Board and (4) action upon the report of the Advisory Board. These rights are essentially rights within the concept of fundamental right. Corresponding provision can be found from the Indian Constitution in Article 22 the Proclamation and Presidential Order dated 28.12.74 is still in force then the rights mentioned in Article 33(4)(5) are not available. Martial Law proclamation continues Orders subject to the condition until they are repealed, revoked or amended. By amendment of the Emergency Powers Act in 18. 8. 77 communication of the grounds of the detention order and constitution of Advisory Committee and a reference thereto and the action upon the report of the Advisory Committee have been provided for. As already been noted these are essential concepts within the fundamental rights. If these rights are available by amendment of the Emergency Powers Act then the fundamental rights have been re-conferred. If not, how was it necessary for a regime during Martial Law to confer the rights upon the citizens which have been taken away by proclamation of Emergency under Constitution.

54. Either the Proclamation of Emergency and Presidential Order is dead or alive. If it is dead then, the, rights have re-appeared. If it is not, the rights simply are not there Assuming that these proclamations and Orders are still alive then how this Emergency Powers Act was amended for bringing into the conception of fundamental rights and how correspondingly Articles 44 and 102 of the Constitution were amended by Martial Law Order for the enforcement of these rights?.

55. Law does not contemplate an absurd proposition. Therefore, let us assume that these Presidential Orders and Proclamation of Emergency are not alive. Now whether the laws can be brought into consistent plane. It will appear at once that Article 44 of Constitution which was amended by 4th Amendment of the Constitution, Act-II of 1975 has drastically changed the complexion of the Article. Previously the Article read as under:-

“The right to move the Supreme Court in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this part is guaranteed.”

Sub-Article (2):

“without prejudice the power of the Supreme Court under Article 102 Parliament may by law empower any other Court within the local limits of its jurisdiction to exercise all of any of the powers.”

After 4th Amendment it reads thus:-

“Parliament may by law establish a constitutional Court, tribunal or commission for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this part.”

A drastic change has been made. The guarantee that has been given that has been now taken away by the 4th Amendment.

56. Similarly the machinery that has been provided by Article 102(1) which reads before the 4th Amendment as follows:-

“102(2). The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved may make such direction or to order any person or authority including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of Republic as may by appropriate for the enforcement of any fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution.”

After the 4th Amendment it reads as under:-

“The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law.”

By legislative amendment the complexion of Article 102 is also changed. The guarantee that was given in Article 44 for the enforcement of the fundamental rights mentioned in Part III by the machinery provided under Article 102 was taken away by the Fourth Amendment.

57. Re-conferment of those two provisions in its original character and color by Second Proclamation (7th Amendment) order dated 28-5-76 which was reiterated by the Second Proclamation (10th Amendment) dated 27-11-77 bringing the entire jurisdiction in its original position and introducing the provisions of Article 33 into the Emergency Powers Act, the opinion is the fundamental rights which were taken away by the 4th Amendment have been reconferred by these two Martial Law Proclamations. If Article 33 had been reconferred there is no doubt that other rights are also available because proclamation said that such proclamation is in force until it is amended, revoked and repealed. It is a case of repeal by implication. If this analysis is correct which we think to be, the latest message of the President to the nation wherein the President who is also the Chief Martial Law Administrator in his message to the nation from the national hook up said :-

“I have observed that the independent and free minded people of Bangladesh did not accept the politics and state system introduction through the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution. One party political system and annulment of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in enforcing the fundamental rights etc. were included under the Fourth Amendment. That is why I have already repealed these undemocratic provisions through different ordinance.”(Bangladesh Times dated 22-4-78)."

58. The issue is now clinched to the hilt and the Presidential message shows that the analysis made above is correct, namely, that the fundamental rights have re-appeared and Article 44 has given guarantee for the enforcement of these rights through the machinery of Article 102 of the Constitution. That Article 44 has given a guarantee is clear because a similar provision exists in the Indian Constitution as well and the guarantee to move for enforcement of fundamental rights is itself a fundamental right. This view was taken in the case of K. K. Kochunni vs. State of Madras, reported in AIR 1959. (SC). 725. The Indian Supreme Court took a further view that it is the duty of the Court to grant relief whenever such right is infringed in the case reported in AIR 1961 (SC), 65 (68). To conclude the significant aspect is that Article 44 finds with Part of the Constitution and Part III is captioned as "Fundamental Rights". Therefore, the guarantee in the Article 44 itself is a fundamental right.

59. If this is a fundamental right, which we have held to be so then the transfer of this case from the Court of Special Tribunal to the Special Martial Law Court is hit by Article 27 because in the same circumstances e.g. in cases of murder with fire-arms one case is liable to be tried by the Special Tribunal whereas another case is liable to be tried by Martial Law Court. The procedures are absolutely different-in one case there is an appeal before Appellate Tribunal under the Special Power Act and in the other case there is no appeal.

60. It is contended that no one has right to the procedure and the retrospectivity has been given by the law. Mr. Serazul Huq made an argument that the offence was committed before the Martial Law. The procedure that has been laid down in the Special Powers Act has provided for an appeal. The Regulation 3(2) has not expressly mentioned that the offences committed before Martial Law and pending before Special Tribunal are also liable to be transferred. The accused has a vested right e.g. the right of appeal.

61. In the case of Adnan Afzal Vs.Capt. Sher Afzal reported in (1969)21 DLR (SC) 123=PLD 1969 (SC) 187, Hamoodur Rahman, C.J. while considering the aspect of the retrospectivity of legislation came to the conclusion that an appeal is a valuable right and that is a matter of right. His Lordship questioned what are the matters of procedure and answered thus:-

“The next question, therefore, that arises for consideration is as to what are matters, of procedure. It is obvious that matters relating to the remedy, the mode of trial, the manner of taking evidence and forms of action are all matters relating to procedure. Crawford too takes the view that questions relating to jurisdiction over a cause of action, venue, parties pleadings and rules of evidence also pertain to procedure, provided that burden of proof is not shifted. Thus a statute purporting to transfer jurisdiction over certain causes of action may operate retrospectively. This is what is meant by saying that a change of forum by a law is retrospective being a matter of procedure only. Nevertheless, it must be pointed out that if in this process any existing rights are affected or the giving of retrospective operation causes inconvenience or injustice, then the Courts will not even in the cause of a procedural statute, favour an interpretation giving retrospective effect to the statute. On the other hand, if the new procedural statute is of such a character that its retrospective application will tend to promote justice without any of the parties concerned, the Courts would favourably incline towards giving effecto such procedural statutes retrospectively.”

That eminent Judge took into consideration that transfer of cases from the Court of the Magistrate u/s. 488 Cr. P. C. to the Family Court created by an Act of 1964 was beneficial because it provided for an appeal from the decision of such Court. That was a beneficial legislation and since no appeal was provided for against an order u/s. 488 Cr. P. C. the learned Judge took the view that no exception could be taken for giving the retrospective operation to the Family Court Act but reminded that by giving such retrospective operation of a procedural statute it must be seen that it does not operate unfavourably to the parties and in a criminal case to the accused. A Full Bench decision reported in 30 DLR 49 has dealt with this point exhaustively. Ruhul Islam, J. (as his Lordship then was) has pointed out that the vested right of appeal cannot be taken away.

62. As already been mentioned that Regulation 3(2) if given retrospective operation then at once it will deprive the accused from appeal which was provided for by the Special Powers Act.

63. Next, the point is considered from the angle of Rule of Law. Dicey in his Book on Law of Constitution while dealing with the rule of law has summed up as to the meaning of 'rule of law' amongst others at page 202 as follows :-

(1) it means in the first place the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power and excludes the existence of arbitrariness of prerogative or even of wide discretionary authority on the part of the government;

(2) it means equality before law or equal or subjection of classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law Courts, the rule of law in this sense excludes the idea of any exemption or officials or others from the duly of obedience to the duty of law which governs other citizens or from the jurisdiction of ordinary tribunals.

The conception of equality before law is postulated in the preamble of the Constitution of Bangladesh:-

“A society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice are available, economic and social justice will be secured for all citizens”.

64. The preamble was amended by the Martial Law Proclamation but this part of the preamble has not been changed. Therefore, it can be said without hesitation that the law making authority, has consciously kept this provision of the preamble in tact. Therefore, if the equality before law is the cherished desire of the people of Bangladesh which has been mentioned in the preamble then apart from Article 27 of the Constitution the transfer of this case from the Court of Special jurisdiction to the Court of Martial Law is violative of the clause of equality because no norms or guide-line has been given by law for passing order of transfer. To hold otherwise is to allow the executive to pick and choose according to its own arbitrary decision.

65. In the case of State of West Bengal Vs. Answer Ali, reported in AIR 1952 (SC) 92, the discriminatory treatment without reasonable classification was under challenge when the question was whether these cases could be transferred to the Special Court created by Section 5 of the West Bengal Special Court Act. The Supreme Court by the judgment of the majority declared that since no reasonable classification has been made for as to which offence or what category of case will be transferred to Special Court so created it is discriminatory. Mukherjee, J observed:-

"As I have said already, in the present case the discrimination arises on the terms of the Act itself. The fact that it gives unrestrained power to the State Government to select in any way it likes the particular cases of offences which should go to a Special Tribunal and withdraw in such cases the protection which the accused normally enjoys under the criminal Law of the country, is on the face of it discriminatory”

66. Be it noted that the learned Judge has found in the enactment itself a scope for discriminatory treatment because the enactment has prescribed the procedure which is different from the ordinary criminal law of the country and such protection that is allowed to an accused under the ordinary law is denied by the Special Law.

67. In the case of Basheshar Nath Vs. I.T. Commissioner, reported in AIR 1959 (SC) 149, the Indian Supreme Court per S.R. Das, C.J. while commenting on the Article 14 observed:-

“There can, therefore, be no doubt or dispute that this Article is founded on a sound public policy recognized and Valued in all civilized states.”

68. In the famous case of Keshabananda Vs. State of Kerala, reported in AIR 1973 (SC) the Indian Supreme Court was considering certain amendments of the Constitution. The majority Judges (9-4) took the view that amendments of the Constitution can be made subject to certain conditions. It was held that the basic feature of the Constitution cannot be changed and the fundamental rights cannot be abrogated. The basic feature of our Constitution is found in the preamble as it has been found in the Indian jurisdiction and equality clause has been described as the basic principle of republicanism per Patanjali Sastri, C.J. in AIR, 1952 (SC) 75. Mohajan, J. described as principle of republicanism in the same case, Das, C.J. termed it as founded on a sound public policy recognized and valued in all civilized states in AIR 1959 (SC), 149. Subba Rae, J. termed it as a necessary corollary to the high concept of the rule of law.

69. Thus this equality clause need not be retained fundamentally in a constitution as a fundamental right. It is the part of the organic system itself that no one will be treated discriminatorily. It must not be understood that we have advocated the theory that no classification can be made. Our view is: a law which provides for trial of particular cases by special Courts or by procedure which differs substantially from the ordinary procedure to the prejudice of the accused is violation of equality before law is there is no classification and if the enactment does not give any underlying policy to determine as to which cases will go before Special Court. 9 DLR (SC) 117 is authority for this proposition. But there will be no infringement if any offence or class of offences are specified by legislature to be triable by special Court or under special procedure. Such view is taken in the case of Lachmandas Kewalram and another Vs. State of Bombay, reported in AIR 1952 (SC) 235 where in law a fair and reasonable classification was made and intelligible differential was supplied in law to guide the executive to which case will go to the special Court.

70. Next we further reiterated that the law must state in clear terms so as to guide the executive to take decision to send the cases from one Court to other Court. In that case it will not be bad. The Indian Supreme Court in Kangshari Haldar Vs. West Bengal reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 457 laid down two tests; (1) whether the classification is rational and based on intelligible differentiation, (2) has the basis of differentiation any national nexus with its avowed policy and object.

Keeping these principles in mind we are constrained to mention that we do not see any such guidance in Martial Law Regulation 3(2) or in any other Regulation or order.

71. On the contrary, we find even in the Martial Law Regulation a systematic classification had been made in so far as the Regulation 11 & 12 and 17(b) are concerned. Regulation 11 provides for penalty for corruption and criminal misconduct "whether it was done before or after the commencement of Regulation". Regulation 12 provides for the penalty for the illegally acquired property "whether it was acquired before or after the commencement of the Regulation". Regulation 7(b) provides for fresh trial for withdrawn cases which were withdrawn at any time before the commencement of any Regulation.

72. The law making authority has supplied the guidance by giving retrospectivity to these cases and, therefore when the law making authority has not given retrospectivity under 3(2), on the principle of expressio unins exclusio alterius". Expressed enactment shuts the door to further implication, the conclusion is that, the legislature did not intend to give retrospective effect in all cases.

73. Martial Law Regulation No.16 of 1976 dated 14-16-76 has provides for jurisdiction of special Martial Law tribunal. Sub-clause (4) says the tribunal may try any offence, whether committed before or after the commencement of this Regulation punishable (a) under chapter-VI or VII of the Penal Code, (b) under the Army Act, the Air Force Act, he Nevy ordinance or any other Rules or Regulations made thereunder, (c) under Regulations 13 or 17 of the Martial Law Regulations (d) attempts or conspires to commit or abetment of etc. and also provided that the tribunal may also try such other offences punishable under any other Martial Law Regulation or law for the time being in force as the Government may, by order in writing, direct. Thus a classification has been made and whenever retrospectivity has been given it has been said so expressly even by the Martial Law Regulation. Therefore, it is laic in the day to argue (hat the enabling power given under Martial Law Regulation 2(3) provides for transfer of cases from ordinary criminal Court to Martial Law Court only because an order has been passed by the Government in respect of offence committed before the Martial Law. In this connection section 94 of the Army Act 1952 may be considered which contemplates a case of concurrent jurisdiction of a criminal Court and a Court martial in respect of "civil offence" and section 95 provides that if the criminal Court is of the opinion that the proceedings ought to 'have been instituted before it in respect of "civil offence" then the controversy can be resolved by referring the matter to the Central Government whose order upon such reference is final. No such provision has been made by the Proclamation or Regulation.

74. We have already found that present Martial Law is completely different from that of 1958 or 1969. The constitution has not been abrogated; only certain part of it has been circumscribed by the Martial Law Proclamation out of necessity. This Martial Law is a mere constitutional deviation and not one of Wellingtonian style. The Chief Justice of Bangladesh, instead of the Speaker, had to administer oath to the President after proclamation of Martial Law. Not only that the Chief Justice had to perform the task of both President and Chief Martial Law. Administrator for some time until the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator was handed over to the Army Chief. The Martial Law Courts had been set up to try certain specific offences and certain now offences as was created by Martial Law Regulations. The function and jurisdiction of the normal Courts were not disturbed. Remedial measures were taken by amendment of Emergency Powers Act and Special Powers Act; provisions of bail were free from restrictive conditions. Thus on the Whole, the declared policy to take the county to the cherished goal through democracy was being pursued. In such setting, the contention that jurisdiction of the superior Court has been ousted in so far as Martial Law Courts are concerned do not appear to be sound Moreover, in this trial five accused had been sentenced to death by a Tribunal which was not composed by persons having judicial experience in civil offence. Without mean in any disrespect, the Martial Law Court has purported to try an ordinary penal offence of murder punishable under section 302 BPC The offence was not one of those Military offences. It was a simple "civil offence". To deny an appeal from such conviction is to treat discriminately. In such situation the judicial power of the superior Court is all the more attracted to examine whether the trial was held in the exercise of jurisdiction. Viewing the matter from this angle, we have come to the conclusion that the transfer itself was defective and illegal. It was a case pending before Special Tribunal. Had it been the case that the Martial Law Regulations have provided that all the cases under suction 302 BPC are triable by Special Martial Law, then possibly an argument would be advanced in support of the proposition that this petition is not maintainable.

75. Next, the offence was committed before proclamation of Martial Law e.g. on 18. 3.75. This point was considered elaborately in Criminal Revision Case No. 381 of 1976. K.M. Subhan, J (as his Lordship then was) observed:-

“There is nothing in the preamble of the First Proclamation or for that matter the Second proclamation which seeks to confer jurisdiction to the Martial Law Court to try certain offences committed even before the birth of Bangladesh.”

His Lordship considered the question of retrospectivity and observed:-

“In our opinion, the use of the word ''before" can not be stretched beyond |he period immediately before the proclamation was issued.”

With respect, we have no reason to take a different view.

76. In this view of the matter we have come to the conclusion that (1) the petitioner is an aggrieved party and the petition is maintainable, (2) the judicial power of this Court is preserved and cannot be taken away, (3) fundamental rights are available to the citizens inasmuch as the proclamation and Presidential Order dated 28.12.74 have been repealed by implication, (4) retrospectivity whenever is to be given has been done expressly and nothing can be implied, (5) procedural law may be changed but if it is meant taking away of right e.g. appeal which is vested in the accused that can not be taken away, (6) equality before law is a high concept of rule of law and cherished by all civilized states. Therefore, whenever any special Court is created or any special procedure is provided the law must lay down standards or at least indicate in clear terms the underlying policy and purpose which will guide the executive to determine as to which class or class of cases are to be sent to Special Court, (7) whenever concurrent jurisdiction is created the law creating such concurrent jurisdiction must give clear guide-line for deciding which are to be sent to the Special Court or to the Ordinary Court, (8) whenever there are Courts having general jurisdiction and special jurisdiction the cases triable exclusively by Special Courts cannot be transferred to the Court of general jurisdiction, (9) the transfer of the present case from the Special Tribunal, Mymensingh to Special Martial Law Court was arbitrary and therefore, illegal. Such illegality has rendered the conviction a nullity, and (10) offences committed before the Martial Law cannot be tried by Martial Law Courts in the absence of any expressed retrospectivity.

77. In the result, therefore, this Rule is made absolute. The order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special Martial Law Court No.11 is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The condemned prisoners will be tried in accordance with law by competent Court and till then they will be in custody as under-trial prisoners.

We acknowledge the assistance that has been given particularly by Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney-General and Mr. Serajul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner and we also acknowledge the assistance of Mr. N.H. Khondkar, the learned Advocate who has appeared in this case as Amicus Curiae.

Abdul Malek J.- I agree.

End.

parties:
Redwan Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Election Tribunal District Judge and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: In this Rule, respondents have been called upon to show cause why order dated 23.5.93 passed by the Parliamentary Election Tribunal, Comilla, in Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1991 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or to pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may deem fit and proper.

2. In this case the petitioner, Redwan Ahmed was elected as member of the Parliament in the election held on 27.2.91 from No. 253 Parliament Constituency (Comilla-6), securing 31,179 votes i.e. 548 votes more than his rival candidate Md.Ali Ashraf, respondent No. 2 who secured 30,631 votes and his name was duly published in the official gazette on 6.3.91 and the petitioner was administered oath of office as member of the Parliament. Thereafter the respondent No. 2 filed the aforesaid Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1991 alleging, inter alia, that his agents were forcibly ousted from the polling station and were not allowed to perform their duties and counting of the votes were made in their absence and that large number of ballot papers with his symbol 'Boat' were declared invalid arbitrarily so as to show larger number of votes in favour of the symbol 'Clock' of the petitioner and that result declared was not consistent with the actual votes cast in favour of the petitioner and the respondent No. 2. Respondent No. 2 further alleged in that case that such illegalities took place in 18 polling stations as detailed in Paragraph Nos. 7, 10 and 17 of the election petition and further that some lost ballot papers were not accounted for.

3. The petitioner contested the said election petition by filing written statement denying the allegations and asserted the election was held and votes were counted according to law and rules and there was no illegality and irregularity in the same and the polling agents of respondent No. 2 never complained or raised objection before the Presiding Officers nor before the Returning Officer and did not seek recounting of ballot papers of any centre except filing an application on 5.3.91 before the Chief Election Commissioner by the election agent of the respondent No. 2.

4. During pendency of the election petition the respondent No. 2 prayed for calling for the election materials and recounting of the ballot papers. Election Tribunal by order dated 21.5.91 called for the election materials and by order dated 6.6.91 decided that prayer for recounting of the ballot papers will be considered after recording the evidence of the witnesses.

The petitioner produced and examined 50 witnesses and the respondent No. 2 examined 39 witnesses in support of their respective case. Thereafter by impugned order dated 23.5.93 Election Tribunal directed recounting of ballot papers in 12 centres. Being aggrieved by the said order the petitioner moved this court and obtained the Rule.

5. The Rule is contested by the respondent No. 2 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations made in paragraph No. 12 of the petition and asserting that there was large scale rigging in the poll and the same was brought to the notice of the proper authority and the Election Tribunal upon hearing the parties rightly and justly passed the order for recounting and the writ petition has been filed to delay the disposal of the election petition.

6. Mr. Khondker M Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner placed before us the petition and other materials on record and the impugned order. He submitted that Election Tribunal acted illegally and with material irregularity in exercise of its jurisdiction in passing the impugned order violating the law laid down by this court to direct recounting. He specially drew our attention to paragraphs 8 to 12 of the writ petition. His main contention is that the Election Tribunal though mentioned in the impugned order that 19 PWs. deposed in support of the alleged unfair means adopted by the election staffs during the counting of votes but discussed cursorily the evidence of PWs 3, 33 and 34 only. His further contention is that though the Election Tribunal mentioned that 22.0 PWs. deposed that counting of votes were fair but did not discuss their evidence at all and did not assign any reason for discarding the same. He, therefore, submitted that non-consideration of material evidence on record has vitiated the impugned order and as such the impugned order should be quashed and the case remanded to the Election Tribunal to decide the matter after detailed consideration of the evidence on record.

7. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 submitted that there is no error in the exercise of jurisdiction on the part of the Election Tribunal in passing the impugned order. He further submitted that impugned order being an interlocutory order it is sufficient if the Election Tribunal finds prima facie case for passing the interlocutory order for recounting ballot papers. He also submitted that impugned order has in no way prejudiced the petitioner who filed the case only to delay the disposal of the election petition.

8. It appears that the Election Tribunal considered the evidence of 19 PWs and 22 OPWs with a view to find out the polling stations where the votes are required to be recounted. It further appears that the Election Tribunal after considering the pleadings and said evidence concluded that out of 18 centres there is no evidence whatsoever in respect of 6 centres and as such he found no reason for directing recounting in those 6(six) centres.

9. With respect to the remaining 12 centres the Election Tribunal observed as follows:

"On consideration of the evidence on record I hold that the petitioner has succeeded to make out a prima facie case pressing home the fact that there might have occurred errors and mischiefs in the counting of votes and consequently I am of the opinion that for the ends of justice the votes be recounted in these 12 centres."

It is true that Election Tribunal did not discuss in detail the evidence of the 19 PWs and also the evidence of 22 OPWs and did not assess their evidence in juxtaposition and also did not assign any reason for discarding the evidence of the said OPWs for which learned Advocate for the petitioner made serious grievance before us. But it is not the grievance of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the said 19 PWs did not state anything regarding illegalities and irregularities committed in counting of the votes in the concerned 12 election centres. The Election Tribunal noticed that PW 33, an Asstt. Presiding Officer stated that many invalid ballot papers were counted in favour of the petitioner. PW 34 Manik Lal, a polling officer, stated that there was rigging in counting of the ballot papers and he denied the suggestion that the signatures appearing in the result sheet were those of the Election Officers. The Election Tribunal though did not discuss the evidence in detail in passing the impugned order it is clear that the Election Tribunal considered the relevant evidence from both sides and came to the finding that the respondent No. 2 was able to make out a prima facie case for recounting the ballot papers in 12 centres mentioned therein. The impugned order undoubtedly is an interlocutory order passed during the trial of the case and at this stage it is not necessary to mention the evidence of witnesses in detail. It is sufficient for passing an interlocutory order that there is evidence on record for justifying the same. Since there is nothing to show that there was any evidence to justify the impugned order simply because no reason was assigned for discarding the evidence of OPWs no fault could be found with the impugned order at this stage. We also do not find at this stage that the impugned order has been passed to the prejudice of the petitioner inasmuch as there is no grievance that the election materials were tampered with. That stage has not yet came.

10. Election Tribunal is entrusted with disposal of an election petition expeditiously. Though the Election Rules do not authorise the Election Tribunal to order recounting of the ballot papers it is now well settled by the decision of this Court (27 DLR 594) as well as of the Appellate Division (27 DLR (AD) 117, 31 DLR (AD) 296, 32 DLR (AD) 186 & 38 DLR (AD) 275 that Election Tribunal can order recounting of ballot papers when it is a material issue before the Election Tribunal and the Tribunal is satisfied from evidence on record that recounting is indispensably necessary for deciding the case.

<u>11. Election Tribunal has power to decide a question before it rightly as well as wrongly. A court of appeal can only correct a wrong decision made by a subordinate Court or Tribunal after considering the evidence on record taking a different view. High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction can only interfere in a writ of certiorari when a subordinate Court or Tribunal acted without jurisdiction or failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it or when it acted illegally and or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction. Had the 19 PWs not stated anything from which the Election Tribunal could have arrived at the conclusion as it did, it could be said that it acted illegally and/or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction. Passing of the impugned order in the manner done by the Election Tribunal noticed before is neither an illegality nor material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction. No wrong could be pointed out before us except that the Election Tribunal did not discuss the evidence in detail. Since the Election Tribunal has jurisdiction to direct the recounting of ballot papers and it has passed the impugned order on consideration of evidence though not in detail it cannot be said that Election Tribunal acted illegally and or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction. We, therefore, find no merit in the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Rather we find merit in the contention of the learned Advocate of the respondent No. 2 that the petition has been filed to delay the disposal of the case before the Election Tribunal.</u>

12. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs assessed at Taka 2,000.00. The order of stay stands vacated and the Election Tribunal is directed to dispose of the case expeditiously.

Let a copy of the order be sent to the Election Tribunal expeditiously.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J. This is an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh challenging an order dated 1-10-75 of the Election Tribunal at Chittagong Sadar setting aside the election of the petitioner as Chairman of a Union Parishad and declaring a defeated candidate (Respdt. No. 2) elected in his place. The impugned order eras made by Mr. M.A. Hoque Election Tribunal and Munsif, 4th Court, Chittagong in Election Tribunal Case No. 6 of 1975.

2. The election was held on 30-12-73 simultaneously in three Wards for electing a Chairman for the Suabil Union Parishad. The petitioner and Respdt Nos. 2, 3 and 4 were the contesting candidates and their Election Symbols were respectively Hurricane, Datetree, Bicycle and Balance. In this election the petitioner secured 2615 votes and the respondents Nos. 2, 3 and 4 secured respectively 2375, 865 and 97 votes, and on the basis of these results, the Returning Officer (Respdt. No. 5) declared the petitioner elected as Chairman.

3. Respdt. No. 2, however, made a petition under section 56(2) of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973, briefly the 'Election Rules' before the Tribunal at Fatikehari challenging the petitioner's election on a number of grounds, such as, the petitioner had threatened the supporters of the respondent and intimidated his voters, snatched away their ballot papers, procured votes of dead persons and also by false personation, set up canvassing camps within the prohibited areas of the Polling centres, entertained the voters as well as the Presiding Officers and Polling Officers and that he also procured unauthorised arms from Rajakars and that the Presiding Officers being biased wrongly counted the ballot paper rejecting many of his valid votes but accepting invalid votes of the petitioner and thereby rendered the entire election a farce. He prayed that he be declared elected in place of the petitioner, in the alternative, the election as a whole be set aside.

4. The petitioner denied the allegations by filling a written statement and contested the petition. Respondent No. 5 and respondents 8 to 10 respectively denied the allegations by tiling two separate written objections but they did not contest the petition. For some reasons this case was transferred from Fatikehari to Chittagong by the Election Commission, whereupon the transferee Tribunal heard the matter on 23rd, 25th, 26th and 30th September, 1975 and delivered its judgment on the 1st October, 1975. The learned Tribunal rejected all the allegations brought against the petitioner except one which related to the alleged wrong counting of ballot papers  He re-opened three sealed gunny bags containing the election materials, examined the ballot papers and rejected 459 ballot papers of the petitioner as invalid which had been found valid by the Presiding Officers. He also rejected as invalid 127, 21 and 2 ballot papers respectively of respondents 2, 3 and 4. The Tribunal discovered 12 valid ballot papers 7 for the Hurricane, 2 for the Date-tree, 2 for the Bicycle and 1 for the Balance-mixed up with the invalid ones. He salvaged them and added them to the account of the respective candidates. The result of recounting is as shown below:

Petitioner 2163 as against 2615

Respondent No. 2 2249 as against 2375

Respondent No. 3 846 as against 865

Respondent No. 4 	96 as against 97.

The Tribunal, in view of this finding, declared the Respondent No. 2 elected on setting aside the petitioner's election.

5. As to how these results of counting were arrived at, the learned Tribunal observed that the Presiding Officers committed error by counting "some ballot papers" having no official seal on their back, "a good number" of ballot papers had double marking and "a good number" of ballot papers were either "illegible" or had marks done by "hard substance other than rubber stamp". The Tribunal, however, did not state how many ballot papers fell under each of these classes and as such a clear picture of the matter is not available from the judgment.

6. The petitioner did no accept this result as the correct state of things but assailed the Tribunal's order by this application as no other remedy was available to him. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, learned .Advocate appearing for the petitioner, assailed the cider taking a number of grounds. He contended that no ballot papers, "illegible" or with "double marks" were there when, at the close of the polls, the ballot boxes were opened by the Presiding Officers in presence of the candidates or their agents and that no objection was raised, nor any allegation was made by the candidates even when the Presiding Officers checked and counted the ballot papers in their presence and then put them into gunny bags and sealed them in their presence. But the Tribunal at Fatikchari and the Electron Officer (P.W. 1 who opened the sealed bags before the Tribunal at Chittagong) found the bags "damaged" having stitched up holes. The Tribunal ignoring these facts proceeded to recount the ballot papers. The petitioner wanted to examine the Presiding Officers in this context and submitted as many as three applications for that purpose but the Tribunal arbitrarily rejected these applications and hurriedly delivered the judgment on the following day. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the Respdt. No. 2 contended that the petitioner's applications were rightly rejected as they were not filed in due time. In the judgment the Tribunal also observed that the examination of the Presiding Officers was a necessity, but the petitioner did not summon them. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan produced before us copies of the three applications of the petitioner and the orders of the Tribunal rejecting them. These orders did not support the Tribunal's observations. In the circumstances, examination of the ballot papers along with the case records appeared to us to be very much necessary.

<u>7. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed contended that when the Tribunal re-examined and recounted the ballot papers in presence of the parties and held some of them invalid, then the Tribunal's finding is a finding of facts which can hardly be disturbed in a writ-petition. He further contended that the Tribunal is not even required to give reasons for rejection of such ballot papers. In support of this contention he referred to two recent decisions of the Appellate Division reported in 27 D.L.R. at pages 117 and 118 respectively. We have perused these decisions. The numbers of invalid ballot papers involved in those two cases were very small- 5 (five) in one and 11(eleven) in another, whereas, the position in the present case is altogether different. These decisions of the Appellate Division cannot be interpreted to hold that the ballot papers found valid by the Presiding Officers in presence of the parties can be arbitrarily rejected by the Tribunal. In "Akbar Ali Vs. Raziur Rahman," 18 DLR (SC), 426, the Supreme Court confirmed a judgment of the High Court which interfered with a finding of an Election Tribunal on the ground of "wanton rejection of ballot papers". The number of ballot papers found wantonly rejected in that case was only six and those six ballot papers being the determining factor in the election result, the High Court called for them in order to see whether they were "spoilt" as found by the Tribunal, or "clean" as claimed by the petitioner. The High Court having held these votes valid set aside the Tribunal's order and directed that the petitioner be declared elected, In appeal before the Supreme Court it was contended that the High Court had assumed the role of an Appellate Court and substituted its finding for that of the Tribunal. The contention was rejected by the Supreme Court which observed that "it was not a case in which the High Court has substituted its own finding in place of the finding of the Tribunal". In view of the peculiar circumstances of the instant case; we called for the ballot papers and all other election materials.</u>

8. On opening the packets of ballot papers we found out the 459 ballot papers of the petitioner which were declared invalid by the Tribunal. Class-wise, 21 ballot papers had no official seals thereon, 295 ballot papers had double marks and 143 ballot papers were shown as "illegible" or having marks made with substances other than rubber stamps. Of the 295 ballot papers having double marks, 245 were marked for the symbols "Hurricane" (of the petitioner) and "Balance" (of Respdt. No. 4); 45 ballot papers were marked for "Hurricane" and "Bicycle" (of Respdt. No.3); 3 ballot papers were marked for "Hurricane" on one hand and "Ink-pot", "Date-tree" and "Clock' on the other, It may be mentioned here that in respect of Symbols, Ink-pot and Cheek, there was no contesting candidate and accordingly to rules these two ballot papers would go to Hurricane; but this is not an important point. These 295 ballot papers having "double marks" are found to be in different ink and of different shapes, clearly indicating that these marks were not made at one time and place they bore official seals and as such were presumably handed over to voters. A voter who intended to vote for the "Hurricane" would not have marked the other symbol such as Balance or Bicycle unless, of course, he was totally ignorant about the procedure of voting. If he had marked both the places, the marks would have been of same size and ink. Different ink and size of the marks clearly indicate that these were made at different places out of motive which was not certainly good.

9. As to the 143 ballot papers found "illegible", it appears that the marks are well within the space of the Symbol "Hurricane" showing without any ambiguity that these ballot papers were marked for the petitioner. But the Election Rule, 40(3) requites that the marks should be made only with a rubber stamp. The Tribunal observed that some of the marks were made with hard substances. What we find is that it is not a case of "illegible marks" or "marks by any hard substance", but a case of deliberately defacing, blurring, mutilating and disfiguring the original marks in various crude ways, such as, by repeatedly pressing a rubber stamp or any other substance on the original marks and in some cases by putting thumb impressions thereon. In spite of this violence the original marks are discernible hi some cases. The purpose behind this was just to tamper with the ballot papers so that they could not be counted in favour of the candidate for whom they were intended. Of these 143 ballot papers, about 30 were found "indistinct" by the Tribunal. Marks may be indistinct if the rubber stamp is not adequately soaked with ink in the pad. Indistinct markings are found in some of the valid ballot papers as well. The ballot papers "illegible" and with "double marks" are found to have been tampered with from sinister motives. Ballot papers of this condition stand rejected under rules and the determination of their validity is a mere formality. As to 127 ballot papers of Respondent No. 2 which were held invalid by the Tribunal, most of them bore double marks like that of the petitioner. These ballot papers were, also tampered with, not for harming Respondent No. 2, but for putting up a "show". For, deduction of 127 ballot papers of Respondent No. 2 as against 459 ballot papers of the petitioner does not affect his interest in any way. As to 21 ballot papers having no office-seal, they are invalid according to rules. Inclusion thereof in the petitioners total might have been due to oversight as 23 ballot papers out of 127 of the Respondent No. 2 also had no office-seal but were nevertheless held valid by the Presiding Officers.

10. Now excluding these 21 ballot papers which had no official stamp, 438 ballot papers of the petitioner are found to have been tampered with. But the Tribunal did not direct its attention to this side of the matter, it presumed that the ballot papers had been there before the presiding officers who wrongly counted shall in favour of the petitioner. The case of the petitioner is that this kind of ballot papers was not there in the ballot boxes when these were opened by the Presiding Officers in presence of the candidates or their agents, but they were tampered with after the election papers were packed and dispatched in sealed gunny bags Exts. (1), (1a) and (1) by the Presiding Officers In support of this contention he relied upon the following facts and circumstances:

(i) If s many invalid votes were found before counting, all other candidates or their agents would have not only raised Objection to their being counted for the petitioner but also they would have brought allegations against the Presiding Officers; when ore single questionable ballot papers cannot be counted in favour of a candidate, inclusion of so many questioned ballot papers which could have been also claimed by other candidates, such as Respdt. Nos. 3 and 4 would not have gone unchallenged.

(ii) The Presiding Officers after examining the ballot papers and counting them filled Form 'M' in presence of the candidates who did not raise any protest. Again, when the Returning Officer, after receiving reports in Form 'M' declared the result of the election officially, of allegation or objection was made to him;

(iii) 'The Tribunal at Fatikchari to whom the three sealed gunny bags of ballot papers were first produced, four’s them in damaged condition and when these gunny bags were porch before the Tribunal by the Election Officer (P.W. 1) these bags were found cut and stitched-up, a fact admitted by P. W. 1 himself, P.W. 1 further said that no stitched-up gunny bags were supplied to the Presiding Officers by the Election Authorities. We have also found these bags stitched; one bag has two stitches one 8" long and the other 9'' long; another bag has got a stitch 6" long and the 3rd bag has a stitch 9" long. The holes by cut which are stitched are big enough to enable a person to take out any packet of ballot papers from the bass.

(iv) When he bags were opened by the Tribunal at Chittagong 011 29-9-75 this state of ballot papers was revealed for the first time. In fact the ballot papers ill respect of Ward Nos. 1 and 2 were opened on 29-9-75 undo before the ballot papers of Ward No. 3 were opened for examination on 1-10-75, the petitioner filed three applications one after another before the Tribunal for summoning the Presiding Officers in order to clarify these glaring anomalies but all these applications were rejected by the Tribunal on the ground that those were "belated" and filed "at the fag end". The petitioner also prayed for recalling P.W. 2 respondent No. 2 who had deposed on 25-9-75 so that he could be cross-examined in respect of this state of affairs revealed on 29-9-75 but the prayer was rejected. Orders of the Tribunal rejecting the petitioner's applications are quoted below:

a) "Prayer is a very belated one. We cannot re-open hearing afresh. Hence the petition is rejected.

M.A. Haque,

Munsif,

30-9-75."

b) "Such a petition was rejected yesterday on the ground stated in the order sheet. Prayer is rejected.

A. Haque, Munsif,

30-9-75."

c) "The Tribunal will form its own opinion about the election materials. It is not possible to postpone inspection at this fag end of hearing. Prayer is rejected.

A. Haque, Munsif,

30-9-75."

v) Respondent No. 2 brought a number of wild allegations against the petitioner to have his election set aside but all these allegations were rejected by the Tribunal. His allegation that his valid ballot papers were rejected by the Presiding Officers also fell through. He, however, showed unusual interest in getting the gunny bags opened and made application after application to recurring the ballot papers. This led to serious complications as stated in paragraph 10 of the Writ Petition:

He stated that the Tribunal at Fatikchari made an order for opening the sealed gunny bags on repeated applications of Respondent No. 2, but the petitioner prayed for an adjournment so that he could get a prohibitory order from the High Court against the premature opening of the ballot papers. The Tribunal, he stated, retaliated by imposing upon him a heavy penalty of Tk. 1,500/- (fifteen hundred) as compensatory costs. The petitioner challenged the order of cost by two Writ Petitions, No. 128/75 and No. 174/75. When these two matters were pending before this Court the petitioner filed another application to this Court alleging that the Tribunal willfully disregarded certain order of this Court whereupon another Rule (Contempt Rule No. 5/75) was issued upon the Tribunal for contempt. All the three Rules were made absolute—a fact not disputed by the Respondent No, 2. Under these circumstances, the Election Case was transferred from Fatikchari to Chittagong. The petitioner apprehends that justice was denied to him when the Tribunal at Chittagong rejected his applications for examining the Presiding Officers on a most vital issue.

11. The Tribunal after rejecting the petitioner's applications for examining the Presiding Officers passed the judgment shifting the blame upon the petitioner as he had not summoned them. This is a travesty of truth. The Tribunal also could have summoned the Presiding Officers. The observation that the applications dated 1.10.75 were filed "belated" or "at the fag-end" is inconsistent with its own record; the applications were not at all belated but were filed at the earliest possible time. The Presiding Officers also had no opportunity to defend themselves as this state of things came to light for the first time on 29.9.75 The entire hearing of the case, it may be noted, took only 7 days time, beginning on 23.9.75 and ending on 30.9.75, judgment being delivered on the following day-1.10.75. Examination of the Presiding Officers was indispensably necessary for arriving at a correct finding as to whether the questionable ballot papers were found in the ballot boxes just on close of the polls or whether they were subsequently tampered with. Respondent No. 2, at the beginning, had made an application for summoning the Presiding Officers but subsequently did not examine them. But when the petitioner wanted to examine them he was refused.

12. The Presiding Officers are found to have opened the ballot boxes, scrutinised ballot papers and counted them in presence of the candidates or their agents who did Dot raise any object ion or made any allegation whatever. They then filled the Forms 'M' under. Rule 41(4) in their presence after which they enclosed and sealed into separate packets the ballot papers and dispatched them in sealed gunny bags, again, in their presence to the Returning Officer. The latter on receipt of the reports of the Presiding Officers in Form 'M' declared the result in presence of the candidates or their agents without receiving any objection or any allegation. Two of the Presiding Officers were Headmaster and Assistant Headmaster of a High School, or Presiding Officer was an Officer of the Power Development Authority and r e Returning Officer was a Thana Revenue Officer. There is evidence that they sided with the petitioner. They ere found to have discharged their duties in strict observance of the Election Rules. In the circumstances, it must be presumed that they acted in good faith and with due care and attention. From these facts and circumstances, the irascible conclusion is that the ballot papers in question were tampered we after they were dispatched by these officers.

13. As to proper custody of the scaled gunny bags of election papers the Election Officer (P.W. 1) has said that he produced them before the Tribunal from his custody. The Sub divisional Officer (Repndt.No. 6) therefore, did not come to the picture in this case under Rule 44. Nevertheless he has been represented before us by the Deputy Attorney-General. Usually the Sub-divisional Officers are not represented by lawyers in election cases, No written statement was, however, filed by the Sub-divisional Officer Respdt. No. 6 in this case

<u>14. At the last stage of the hearing before us, the learned Attorney-General appeared in private capacity for Respdt. No. 2. He supported the contention of Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and limited himself to the question of powers of this Court in Writ jurisdiction as to "Certiorari". He has contended that the finding of facts arrived at by the Tribunal on re-examination of ballot papers in presence of the parties can hardly be interfered with under Article 102 of the Constitution. Firstly we do not think that determination of validity elf ballot papers is a question of facts; it is a mixed, question of law and facts. As to our jurisdiction under Article 102, we need not have been reminded that writ is a writ and not an appeal. Ordinarily, this Court does not interfere with the findings of a Sub-ordinate Court if the findings are arrived at on due consideration of relevant facts and correct appreciation of evidence being free from any unfairness of mired. If the findings are not so arrived at this Court has got every power to interfere therewith. In the case of Jamal Shah, reported in 18 D.L.R. (S.C.) the Supreme Court held that the High Court got jurisdiction under Article 98 of the late Constitution to interfere with the finding of an Election Tribunal. It was held by the Shifted Court:</u>

<u>"If the authority functioning under section 53 of the National and Provincial Assemblies Act or the Election Tribunal has either failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it or exceeded that jurisdiction or if the order in question is tainted with malafide the aggrieved party may invoke the provisions of Article 98 of the Constitution to obtain relief."</u>

<u>15. In the instant case, the Tribunal acted with material irregularity when it proceeded of examines the ballot papers ignoring the broad fact that the gunny bags containing the election papers were tampered with having a number of stitched up holes. Again, when, on discovery of apparently tampered ballot papers, so many in number, examination of the Presiding Officers was in dispensable by necessary in the interest of justice, he arbitrarily refused to examine them and thereby failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in him. Findings arrived at in these circumstances, cannot claim any sanctity nor can they be ermine from interference. When the election was held in a peaceful atmosphere and scrutiny and counting of ballot papers were made in an orderly manner, without any objection for many quarter, reports of the Presiding Officers as to due performance of their duties must be accepted, Otherwise, there will be no sanctity of a free election which is a must for running democratic institutions. The facts and circumstances of the case unerringly show that the questioned ballot papers of the petitioner were tampered with by some malicious hand after their dispatch from the local officers. Subsequent act of tampering with the ballot papers cannot be a ground for undoing the election. To co would be to give premium of corrupt practices. To ensure face, and fair election of peoples representatives Election laws against Court practices should be made stringent. In this case the authorities may direct an enquiry as to how the ballot papers were tampered with.</u>

16. For the reasons given above we reject the Tribunal's finding as having no basis and we find that there was no reason to set aside the petitioner's election as declared by the Returning Officer. In the result, the impugned order of the Tribunal is declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The order declaring Respondent No. 2 elected is set aside arid it is declared that the petitioner was lawfully elected a Chairman. The Rule is made absolute with costs which we assess at Taka 1,000/- (one thousand) only.

Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.-I agree.

End.
