case_source: (From the judgment and order dated April 11, 1994 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 43 of 1989)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This appeal, among other, raises a very serious and important question, whether a Tribunal established under a law can sit on judgment over a decision of the High Court Division given in the writ jurisdiction interpreting a provision of law. The Tribunal here is the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka and the extraordinary judgment which has been impugned in this appeal was passed by it on 11-4-94 in Appeal No. 43 of 1989.

2. Facts material for the purpose of disposal of this appeal, briefly, are that the appellant who was a Superintendent of Customs challenged the order of her dismissal from service dated 26-8-87 by filing Administrative Tribunal Case No. 183 of 1988 before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka. The Tribunal dismissed the case by its judgment and order dated 21-8-89 whereupon the appellant preferred aforesaid appeal No. 43 of 1989 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. The hearing of the appeal started before a duly constituted Appellate Tribunal consisting of the Chairman and two members but subsequently the Chairman could not attend the hearing due to his personal difficulties and the hearing of the appeal continued before the two members of the Tribunal and after conclusion of the hearing judgment was delivered on 7-6-90 dismissing the appeal.

3. The appellant then moved the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution against the said judgment of the Appellate Tribunal and a Rule Nisi was issued in Writ Petition No. 1637 of 1990. A Division Bench of the High Court Division, by its judgment and order dated 6-8-92, made the Rule absolute in the writ petition holding that the judgment and order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal consisting of two members only were passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The appeal was remanded to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal to be heard and disposed of by a properly constituted Tribunal in accordance with law.

4. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal in the impugned judgment raised the question whether the Appellate Tribunal was amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court and observed relying on the case of Mujibur Rahman vs. Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 111 that it was not. Then it was noticed that the High Court Division had held in the writ petition that the judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal by two members only was a nullity because the Tribunal was coram non judice and, as such, the writ petition was maintainable. Then the Tribunal expressed the view that in its opinion the Appellate Tribunal consisting of two members was not coram non judice rendering its judgment a nullity as held by the High Court Division. It then went on to say that the question could have been settled by this Division by taking an appeal under section 6A of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981), briefly the Act, which was incorporated by amendment dated 22-7-1991 (by Act No. XXIII of 1991). The Appellate Tribunal took exception to the appellant's continuing with the writ petition (against the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal) even though the decision of this Division in Mujibur Rahman's case had in the meantime been given on 28-11-1991 and the provision for appeal to this Division was already made on 22-7-1991.

5. It was argued on behalf of the appellant that notwithstanding the decision in Mujibur Rahman's case, the decision by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal consisting of two members was a nullity, the Tribunal being coram non judice and, as such, the writ petition was maintainable and the judgment given by the High Court Division directing a re-hearing of the appeal by a properly constituted Tribunal ought to be followed. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal replied to the above contention as follows:

"We are sorry to say that we cannot accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant because (i) we think that the judgment, dated 6-8-92 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1637/90 is without jurisdiction and (ii) the decision of the Appellate Tribunal holds good unless it is set aside by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court."

6. It was further held that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal "is in no way amenable to the decision of the High Court Division" and ultimately, without passing any positive order the matter was simply disposed of holding that "as the judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal, dated 7-6-90 still stands we have nothing to do in this matter".

7. Leave to appeal from the impugned judgment was obtained raising the following grounds (1) that having regard to the fact that the Appellate Tribunal while passing the judgment and order on 7-6-90 was coram non judice and the said judgment and order were declared to be a nullity by the High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 6-8-92 in Writ Petition No. 1637 of 1990, the Appellate Tribunal acted illegally in not deciding the appeal on merit on remand; (2) that the Appellate Tribunal upon a myopic view of Mujibur Rahman's case illegally held that the judgment of the High Court Division in the writ petition was passed without jurisdiction; (3) that in view of the decision in the case of Abu Taleb vs. Bangladesh 45 DLR (AD) 45 which unfortunately, could not be placed before the Appellate Tribunal due to inadvertence, the Appellate Tribunal was required to hear the appeal on merit in any case and (4) that having regard to the special facts of the case i.e., the writ petition was filed before section 6A was incorporated in the Act on 22-7-91, the Appellate Tribunal acted illegally in not deciding the appeal on merit upon a wrong view of the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

8. The third contention as above may be disposed of first because Abu Taleb's case has no application in the facts of the present case. In that case during re-hearing of an appeal only two members took part and the Chairman was absent but the judgment was signed by all the three members. That was not a case of coram non judice but it was held that re-hearing of the appeal was to be done by all the three members who had earlier decided the matter.

9. The first important question that falls to be decided in this appeal is whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal acted legally and properly in holding that the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1637 of 1990 was passed without jurisdiction and further that the judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal dated 7-6-90 remained valid in spite of the judgment of the High Court Division. The core issue, however, is whether the Appellate Tribunal in the facts of the present case could defy the finding of the High Court Division that the two-member Appellate Tribunal was coram non judice and go to the extent of giving its own finding that it was not coram non judice.

<u>10. The Administrative Tribunal relying upon Mujibur Rahman's case correctly held that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. So far so good, but what it has failed to notice, however, is that Mujibur Rahman's case is not the only case which defines the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division. We regret to say that the Appellate Tribunal seems to be totally unaware of the settled law that notwithstanding the ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division by any legislative provision or even under Article 102 itself the High Court Division is yet entitled to exercise its power of judicial review under Article 102 if the action complained of before the High Court Division is found to be coram non judice, without jurisdiction or taken malafide. The cases of Ehteshamuddin vs. Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 154, Jamil Haq vs. Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 125, Moshtaque Ahmed vs. Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 222, Helaluddin Ahmed vs. Bangladesh 45 DLR (AD) 1 illustrate the settled law as referred to above. The learned Advocates for the parties before us are agreed in their submission that the view taken by the Appellate Tribunal as to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division was based upon a partial view of the law (as declared in Mujibur Rahman's case) and ignoring the other decisions extending the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division in spite of an ouster clause.</u>

<u>11. The High Court Division having held that the decision of the two-member Tribunal was a nullity because the Tribunal was coram non judice, it was clear that the writ jurisdiction of High Court Division was attracted and it was not anymore open for the Appellate Tribunal to pronounce that the judgment of the High Court Division was passed without jurisdiction. The question of maintainability was also raised in the writ petition and the learned Deputy Attorney-General who was representing the respondents fairly conceded the settled position of law as referred to above. Not only that the learned Deputy Attorney-General supported the contention of the appellant that the judgment passed in the absence of a member of the Appellate Tribunal will be a judgment of individuals and not of the Tribunal and, as such, it will be a nullity, the Tribunal being coram non judice. It is to be deprecated, mere regretting is not enough, that the Appellate Tribunal has not at all considered the reasons given in the judgment of the High Court Division and in an over-bearing manner bluntly declared that it did not agree that the Appellate Tribunal with two members was coram non judice.</u>

12. The High Court Division in the facts of the case having correctly exercised its power of judicial review and pronounced upon the incompetence of the Appellate Tribunal, it was not at all legal and proper on the part of the Appellate Tribunal to hold and find that the view taken by the High Court Division was wrong. It is true that the Appellate Tribunal is not subordinate to the High Court Division but judicial decorum, propriety and discipline demand that when an interpretation of law is given by the High Court Division all Courts and Tribunals in Bangladesh should abide by such interpretation until the said interpretation is set aside or varied by the Appellate Division. It will give rise to anarchical situation if a Tribunal were to give its own interpretation of law when the matter is settled by a decision of the High Court Division passed in its constitutional jurisdiction. The Tribunal has no authority to sit on judgment over the decision of the High Court Division in such matters. It may express its own opinion but will be always obliged to follow the decision of the High Court Division in the absence of any contrary opinion of the Appellate Division on the subject.

13. If the respondents were aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court Division, they could move this Division with a petition for leave to appeal from the said judgment. But the respondents did not take any objection to the said judgment, rather it has been noticed that they supported the view taken by the High Court Division and, in our opinion, rightly. The decision in Mujibur Rahman's case was correct because of the provisions of Article 102(5) read with Article 117 of the Constitution. But that decision has nothing to do in the facts of the present case because the High Court Division exercised its jurisdiction on the premise that the Appellate Tribunal had acted coram non judice. Further, the writ petition was filed before section 6A was added to the Act on 22-7-91. The Appellate Tribunal has been needlessly presumptuous in observing that the appellant ought to have withdrawn his writ petition after the introduction of section 6A and filed appeal before this Division because the writ petition was still maintainable on the ground raised ie of coram non judice. The Tribunal went on to surmise that Mujibur Rahman's decision was not brought to the notice of the High Court Division and the judgment was obtained, as if, surreptitiously. The learned Advocate for the appellant who himself appeared in the High Court Division submitted that the observation of the Appellate Tribunal is incorrect because the High Court Division was quite aware of the said decision and was initially reluctant to interfere but ultimately did interfere being persuaded that the Appellate Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction by giving a two-member judgment and the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Govt. also supported the stand taken by the appellant. In the circumstances of the case it must be observed that the Appellate Tribunal quite gratuitously and unwarrantedly opened the question of maintainability of the writ petition, manifested a lack of understanding of the writ jurisdiction and made improper observation on the judgment of the High Court Division. The height of impropriety was its solicitous finding that the High Court Division acted without jurisdiction which is strongly disapproved.

14. We have already held that the High Court Division, in the facts of the present case, acted fully within its competence and if was the plain duty of the Appellate Tribunal to abide by the decision of the High Court Division and to dispose of the appeal on merit.

15. The Appellate Tribunal expressed the view contrary to that taken by the High Court Division that if two members of the Appellate Tribunal pronounce a judgment it would not be a case of coram non judice. We would have examined this view if there was an appeal by the respondents from the judgment of the High Court Division in the writ petition. But since there is no appeal from that decision before us, we shall dispose of this appeal on the basis that it was not for the Appellate Tribunal to question the correctness of the decision of the High Court Division given in its constitutional jurisdiction. It was plainly and completely obligatory on the part of the Appellate Tribunal to act in accordance with the law declared by the High Court Division. The letters of Article 111 of the Constitution may not apply in terms to the Tribunal but the spirit behind them, we have no hesitation to hold, clearly requires that the decision given by the High Court Division must be followed by the Tribunal.

16. The discussion made so far answers the issues raised in this appeal but we would like to observe that the Appellate Tribunal also laboured under a misconception in holding that section (3B) of the Act permitted a judgment to be delivered by the Appellate Tribunal even with two members. It has been noticed that the Appellate Tribunal did not at all appreciate the weighty and substantial reasons given by the High Court Division for its view that it would be a case of coram non judice. We, however, find great force in the reasons given by the High Court Division for the view it has taken.

17. It is true that the word ''hearing'' in the context of certain enactments has been interpreted in a broad sense to cover the entire stage of trial and not in the restricted sense of only a particular stage beginning with the examination of parties and ending with the arguments in the case. There are, however, contrary views where it has been held that trial does not include the stage of judgment and the word ''hearing'' denotes a stage before the stage of judgment or order. But those decisions are not relevant for our purpose because the word ''hearing'' as used in section (3B) of the Act has to be interpreted in the context of the Act itself.

18. It is provided in section 6(1) that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals...... ...... .... Hearing and determination are undisputedly attributes of judicial function and are requirements for disposal of an appeal. Since the legislature has expressed the two functions separately in section 6, it will be in consonance with the principle of interpretation of law that this separation should be kept in view while construing the other provisions of the Act. Read in this light section (3B) cannot be construed to mean that when continuation of hearing has been made permissible before two members only, it also includes permission for pronouncing judgment by two members as well. Continuation of hearing by two members only has been provided for apparently to overcome the contingency of sudden absence of a member to attend any particular sitting or sittings of the Tribunal, but when it comes to determination or giving judgment it must be participated by all the three members and all of them must be parties to the judgment. The absurdity of the view of the Appellate Tribunal that two members can also validly pronounce a judgment will be apparent if the provisions of section (3A) are noticed which provide that in the event of a difference of opinion amongst the members of the Appellate Tribunal, opinion of the majority shall prevail. Evidently the question of majority can arise only when more than two members are parties to a decision. The view expressed by the Appellate Tribunal is therefore in direct conflict with the provision of section (3A). It is not necessary to repeat the others substantial reasons given by the High Court Division in support of the view that the decision of two members is a decision of individuals and not of the Tribunal and therefore it is a case of coram non judice. It has already been held that since there was no appeal against the judgment of the High Court Division, the interpretation given by it must prevail.

19. Mr. B Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney-General, upon drawing our attention to the earlier judgment of the Appellate Tribunal (dated 7-6-90 passed by two members) has submitted that may be it was coram non judice but it was an excellent judgment on merit and the appellant does not and cannot have any valid ground to complain about it. The misconduct committed by the appellant was found to be well proved and the punishment awarded was found to be fully justified and not liable to be reduced even. Therefore even if the appeal was not disposed of on merit on remand by the High Court Division, there was no failure of justice. For the same reason, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits, there need not be a remand again because it will serve no useful purpose.

20. We shall refrain from saying anything on the merit of the appellant's case but we shall interfere with the impugned judgment because of its appalling nature. The appeal should be heard and decided again, for, justice should be seen to have been done.

21. For the reasons, this appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and order are set aside. The appeal is remanded to the Appellate Tribunal for disposal on merit. There will be no order as to costs.

<u>Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury J: I have gone through the proposed judgment of my Lord the Chief Justice. I fully concur with his decision and the reasoning’s. I would, however, like make a small observation about the construction of section 7(3B) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980, which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"If, in the course of a hearing, the Chairman or any other member of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is, for any reason, unable to attend any sitting thereof, the hearing may continue before the other two members".</u>

<u>To me it appears that absence of the Chairman or any other member is conceived in a situation where in the midst of a hearing by all the three members one departs temporarily for any reason so that he remains a party to the deliberations and, therefore, competent to sign the judgment.</u>

End.

Mahmudul Islam, Advocate — For the Opposite Party No.1.

Abu Musa Mazumder and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the elected Chairman of Galiara Union Parishad of Sadar PS of Comilla District is against Judgment dated 9.3.94 passed by the Election Appellate Tribunal, Comilla in Election Tribunal Appeal No. 2 of 1993 affirming Judgment dated 30.1.93 passed by the Election Tribunal, Comilla in Election Tribunal Case No. 15 of 1992.

2. Election for the office of Chairman of the said Union Parishad was held on 3-2-92 in which petitioner and opposite party Nos.1-5 contested the election and the petitioner was declared elected securing 3308 votes including 639 votes in the disputed Subhapur School centre, opposite party No. 1 securing 3049 votes including 616 votes in the said centre and other candidates securing much less votes than the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1.

3. Opposite party No.1 challenged the election of the petitioner before the Election Tribunal alleging that employees of Forest Department and members of Bangladesh Rifles in collusion with the petitioner and his agents created terror and rigging in Subhapur School centre and that many invalid ballot papers were shown as valid in favour of the petitioner; that many valid ballot papers of the opposite party No. 1 were rejected as invalid and subsequently counted in favour of the petitioner and mixed up with cancelled ballots; that cancelled ballot papers were not shown in the result sheet; that prayer for recounting was refused by the Presiding Officer; and that the opposite party No.1 submitted an application on 4-2-92 to the Returning Officer making the said allegations for recounting the ballot papers of the said center and the same was sent to the Election Commission without recounting ballot papers. Petitioner denied all the allegations and asserted that election and counting of ballot papers in that center were held peacefully and in accordance with law and no objection was raised at the time of counting of ballot papers and no prayer for recounting was made.

4. On consideration of evidence Election Tribunal found that the opposite party No. 1 failed to prove creating terror in the disputed centre or casting false votes or votes of dead persons by the petitioner's men. It further found that the Presiding Officer counted votes himself but also held that counting of votes in that centre was not correctly made and result sheet was not correctly prepared as the Presiding Officer failed to show cancelled votes in the result sheet. He therefore ordered for recounting of ballot papers of Chairman election of the disputed centre. On the date of re-counting of ballot papers petitioner pointed out that there was no seal in the gunny bag containing election materials and there was 9" x 4" hole at the bottom of the gunny bag and that ballot papers should be proved by examining witnesses. But Election Tribunal rejected the prayer for examining the Presiding Officer to prove the ballot papers and kept with the record other two applications of the petitioner on the ground that the gunny bag was received by the Tribunal on 19.4.92 with a hole therein. After opening the gunny bag containing election materials of disputed centre Election Tribunal found 639 ballot papers in the packet of the petitioner and out of the same found 332 ballot paper bearing double marks, 33 ballot papers bearing no official seal and one ballot paper bearing marking on candle light of another candidate and thus deducting these he found 283 valid ballot papers in favour of the petitioner. In the packet of opposite party No. 1 Election Tribunal found 616 ballot papers out of which 86 ballot papers were found bearing no official seal and thus deducting those found 530 valid votes in favour of opposite party No. 1. Tribunal found 99 cancelled ballot papers in the packet of cancelled ballots and found ballot papers of other candidates tally with the result sheet. Thus on re-counting petitioner's votes were reduced to 2952 from official result of 3308 votes and opposite party No. 1's votes were also reduced to 2963 from official result of 3049 votes. Therefore, Election Tribunal declared election of petitioner void and declared opposite party No. 1 elected as Chairman.

5. Petitioner's appeal was dismissed by the impugned judgment holding that neither party challenged fairness of re-counting by filing petition, nor did they question the result of the re-counting nor raised specific allegation as regards rigging of poll in the disputed centre and that the Election Tribunal has jurisdiction to recount the ballot papers. But the Election Appellate Tribunal did not give its decision on the question raised in the appeal that the gunny bag containing the election materials and the packets therein were tampered with and that opportunity was not given to the petitioner to re-examine the Presiding Officer to prove that ballot papers were tampered with subsequent to the declaration of result.

6. Important question as contended by the learned Advocate of the petitioner is, whether there was double marks in 332 ballot papers counted in favour of the petitioner at the time of counting the ballot papers in the disputed centre by the Presiding Officer, RW 2 ABM Abdul Matin, or the same is post-election manipulation.

<u>7. There is no specific allegation in the election petition or evidence of counting double marked ballot papers in favour of the petitioners by the Presiding Officer or raising objection about the same before the Presiding Officer. Presiding Officer deposing as RW 2 and the two Assistant Presiding Officers deposing as PWs. 2 and 3 did not support the vague allegation of opposite party No. 1 that many invalid ballot papers were counted in favour of the petitioner or that objection was raised to the same or that re-counting was demanded from the Presiding Officer on behalf of the opposite party No. 1. Election Tribunal as well as the Election Appellate Tribunal did not decide whether the double marks were there in the 332 ballot papers at the time of counting the same by the Presiding Officer in favour of the petitioner or those were double marked after the declaration of the result though petitioner raised the question by filing three petitions before the Tribunal and contending before the Appellate Tribunal.</u>

<u>8. Election Tribunal found 639 ballot papers in the packet containing ballot papers of the petitioner and 616 ballot papers in the packet containing ballot papers of the opposite party No. 1 exactly as shown in the result sheet of the disputed Subhapur School centre. Deduction of 33 ballot papers of the petitioner and 86 ballot papers of the opposite party No.1 on the ground of bearing no official seal can hardly be disputed and rightly not disputed by either of the parties and the same might have been counted due to oversight as there was no objection raised at the time of counting. As regards 332 ballot papers bearing double marks Election Tribunal has not noticed nature of the double marks. There is no finding that in addition to the petitioner in favour of which other candidate additional mark was given and by what kind of rubber stamp and what kind of ink; whether of the same or different size and ink. There is no finding that any of those double marked ballot papers were marked in favour of the opposite party No. 1 also. There is also no finding that any of the 99 cancelled ballot papers was illegally concealed though validly cast in favour of the opposite party No. 1. So the election petitioner opposite party No. 1 failed to establish his allegation that his many valid ballot papers were treated as invalid and counted as valid votes in favour of the petitioner or cancelled. It is true that presumption of correctness of the result declared by the Presiding Officer was lost as the Presiding Officer failed to show cancelled ballot papers in the result sheet. Since the 99 cancelled ballot papers did not contain a single ballot paper validly cast in favour of the opposite party No. 1 and votes counted in his favour were not increased, such incorrect result sheet is of no help to him. In such circumstances merely because the Presiding Officer did not show 99 cancelled ballot papers in the result sheet it cannot be inferred that 332 ballot papers were double marked at the time of counting the same by the Presiding Officer.</u>

<u>9. When the gunny bag was found torn and seal not intact and when the Presiding Officer was not recalled and reexamined as to the condition of gunny bag and double marks in the ballot papers though demanded by the petitioner, I find that there is no basis for the finding of the Election Appellate Tribunal that fairness of re-counting or result of re-counting by the Tribunal was not challenged.</u>

<u>10. On the ground of refusal of the Election Tribunal to examine the Presiding Officer in spite of prayer for the same when the gunny bag containing election materials was found with stitched up holes at the time of re-counting, rejection of double marks ballot papers was not upheld in the case of Nurul Islam vs. Munsif, Chittagong reported in 28 DLR 375. Similarly in the case of Md. Shahjahan vs. Md. Sadeque reported in 38 DLR (AD) 275=1986 BLD (AD) 236 rejection of double marked ballot papers was not approved with the following observations:</u>

<u>"Double mark indicating a vote for more than one candidate where only one candidate is to be elected is such a glaring defect that it cannot escape notice of the parties or their representatives in whose presence ballot papers were counted. Had 68 ballot papers bearing double marks been counted in favour of the respondent the election agent of the appellant would have certainly raised objection. Secondly, this allegation would have been taken as a specific ground by the appellant in his election petition in which a number of vague and baseless allegations were made."</u>

<u>11. It has already been found that the election petitioner opposite party No. 1 failed to prove that he raised any objection before the Presiding Officer about counting of votes in favour of the petitioner. He also did not specifically raise objection neither regarding counting of double marked ballot papers in favour of the petitioner in the election petition nor led any evidence to that effect. Opposite party No. 1 also did not produce copy of his application filed on 4-2-92 to the Returning Officer praying for re-counting to show what specific allegations were made by him one day after the election. On the other hand, without considering petitioner's objection regarding tampering with the gunny bag containing election materials and prayer for re-examining the Presiding Officer ballot papers were recounted. Election Appellate Tribunal even did not care to examine evidence on record and the election materials to meet the objections raised by the petitioner in the appeal though as the last Tribunal of fact it was its duty to come to a definite finding as to whether double marks were there at the time of counting by the Presiding Officer or not. Without finding that double marks were there in the ballot papers at the time of counting the same in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer election of such a returned candidate cannot be declared void by deducting double marked ballot papers as invalid by the Election Tribunal. As there is no such finding in the instant case, I find it difficult to uphold the impugned judgment affirming the judgment of the Election Tribunal.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute with costs and the impugned judgment of the Election Appellate Tribunal affirming that of the Election Tribunal is set aside.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Abdul Quayum with Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakraborty and Mr. Manabendra Batabyal, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq with Mr. Subodh Ranjan Datta, Mr. Muslem Ali Howlader and Mr. Md. Mostafa, Advocates ----- For Opp. Party. No.1
parties:
Jalaluddin Ahmed ----- Petitioner 
VS
Matiur Rahman Khan & ors ----- Opposite party
full_judgment:
Md. Badruzzaman, J :- This Rule, obtained by added defendant No.3 on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, is directed against an order dated 7.5.88 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati, in Title Suit No. 26 of 1988, by which the application of the defendant-petitioner under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code was rejected.

2. Opposite party No. 1 Matiur Rahman Khan as plaintiff filed the suit on 9.4.88 for declaration that the polling station at Bahadurapur B.G. Union Academy High School for Ward No. 2 of No. 5 Subidpur Union Parishad of Nalchity Upazilla, District Jhalakati, falls outside the area of that ward and for not holding poll in that polling station on the averments that he is the sitting chairman of that Union Parishad. Petitioner, opposite party No.1 and one Abdul Kader Jamader are contesting candidates for the office of the chairman in the election of that Union Parishad initially scheduled to be held on 10.2.88. The Election Officials namely opposite party Nos. 2 and 3, in collusion with the petitioner, set up the polling station of Ward No.2 at Bahadurpur G.G. Union Academy High School which is situated outside its area in contravention of the Election Rules. The petitioner verbally raised objection against the setting up of that polling station but opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 paid no heed to it. One Mosharref Hossain Khan also made a representation to the Election Commission Under Rule 70 of the Union Parishads (Election), Rules 1983 against the setting up of polling station of Ward No.2 outside its area and the Election Commission directed opposite party No.2 to set up the polling station of Ward No.2 at West Gopalpur Free Primary School, if it was found on enquiry that Bahadurpur, B.G. Union Academy High School fell outside the area of that ward but the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3, without making any enquiry as directed made arrangement for holding the fresh poll on 11.4.88 at the old polling station at Bahadurpur B.G. Union Academy High School by disregarding the direction of the Election Commission. Hence the opposite party No. 1 brought the suit for the said declaration and prayed for an order of temporary injunction restraining of holding of fresh poll at Bahadurpur B.G. Union Academy High School polling station.

3. The learned District Judge, who was in charge of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati, on 10.4.88, passed an order of status quo. On his prayer the petitioner was added as defendant No.3 in the suit and he thereafter filed an application under order 7 rule 11 of the Code for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was barred under section 26 of the Ordinance.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge heard together the injunction matter and the petitioner's application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code and by his order dated 7.5.88 allowed the prayer for temporary injunction and restrained the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 from holding the fresh poll of Ward No.2 at Bahadurpur B.G. Union Academy High School Polling station till disposal of the suit but rejected the petitioners' application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code on the view that the Jurisdiction of the Civil court was not barred as a completed election was not challenged but the suit was filed merely challenging the legality of an intermediate process for holding the election which fell outside the purview of the Election Tribunal. Against the order of temporary injunction the petitioner filed Misc. Appeal No. 12 of 1988 before the District Judge, Jhalakati which is still pending. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code, the petitioner moved this court in its provisional jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Civil Court has got no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the same was barred under section 26 of the Ordinance and the rules made thereunder and that the election when completed can only be challenged by filing an election petition to the Election Tribunal appointed under section 27 and that the learned Subordinate Judge, by rejecting the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code, has committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice.

6. Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, submits that the subject-matter of the suit does not fall within the term "election dispute" and consequently it falls outside the jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal. He further submits that the Civil Court has got jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the act complained of (i.e. selling up of the polling station concerned) was made in contravention of the provision of Rule 6 and the direction of the Election Commission in that regard. According to him there is no error of law in the impugned decision and consequently the Rule is liable to be discharged.

7. Rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure lays down the circumstances when the plaint is liable to be rejected and it reads as follows :-

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action:

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so :

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so :

d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

Provided that the time fixed by the court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days."

8. In the instant case we are concerned with clause (d) of Rule 11 which provides that for rejecting the plaint the finding of the suit to be barred by any law must be based on the statement in the plaint. In other words, the plaint cannot be rejected on that ground on the basis of statement made by the defendant in his pleading or in his application under Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code. The plaintiff-opposite party filed the suit on the basis of averment in the plaint that the polling station at Bahadurpur B.G.Union Academy High School for Ward No.1 was set up outside its area in contravention of Rule 6 and the direction of the Election Commission in this regard and we shall therefore, for the purpose of deciding the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code, proceed on the assumption that tile said averment was correct.

9. Under section 9 of the Code, the Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature excepting suits of which the cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. Section 4 of the Code provides that in the absence of any specific provision to the contrary, nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any special law now in force or any special jurisdiction or power conferred, or any Special form of procedure prescribed by or under any other law for the time being in force. It appears from section 4 that the provision in the special law is not affected by the provision in the Code and that the provision in the special law must prevail in the absence of any specific provision to the contrary. It has been held in the case of Nawal Kishore Agarwala- vs.- Municipal Board, Gorakhpur and others, 'A.I.R. 1937 Allahabad 365 that it follows from section 4 that where there is a special or local law the Civil Court would not have jurisdiction under section 9 of the Code to entertain a claim merely because it is of a civil nature and that the special law overrides the general jurisdiction conferred on Civil Courts to entertain suits of Civil nature. Sections 4 and 9 of the Code read together therefore, indicate that where a right is created by a special law and a method of enforcing the right is pointed out by the law creating such right, the general remedy of suit under section 9 of the Code will be impliedly barred and the method provided by the special law must be followed.

10. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court has not been expressly barred by anything contained in the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 and the Rules made thereunder, Now we are to see if the jurisdiction of the Civil Court is barred by implication that arises by the creation of a special jurisdiction under the Ordinance.

11. In the case of Main Sultan Ali Nanghiana- Vs.-Mian Nur Hussain, P.L.D. 1949 Lahore 301, the Full Bench of the Lahore High Court after considering the several decisions cited before them observed as follows:

"The rule is fundamental both here and in England that where a right is created by a statute which also prescribes the manner in which that right may be enforced, the party complaining of any infringement of such, right can only seek such remedy as is provided by that statute."

12. In that case, the observation by Wills, J. in the case of Wolverhampton New Water Works Company-Vs.-Hawkesford 37 LJ. 248 was cited with approval and it was further observed:

"Wills, J. dealing with the question said:- There are three classes of cases in which a liability may be established by statute. There is that class where there is a liability existing at common law, and which is only re-enacted by the statute with a special form of remedy there, unless the statute contains words necessarily excluding the common law remedy, the plaintiff has his election of proceeding either under the statute or common law. Then there is a second class, which consists of those cases in which a statute has created a liability, but has given no special remedy for it; there the party may adopt an action of debt or other remedy at common law to enforce it. The third class is where the statute creates a liability not existing at common law and gives also a particular remedy for enforcing it. Now it appears to me that the present case falls within such third class; and as with respect to that class it has been always held that the party must adopt the form of remedy given by the statute; So I think the company are bound here to follow the form given by this statute which creates the right."

The rule was enunciated by Wills, J. in relation to a liability created by a statute but the position is exactly the same where a new right is created by a statute, the law being settled beyond question that where a special Tribunal out of the ordinary course is appointed by an Act to determine questions as to rights which arc the creation of that Act, then, except so far as otherwise expressly provided or necessarily implied, that tribunal's jurisdiction to determine those questions is exclusive. This principle has been generally accepted in this country and freely applied to the determination of disputes arising out of election to the District or Municipal Boards and Legislative bodies.

13. In the case of Imtiaz Ahmed-Vs.-Ghulam Ali, 15 D.L.R. (S.C.) 283 the Court proceeded to observe thus :-

"It is well recognized that where a right or liability is created by statute which gives a special remedy for enforcing it, the remedy provided by that statute must be availed of."

14. The same principle has been followed by a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Syed Shah Mohammad Osman Ghani Vs. Bangladesh 39 D.L.R. 451 where it has been held as follows: "Where a statute creates a new right or a new liability which has no existence apart from the statute creating it and the statute creating the right or liability at the same time prescribes a particular method of enforcing it, then the remedy provided by the statute must be followed and it is not competent to the party to pursue any other remedy."

15. Election rights are not common law rights. They are the creation of a statute and should be exercised only in the manner in which the law which create them provided. In the course of the arguments the learned Advocate for the opposite party did not    dispute the correctness of the said proposition of law but he has contended that the bar of jurisdiction of   the Civil Court is conditional on the existence or functioning of the tribunal created by the special law. In support of this contention he has relied on the decision in the case of Sat Narain Gurwala-Vs.- Hanuman Parshad and another, A.I.R. 1946 Lahore 85 where it has been observed thus:

"In my opinion there is no ouster of the Jurisdiction of the courts till the special courts created by the statute function in accordance with the intent and spirit of the statute. Mere contemplation of a tribunal is not enough. It must come into being and having come into being it must function effectively and till that stage is reached the right which is a civil right is enforceable in the ordinary Civil Courts under the provisions of section 9 and it cannot be held that something illusory can take away the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts."

16. The learned Advocate then submits that since the Election Tribunal was not constituted by the time when plaintiff filed the suit, the Civil Court had Jurisdiction to entertain the suit as it was a suit of Civil nature. In this case there is no allegation in the plaint that the Election Tribunal contemplated under section 26 of the Ordinance was not in existence when the suit was filed. In fact in the instant case the Election had not been completed as yet and no cause of action arose for filing election petition to the Election Tribunal inasmuch as the election petition could not be filed before completion of the election and the publication of the names of the returned candidate in official Gazette under Rule 41. This being the position the existence or non-existence of the Election Tribunal at the time of the filing of the suit was of no significance in the case before us.

17. The learned Advocate for the opposite party-next submits that the Civil Courts have the jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with or the statutory Tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of Judicial Procedure. In support of this contentions, he has relied on the Privy Council decision in the case of Secretary of State-Mask and Co. 44 C.W.N.709 where their Lordships made observations which runs thus:-

"It is settled law that the exclusion of the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is not to be readily inferred, but that such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. It is also well settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure."

18. This Privy Council case was also referred to in the case of Mian Sultan Ali Nanghiana- Vs.-Mian Nur Hussain, P.L.D. 1949 and it was observed that those observations were made in reference to a case where initially the Civil Courts had jurisdiction in the matter which was subsequently taken away from them and entrusted to a special tribunal and they have no application to cases where the right never had been within the cognizance of the Civil Courts. We are in respectful agreement with this view. The election rights on which the suit has been based had never been within the cognizance of the Civil Courts as it was not a common law right but it was a right created by the special law which provided a special jurisdiction to enforce it. Hence the above contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite party has no relevance in the facts of the case before us.

19. It is now well settled that the term "election" embraces the entire process of election and not only the taking of poll and subsequent declaration of result. It has been held in the case of Md. Nazir Hakim- Vs-Said Muhammad and another; P.L.D. 1962 (W.P.) 421 that the election is a single process from the date of publication of the electoral roll to the date on which the result of the election is declared, like a chain with a number of links.

<u>20. In the case of Syed Mofazzal Hossain-Vs. The Election Commissioner and others, 28 D.L.R. (A.D.) 51 the meaning of term "election" was considered by the Appellate Division and it was observed thus:</u>

<u>"Election, therefore, means to be the final act of selection of a person for a particular office and this right to office is ascertained on the basis of the highest aggregate number of votes which a candidate may have received at different polling stations set up for the said purpose. The expressions "Election" sometimes is used popularly in a very wide sense. It then means the whole process of choosing a representative starting with the filing of a nomination paper and ending with the declaration of the result. The polling of Votes, which means the casting of votes at a Polling Centre, is only a part of the said process."</u>

<u>21. Now the point that arises is whether the setting up of polling station as provided in Rule 6 falls within the term "Election" or if it was a step prior to the election process. The heading of Part II of the Union Parishads (Election) Rules, 1983 is "Election" which provides the whole of process of election beginning from arrangement of electoral roll in Rule 4 upto the delivery of election papers to the concerned official after the publication of the result in Rule 42 and consequently the alleged contravention of Rule 6 on which the suit is based is included within the term "election". The setting up of polling station and the publication of the list of polling station are to be made at least fifteen days before the polling day as provided in Rule 6(AI) which therefore can be done after the filing of the nomination papers as well, as the day for filing nomination papers must be fixed on a date more than fifteen days before the polling day as it is evident from Rule 9. Hence the election process as detailed in Part II of the Rules which also provide for setting up of polling station will not come in conflict with the observation of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 28 DLR (AD) 51.</u>

22. Section 26 of the Ordinance provides that no election under this Ordinance shall be called in question except by an election petition under sub- section (2) and that any candidate may make an election petition in the prescribed manner to the Election Tribunal appointed under section 27 challenging election at which he was a candidate. Section 29 lays down that the decision of the Election Tribunal on the petition shall be final subject of the decision of the District Judge. An appeal provided for in Sub-Section (4), Rule 45 enumerates the relief which the petitioner may claim in the election petition. Under Rule 48 the Tribunal shall have all the powers of the Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 48 indicates that the Election Tribunal shall be competent to give reliefs mentioned in Rule 45 or make such orders as it may think fit but the Election Tribunal shall not declare the election of any returned candidate or the election as a whole void unless it is satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected by reason of the failure of any person to comply with or the contravention of these rules. The Ordinance and the Rules made thereunder, clearly provide for a special forum in the Election Tribunal to determine the election dispute which is to be brought before the Election by an election petition after the publication of the result in official Gazette under Rule 41. The contravention of Rules during election process can however, be made a ground to call the election in question by filing election petition.

23. Any matter which has the effect of vitiating an election of the Union Parishad for contravention of any of the rules in Part II or on any other ground cannot be brought up, at an intermediate stage, before the Elections Tribunal. No disputes arising in the course of an election will be entertained until the election is completed.

24. The Electoral right, on which the plaintiff- opposite party' based the suit, being a right created by the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 and it having prescribed the manner in which that right may be enforced, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to entertain the suit was impliedly barred u/s. 26 of the Ordinance. The Civil Courts have got no jurisdiction to entertain any suit challenging the election on the ground of contravention of rules or an any other ground at any stage either during election process or after publication of result of the election of the Union Parishad. The Jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal in this matter is exclusive. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed a jurisdiction not vested in him by law. Since the jurisdiction of the Civil Court has impliedly barred which was also evident from the Statement made in the plaint, the learned Subordinate Judge, by not rejecting the plaint, had committed an error of law resulting in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The petitioners application under Order 7 Rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed and the plaint of Title Suit No. 26 of 1988 of the court of Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati, is rejected.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Kazi Shamsunnahar & others ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Commandant RRF Khulna and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Haque J : Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the order No. 159 dated 6-3-88 removing late Kazi Matiur Rahman, Accountant, Range Reserved Force, Mirer Danga, Khulna, husband of the petitioner No. 1 and father of the petitioner Nos. 2-4 as contained in Memo. No. 811/E dated 8-6-89 evidenced by Annexure-L to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioners on 30-3-93 corresponding to Annexue-C to the petition passed by the respondent No.1 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to pay all arrear salary and other benefits admissible to the petitioners, the heirs of late Kazi Matiur Rahman.

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule, in short, are that late Kazi Matiur Rahman, the husband of the petitioner No.1 and the father of the petitioner Nos. 2, 3, and 4 during his life time joined as a sales clerk of "Ration Store" in the Kushtia police line and subsequently he was promoted to the rank of "Ration Clerk" with effect from 10-11-53 vide DO No. 3034 dated 23-11-53. During the continuance of service he was transferred from Kushtia Police Line to the Police Office at Jessore. Late Matiur Rahman had received there many laurels for his excellent service, and thereafter he was transferred to Khulna Range on promotion as an "Accountant vide Memo No. 7451-E dated 27-7-73 and he joined there as an "Accountant" in the office of the Khulna Police on 2-8-73.

3. During the continuance of service he was implicated in Khulna PS Case Nos. 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41 dated 16-9-78 and was arrested along with other persons on 7-10-78. The aforesaid criminal cases were subsequently re-numbered as Special Case Nos. 13/81, 14/81, 15/81, 19/81 and 20/81 of Divisional Special Judge, Khulna Division, Khulna, During the pendency of the aforesaid special Criminal Cases Mr Kazi Matiur Rahman died on 5-9-86 leaving behind the petitioners as his heirs. Since Kazi Matiur Rahman died the aforesaid Special Criminal Cases abated as against him. In support of the assertion the petitioners have annexed certified copy of the judgment of the Special Case No. 13/81 arising out of Khulna PS Case No. 38 dated 16-9-78 as Annexure-B. Similarly, other Special Case Nos. 14/81, 15/81, 19/81, 20/81 also abated against deceased Kazi Matiur Rahman.

4. It appears from the Annexures-A, C & L that Kazi Matiur Rahman died on 5-9-86 an by order No. 159 on 6-3-86 as contained in Annexure-C, an extract from the deceased Kazi Matiur Rahman's service book, he was removed from the service with effect from 6-9-86. Subsequently, the petitioners have filed the formal order of removal dated 8-6-89 and the same has been annexed as Annexure-L to the supplementary affidavit, which is under challenge before this court.

5. The petitioners have asserted that they being the only heirs of late Kazi Matiur Rahman are entitled to get arrear salaries, gratuity, pension and other benefits due to him. Accordingly, the petitioners herein made several applications to the proper authority time and again but without any result. However, the petitioners received information that on account of non-availability of his service book nothing could be done as to their claim of pension, etc. They were also informed that until the service book of late Kazi Matiur Rahman is traced out and/or reconstructed nothing could be done. However, his service book was subsequently reported to have been reconstructed and was sent to Jessore for necessary order but no order was passed in favour of the petitioners.

6. The petitioners having failed to obtain any relief went to the Administrative Tribunal. Dhaka for necessary relief in the matter but the learned Administrative Tribunal. Dhaka returned their application with a verbal instruction to move the same before the Hon'ble High Court Division in its Writ Jurisdiction for necessary relief in the matter as the Tribunal does not have any jurisdiction to entertain the application at the instance of the petitioners who are admittedly not the persons in the service of the Republic. The petitioners, therefore, served a legal notice demanding justice in the matter before coming to this court. It was clearly stated in the said notice demanding justice that in the case of default, the petitioners would be compelled to file and move a writ petition in the High Court Division without any further reference. The respondents though received the notice demanding justice but they did not comply with the requests of the petitioners. The petitioners having failed to obtain any relief, moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Miah Abdul Gafur, appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the impugned order is ex facie illegal inasmuch as the deceased person cannot be removed and/or dismissed from the service. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioners being aggrieved went to the Administrative Tribunal but the Tribunal returned their application on the ground that the Administrative Tribunal does not have any jurisdiction to entertain an application at the instance of the petitioners, who are admittedly not the persons in the service of the Republic or of any public statutory authority. Mr Miah Abdul Gafur submits that the petitioners do not have any other efficacious and alternative remedy and as such they have filed this instant writ petition for necessary relief in the matter.

8. The respondent No. 2, Inspector General of Police. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has made appearance before this Court through the learned Deputy Attorney-General and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the petition. It has been stated in paragraph 5 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the statements made in paragraphs 4 and 5 of the petition are matters of record, but the petitioners are required to prove the same. The respondent No. 2 has further stated in paragraph 8 of the affidavit-in-opposition that no notice whatsoever was served upon the respondents about the death of Kazi Matiur Rahman but on receipt of the information about his death from his widow, a report was sent to the Police Head Quarter on 21-10-86. In paragraph 10 of the affidavit-in-opposition it has been stated by the respondent No. 2 that due to involvement of the deceased Kazi Matiur Rahman in the criminal cases, the department could not consider his pension and other claims like gratuity, family pension and arrear of salaries, etc.

9. On the basis of the aforesaid averments Mr Mumtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attoreny-General submits that Ex-Accountant Kazi Matiur Rahman and his other co-accused committed defalcation of Government money by preparing false bills. Thereby the Government has suffered a pecuniary loss of Taka 1,92,372.00 only. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that Kazi Matiur Rahman was the principal FIR accused, inasmuch as six criminal cases were instituted by the District Anti-Corruption Bureau (DAB) Khulna vide Khulna PS Case Nos. 37(9)78, 38 (9)78, 39 (9)78, 40(9)78 41(9)78 and 66(9)78 under sections 409/467/468/471/34 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and in all these cases co-accused of Kazi Matiur Rahman has been convicted by the learned Divisional Special Judge, Khulna and due to the death of Kazi Matiur Rahman, the learned Special Judge simply had to stop the trial of the cases as against him. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that Kazi Matiur Rahman was not acquitted of charges levelled against him. Therefore, the prayer of the petitioners for arrear salaries, gratuity, pension and family pension, etc. in respect of Kazi Matiur Rahman Ex-Accountant, RRF Khulna could not be considered. Further, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the present petition is not maintainable in writ jurisdiction. The petitioner ought to have gone to the Administrative Tribunal for necessary relief in the matter.

10. Let us first consider the objection of maintainability of the petition raised by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. The jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal has been set forth in section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980. For conveniences section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1980 is quoted as under.

"(1) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of Republic (or any statutory public authority)."

11. It is also provided in sub-section (2) of section-4 that:

"a person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) may make an application to an Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (1), if he is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority."

"Provided that no application in respect of an order, decision or action which can be set aside, varied or modified by a higher administrative authority under any law for the time being in force relating to the terms and conditions of the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) or the discipline of that service, can be made to the Administrative Tribunal until such higher authority has taken a decision on the matter. Provided further that no such application shall be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal unless it is made within six months from the date of making or taking of the order, decision or action concerned or making of the decision on the matter by the higher administrative authority as the case may be."

12. It appears that a "person" in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority may make an application to an Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (1), if he is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority. In this connection sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act is also relevant which is as follows:

"(3) In this section "person" in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) includes a person who is or has retired or is dismissed, removed or discharged from such service, but does not include a person in the defence service of Bangladesh (or of the Bangladesh Rifles)."

<u>13. Therefore, it appears that a person, who was in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority but he has been retired, dismissed, removed or discharged from the service, can also file an application before the Administrative Tribunal provided he is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority. Even if Matiur Rahman was removed from the service, he could have filed an application under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 provided he was alive. In this connection we have also considered section 19 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 of India, as similar provision as section 4 of our Act, wherein it is provided that "(1) Subject to the other provisions of this Act, a person aggrieved by any order pertaining to any matter within the jurisdiction of a Tribunal may make an application to the Tribunal for the redressal of his grievance."</u>

14. The word "person" occurring in sub-section (1) of section-19 of the said Act, 1985 covers Government and its departments. Hence, the Government or its department can also maintain an application in a matter relating to service matters of an employee. In the said section 19 of Act. 1985 the "person aggrieved" has been held to mean that a person who makes an application must be one having an enforceable legal right and in a decision of the Indian jurisdiction it has been held that not only a public servant but even "heirs of a ''deceased servant" can be "persons aggrieved" within the meaning of section 19 of the Administrative Tribunal, Act, 1985 of India and it has been decided so in the case of PR Somau vs. Anuradha (1988) 6A TC 173.

15. Further, that a person, who is not yet a public servant but claims right to appointment to a civil post can also be a "person aggrieved" and can maintain an application before the Administrative Tribunal and the same has been decided in the case of Ginder Kaur vs Delhi Admn. (1987) 4 ATC 675.

16. But in our Act, 1980 "person" who is in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority may make an application to an Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (1), if he is aggrieved by any order or decision, etc. The only exception that has been made under section (4)3 of our Act. 1980 that a "person" who is or has retired or is dismissed or removed or discharged from service can also maintain an application as if he is still in the service of the Republic or of public statutory authority. There is nowhere in the four corners of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 that "any person who is aggrieved by any order or decision may make an application before the Administrative Tribunal. There is no such expression in our Act that an aggrieved person may make an application under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act. 1980 as is possible, under section 19 of the Administrative Tribunals Act. 1985 of India. The scope of section 19 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 of India is much wider than section 4 of our Administrative Tribunals Act. 1980.

17. Although the Administrative Tribunal has been given the exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine application made by any person in the service of the Republic in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory Public Authority, nevertheless there is no such expression that not only a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory Public Authority but even heirs of a deceased servant may make an application to the Administrative Tribunal under section 4 of our Act for redressal of his grievance.

<u>18. After having considered and compared the relevant provisions of section 4 of our Administrative Tribunals Act. 1980 as well as section 19 of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1985 of India, we are of the view that only "a person" who is in the service of the Republic or of any statutory Public Authority and or who has been retired dismissed, removed or discharged from service may make an application before the Administrative Tribunal for necessary relief in the matter No. person other than the "person" in the service of the Republic or of any statutory Public Authority as contemplated under section 4(1)(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 can maintain an application before the Administrative Tribunal. But under section 19 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 of India, "a person aggrieved" may make any application before the Administrative Tribunal. In that view of the matter we are inclined to hold that the petitioners before us had or have no locus standi to file any application before the Administrative Tribunal. If their application was returned by the Chairman of the Administrative Tribunal there was no illegality in it.</u>

<u>19. It also appears that the petitioners are admittedly persons who are aggrieved within the meaning of Article 102 of our Constitution and they, having no other equally efficacious and alternative remedy, can validly maintain an application under Article 102 of our Constitution in the High Court Division.</u>

20. With regard to the merit of the case we have heard the learned Advocates and perused the necessary papers. It appears from Annexure ''C'' to the petition that late Kazi Matiur Rahman was in the service of the People's Republic of Bangladesh before he was removed vide Annexure-C to the petition corresponding to Annexure-L to the supplementary affidavit. It also appears that the said Matiur Rahman was named— accused person in Khulna PS Case Nos. 37(9)78, 38 (9)78, 40(9)78, 41(9)78 and 66(9)78, all were under sections 409/467/468/471/34 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II 1947. On this point the learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that all other accuseds were convicted by the court of Divisional Special Judge, Khulna but due to the death of Kazi Matiur Rahman, the learned Court simply stopped the cases against Kazi Matiur Rahman. We have perused annexure-B, the certified copy of the judgment and order passed by the Divisional Special Judge, Khulna Division in Special Case No. 13 of 1981 (arising out of Khulna PS Case No. 38 dated 16-9-78) wherein the learned Divisional Special Judge has come to a decision that "It is a fact accused. Kazi Matiur Rahman died during the pendency of the present proceeding. As such, it appears that the case has abated as against deceased Kazi Matiur Rahman." Therefore, the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General is factually not correct. Further, it is nobody's case that Kazi Matiur Rahman was acquitted of the charges that were brought against him. The learnd Deputy Attorney-General submits that this is the reason why the respondent No.1 did not consider the application of the petitioners for getting gratuity, pension and arrears of salary, etc. in respect of late Kazi Matiur Rahman. Ex-Accountant, RRF Khulna. It also appears that the respondent No. 2, after coming to know that Kazi Matiur Rahman died on 5-9-86 by heart attack initiated the order No. 159 dated 6-3-88 annexure-''C'' removing Kazi Matiur Rahman from his service which culminated in the issuance of annexure-''L'' to the supplementary affidavit. In fact, Annexure-L is the formal order of removal corresponding to Annexue-''C''. It is also not disputed that said Kazi Matiur Rahman was removed from the service with effect from 6-9-86 immediately after his death on 5-9-86.

21. It is not understood as to why a dead person was removed from the service. It further appears that Kazi Matiur Rahman was still in the service before his death though the said criminal cases were pending against him and others. There is no dispute that Kazi Matiur Rahman was neither convicted nor removed, dismissed or retired from service prior to his death. In fact, Kazi Matiur Rahman died during the continuance of his service. Further; death of a person cannot be a ground of dismissal or removal from service. In that view of the matter we are inclined to hold that the impugned order Annexure ''L'' corresponding to Annexure-''C'' removing late Kazi Matiur Rahman, from service is ex facie illegal and the same has been issued without any lawful authority.

<u>22. Since we have already held that Kazi Matiur Rahman died while he was still in the service of the Republic the petitioners as heirs of late Kazi Matiur Rahman are entitled to receive the arrear salary, pension, gratuity, etc. as permissible under the law.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned Order No. 159 dated 6-3-88 removing late Kazi Matiur Rahman as contained in Memo. No. B1 1 /E dated 8-6-89 Annexure-L to the supplementary affidavit corresponding to Annexure-C to the petition has been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to pay to the petitioners the arrear salaries if any, gratuity, pension and family pension, etc. in respect of late Kazi Matiur Rahman as permissible under the law.</u>

End.
