parties:
Kamrun Nahar Begum ------ Appellant
Vs.
Nurul Alam Chowdhury & another ------ Respondent
case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated February 23, 1995 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 568 of 1990 [heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 567 of 1990])
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: These appeals by leave are by the preempted against the common judgment in Civil Revision Nos. 567 and 568 of 1990 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rules. The Civil Revisions were filed against the judgment and order dated January 24, 1990 in Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 120 and 121 of 1987 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka affirming the judgment and order dated April 23, 1987 of the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 allowing the same. The Miscellaneous Cases were filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 seeking pre-emption in respect of the land in Dhanmondi Residential Area (Dhanmondi RA). 

	2. The pre-emptor acquired ownership of the major part of the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13 of Dhanmondi RA by purchase in between 1975 and 1981 from some of the heirs of original allottee of the aforesaid plot and that he sought for pre-emption as regard the transfer made in February 1984 to the appellant (opposite party No. 1 in the miscellaneous' cases) by the heirs of original allottee. 

	3. Late Kala Miah became owner of 10 kathas of land of plot No. 543/A, Road No. 13, Dhanmondi RA,-upon obtaining lease from the Government. He died leaving 2 widows 8 sons and 10 daughters. Pre-emptor-respondent No. 1 by purchase in between the years 1975-1981 became co-sharer to the extent of 14 annas in the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13, Dhanmondi, RA. The appellant in February 1984 by 2 different deeds purchased shares of some of the heirs (4 daughters) of Kala Miah. Thereupon the respondent No. 1 filed the aforesaid Miscellaneous Cases claiming to be the co-sharer of the land transferred to the appellant. 

	4. The Miscellaneous Cases were opposed by the appellant and another (respondent No. 2) by filing written objection contending, inter alma, that in respect of the land transferred in the year 1984 there were agreements of the year 1977 between the vendor and the vendees and that the pre-emptor had knowledge about the sale long before 17-8-1984. It was also contended by the pre-emptee that Miscellaneous cases were barred by limitation and that same were not maintainable because of the provisions of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

	5. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that Miscellaneous cases were not barred by limitation and that also not barred under the provision of section 85(2) of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, 1949. The preempted-appellant went on appeal against the judgment and order of the Court of Assistant Judge before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. The Miscellaneous Appeals were heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka and he dismissed the appeals. 

	6. The preempted-appellant thereafter moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction' and obtained Rules in the Civil Revisions as mentioned herein before. The High Court Division discharged the Rules on the finding the land was acquired by the Government only to develop, demarcate plots and lease out to interested persons retaining its superior right in respect of transfer, correction of record, fixing of rent or subsequent enhancement of rent or any other terms on expiry of the lease of 99 years but by this Government does not create obstacle in the beneficial enjoyment of the property, its transferability and. inheritance by the descendants but the transferability will be always controlled on principle that the land as far as possible should be retained by the heirs of lessee under principles and policy of the pre-emption law. Therefore, I hold that pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is very much applicable to the Dhanmondi. Residential plot sold to others by the co-sharers". 

	7. Leave was granted to consider the contention of the appellant as in view of the provision of sub-section 1(c) of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 as well as in view of the discussion in the case of Md Mosaddeque Hossain vs Dr Esmat Mirza and others reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 57 Pre-emption sought under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 was not maintainable, the High Court Division was in error in discharging the Rule and not holding that pre-emption was not available under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as against the transfer to the preempted-appellant by the co-sharers of the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13 of Dhanmondi RA. 

	8. The learned Counsel for the appellant primarily argued in the background of the decision of this court in the case reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 57 as to the maintainability of the Miscellaneous cases filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as regard non-agricultural land in Dhanmondi RA.

	9. The question similar to the question involved in the present appeals came up for consideration before this court in the case mentioned hereinabove. This court upon considering the provisions of section 85(2) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 which reads as : 

	"Nothing in this Act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government: 

	Provided that the right vested in a tenant by the provisions of this Act shall not be divested by the acquisition of the superior right only in the land by the Government." and the provisions of section 81A (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which reads as The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall, except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Act IV of 1882)" (proviso to the sub-section is not relevant for the present purpose) has held"  that the object of section 85(2) of the Act was to retain control over non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government unencumbered by the provisions of the NAT Act. Section 81A(2) stated positively how the rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants other than those who have become tenants under the Government by virtue of compulsory acquisition of land shall be determined. The NAT Act has not been mentioned to be a governing law in respect of such tenants of non-agricultural land under the Government. Hence, on both accounts, under section 85(2) of the NAT Act and section 81A(2) of the SAT Act, the ouster of NAT Act from the categories mentioned therein are complete. Section 24 of the NAT Act has no manner of application to lands of Dhanmondi Residential Area". 

	10. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 made submissions amongst others, that prayer for pre-emption was very much maintainable since the land sought to be pre-empted was not acquired for the use of the Government directly or for any Office or Department of the Government but for the use of the lessees of the Government which in no way can be considered that the land so acquired is being used by the Government or by any office or Department of the Government and that denying of right of pre-emption in respect of the land of Dhanmondi Residential Area which is non-agricultural land but exercise of right of pre-emption in respect of other non-agricultural land while available under the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act would result in discrimination as regard the right of pre-emption amongst the non-agricultural tenants. This particular contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent in our view is not well founded in law in that in barring pre-emption in respect of the land of Dhanmondi Residential Area upon resorting to the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act no discrimination has been made in between the tenants of the said residential area. The tenants of the other non-agricultural land are being in the different category the bar of pre-emption as has been made to land of Dhanmondi RA cannot be said discrimination in any respect amongst the class of non-agricultural tenants in general. The bar as to pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is limited amongst the tenants of Non-Agricultural land in Dhanmondi RA and thereby no discrimination has been done amongst the non-agricultural tenants of the said particular area, rather the tenants of the said limited area have been treated equally. The bar so made as to pre-emption of the land of Dhanmondi RA appears to be rational and does not offend the rule of non-discrimination amongst the, same class of person or persons placed in the same situation. The other contention that the land sought to be pre-empted as is not used by the Government or by any Office or Department of the Government cannot be said immune from being pre-empted under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act also not well founded in law because of the fact that the land sought to be pre-empted is being held by the lessee tenants under the Government in respect of acquisitioned land being same leased out. Provision of sub-section 2 of section 85 of NAT Act clearly shows that provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act shall not be applicable in respect of non-agricultural land as mentioned in section 85(1) of NAT Act and that land of Dhanmondi RA being the land of one of those categories as the same is held by special kind of tenant of the Government pre-emption is not available. There is no dispute that the lands in Dhanmondi Residential Area are non-agricultural land and the same are being held by the lessees as being the tenants under the Government. Proviso to sub-section (2) of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, and the sub-section (1) of section 81A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 clearly show that non-agricultural tenants who have become tenants under the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior right in non-agricultural land by the provision of SAT Act, the provisions of NAT Act, if so were application to such tenants at the time of acquisition, would be regulated by the provision of NAT Act. The application of section 24 NAT Act has been excluded by the provision of section 85(2) of NAT Act in respect of the land mentioned in section 85(1) (a,b,c,d,e) and land of Dhanmondi RA being the land of one of the categories of land as in section 85(1)(a,b,c,d,e) application of provision of section 24 NAT Act has been excluded by section 85(2) NAT Act. 

	11. The learned Counsel for the respondent in spite of best endeavor could not make out any distinction as to question of law involved in the present appeal and question of law considered and decided in the case reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 57. The respondent could not make out any case to persuade us to take a different view as to the ratio of the reported case, nor could the respondent distinguish the reported case, either on facts or law involved therein, from the instant appeals. 

	12. Since the point involved in the appeals is as to whether lands in the Dhanmondi Residential Area are or not subject to pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and as the said point is covered by the decision in the case reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 57 and that as the decision in the reported case fully applicable to the facts as well as law involved in the appeals and that also to the points urged for consideration in the appeals we are of the view that in the afore state of the matter and also in the light of our discussions made herein over the judgment and decision of the High Court Division calls for interference. 

	13. Accordingly the appeals are allowed 

	14. The judgment and the order of the High Court Division in the Civil Revisions affirming the judgment and the order of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in the Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 120 and 121 affirming the judgment and the order of the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 are dismissed. 
	
	There is no order as to costs. 
	
End.

lawyer:
Shah Azizur Rahman with Latifur Rahman Advocates, instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record for the Appellant.
Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmad, Attorney-General, instructed by A. M. Khan Chowdhury, Advocate-on-Record-U/O-XLV Rule 1 (S.C) A.D. Rules 1973.
parties:
Syed Mofazzal Hossain ----- Appellant.
Vs.
The Election Commissioner and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Order dated 3-12-1974 passed by the High Court Division in Petition No. 1473 of 1974).
full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J. This appeal by Special Leave is against an order of a Bench of the High Court Division summarily rejecting an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and refusing to interfere with the judgment of an Election Tribunal which set aside the election of the appellant as Chairman of a Union Parishad and certain other persons, held under the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973 and the rules framed thereunder.

2. An election was held under the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules in respect of Bechali Union Parishad within the Sub-Division of Narail in the district of Jessore and the appellant contested the said election for the office of Chairman of the said Union Parishad, which was held on 21.12.73. The appellant having secured the highest number of votes was declared elected as Chairman of the said Union Parishad and his name was duly published in the Bangladesh Gazette as per Rule 43 of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973. Respondent No. 3 thereafter filed an election petition under Rule 56(2) of the said Rules on 7-3-74 before the Electron Tribunal (3rd Court of Munsif) at Narail, challenging the validity of the polling in Ward No. 1 only on the allegations that there were no enclosures at the polling booth which was full of unauthorized persons, that there were occasional disturbances by the goonda elements who snatched away ballot papers and dropped them in the ballot boxes, that there was no arrangement of light and as such the voting was suspended for half an hour after dusk, but the polling continued upto 12 P.M., that the votes were not counted just after the completion of the election and the ballot boxes were taken to nearby Seed Store where the counting started in the morning of 22. 12. 73, that there were disturbances and the counting could not be completed there, that the Presiding Officer was gained over by the appellant and as such 255 ballot papers were removed and utilised for declaring the appellant elected.

3. It is to be noticed that no candidate who contested for the office of Vice-Chairman or of any of the members disputed the result of the election to any of the said offices, and none of the successful candidates for the said offices was made a party to the said proceeding before the Election Tribunal.

4. The election petition was opposed by the appellant as well as by the Presiding Officer who filed separate sets of written objection, in which the material allegations In the election petition were denied. It was specifically asserted in the said written objections that the counting of the votes cast in the election commenced in the morning of 22-12-73 at the Seed Store and was completed at 1 P. M. and that after counting it was found that the appellant received 1016 votes and Respondent No. 3 obtained 737 votes.

5. Evidence was adduced by the contesting parties to the election petition in support of their respective cases and the Tribunal on a consideration of the materials on record, Came to the finding that the counting of votes which commenced in the morning on 22.12.73 at the Seed Store could not be completed that the Presiding Officer did not declare the result after counting the votes and that he did not fill up the requisite forms as per Rule 41. Being of the view that the election held in respect of Ward No. 1 had been vitiated on account of the failure of the election officials to count the votes at the spot and to fill up 'L' and 'M' forms in presence of the contesting candidates or their agents, the Election Tribunal set aside the election, not only of the Chairman, but also of the Vice-Chairman and members as held at Ward No. 1.

6. The appellant moved the High Court Division under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh against the said order of the Election Tribunal but the learned Judges of the High Court Division rejected the said application summarily being of the view that there having been no counting according to Rules, the result of the election must be held to have been materially affected thereby.

7. Special Leave has been granted to appeal against the said Order of the High Court Division to consider the question whether the Election Tribunal acted within its authority in setting aside the election partially i.e., in respect of one Ward only.

8. Mr. Shah Azizur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, has submitted that the rules, as framed in the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973, according to which the election of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman and the Members of a Union Parishad are held do not contemplate that an election of any such person can be set aside in part in respect of one Ward only and that if an election of the office of Chairman of the Union Parishad is to be set aside, it shall have to be set aside in respect of all the Wards.

9. No one has appeared on behalf of Respondent No. 3 at whose instance the election of the appellant has been set aside Learned. Attorney-General, being called upon to assist the Court, has however, appeared in this case and has supported that part of the order of the Election Tribunal, by which the election result in respect of Ward No. 1 as to the office of Chairman has been nullified. He has submitted that there is nothing in the Rules which prevents the Tribunal from disturbing the result of the polling at one centre only and maintaining the result at other centres. Learned Attorney-General has referred to Rule 30 of the Election Rules which provides for adjournment of poll of a particular polling station in case of interruption or obstruction beyond control of the Presiding Officer without affecting the polling at other stations.

10. In course of his submission, learned Attorney-General has, however, raised a new and a very important point as to the validity of the other part of the Order of the Election Tribunal, which has purported to set aside the election of the Vice-Chairman and the members of the Union Parishad for Ward No. 1. Learned Attorney-General has drawn the attention of the Court to the facts that Respondent No. 3 who presented the election petition to the Election Tribunal was a candidate only for the office of Chairman and was interested in the election to the said office alone and that none of the successful candidates for the office of the Vice Chairman and members concerned were made parties in the election petition nor were they given any opportunity to defend the validity of their election. In the premises, it has been submitted by the learned Attorney-General the Election Tribunal had no jurisdiction to act aside the election to the said offices and the part of the order purporting to invalidate the election to the said offices was patently with-out any lawful authority. This point has not taken by the appellant before the High Court Division nor has it been taken before this Division, presumably because he is not interested in it, but as the question relates to the jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal in making the impugned order and is of great public importance, we halve allowed the learned Attorney-General to raise this important question of law before this Division, although it was not mentioned in the order granting special leave and have heard him as well as the learned Counsel for the appellant on this question.

11. The learned Counsel for the appellant has contended, in support of his appeal regarding the setting aside of his election as Chairman, that the Election Rules do not authorise such partial setting aside of election, and has referred to rule 60 which provides what kind of relief a petitioner of an election petition may claim and also to the proviso to rule 62(2) which prescribes that the Tribunal shall not declare the election of any returned candidate or election as a whole void unless it is satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected by reason of the irregularity or the contravention of the Rules complained of.

12. For proper appreciation the point, the relevant rules may be quoted as follows:—

"60. Relief the petitioner may claim as relief any of the following declaration:

(a) That the election of any returned candidate is void and that the petitioner or some other person has been duly elected; or

(b) That the election as a whole void. 62. The trial of petition—(1) A Tribunal shall, upon receipt of an election petition, give notice thereof to all the contesting candidates and such other candidates against whom any allegation, if any, of any corrupt or illegal practice is made at the election to which the election relates.

(2) The Tribunal shall, after giving the contesting candidates and such other candidates against whom any allegation, if any, of any corrupt or illegal practice is made an opportunity of being heard and taking such evidence as may be produced before it, make such orders as it may think fit;

Provided that the Tribunal shall not declare the election of any returned candidate or election as a whole void unless it is satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected by reason of the failure of any person to comply with or the contravention of these rules;

(3) The decision of the Tribunal on an election petition shall be final".

<u>13. The perusal of the above quoted rules indicates that the aggrieved candidate may challenge the validity of the election of a returned candidate and pray that some other person has been duly elected to the office. In such a case the election as a whole is not set aside and there is no necessity for holding a fresh poll for the purpose of an election to the disputed office. Under clause (b) of rule 60 the election may be challenged to have been bad as a whole in which case fresh polling is, of necessity, to take place. This election must necessarily mean the election of a returned candidate for which the petitioner was a candidate.</u>

<u>14. In the instant case, the Election Tribunal, by setting aside the election held at Ward No. 1 only for the office of the Chairman, does not appear to have conformed to the direction as contained in the said Rules in framing the final order in the case. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that the Rules as framed under the Bangladesh Local Government Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Order, 1973 do not contemplate a partial setting aside of an election. Election has been defined in the definition clause i.e., Rule 2(a) as meaning election of a Member, Commissioner, Woman Commissioner, Chairman or Vice-Chairman of a Union Parishad or Paurashava, as the case may be Election, therefore, means to be the final act of selection of a person for a particular office and this right to office is ascertained on the basis of the highest aggregate number of votes which a candidate may have received at different polling stations set up for the said purpose. The expression "Election" sometimes is used popularly in a very wide sense. It then means the whole process of choosing a representative starting with the filing of a nomination paper and ending with the declaration of the result. The polling of votes, which means the casting of votes at a Polling Centre, is only a part of the said process. It may be that if a certain irregularity has taken place in a particular polling centre in respect of the election of a person to a particular office and the Tribunal is satisfied that the final result has been affected by such irregularity and no other candidate can be declared elected in his place, the election to that particular office is to be declared void as a whole. But that does not mean that the result of the polling at other centres, in respect of which no irregularity or illegality has been complained of, should also be nullified. Having regard to rule 62(2) which authorise a Tribunal to make such order as may be deemed fit in a particular case, the Tribunal shall have, no doubt, to declare the election to a particular office to be void as a whole but it would be perfectly within its power to direct that fresh polling shall take place only with regard to the polling centre where the irregularity or illegality has been committed and the final result will be ascertained by aggregating the results of the newly held poll and of the former polls which have remained undisturbed.</u>

<u>15. Proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 62, however, enjoins that before declaring the election of any returned candidate or the election as a whole void because of any irregularity or illegality the Tribunal shall have to be satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected because of such irregularity or illegality. What has been found by the Election Tribunal in this case is that there were certain irregularities and contravention of Rules in respect of the polling station of one of the 3 wards of the Union in question and this finding of the Tribunal on the basis of the materials brought before it is not open to challenge in this court. But what the Tribunal was required under the Rules to do after such a finding was that it should have also been satisfied as to whether the final result of the Election was affected because of the irregularity or contravention of Rules in respect of Ward No. 1 alone, which were found by the Tribunal to have occurred, that is to say, whether, if the result of the polling at Ward No. 1 was excluded the position of the successful candidate would have been affected by such exclusion. In the present case, of course, it has been conceded by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the successful candidate obtained the highest number of votes in this ward and that he did not poll sufficient number of votes in other centres, which could have off-set the reduction in the number of his votes in consequence of the exclusion of the votes obtained by him in that particular ward. It appears therefore, that although the Election Tribunal has not specifically referred to the proviso to rule 62(2) it was satisfied that the entire election of the Chairman was affected as a result of the exclusion of the votes cast at the polling centre of the said ward.</u>

16. On a perusal of the judgment of the Election Tribunal as a whole, it appears to us that what was really meant by the Election Tribunal by setting aside the election held at Ward No. 1 of Bechali Union for the election of Chairman, was that the election to the said office was set aside as a Whole but that the fresh polling for such office would take place only at Ward No. 1 of the said Union. This was, according to us, perfectly within the jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal to direct.

17. We are, therefore, of opinion that although the final order of the Election Tribunal has not been properly drawn tip, the order so far as it relates to the election of Chairman has, in substance, set aside the election of the Chairman as a whole, but has directed that there will be fresh poll only in respect of Ward No. 1 and there seems to be no valid reason to interfere with this order, so far as the election of the Chairman is concerned.

18. The order of the Election Tribunal so far as it relates to the election of the Vice-Chairman and Members of the Union Parishad however, stands on a different footing. As it has already been noted none of the candidates for any of said offices has challenged the validity of the election of any of the successful candidates for the said offices nor any of the said successful candidates was given any opportunity to appear in the proceeding before the Election Tribunal and be heard before the adverse order was passed against him.

<u>19. The scheme of the rules framed under section 24 of the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973 relating to an election dispute seems to be that an election to an office of a Union Parishad can be challenged only by a candidate to the said office and that before an election is set aside, an opportunity shall have to be given to all the contesting candidates at the disputed election.</u>

20. Rule S6 of the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules clearly provides that no election shall be called in question except by an election petition made by a candidate challenging the election at which he was a candidate. It shows that a dispute as to the validity of an election of Chairman, Vice-Chairman and the members, as the case may be, can be raised only by a person who was a contestant in the said election and that by means of an election petition, which is to be presented to the Tribunal in the mariner as provided in Rule 59 which by sub-rule (2) provides that it shall be presented either by the candidate or by a person duly authorised by him in writing in that behalf.

21. In the instant case no dispute appears to have been raised as to the validity of the election of the Vice-Chairman or any of the Members by means of an election petition nor has such a dispute been raised by a candidate at such an election. In the circumstances, it appears to us that the Election Tribunal has gone out of its way in setting aside the election of the Vice-Chairman or the members and such an action is on the face of it without jurisdiction.

<u>22. Furthermore, rule 62 enacts that the Tribunal shall, upon a receipt of an election petition give notice thereof to all the contesting candidates at the election to which the election petition relates and shall decide the case only after giving such contesting candidates an opportunity of being heard. We find the statutory rule clearly lays down that the Tribunal shall adjudicate the dispute only after giving all the interested parties necessary facility for representing their case in support or otherwise of the validity of the election. The provision of this statutory rule cannot be read as merely directory in the case of a successful candidate, whose position is entirely different from that of the other contesting candidates. The valuable right to a representative office which has been acquired by him as a result of the election is not simply a personal or individual right; it is concerned with the interest of numerous persons inhabiting the constituency, who arc sought to be represented by the successful candidate in the particular office and it does also involve, undoubtedly, question of public policy. The positive provision in the statutory rule for affording an opportunity to the Contesting candidates of being heard in a trial of an election petition should therefore, be read, in our opinion, as a mandatory provision of law, so far as the successful candidate is concerned, and setting an election of a successful candidate at nought without giving him an opportunity of being heard in contravention of the said mandatory provision would be clearly in excess of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal all concerned.</u>

23. On all these considerations, we have no manner of doubt that the order of the Election Tribunal so far as it relates to the setting aside of the election of the Vice-Chairman and the members was without jurisdiction and cannot, therefore, be sustained.

24. We, therefore, hold that there is no infirmity in the order of the Election Tribunal by which the election of Chairman was set aside and repelling was purported to be directed in respect of Ward No. 1 only but the order of the said Tribunal setting aside the election of the Vice-Chairman and the members of Ward No. 1 was without any lawful authority and was, therefore, a nullity.

25. In the result this appeal, for which special leave was granted is dismissed without any order as to cost subject to the observation made above in respect of the import of the oilier made by the Election Tribunal relating to the election of Chairman but the order of the said Tribunal so far as it relates to the setting aside of the election of the Vice-Chairman and the members is declared to have been without jurisdiction and as such void.

End.

full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury J: On an application filed by the petitioner under Article 102(1) and (2) of the Constitution of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the impugned Gazette Notification dated 3-9-92, as evidenced by Annexure-K and the acquisition of the property covered by the said notification shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

2. The case of the petitioners is as follows: 

1.56 acre of land of SA Plot Nos. 31, 32 and 31/193 of mouza Baje Kakrail within Police Station Ramna, Dhaka forming Municipal Holding No. 85 Kakrail, Ramna, Dhaka belonged to one Lawrence Aloysius Noronha died intestate on 15-2-63 and his right, title and interest in the said property devolved on his two sons-Clifford Noronha and George Eric Noronha and two daughters-Winifred Rubie and Josephine Willes, who died intestate, as a result half of her share devolved on her husband DR Willes and the rest devolved on her two brothers and one sister. Thereafter Winifred Rubie filed a partition suit being Partition Suit No. 113 of 1996 against DR Willes and others which was dismissed. Winifred Rubie preferred an appeal being FA No. 318 of 1970 before the High Court of the then East Pakistan and the appeal was allowed and the suit was decreed by the High Court of Bangladesh by judgment dated 25-5-97. Winifred Rubie and her two brothers each got 7/24th share and DR Willes got 3/24th share. Thereafter the final decree was passed on 2-5-93 and DR Willes got half of the main building in the western side and the land underneath in his 3/24th share. Rest of the property was allotted to the saham of the surviving sons and daughters of Laurence Aloysius Noronha. The aforesaid property was requisitioned under the provisions of Emergency Requisition of Property Act. 1948 by an order dated 19-7-77 for accommodation of Willes Little Flower School. The said requisition was challenged by Winifred Rubie, but was found by the Appellate Division to have been validly made. The petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury 16 (sic) executed and registered between 20-7-81 and 9-9-81 purchased the entire share of the aforesaid property allotted 21/24th share to Clifford Noronha, George Eric Noronha and Winifred Rubie. Moshahid Ali Chowdhury died in April 1993 leaving behind wife petitioner No. 3, two sons, petitioner Nos. 1 and 2, three daughters, Mrs. Suraiya Islam, Mrs Aleya Chowdhury and Mrs Rabeya Chowdhury as his heirs. The petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury, after the aforesaid purchase, applied to the Government of Bangladesh for derequisition of the same. The Government of Bangladesh through the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms after hearing the petitioners and the Willes Little Flower School authority on 16-1-85 issued an order of derequisition directing the Deputy Commissioner, respondent No. 2, to release specified and demarcated 0.63 acre of the aforesaid property together with the building standing thereon and deliver possession of the derequisitioned property to the "original owners from whom the property was requisitioned or to their successor-in-interest after verification of title. A true copy of the said order dated 16-10-85 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure "A". Thereafter, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) respondent No. 1 issued a notice under Rule 10(1) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Rules for verification of title and after verification of the title documents and other papers produced by the petitioners respondent No. 1 was satisfied about the title of the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury to the aforesaid property. The names of the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury were mutated in the Revenue recorls of the Government of Bangladesh in respect of the aforesaid property and the rent of the said property was accepted by the Government. The true copies of the mutation order, Mutation DCR, Mutation Khatian and the rent receipt are annexed to the petition and marked as Annexures B, B(1), B(2), B(3) and B(4). Thereafter the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) issued notice upon the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury under rule 10(2) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Rules in Form E on 26-12-85. True copy of the said notice is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-G. Respondent No. 1 also issued a Memo dated 26-12-85 (true copy of which is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-D by which he requested the Head Mistress of the said School to deliver vacant possession of the derequisitioned property to Surveyor of Land Acquisition Office. The possession could not be taken over due to the obstruction created by the School authority. On 13-1-86 the Additional Deputy Commissioner wrote to the Head Mistress of the school requesting her to hand over vacant possession on 16-1-86. True copy of the said Memo is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure "E". On 16-1-86 the officials of Dhaka Collect orate went to take over the possession of the derequisitioned property, but possession could not be taken due to obstruction created by the school authority. The Head Mistress of the said school filed a suit being title suit No. 3 of 1986 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the Government of Bangladesh and respondent No. 1 praying for a declaration that the order dated 26-12-85 (Annexure-"C") issued by respondent No. 1 was illegal and of no legal effect. A true copy of the plaint of the said suit is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-"F''. In the said suit the Government filed written statement stating, inter (ilia, that Moshahid Ali Chowdhury and 5 others purchased the suit property by 60 registered sale deeds with an area of 1.56 acre of land covering the holding No. 85 Kakrail Road out of which the share of Clifford Noronha measuring an area 0.56 acre of land was declared as vested in VP Case No. 5 of 1974. The Ministry of LA and LR took decision on 16-10-85 on the application submitted by Mr. Moshahid Ali Chowdhury, in presence" of the Head Mistress and the Members of the School Managing Committee, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka Division communicated the same under Memo No. DA-54/84/835 dated 16-10-85 for implementation. As per decision of the Ministry of LA and LR dated 16-10-85 the school was asked to hand over possession of the derequisitioned portion to the representative of the requisitioning authority on 29-12-85 but the possession could not be taken as the Head Mistress showed an injunction passed in TS 1244/85 of the 4th Court of Munsif, Dhaka. Subsequently in Misc. Appeal No. 352/85 in the court of the District Judge Dhaka an order staying operation of impugned injunction in TS 1244/85 was passed. The plaintiff was informed regarding derequisition of 0.63 1/2 acre of land out of 1.50 1/2 as per order passed by the Ministry of LA and LR under Memo No. 2226/Reqn/85 dated. 26-12-85. Having failed to obtain possession of the derequisitioned portion of the aforesaid property the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury filed Writ Petition No. 512 of 1987 for implementation of the derequisition order passed by the Government on 16-10-85. After hearing this Court by judgment dated 13-12-90 made the Rule absolute passing the following order 

"In this view of the matter we make the Rule absolute without any order as to cost and direct the respondents to implement the impugned Order of derequisition contained in Memo No. DA-54/84/85-Acqn dated 16-10-85 and to hand over possession of the property in question to its owners in terms of the said order within one month from date and respondent No. 4 is directed to vacate the same within 31st December, 1990." 

A true copy of the judgment dated 13-12-90 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-"H". The Government filed leave application before the Appellate Division against the judgment of the High Court Division and similar application was also filed by the School Authority. The Appellate Division after hearing was unwilling to grant leave and, as such, the Government and the School Authority withdrew their respective leave applications and filed review applications before the High Court Division. The High Court Division rejected the review application and against the said rejection order the Government and also the School Authority filed leave applications before the Appellate Division which was rejected by order dated 6-3-91. A true copy of the order of the Appellate Division dated 6-3-91 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-I. The respondents did not comply with the order of the Court and instead the Land Acquisition Officer on 8-4-91 served notice dated 1-4-91 under Rule (10)1 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Rules stating therein that enquiry would be held on 10-4-91 in respect of right and title of the aforesaid derequisitioned property and requiring the petitioners to submit statement regarding their title on 9-4-91 and to be present with papers on 10-4-91. The petitioners submitted a petition before respondent No. 2 saying that formalities and requirements of rule 10(1) of the aforesaid Rules had been completed long before and the petitioners were given notice under Rule 10(2) of the said Rules and the Officers of the District Administration twice endeavored to hand over possession of the derequisitioned property but failed due to the obstructions created by the School Authority and therefore question of determining right, title and interest in the aforesaid property did not arise. It was alleged that the notice dated 1-4-91 was nothing but a device and cloak to delay and/or avoid implementation of the Judgment of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 512 of 1987. On 10-4-91 the petitioner No. 1 appeared before the Land Acquisition Officer. In this situation the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury were compelled to file a wit petition for drawing up contempt proceeding against the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA), Dhaka, Land Acquisition Officer, Dhaka and Head Master of Willes Little Flower School and the High Court in Contempt Petition No. 15 of 1991 was pleased to draw up the proceeding till final hearing. 

3. On 7-7-93 the petitioners saw a news item in Daily Star about a function of the managing committee of the school where the managing committee thanked the Government for permanently leasing out 0.87 acre of land to the school. Petitioner No. 1 went to the office of respondent No. 1 seeking information. The petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury had earlier filed Title Suit No. 246 of 1984, subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 143 of 1988 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others including the school as defendant No. 4. On 30-8-93, the school authority filed an application in that suit stating that 0.87 acre of the aforesaid property had been permanently acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 14 of 1990-91 and it has been transferred to the school authority for valuable consideration of Taka 1,34,50,668/84. A true copy of the said petition is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-J (i). After making frantic effort petitioner No. 1 succeeded in finding out the Gazette Notification regarding the alleged acquisition in the first part of November, 1993 and obtained copy of the Gazette notification dated 3-9-92 published in the Bangladesh Gazette which is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-K. Annexure-K shows that 0.08 acre of plot No. 31/193, 0.07 acre of plot No. 31 and 0.72 acre of plot No. 32, in total 0.87 acre of land had been acquired under provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 in LA Case No. 14 of 1990-91. It is submitted that for acquisition of any immovable property section 3 of the Ordinance requires publication of preliminary notice of acquisition on or near the property in the prescribed form, but no such notice was issued to the knowledge of the petitioners. Had any such notice been published in any convenient place, the petitioners would have known about it. The petitioners have every reason to believe that in collusion with the school authority respondent Nos. 1-2 may have shown publication of such notice on record without actually publishing any such notice at any convenient place of the property in question so as to keep the petitioners in dark about it. It is further submitted that section 6 of the Ordinance requires that after making decision for acquiring property public notice of the proposed acquisition has to be given in the prescribed manner and convenient places on or near the property and section 6(3) of the Ordinance requires service of such notice on all persohs known or believed to be interested therein. The petitioners are certainly interested in the said property and the respondents also knew about it. Not only that no such notice was published at convenient places on or near the property in question, no notice under section 6(3) of the Ordinance was served on the petitioners even though the respondents had full knowledge that the petitioners are owners of the said property. It is alleged that the respondents had fraudulently and collusively with the school authority omitted to publish and serve such notices so that the petitioner might not be able to raise any lawful objection to the acquisition and the property could not be acquired for a price below the price permissible under the Ordinance and to prevent them from referring the matter to arbitration. That no notice of passing of the award made by the respondents was given to the petitioners. Everything had been done secretly and without complying with the requirements of the law. After coming to know of the acquisition from the petition submitted by the school authority in the aforesaid suit, petitioner No. 1 met respondent No. 1 and wanted to see the award, but respondent No. 1 flatly refused to show it to him. It is also submitted that the holding of 85, Kakrail, Dhaka is situated on the Kakrail Road. The property in question is situated in the commercial centre of Dhaka and the land is being sold in this locality at the rate of Taka 12 to 15 lakh per katha and the value of 0.87 acre of the acquired land alone without the structure would not be less than Taka 7 crore. Because the people under valued the sale price of properties at Dhaka the Government issued notification stating the minimum price of lands in different localities in Dhaka city for the purpose of payment of stamp duty, gift tax, etc. The price so stated in the notification is much below the actual market price. On 3-1-91 the Government by Gazette Notification refixed the price of lands at Dhaka and photocopy of the Gazette Notification is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-L. Again on 20-12-92 the Government refixed the price and by a circular dated 11-1-93 stated the existing price and re-fixed price. True copy of the said circular dated 11-1-93 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure L(1). It is seen from the Gazette Notification dated 3-1-91 and the circular dated 20-12-92 that the Government stated the minimum price of land on the main road side in Kakrail area to be Taka 1 crone per bigha which means Taka 5 lakh per katha. At the Government stated rate the price of 0.87 acre of land alone was at least Taka 2,63,63,636.00 but the respondents assessed the compensation of 0.87 acre together with the building standing thereon at Taka 1,34,50,668.84 as stated by the school authority. The Government having fixed the minimum rate of price of land and publishing the notification dated 4-12-90 in the official gazette if the respondent acted bona fide they could not have assessed compensation at half the rate fixed by the Government. The whole transaction of the respondents smacks of mala fide and the gross under assessment of compensation explains why the respondents kept the petitioners completely in the dark about the transaction which clearly established the collusion of the respondents 1-2 with the school authority. The respondents are so biased that they gave no notice to the petitioners so as to deprive the petitioners an opportunity of seeking arbitration against the gross under assessment. The acquiring authority having not complied with the requirement of law, the entire process of the acquisition of the property in question is illegal and without lawful authority and has not been any lawful acquisition in the eye of law. 

4. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-3. It appears that the respondents have admitted that the property in question belonged to one Laurence Alloysius Noronha and his heirs. The respondents however dispute the alleged transfers of property by the heirs in favour of the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury. It is stated that the alleged transfer were made by non-residents by means of various deeds registered in seven sub-registry Offices in Dhaka simultaneously and consecutively ranging between 20-7-81 and 9-9-81 valued only at Taka fifty thousand each, obviously for avoiding payment of Gain-Tax to the Government. The petitioners have not stated why sixty documents had to be created in respect of 4-1/3 bighas land for taking transfer from the owners. Clifford Eric Noronha and George Eric Noronha did not execute and register any instrument of transfer. The alleged powers of attorney by virtue of which the transfer documents were executed and registered are not genuine and these were not signed or executed or given by Clifford Noronha and/or George Eric Norona. The statement made in paragraph 7 of the petition has been denied. It is stated that after issuance of the order of de-requisition dated 16-10-85 by the Government, enquiry which is the mandatory requirement of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 was not made to ascertain as to who are entitled to restoration of possession of the property and notice under Rule 10(1). It is stated that the notice under the Emergency Requisition of Property Rules in prescribed form was issued without verification of title. It is also stated that some Civil Suits relating to the title of the acquisitioned land are pending for adjudication in the civil Court. Since the petitioners were not in possession they were not served with notice under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Ordinance, 1982. (a) Mrs Josephine Willes wife of DR Willes (b) Mrs Clifford A Noronha (c) Dr George Eric A. Noronha, son of Lawrence Alloysius Noronha (d) DR Willes son of HJ Willes (e) Mrs. Winifred Ruby daughter of Mr Lawrence Alloysius Noronha who were the undisputed original owners were served with notice under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Ordinance, 1982 at Kakrail 85. As the title to the land could not be established none has been paid compensation. The compensation of the Government was deposited in Government Accounts Deposit Accounts Head under section 10(2) of the Land Acquisition Ordinance, 1982. Since the petitioners'' title to the property under acquisition is sub judice in the civil Court the question of informing them in any matter did not arise at all. It ''is stated that the land in question was decided to be acquired for the project of Willes Little Flower School under PS Ramna within Mouza Baje Kakrail appertaining to SA Plot No. 31 (part) 32 (part) and 31/193 (part) measuring 0.87 acre pending approval of the Central Land Acquisition Committee vide Land Ministry Memo No. Bhu/Mah/Sha-10/Who/ DA-54/84/150/-Acqn. dated 14-3-91. In the light of the Resolution, Land Ordinance No. 2/82 (which was later converted into Land Acquisition Act, 1987) notice under section 3 was served on 24-3-91. After the service of notice under section 3 no objection notice was received within 15 days from the service of notice. The Deputy Commissioner on 4-4-91 accorded permission under section 4(3) for acquisition and according to the provisions of that Act notice was served fixing 22-4-91 for giving written objection within that time but no objection was received within that time. 8. The petitioners in their petition have given a brief history about the owners of 1.56 acres of land being holding No. 85, Kakrail, Ramna, Dhaka and how they claimed to be the owner of the said property. In this writ petition we are only to see whether the acquisition of 0.87 acre of land for the requiring body Willes Little Flower School was made in accordance with the provision of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. The requisition and acquisition of land was for the purpose of establishment of a school. The petitioner has not seriously challenged that the land was acquired for public purpose. They have challenged the acquisition on the ground that it was not done in accordance with the provision of the Ordinance that is, without notice to the petitioner. They have further submitted that by not serving notice on them they have been deprived of the opportunity to go for arbitration against the amount of compensation awarded by the Additional Deputy Commissioner which is far below the market price. We will first take up the question whether the acquisition of 0.87 acre of land was made in accordance with the Ordinance, 1982. Admittedly, no notice was served on the petitioners of late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury. 

9. Section 6(1) of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 provides that "when the Government, the Divisional Commissioner or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be, has made a decision for acquisition of any property under section 5 of the proviso to section 4(3)(b), as the case may be, the Deputy Commissioner shall cause public notice to be given in the prescribed manner at convenient places on or near such property stating that the Government, (the Divisional Commissioner or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be,) has decided to acquire the property and intends to take possession thereof and that claims to compensation for all interests in such property may be made to him." 

10. Section 6(2) of the said Ordinance, 1982 provides that "such notice shall state the particulars of the property to be acquired and taken possession of, and shall require all persons interested in the property to appear personally or by agent before the Deputy Commissioner at a time, not being earlier than fifteen days after the date of publication of the notice, and place mentioned therein and to state the nature of their respective interests in the property and the amount and particulars of their claims to compensation for such interests." 

11. Sub-section (3) of section 6 of the said Ordinance 1982 "the Deputy Commissioner shall also serve notice to the same effect in the prescribed form on the occupier, if any, of such property and on all persons known or believed to be interested therein." 

12. The petitioners have given background with facts which clearly show that the respondents knew that they were persons who claimed interest in the property which was acquired. Annexure-A to the petition dated 16-10-85 is a letter in reply to the prayer for derequisition and restoration of vacant possession made by the petitioner. In the said Annexure signed by one M Wajihullah Senior, Scale Section Officer of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms Section, it said that the Ministry heard and considered the petition of Janab Moshahid Ali Chowdhury and the Head Mistress and Members of the School Managing Committee in the presence of Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka Division. iii) the block ''B'' shown in the sketch map falling within SA Plot Nos. 32, 36, 28, 29 & 31/193 will continue to remain under requisition in favour of the Willes Little Flower School till it is acquired permanently under normal LA proceedings. 

13. It was further directed in the Memo that necessary action might be taken to implement the above decision as quickly as possible.

The said notice is addressed to the petitioners and late Moshahid Ali Chowdhury signed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka. ২৯-০৫-৯১ আজ অত্র কেইসের প্রত্যাশী সংস্থা উইলস লিটল ফ্লাওয়ার স্কুলের প্রধান শিক্ষক উপস্থিত হয়ে এক দরখাস্ত দিয়ে জানান যে, বাজে কাকরাইল মৌজায় ২৬২ নং দাগের যে বিক্রয় তথ্য সংগ্রহ করা হয়েছে তা উদ্দেশ্য প্ৰনােদিতভাবে নাল লেখা হ্ইয়াছে৷ আসলে তাহা পাকা বাড়ী গ্রেনীভূক্ত এর সমর্থনে তিনি ঐ মৌজায় একটি এস, এ, খতিয়ান দাখিল করেছেন যাহাতে প্রতীয়মান হয়ে যে, আলোচ্য জমি পাকা বাড়ী প্রেনীৱ । রেক্যর্ড পাকা বাড়ী৷পরে তাহার প্রকৃতি পরিবর্তীত হয়েছে কিনা সে বিষয়ে নিশ্চিত হওয়ার জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট কানূনগোকে সরজমিনে তদন্ত অন্তে মূল্যায়ন নিরুপনের জন্য বলা যেতে পারে৷

                                                                                                                            স্বাক্ষর/অস্পষ্ট

০৮-১-৯২৷আলোচ্য বিষয়টি ১৪-/৯০-৯১নং-এ্ল, এ, কেইসের অন্তর্গত বাজে কাকরাইল মৌজার ০.৮৭একর জমি যাহা উইলস লিটল ফ্লাওয়ার স্কুলের অনুকুলে হূকুম দখলের জন্য প্রস্তাবিত এযুরনহার অনুমোদন সংক্রান্ত৷

ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয় ২৯-১১-৯৭ বাং ১৪-৩-৯১ইং তারিখের ভূমঃসাঃ-১০/হূদঃভিএ-৫৪/৮8/১৫০-এ টুনে নং-ম্মারকে উইলস লিটল ফ্লাওয়ার স্কুলের অনূকৃলে বাজে কাকরাইল মৌজার এস, এ, দাগ নং-৩১(অংশ), ৩২(অংশ) ও৩১/১৯৩ (অংশ) এর০.৮৭ একর জমি বরাদ্দের জন্য ‍কেন্দ্রীয় ভূমি বরাদ্দ কমিটির ৩৬তম সভায় ০.৮৭ একর জমি উক্ত স্কুলের অনূকূলে এই শর্তে বরাদ্দ করা হয় যে, ০.৮৭ একর জমির দাগসমূহ এর মধ্যে রীট মামলার রায়ের জমি থাকিলে জেলা প্রশাসক তাহা নির্ধারন পূর্বক বাদ দিবেন (পথ) ।

এখানে উল্লেখ্য ৩২নং দাপেঁর ১.৩৩ একর জমির মধ্যে ০৬৩৫ একর (সাড়ে তিওট্রি শতাংশ) জমি নিয়া ৫১২/৮৭নং রীট

কেস ছিল, যাহার রায় ইতিমধ্য হইয়া গিয়াছে, এবং আলোচ্য ১৪/৯০-৯১নং এল, এ, কেইসের প্রস্তাবিত জমি অবশ্যই উক্ত রীট কেসের ০.৬৩৫ একর জমি বাদ দিয়া প্রস্তাব করাহ ইয়াছে৷ 

আলোচ্য এর, এ, কেইসে বরাদ্দকৃত ০.৮৭ একর জমির মূল্য নির্ধারনের জন্য কানূনগাে সংশ্লিষ্ট সাব-রেজিস্ট্রী অফিস হইতে বিক্রয় তথ্য সংগ্রহ করিয়া মুল্য হার প্রতিবেদন দাখিল করিয়াছেন (প/গ) সদয় দ্রষ্টব্য ৷ উক্ত প্রতিবেদন দৃষ্টে দেখা যাইতেছে যে, সংগৃহীত তথ্যের তত্ত্ব পুলিনাল জমির বিক্রয় তথ্য এবং সেই বিক্রয় তথ্য অনযায়ী প্রতি একর নাল জমির মূল্য ১,২০,৪৮,৬০০.০০ (এক কোটি বিশ লক্ষ আট চল্লিশ হাজার তিনশত টাকা মাত্র) সকল জমির মূল্যের সহিত নিয়মানূযায়ী ৫০% যোগ করিয়া ভিটি শ্রেণীর জমির একর প্রতি মূল্য দাড়ায় ১ ,৮০ , ৭২,৩০০.০০ এক কোটি আশিলক্ষ বাহাত্তর হাজার জ্যিশত টাকা মাত্র ।


স্কুল কর্তৃপক্ষের তরফ থেকে প্রধান শিক্ষক এর দরখাস্তের (প/থ) মাধ্যমে নিজে উপস্থিত হইয়া জানান যে, যে জমির বিক্রয় তথ্য নেওয়া হইয়1ছে তাহা আসলে নাল নয়, প্রকৃত পক্ষে তাহা পাকা বাড়ী, এবং তিনি সেই জমির অর্থাৎ ২৬২নং দাগের এস, এ, খতিয়ানের একটি কপি দাখিল করিয়া জানান যে, ঐ জমির রেকডীয়প্রেনী পাকা বাড়ী৷ প্রধান শিক্ষক-এর এই আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে এস, এ, ৬ এবং আঃজেঃপ্রঃ (এল, এ) মহােদয়ের নির্দেশে কানূনগাে উক্ত ২৬২নং দাগের জমি সর জমিনে তদন্ত করিয়া সেখানে বহূতপ্স বিশিষ্ট ইমারত দেখিতে পান বলিয়ে প্রতিবেদন দৃন্টে দেখা যায়, এবং সেই জন্য 
কানূন গাে জনাব ক্ষিতিশ কর্মকারতার প্রতিবেদনে বিক্রয় তথ্য নাল হিসাবে না ধরিয়া ভিঢি বাড়ী হিসাবে ধরিয়া জমির একর প্রতিমূল্য ১,২০,8৮,২০০.০০ (এক কোটি বিশ লক্ষ আটচল্লিশ হাজার দূইশত টাকা মাত্র) টাকা নির্ধারন করিয়াছেন৷ পূনাংশের ৩২.৩৩ পৃষ্ঠায় প্রতিবেদন (প/গ) অনুগত পূর্বক দেখা যাইতে পারে৷

উপরোক্ত আলোচনার ভিত্তিতে আলোচ্যকেই সে উইলস লিটল ফ্লাওয়ার স্কুলের অনুকূলে হূকুম দখলের জন্য প্রস্তাবিত জমির মূল্য একর প্রতি ১,২০,৮8,২০০.০০ (এক কোটি বিশ লক্ষ আটচল্লিশ হাজার দৃইশত টাকা মাত্র) টাকা সময় অনুমোদন করা যাইতে পারে৷

২৭-২-৯২ পার্শ্বে কানুনগ সাহেবরে নোটিশ অনুগ্রহ্পূর্বক দেখা যেতে পারে৷ উহাতে দেখা যেতে পারে৷ঊহাতে দেখা যায় যে আলোচ্য কেইসের যৌথ তদন্তের তালিকায় (প/ক) ১-২৩নং ক্রমিকের আইটেম পুলি আলোচ্য ফেইসের প্রত্যাশী সংস্থা (উইলস লিটল ফ্লাওয়ার স্কুল) কর্তৃক নির্মিত বিধায় কেইসের প্রাক্কালন হইতে ঐ সমস্ত আইটেম পুলিবাদ রাখার জন্য স্কুলের প্রধান শিক্ষক অনুরোধ জানাইয়াছো (প/থ) সদয় দ্রষ্টব্য।

16. It appears to us from the proceedings record of LA case No. 14/90-91 that the procedure for acquiring 0.87 acre of land as required under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 has been followed save and except the requirement of sub-section 3 of section 6 of the Ordinance, 1982 which requires notice to be served on all persons known or believed to be interested in the property. We have already expressed our view for reasons given that notice ought to have been served on the petitioners. The proceedings of the LA Case as contained in Annexure-4 series of the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-3 show that notice under section 6 of the Ordinance, 1982 were served on Mrs Josephine Willes, Mrs Clifford A Noronha, Dr George Eric Noronha, DR Willes, Mrs. Winifred Rubie and Secretary, Willes Little Flower School at 85, Kakrail, Rarnna Dhaka who are undisputed original owners of the land. The respondents, as it appears from the affidavit-in-opposition, did not serve notice on the petitioners on the ground that their title had not been proved. There were several suits filed by the petitioners connected with the property including for a suit for declaration that they are the owners of 1.56 acre of land which are still pending. Further, in Annexure-A to the petition it was said that the block marked-A which was to be withdrawn from requisition possession was to be made over to the original owner/owners-from whom it was requisitioned or to his/ their successor-in-interest after verification of their right and title. The land was requisitioned from the original owners and the petitioners were still to establish their title and interest. It was for these reasons the respondents said that no notice was served on the petitioners under section 6 of the Ordinance, 1982, but the respondents having made a claim of ownership of 1.56 acre of land and having also filed a petition against failure to de-requisition 0.63 acre of land as directed by the High Court, the respondents ought to have known or believed that the petitioners are interested parties. The question therefore arises whether under the circumstances non-service of notice under sub-section 3 of section 6 of the Ordinance, 1982 will render the acquisition of property by Annexure-K illegal. 

17. The learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners has not cited any decision that in default of such notice the acquisition is illegal. It is our considered view that an irregularity in the procedure will not ipso facto render the acquisition illegal provided the acquisition was for a public purpose and the compensation amount was adequate and fixed in accordance with law. In the instant case the petitioners have not seriously challenged that the acquisition was for a public purpose. On the question of awarding the compensation it is correct that the petitioners did not have any notice of the acquisition and were thus deprived of opportunity to file an application to the Arbitrator within 45 days of the date of service of award for revision of the award under section 28 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. However, it appears from the order sheet in LA Case No. 14/90-91 that while fixing the value of 0.87 acre of acquired land the ''Kanungo'' after obtaining information and consultation with the Sub-Registry Office submitted the valuation of the land in that area. It appears from that report and information that the price of Nal land per acre was 1,20,48,200.00 and by adding 50% over that price, the price of bhiti land per acre came to Taka 1,80,72,300.00. It was on this basis that the price of 0.87 acre of land was fixed at Taka 1,34,50,668.00 which amount was duly paid by the requiring body Willes Little Flower School. This amount, it is stated by the respondents, is now kept in the block account as nobody came forward to claim the compensation and the title to the land has not been established.'' This amount has been kept in the block account under sub-section 2 of section 10 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 which provides that if the persons entitled to compensation do not consent to receive it, or if there be no person competent to receive the compensation or if there be any dispute as to title to receive the compensation or as to the apportionment of it, the Deputy Commissioner shall keep the amount of the compensation in a deposit account in the Public Account of the Republic which shall be deemed payment for the purpose of taking over possession of the property without any prejudice to the claim of the parties to be determined by the Arbitrator. The petitioners therefore may claim the compensation to be paid from this account on proof of their interest and title. 

18. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case that the land in question was acquired for a public purpose, the compensation money having been paid by the requiring body on the basis of enquiry and report in LA Case No. 14/90-91 and the acquired land having been given on permanent lease in favour of the requiring body by a registered lease deed, we do not think that the acquisition order Annexure-K to be illegal only on the ground of procedural irregularity. 

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

M Nurullah with Shamsuddin, AQM Shafiullah, Advocates—For the Appellants.
